source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VI (Montreuil)

1.title: Quid sit prophetia, et de gradibus ejus, et qualis prophetia sit dignior
1.title_en: What prophecy is, and of its degrees, and which prophecy is the more worthy
1.note: The first of Denis's introductory articles to his commentary on the Psalter, on prophecy; it expounds no verse of Psalm 1.

paras.t: Prophetia autem ad intellectum potissimum pertinet. Est enim prophetia, supernaturalis futurorum cognitio, ex divina inspiratione adepta. Prophetæ namque dicuntur, qui Deo revelante cognoscunt ea, quæ ceteris abscondita sunt, et procul ab ipsis posita. Propter quod in libro Regum dicitur: Qui nunc dicitur Propheta, olim vocabatur Videns. Et Samuel ad Saul dixit: Ego sum Videns.
paras.en: Now prophecy belongs chiefly to the intellect. For prophecy is a supernatural knowledge of things to come, obtained by divine inspiration. For they are called prophets who, by God's revealing, know the things that are hidden from others and set far from them. That is why it is said in the book of Kings: [[1 Kings 9:9|he that is now called a prophet, in time past was called a seer|Qui nunc dicitur Propheta, olim vocabatur Videns]]. And Samuel said to Saul: [[1 Kings 9:19|I am the seer|Ego sum Videns]].

paras.t: Porro prophetia ad gratias gratis datas pertinere cognoscitur, sicut operatio miraculorum, interpretatio sermonum, discretio spirituum. Tales enim ac similes gratiæ, communes sunt bonis et malis. Gratiæ vero gratis datæ, ad aliorum utilitatem dantur et ordinantur, quemadmodum ad Corinthios ait Apostolus: Unicuique datur manifestatio Spiritus ad utilitatem. In quantum igitur prophetalis notitia ordinatur ad hoc, ut aliis innotescat, sic prophetia secundario pertinet ad locutionem: sicque Propheta a præfando nomen accepit. Sed quoniam prophetia est de his, quæ naturalem rationem excedunt, neque naturali ratione probari possunt; idcirco tertio ad prophetiam pertinet operatio miraculorum, tanquam confirmatio horum quæ prophetice annuntiantur. Et ita intelligendum est quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Eliseus non timuit principem; et mortuum prophetavit corpus ejus, videlicet quia post mortem mortuum suscitavit. In quo ostendebatur, eum verum fuisse Prophetam. Et simile de ossibus Joseph ait Scriptura.
paras.en: Further, prophecy is known to belong to the graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts given for the good of others, as distinct from the grace that makes a man holy], like the working of miracles, the interpretation of speeches, and the discerning of spirits. For such graces and the like are common to the good and the wicked. And graces freely given are given and ordered to the profit of others, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 12:7|the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man unto profit|Unicuique datur manifestatio Spiritus ad utilitatem]]. So, in so far as prophetic knowledge is ordered to being made known to others, prophecy belongs secondarily to speech: and so the prophet took his name from speaking beforehand [*a præfando*: Denis derives *propheta* from *præfari*, to speak before]. But since prophecy is about things which exceed natural reason and cannot be proved by natural reason, therefore, in the third place, the working of miracles belongs to prophecy, as a confirmation of the things that are announced prophetically. And so is to be understood what is written in Ecclesiasticus: Eliseus [[Ecclus 48:13|feared not the prince|non timuit principem]]; [[Ecclus 48:14|and after death his body prophesied|et mortuum prophetavit corpus ejus]]: namely, because after his death it raised a dead man to life. By this it was shown that he had been a true prophet. And Scripture says the like of the bones of Joseph[[Ecclus 49:18||]].

paras.t: Porro, quemadmodum naturale lumen intellectus agentis, est omnium naturalium cognitionum intellectus possibilis principium; sic lumen supernaturale atque divinum, est prophetalium cognitionum principium. Ideo, sicut naturalis cognitio intellectus possibilis ad omnia se extendit, seu omnium capax est, quæ per naturale lumen intellectus agentis, inveniri agnoscique possunt; sic prophetalis cognitio circa omnia illa versatur, quæ per lumen supernaturale ac divinum ostendi valent ac sciri. Per lumen autem divinum omnia utique manifestari queunt, videlicet divina et humana, creata et increata, spiritualia et corporalia, naturalia atque moralia. Unde ad omnia ista extendit se prophetia. Facta est enim aliquando prophetica revelatio de his, quæ ad Dei majestatem seu excellentiam pertinent: sicut Isaias de se loquens, Vidi, inquit, Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum et elevatum: et quod audivit Seraphim ter clamantia, Sanctus: quod ad superbenedictæ Trinitatis pertinet revelationem. Danieli quoque prophetæ ostensum est, qualiter millia millium ministrabant Deo, et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei: quod ad supernorum spirituum prophetalem revelationem spectare non dubium est. Continet etiam prophetia, illa quæ ad mores hominum instruendos respiciunt, ut est illud: Frange esurienti panem tuum. Et Michæas propheta: Indicabo (ait) tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, et quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium et justitiam, et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo.
paras.en: Again, as the natural light of the agent intellect is the principle of all the natural knowledge of the possible intellect [terms of scholastic philosophy: the *agent intellect* is the power that makes things actually understandable, the *possible intellect* the power that receives and knows them], so the supernatural and divine light is the principle of prophetic knowledge. Therefore, as the natural knowledge of the possible intellect extends to all things, or is capable of all things, that can be found out and known by the natural light of the agent intellect, so prophetic knowledge is concerned with all those things that can be shown and known by the supernatural and divine light. But by the divine light all things whatever can be made manifest: things divine and human, created and uncreated, spiritual and bodily, natural and moral. Hence prophecy extends to all these. For prophetic revelation has at times been made of things belonging to the majesty or excellence of God: as Isaias, speaking of himself, says: [[Is 6:1|I saw|Vidi]], [[Is 6:1|the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated|Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum et elevatum]]: and that he heard the Seraphim crying thrice, Holy[[Is 6:3||]]: which belongs to the revelation of the most blessed Trinity. To Daniel the prophet also it was shown how [[Dan 7:10|thousands of thousands ministered to him|millia millium ministrabant Deo]], [[Dan 7:10|and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him|et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei]]: which beyond doubt concerns the prophetic revelation of the spirits on high. Prophecy also contains the things that look to the instruction of men's morals, as is that saying: [[Is 58:7|Deal thy bread to the hungry|Frange esurienti panem tuum]]. And Michæas the prophet: [[Mich 6:8|I will shew|Indicabo]] (he says) [[Mich 6:8|thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment|tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, et quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium]] and justice, [[Mich 6:8|and to walk solicitous with thy God|et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo]] [Denis reads "judgment and justice" and leaves out "to love mercy"].

paras.t: Quanto autem aliqua naturalem rationem magis excedunt, remotiusque a nostra cognitione distant, tanto amplius magisque proprie rationem prophetiæ concernunt, sicut sunt futura pure contingentia, ut actus humani. Propterea prophetia propriissime pertinet ad futurorum eventuum cognitionem. Sic namque Cassiodorus prophetiam definit, quum ait: Prophetia est inspiratio seu revelatio divina, rerum eventus immobili denuntians veritate. Et ideo Gregorius super Ezechielem testatur, quia prophetia ita vocatur, quoniam futura prænuntiat; dum vero præterita aut præsentia manifestat, nominis sui rationem amittit.
paras.en: But the more some things exceed natural reason and the further they stand from our knowledge, the more fully and properly they concern the nature of prophecy: such as purely contingent future things, like human acts. Therefore prophecy belongs most properly to the knowledge of future events. For so Cassiodorus defines prophecy, when he says: Prophecy is a divine inspiration or revelation, announcing the outcome of things with unchangeable truth. And so Gregory, on Ezechiel, testifies that prophecy is so called because it foretells things to come; but when it makes known things past or present, it loses the reason for its name.

paras.t: Præterea, multi sunt gradus prophetiæ, quorum infimus dicitur, dum aliquis ex interiori Spiritus Sancti instinctu movetur ad exteriora opera: sicut frequenter in libro Judicum scribitur, quod Spiritus Domini irruit in Jephthe vel Samson, ex quo inducebantur ad aliqua opera exterius exercenda. Secundus et altior prophetiæ gradus est, dum aliquis ex illustratione Spiritus Sancti, quædam supernaturali modo cognoscit et percipit, quæ tamen naturaliter cognosci possunt: quemadmodum de Salomone habetur, quod Dominus dedit ei sapientiam et prudentiam multam nimis, ita quod disputavit super lignis, a cedro qui est in Libano usque ad hyssopum quæ egreditur de pariete; disseruitque de jumentis et volucribus, reptilibus ac piscibus. De talibus enim gentiles quoque philosophi plura disseruisse subtiliter inveniuntur. Unde hi duo gradus ad perfectam prophetiæ rationem non attingunt, quia ad supernaturalem veritatem non pertinent. Nihilo minus aliqua Salomoni revelata sunt, quæ naturalis rationis limites omnino excedunt, præsertim in Canticis: propter quorum cognitionem, Salomon vere et proprie Propheta vocatur.
paras.en: Moreover, there are many degrees of prophecy. The lowest of them is said to be when someone is moved to outward works by an inward prompting of the Holy Ghost: as it is often written in the book of Judges that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte or Samson[[Judg 11:29||]][[Judg 14:6||]][[Judg 15:14||]], by which they were led to carry out certain outward works. The second and higher degree of prophecy is when someone, by the enlightening of the Holy Ghost, knows and perceives in a supernatural way certain things which can nevertheless be known naturally: as we have it of Solomon, that [[3 Kings 4:29|God gave to Solomon wisdom, and understanding exceeding much|Dominus dedit ei sapientiam et prudentiam multam nimis]], so that [[3 Kings 4:33|he treated about trees, from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes|disputavit super lignis, a cedro qui est in Libano usque ad hyssopum quæ egreditur de pariete; disseruitque de jumentis et volucribus, reptilibus ac piscibus]]. For heathen philosophers too are found to have discoursed subtly on many such things. Hence these two degrees do not reach the perfect nature of prophecy, because they do not concern supernatural truth. Nevertheless some things were revealed to Solomon which altogether exceed the limits of natural reason, above all in the Canticles: because of his knowledge of these, Solomon is truly and properly called a prophet.

paras.t: Est ergo tertius gradus propheticæ cognitionis, quando per imaginariam visionem alicui supernaturalis veritas revelatur: quemadmodum Daniel vidit Antiquum dierum, id est Deum æternum, sub similitudine imaginabilium rerum, quemadmodum apud Danielem legitur: Adspiciebam, inquit, donec throni positi sunt, et Antiquus dierum sedit; vestimentum ejus quasi nix candidum, et capilli capitis ejus quasi lana alba. Istiusmodi vero prophetiæ multi sunt gradus, prout Doctor sanctus in secunda secundæ pulchre deducit.
paras.en: The third degree of prophetic knowledge, then, is when a supernatural truth is revealed to someone through an imaginary vision [that is, a vision in the imagination, of images, as distinct from a bodily or a purely intellectual vision]: as Daniel saw the Ancient of days, that is, the eternal God, under the likeness of things that can be imagined, as we read in Daniel: [[Dan 7:9|I beheld|Adspiciebam]], he says, [[Dan 7:9|till thrones were placed, and the ancient of days sat: his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool|donec throni positi sunt, et Antiquus dierum sedit; vestimentum ejus quasi nix candidum, et capilli capitis ejus quasi lana alba]]. But of this kind of prophecy there are many degrees, as the holy Doctor finely sets out in the Secunda Secundæ [St Thomas, Summa theologiae II-II, q. 174, a. 3, as the margin notes].

paras.t: Prima distinctio est penes differentiam somnii et visionis sive vigiliæ. Interdum namque prophetica revelatio in somnio infunditur, sicut scriptum est: Per somnium in visione nocturna, aperit aures virorum. Interdum autem infunditur prophetia in visione vigiliæ, quemadmodum Danieli factum legimus. Et hic gradus est dignior primo: quoniam major est vigor prophetici luminis, quando animam vigilantis et circa sensibilia occupati, ad supernaturalia erigit, quam dum animam dormientis, atque a sensibilibus jam vacantis, ad divina ac supernaturalia elevat.
paras.en: The first distinction is according to the difference between a dream and a vision, that is, a waking one. For sometimes prophetic revelation is poured in during a dream, as it is written: [[Job 33:15|By a dream in a vision by night|Per somnium in visione nocturna]], [[Job 33:16|he openeth the ears of men|aperit aures virorum]]. But sometimes prophecy is poured in in a waking vision, as we read was done to Daniel[[Dan 10:1||]]. And this degree is worthier than the first: for the vigour of the prophetic light is greater when it raises to supernatural things the soul of one who is awake and busy about the things of sense, than when it lifts to divine and supernatural things the soul of one asleep and already free of the things of sense.

paras.t: Secundo autem attenditur gradus prophetiæ penes differentiam imaginabilium sensibiliumque signorum, quibus mens Prophetæ ad intellectualem supernaturalis veritatis notitiam elevatur. Quanto enim signa hujusmodi fuerint expressiora, tanto prophetia erit sublimior. Quum ergo, secundum Augustinum, inter signa primum ac summum locum teneant verba, constat quod prophetia ejus qui vel in vigilando vel in dormiendo audit verba secum loquentis, sit altior prophetia ejus cui dumtaxat ostenduntur res quædam seu similitudines aliarum rerum significativæ: quemadmodum septem spicæ Pharaoni ostensæ, septem fertilitatis annos præfigurabant; et olla succensa Jeremiæ ostensa, civitatis Jerusalem incendium designavit.
paras.en: Secondly, the degree of prophecy is judged according to the difference of the imaginable and sensible signs by which the prophet's mind is raised to an intellectual knowledge of supernatural truth. For the more expressive such signs are, the more sublime the prophecy will be. Since, then, according to Augustine, words hold the first and highest place among signs, it is plain that the prophecy of one who, waking or sleeping, hears the words of one speaking with him is higher than the prophecy of one to whom are shown only certain things, or likenesses signifying other things: as the seven ears of corn shown to Pharao foreshadowed seven years of plenty[[Gen 41:26||]]; and the pot set on fire shown to Jeremias[[Jer 1:13||]] signified the burning of the city of Jerusalem.

paras.t: Tertio insuper gradus prophetiæ attenditur penes accessum ad causam ipsam propheticæ cognitionis. Altior enim est gradus prophetiæ, dum non solum verba loquentis percipiuntur, sed ipse quoque loquens adspicitur: sicut Zachariæ prophetæ ac Danieli multisque aliis angeli, per quos (teste Dionysio) prophetiæ revelationes administrantur ac infunduntur, apparuerunt.
paras.en: Thirdly, moreover, the degree of prophecy is judged according to the approach to the very cause of the prophetic knowledge. For the degree of prophecy is higher when not only the words of the speaker are perceived, but the speaker himself is also seen: as angels appeared to Zachary the prophet[[Zach 1:1||]] and to Daniel [the margin also gives a chapter of Daniel, hard to read] and to many others: angels, through whom (as Dionysius testifies) the revelations of prophecy are ministered and poured in.

paras.t: Quarto autem gradus prophetiæ pensatur ex conditione apparentis atque docentis. Si enim qui videtur, apparet in persona hominis, inferior erit prophetia, quam si appareret in persona angeli. Altissima vero censetur, si apparet in persona Dei, quemadmodum Michæas ait: Vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum, et omnem exercitum cœli adsistentem ei a dextris et a sinistris.
paras.en: Fourthly, the degree of prophecy is weighed from the condition of the one who appears and teaches. For if the one who is seen appears in the person of a man, the prophecy will be lower than if he appeared in the person of an angel. But it is reckoned highest if he appears in the person of God, as Michæas says: [[3 Kings 22:19|I saw the Lord sitting|Vidi Dominum sedentem]] upon a throne high [Denis reads *super solium excelsum*, "upon a high throne", as in Is 6:1; in 3 Kings the Vulgate has *super solium suum*, "on his throne"], [[3 Kings 22:19|and all the army of heaven standing by him on the right hand and on the left|et omnem exercitum cœli adsistentem ei a dextris et a sinistris]].

paras.t: Postremo, summus atque dignissimus prophetiæ gradus est, quando intelligibilis supernaturalisque veritas absque imaginaria visione ostenditur, puta per solam anagogicam ac intellectualem illuminationem. Et hic modus excedit rationem prophetiæ proprie dictæ, ut Thomas affirmat. Unde hujusmodi modus potius dicitur tertium genus prophetandi, quam gradus prophetiæ. In ratione enim prophetiæ quædam obscuritas includi videtur, sicut in ratione fidei. Propterea nec prophetia, nec fides, comprehensoribus seu Beatis in patria convenit. Sed ad rationem prophetiæ proprie sumptæ requiritur, ut per imaginariam visionem, tanquam per medium, mens Prophetæ ad intellectualem notitiam perducatur. Hoc aliqui asserunt. Ideoque secundum hos, gradus prophetiæ secundum imaginariam visionem distinguuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, the highest and worthiest degree of prophecy is when an intelligible and supernatural truth is shown without any imaginary vision, that is, by an anagogical and intellectual enlightenment alone. And this mode exceeds the nature of prophecy properly so called, as Thomas affirms [the margin refers to II-II, q. 174]. Hence such a mode is rather called a third kind of prophesying than a degree of prophecy. For a certain obscurity seems to be included in the nature of prophecy, as in the nature of faith. Therefore neither prophecy nor faith befits those who have attained [*comprehensores*: those who already possess God], that is, the Blessed in the fatherland. But for the nature of prophecy taken properly it is required that the prophet's mind be led to intellectual knowledge through an imaginary vision as through a means. So some assert. And therefore, according to them, the degrees of prophecy are distinguished according to the imaginary vision.

1.title: DE SPECIEBUS PROPHETIÆ, ET QUOMODO PROPHETIA INFALLIBILITER IMPLEATUR.
1.title_en: On the kinds of prophecy, and how prophecy is infallibly fulfilled

paras.t: Sicut denique gloriosissimus Apostolorum princeps in secunda sua Canonica ait, Non voluntate humana allata est aliquando prophetia; sed Spiritu Sancto inspirati, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Objectum enim prophetiæ est veritas supernaturalis, prout in divina cognitione consistit, ac naturalem rationem transcendit. Intellectus vero divinus futura ac prophetabilia dupliciter cognoscit, videlicet secundum se ipsa seu in se ipsis, prout scilicet sunt fienda a Deo. Secundo cognoscit ea in suis immediatis ac propriis causis, id est secundum ordinem quem habent ad eas. Prophetalis autem cognitio, est quædam expressio seu derivatio a divina scientia fluens, ac Prophetis infusa.
paras.en: Now, as the most glorious prince of the Apostles says in his second canonical Epistle: [[2 Pet 1:21|prophecy came not by the will of man at any time: but the holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Ghost|Non voluntate humana allata est aliquando prophetia; sed Spiritu Sancto inspirati, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines]]. For the object of prophecy is supernatural truth, as it stands in the divine knowledge and transcends natural reason. And the divine intellect knows things to come, and things that can be prophesied, in two ways: first, according to themselves, or in themselves, that is, as they are to be done by God. Secondly, it knows them in their immediate and proper causes, that is, according to the order which they have to those causes. And prophetic knowledge is a certain expression or derivation flowing from the divine knowledge and infused into the Prophets.

paras.t: In quantum igitur Deus benedictus et sanctus cognoscit res primo modo, accipitur prophetia prædestinationis, quæ de necessitate semper impletur. In quantum vero agnoscit res secundo modo, accipitur prophetia comminationis, quæ non semper impletur, nisi forte secundum secretam intelligentiam, ut de subversione Ninive, et morte Ezechiæ. In hac quippe prophetia annuntiatur aliquid secundum ordinem causæ ad suum effectum. Hic autem ordo, aliis ac fortioribus causis supervenientibus, impediri potest, præsertim dum divinæ voluntati, quæ est omnium rerum prima causa, placuerit. Et ideo talis prophetia non semper impletur, sicut nec prophetia promissionis, quemadmodum apud Jeremiam apertissime declaratur. Ibi enim Dominus ait: Repente loquar adversus gentem et regnum, ut eradicem et destruam illud; si pœnitentiam egerit gens illa a malo suo, agam et ego pœnitentiam. Et hoc ad prophetiam comminationis clarum est pertinere. De prophetia autem promissionis, mox subditur: Subito loquar de gente et regno, ut ædificem et plantem illud; si fecerit gens illa malum in oculis meis, agam et ego pœnitentiam super bono quod locutus sum, ut facerem eis. Unde hujuscemodi propheticæ annuntiationes semper intelligendæ sunt, nisi aliunde proveniat impedimentum, videlicet ex meritis sive demeritis hominum, aut alia simili causa. Hinc enim dicit Gregorius, quod Deus non mutat consilium, quamvis mutet sententiam.
paras.en: Inasmuch, then, as God, blessed and holy, knows things in the first way, we have the prophecy of predestination, which of necessity is always fulfilled. But inasmuch as he knows things in the second way, we have the prophecy of threatening [prophetia comminationis: a prophecy that announces a punishment as the outcome of the causes now at work, and so can be averted], which is not always fulfilled, except perhaps according to a hidden meaning, as in the case of the overthrow of Ninive[[Jon 3:4||]] and the death of Ezechias[[Is 38:1||]] [the margin is partly unreadable here ('… xxxvi, 1'); Isaias 38:1 is the likeliest reading; the same story is told in 4 Kings 20:1]. For in this prophecy something is announced according to the order of a cause to its effect. But this order can be hindered when other and stronger causes supervene, above all when it so pleases the divine will, which is the first cause of all things. And therefore such a prophecy is not always fulfilled, any more than the prophecy of promise, as is most plainly declared in Jeremias. For there the Lord says: [[Jer 18:7|I will suddenly speak against a nation, and against a kingdom, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy it|Repente loquar adversus gentem et regnum, ut eradicem et destruam illud]]; [[Jer 18:8|If that nation against which I have spoken, shall repent of their evil, I also will repent|si pœnitentiam egerit gens illa a malo suo, agam et ego pœnitentiam]]. And it is clear that this belongs to the prophecy of threatening. Of the prophecy of promise, it is added straight after: [[Jer 18:9|I will suddenly speak of a nation and of a kingdom, to build up and plant it|Subito loquar de gente et regno, ut ædificem et plantem illud]]; [[Jer 18:10|If it shall do evil in my sight|si fecerit gens illa malum in oculis meis]], [[Jer 18:10|I will repent of the good that I have spoken to do unto it|agam et ego pœnitentiam super bono quod locutus sum, ut facerem eis]]. Hence prophetic announcements of this kind are always to be understood with this proviso: unless a hindrance should arise from elsewhere, namely from the merits or demerits of men, or some other like cause. For this is why Gregory says that God does not change his counsel, though he changes his sentence.

paras.t: Est autem et alia species prophetiæ, quæ dicitur prophetia præscientiæ, quæ est de rebus, secundum quod Deus prænoscit futura, prout per nostrum arbitrium adimplentur: et ista est bonorum atque malorum.
paras.en: There is also another kind of prophecy, which is called the prophecy of foreknowledge: it is of things according as God foreknows what is to come as it is to be brought about through our free choice; and this is of good things and of evil.

paras.t: Quatuor sunt ergo species prophetiæ; verumtamen Glossa in principio libri Psalmorum, ponit duas dumtaxat species prophetiæ, videlicet præscientiæ et comminationis. Prophetia namque promissionis, sub prophetia comminationis comprehenditur, vel ad eam reducitur. Prophetia quoque prædestinationis, sub prophetia præscientiæ continetur, quia prædestinatio est pars præscientiæ. Dicitur enim præscientia, prænotio tam electorum, quam reproborum. Unde Apostolus interdum utitur nomine præscientiæ, quantum ad bonos, quemadmodum ad Romanos de Deo loquens: Quos, inquit, præscivit et prædestinavit conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui. Sed quoniam electorum prænotio proprium nomen habet, quod est prædestinatio; ideo præscientia communiter sumitur, quantum ad malos, ita quod præsciti dicuntur mali et reprobi. Dicit etiam Glossa prætacta, quod prophetia præscientiæ semper impletur.
paras.en: There are therefore four kinds of prophecy. The Gloss, however, at the beginning of the book of Psalms, sets down only two kinds of prophecy, namely of foreknowledge and of threatening. For the prophecy of promise is included under the prophecy of threatening, or is reduced to it; and the prophecy of predestination is contained under the prophecy of foreknowledge, because predestination is a part of foreknowledge. For foreknowledge is the name given to God's foreknowing of the elect and of the reprobate alike. Hence the Apostle sometimes uses the name of foreknowledge with regard to the good, as when, speaking of God in the Epistle to the Romans, he says: [[Rom 8:29|whom|Quos]], he says, [[Rom 8:29|he foreknew, he also predestinated to be made conformable to the image of his Son|præscivit et prædestinavit conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui]]. But since the foreknowing of the elect has a name of its own, which is predestination, foreknowledge is commonly taken with regard to the wicked, so that the wicked and reprobate are called the foreknown [præsciti: in the usage of the schools, those whom God foresees will be lost]. The aforesaid Gloss also says that the prophecy of foreknowledge is always fulfilled.

1.title: An David fuit excellentissimus prophetarum
1.title_en: Whether David was the most excellent of the prophets
1.note: One of Denis's introductory articles to his commentary on the Psalter; it expounds no verse of Psalm 1.

paras.t: Dionysius, primo Cœlestis hierarchiæ capitulo, duplicem tangit modum revelationis propheticæ, quæ sanctorum theologorum Prophetarumque mentibus est infusa. Interdum enim per sensibilia signa, demonstrata est veritas supernaturalis ac prophetalis; quandoque vero per solam mentis elevationem in divina pure contemplata, sine sensibilium tegumento formarum, et sine imaginariarum similitudine specierum. Prima autem harum revelationum, symbolica dicitur: quoniam symbolum est collatio sensibilium formarum, ad invisibilium demonstrationem. Secunda vero, anagogica nuncupatur. Anagoge namque est pura mentis ascensio ad divina.
paras.en: Dionysius, in the first chapter of the Celestial Hierarchy, touches on a twofold mode of the prophetic revelation poured into the minds of the holy theologians and prophets. For sometimes supernatural and prophetic truth has been shown through signs of sense; and sometimes through the mind's being raised alone to divine things contemplated purely, without the covering of sensible forms and without the likeness of imagined images. The first of these revelations is called symbolic: for a symbol is a bringing together of sensible forms to show things invisible. The second is named anagogical. For anagoge is the pure ascent of the mind to divine things.

paras.t: Denique, secundum Augustinum, tribus modis causatur seu fit prophetalium formarum ostensio. Aliquando enim fit sola imaginaria visione, sine intellectuali revelatione: sicut in Nabuchodonosor, qui vidit statuam grandem; et in Balthasar filio ejus, qui vidit articulos; atque in Pharaone, qui vidit septem boves et septem spicas: et horum nullus erat propheta. Ad prophetiam enim exigitur primo alicujus revelandi ostensio: secundo, propositæ veritatis perceptio. Propter quod in Daniele scriptum est: Intelligentia opus est in visione. Et ideo Joseph et Daniel, qui prædictas visiones imaginarias intelligebant et exponebant, Prophetæ fuerunt. Interdum autem in prophetali revelatione simul infunduntur imaginaria visio et intellectualis perceptio: et hoc modo omnes Prophetæ duodecim, quorum libros habemus, prophetaverunt. Interdum vero infunditur prophetia secundum solam intellectualem illustrationem: et hic modus prophetandi est purior atque præstantior. Sic David prophetasse ab omnibus dicitur. Unde Glossa in exordio Psalterii asserit, quod alii Prophetæ per quasdam rerum imagines et integumenta verborum prophetaverunt, videlicet per somnia, et dicta, ac facta; David autem solus Spiritus Sancti instinctu, sine omni exteriori adminiculo, suam edidit prophetiam.
paras.en: Further, according to Augustine, the showing of prophetic forms is brought about, or comes to pass, in three ways. For sometimes it comes by imaginary vision alone, without intellectual revelation: as in Nabuchodonosor, who saw a great statue[[Dan 2:31||]]; and in Baltassar his son, who saw the joints of a hand[[Dan 5:5||]]; and in Pharao, who saw seven kine and seven ears of corn[[Gen 41:2||]][[Gen 41:5||]]: and none of these was a prophet. For prophecy requires, first, the showing of something to be revealed; second, the perception of the truth set forth. That is why it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 10:1|there is need of understanding in a vision|Intelligentia opus est in visione]]. And therefore Joseph and Daniel, who understood and expounded the imaginary visions just mentioned, were prophets. But sometimes, in prophetic revelation, imaginary vision and intellectual perception are poured in together: and in this way all the twelve prophets whose books we have prophesied. And sometimes prophecy is poured in by intellectual enlightenment alone: and this mode of prophesying is purer and more excellent. In this way David is said by all to have prophesied. Hence the Gloss, at the opening of the Psalter, asserts that the other prophets prophesied through certain images of things and coverings of words, namely through dreams, and sayings, and deeds; but David alone, by the prompting of the Holy Ghost, without any outward aid, gave forth his prophecy.

paras.t: Fit autem prophetia quatuor modis. Primo, per facta, ut arca Noe significavit Ecclesiam, et per sartaginem ferream, inter Ezechielem et Jerusalem positam, designabatur devastatio urbis Jerusalem. Secundo, prophetia fit per verba seu dicta, sicut ad Abraham dictum est: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ. Tertio, per visiones, sicut Moyses vidit rubum ardere, nec tamen consumi. Quarto, per somnium. — Præterea quædam est prophetia de præterito, sicut Moysi prophetica revelatione innotuit creatio mundi. Unde quod ait, In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram, prophetia est. Alia est prophetia de præsenti, sicut dum aliquis Spiritu Sancto revelante cognoscit, quid alius cogitat. Et sic Elisabeth de incarnatione Christi et ejus præsentia prophetavit, Unde (inquiens) hoc mihi, ut veniat Mater Domini mei ad me? Tamen ut dictum est, prophetia proprie dicta, non est nisi de futuro. — Et quia donum prophetiæ pertinet ad gratiam gratis datam, non ad gratiam gratum facientem; idcirco per malos etiam, spiritus prophetiæ aliquando loquitur, sicut per Balaam: qui quamvis ariolus et magus ac pessimus fuerit, pulcherrime tamen prophetavit, quemadmodum in libro Numerorum habetur.
paras.en: Now prophecy is made in four ways. First, by deeds: as the ark of Noe[[Gen 6:14||]] signified the Church, and by the iron pan set between Ezechiel and Jerusalem[[Ezech 4:3||]] the laying waste of the city of Jerusalem was signified. Secondly, prophecy is made by words or sayings, as it was said to Abraham: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ]] [Denis reads *omnes tribus terræ*, "all the tribes of the earth", as in Gen 28:14, for *omnes gentes terræ*]. Thirdly, by visions, as Moses saw the bush burning and yet not consumed[[Ex 3:2||]]. Fourthly, by a dream. — Moreover, there is a certain prophecy of the past, as the creation of the world became known to Moses by prophetic revelation. Hence his saying, [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram]], is prophecy. Another is prophecy of the present, as when someone, by the revelation of the Holy Ghost, knows what another is thinking. And in this way Elisabeth prophesied of the incarnation of Christ and of his presence, saying: [[Luke 1:43|whence|Unde]] [[Luke 1:43|is this to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?|hoc mihi, ut veniat Mater Domini mei ad me?]] Yet, as has been said, prophecy properly so called is only of the future. — And since the gift of prophecy belongs to grace freely given, not to the grace that makes pleasing [*gratia gratum faciens*: sanctifying grace, which makes a man pleasing to God]; therefore the spirit of prophecy sometimes speaks even through the wicked, as through Balaam: who, though he was a soothsayer and a magician and most wicked, yet prophesied most beautifully, as we have it in the book of Numbers[[Num 24:17||]] [the margin, hard to read, seems to give Num. xxiii–xxiv].

paras.t: Est igitur quæstio, an David sit maximus Prophetarum. Et quod sit ceteris Prophetis, qui imaginarias aut corporales visiones habebant, sublimior, palam est ex præinductis. Sed de hoc maxime est quæstio, an sit major Propheta quam Moyses.
paras.en: There is, then, the question whether David is the greatest of the prophets. And that he is higher than the other prophets, who had imaginary or bodily visions, is plain from what has been brought forward. But the chief question about this is whether he is a greater prophet than Moses.

paras.t: Hanc vero quæstionem S. Thomas inducit; eamque solvendo testatur, quod omnibus consideratis, simpliciterque loquendo, Moyses excellit in dono prophetiæ sanctum David, quamvis vel David, vel alii, quantum ad aliquid, possint excedere Moysen: quia videlicet de Christi mysteriis plenius sunt locuti, ut David; vel quia majora fecerunt miracula, ut Josue, ad cujus præceptum sol et luna steterunt immobiles in cœlo unius diei spatio. Quod vero Moyses, absolute loquendo, sit Propheta altissimus, probatur, quia ad prophetiam præcipue spectat visio tam imaginaria, quam intellectualis; item denuntiatio veritatis ostensæ, atque miraculorum ostensio. Moyses autem in omnibus his excellebat. Primo, quoad intellectualem visionem: quoniam secundum Augustinum, in hac vita vidit Deum per essentiam, sicut et Paulus in raptu, ut Augustinus duodecimo super Genesim ad litteram, et in libro de Videndo Deum, fatetur. Unde in libro Numerorum de Moyse dicitur: Palam et non per ænigmata Deum videt. Secundo, Moyses reliquos omnes præcellit, quantum ad imaginariam visionem, quam quasi ad libitum habuit, non solum audiendo et in somno, sed et videndo angelum colloquentem sibi, et vigilando. Et ideo in Exodo dicitur, quod loquebatur ei Dominus, id est angelus Domini, facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum. Tertio, Moyses excellit quoad denuntiationem, quoniam toti populo loquebatur, proponens ei legem. Quarto, excellit Moyses quoad miraculorum ostensionem, quia multa magna fecit miracula coram iniquis et populo universo.
paras.en: St Thomas brings up this question [Summa theologiae II-II, q. 174, a. 4, as the margin notes]; and in resolving it he testifies that, all things considered and speaking simply, Moses excels holy David in the gift of prophecy, although David or others may in some respect exceed Moses: namely because they spoke more fully of the mysteries of Christ, as David did; or because they worked greater miracles, as Josue, at whose command the sun and moon stood still in the heaven for the space of one day[[Jos 10:13||]]. That Moses, speaking absolutely, is the highest prophet is proved thus: to prophecy belong chiefly vision, both imaginary and intellectual; likewise the announcing of the truth shown, and the showing of miracles. And Moses excelled in all of these. First, as to intellectual vision: since, according to Augustine, he saw God in this life through his essence, as Paul did too in his rapture[[2 Cor 12:2||]][[2 Cor 12:4||]], as Augustine acknowledges in the twelfth book on Genesis to the Letter and in the book On Seeing God. Hence it is said of Moses in the book of Numbers: [[Num 12:8|plainly, and not by riddles|Palam et non per ænigmata]] [[Num 12:8|doth he see the Lord|Deum videt]]. Secondly, Moses surpasses all the rest as to imaginary vision, which he had almost at will, not only by hearing and in sleep, but also by seeing an angel speaking with him, and while awake. And therefore it is said in Exodus that [[Ex 33:11|the Lord spoke to Moses|loquebatur ei Dominus]], that is, the angel of the Lord, [[Ex 33:11|face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend|facie ad faciem, sicut loqui solet homo ad amicum suum]]. Thirdly, Moses excels as to the announcing, since he spoke to the whole people, setting the law before them. Fourthly, Moses excels as to the showing of miracles, since he worked many great miracles before the wicked and the whole people.

paras.t: Sed huic responsioni contradicit Nicolaus de Lyra, præsertim in hoc, quod Thomas idcirco præfert Moysen David in dono prophetiæ, quia vidit in præsenti vita Deum per essentiam, quoniam talis visio ad prophetiam nil pertinet. Verumtamen determinatio Thomæ conveniens est. Quamvis enim visio ista directe ad prophetiam non pertinet, tamen eo modo quo miraculorum operatio ad eam pertinere asseritur, ipsa quoque ad eam pertinere censetur. Unde in Deuteronomio scriptum est: Non surrexit ultra Propheta in Israel sicut Moyses, quem nosset Dominus facie ad faciem, in omnibus signis atque portentis quæ per eum fecit Dominus in terra Ægypti.
paras.en: But Nicholas of Lyra contradicts this answer, especially in this, that Thomas prefers Moses to David in the gift of prophecy because he saw God through his essence in the present life; since such a vision has nothing to do with prophecy. Nevertheless, Thomas's conclusion is fitting. For although that vision does not belong to prophecy directly, yet it is judged to belong to it in the same way in which the working of miracles is said to belong to it. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 34:10|there arose no more a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face|Non surrexit ultra Propheta in Israel sicut Moyses, quem nosset Dominus facie ad faciem]], [[Deut 34:11|In all the signs and wonders, which he sent by him, to do in the land of Egypt|in omnibus signis atque portentis quæ per eum fecit Dominus in terra Ægypti]].

paras.t: Quod ergo David dicitur eximius Prophetarum, intelligendum est quantum ad hoc, quod de Christi mysteriis excellentius et evidentius prophetavit.
paras.en: That David, then, is called the foremost of the prophets is to be understood in this respect: that he prophesied of the mysteries of Christ more excellently and more plainly.

1.title: DE QUADRUPLICI EXPOSITIONE SACRÆ SCRIPTURÆ, ET SEPTEM REGULIS AD INTELLIGENTIAM SCRIPTURARUM SANCTARUM VALDE UTILIBUS.
1.title_en: On the fourfold exposition of sacred Scripture, and seven rules most useful for understanding the holy Scriptures

paras.t: Tota fere sacra Scriptura, seu theologicalis doctrina, sub quibusdam figuris ac similitudinibus mirabiliter est velata, quatenus veritas indignis et pravis hominibus occultetur, studiosis vero ac piis occasio bonæ exercitationis præstetur; et item, quoniam secundum Dionysium, impossibile est aliter nobis innotescere divinum radium, nisi varietate sacrorum velaminum anagogice circumvelatum. Unde Damascenus: Scire, inquit, oportet nos homines in hac grossa carne exsistentes, res divinas et immateriales non posse agnoscere, nisi quibusdam notis imaginibus et connaturalibus formis usi fuerimus. Et ideo Augustinus ait: Notitia proprietatum naturalium rerum, reserat nobis sanctarum abdita Scripturarum. Hinc ergo contingit, quod sacra Scriptura multis modis exponitur, eo quod non solum nomina significent res, sed etiam res una significet aliam. Nam res ipsæ comparantur ad intellectum divinum, sicut verba ad proferentem: quoniam ipse dixit, et facta sunt. Sacratissima igitur theologia non solum attendit vocum significationes, sed etiam rerum proprietates.
paras.en: Almost the whole of sacred Scripture, or theological doctrine, is wonderfully veiled under certain figures and likenesses, so that the truth may be hidden from unworthy and wicked men, while the studious and devout are given occasion for good exercise; and also because, according to Dionysius, the divine ray cannot otherwise become known to us than veiled round anagogically [that is, in a way that leads the mind upward] with a variety of sacred veils. Hence Damascene says: We men, living in this gross flesh, must know that we cannot come to know divine and immaterial things unless we make use of certain familiar images and forms connatural to us. And therefore Augustine says: Knowledge of the properties of natural things unlocks for us the hidden things of the holy Scriptures. Hence, then, it comes about that sacred Scripture is expounded in many ways, because not only do words signify things, but one thing also signifies another. For things themselves stand to the divine intellect as words to the one who utters them: since [[Ps 148:5|he spoke, and they were made|ipse dixit, et facta sunt]]. The most sacred theology, therefore, attends not only to what words mean, but also to the properties of things.

paras.t: Quatuor itaque modis exponitur sacra Scriptura: videlicet litteraliter seu historice, et spiritualiter seu mystice. Sed mysticus intellectus est triplex, scilicet allegoricus, tropologicus seu moralis, et anagogicus. Historia enim docet quid sit factum, allegoria quid credendum, tropologia quid faciendum, anagogia quid sperandum. Historia autem est rei gestæ narratio. Sensus vero historicus seu litteralis, est fundamentum seu basis intellectuum aliorum: et ex eo solo valet argumentum ad fidei probationem, sicut in epistola contra Vincentium Donatistam asserit Augustinus. Denique sensus allegoricus est, quando ex dicto vel facto alicujus personæ, aliud quid intelligitur pertinens ad Christum et corpus ejus mysticum, quod est Ecclesia: sicut dum ea quæ in veteri Testamento ad litteram sanctis patribus contigerunt, de Christo intelliguntur; vel ea quæ ad Synagogam spectabant, ad Ecclesiam referuntur. Omnia namque in figura contingebant illis, et scripta sunt ad nostram eruditionem. Sensus vero tropologicus est, quando ea quæ de Christo vel de Sanctis scribuntur et recitantur, ad nostram moralem informationem aptantur et exponuntur. Sensus autem anagogicus est, quando ex his quæ temporaliter facta sunt, ad contemplationem æternorum perducuntur; et ea quæ ad militantem Ecclesiam pertinent, ad statum triumphantis Ecclesiæ referuntur.
paras.en: Sacred Scripture, then, is expounded in four ways: namely literally or historically, and spiritually or mystically. But the mystical understanding is threefold, namely allegorical, tropological or moral, and anagogical. For history teaches what was done, allegory what is to be believed, tropology what is to be done, anagogy what is to be hoped for. Now history is the narration of a thing done. And the historical or literal sense is the foundation or base of the other senses; and from it alone does an argument hold good for proving the faith, as Augustine asserts in the letter against Vincent the Donatist. The allegorical sense, next, is when from the saying or deed of some person something else is understood that belongs to Christ and to his mystical body, which is the Church: as when what befell the holy fathers in the Old Testament according to the letter is understood of Christ; or what concerned the Synagogue is referred to the Church. For [[1 Cor 10:11|all these things happened to them in figure|Omnia namque in figura contingebant illis]], and [[Rom 15:4|were written for our learning|scripta sunt ad nostram eruditionem]]. The tropological sense is when what is written and told of Christ or of the Saints is applied and expounded for the forming of our morals. And the anagogical sense is when from things done in time [our minds] are led on to the contemplation of eternal things, and what belongs to the Church militant is referred to the state of the Church triumphant.

paras.t: Horum autem solet poni exemplum in hac dictione, Jerusalem: quod quia commune est et pene omnibus notum, omitto, ponamque exemplum in integra oratione. Id enim quod de manna scriptum est, secundum litteralem sensum exponitur de cibo illo, quem Deus pluit filiis Israel in deserto. Allegorice vero exponitur de superdignissimo corporis et sanguinis Christi Sacramento. Manna enim figura fuit Sacramenti altaris. Tropologice quoque exponitur de spirituali nutritione, qua Deus quotidie servos suos fideles in præsenti exsilio interius alit, consolatur, ac roborat per caritatem et gratiam. Anagogice autem exponitur de felicissima illa refectione Beatorum in patria, ubi ipsa superessentialis Divinitas est Beatorum edulium per beatissimam fruitionem. Unde et scriptum est: Beatus qui manducabit panem in regno Dei. Et iterum: Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos.
paras.en: An example of these is usually given in the word Jerusalem; but since that is common and known to almost everyone, I leave it aside, and will give an example in a whole statement [*in integra oratione*: in a complete sentence, not a single word]. What is written of the manna[[Ex 16:14||]] [the margin reads Exod. xvi … et seq.; the verse number is unreadable] is expounded in the literal sense of that food which God rained down on the children of Israel in the desert. Allegorically it is expounded of the most worthy Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ: for the manna was a figure of the Sacrament of the altar. Tropologically, too, it is expounded of the spiritual nourishment by which God daily feeds within, consoles and strengthens his faithful servants in this present exile, through charity and grace. And anagogically it is expounded of that most happy refreshment of the Blessed in the fatherland, where the superessential Godhead itself is the food of the Blessed through most blessed fruition. Hence it is also written: [[Luke 14:15|Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God|Beatus qui manducabit panem in regno Dei]]. And again: [[Ps 35:9|They shall be inebriated with the plenty of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure|Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]].

paras.t: Porro septem sunt regulæ, quas Augustinus, Beda et Haymo referunt a Tichonio positas, per quas omnes ambiguitates contrarietatis litteralis explanantur et dissolvuntur. His enim regulis sanctarum Scripturarum series variatur, atque expositio immutatur. Prima regula est, quod interdum de Christo et corpore ejus mystico fit sermo sub una invariataque voce, et ita fit transitus de uno in aliud, ac si de eodem fieret sermo. Tunc ergo considerandum est, quid uni, et quid alteri congruere possit. Christus namque vicissim in persona membrorum suorum aliquid loquitur, quasi de se ipso, ut ibi: Quare me dereliquisti longe a salute mea? Et iterum: Esurivi, et non dedistis mihi manducare. Et rursus: Saule, Saule, quid me persequeris?
paras.en: Further, there are seven rules, which Augustine, Bede and Haymo report as laid down by Tichonius, by which all the ambiguities of apparent contradiction in the letter are explained and resolved. For by these rules the course of the holy Scriptures is varied and their exposition changed. The first rule is that sometimes Christ and his mystical body are spoken of under one and the same unvaried wording, and so there is a passing from the one to the other as if the same were being spoken of. Then, therefore, we must consider what can fit the one, and what the other. For Christ in turn says something in the person of his members as if of himself, as here: [[Ps 21:2|why hast thou forsaken me? Far from my salvation|Quare me dereliquisti longe a salute mea?]]? And again: [[Matt 25:42|I was hungry and you gave me not to eat|Esurivi, et non dedistis mihi manducare]]. And once more: [[Acts 9:4|Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?|Saule, Saule, quid me persequeris?]]

paras.t: Secunda regula est, quod sancta Scriptura aliquando simul loquitur de corpore Christi mystico quod vere ad Christum pertinet, et corpore mystico quod solo nomine ad ipsum spectat, ut sunt reprobi: sicut dum dicitur, Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum, et revertebantur, et diluculo veniebant ad eum. In tali enim locutione videtur Scriptura de eisdem loqui, quum tamen de diversis loquatur. Nam alii occidebantur, et alii quærentes Deum, revertebantur. Tertia regula est, quod sacra Scriptura interdum sub eadem voce, aliquid pro suo tempore faciendum litteraliter indicat, et Spiritus nobis ex hoc alia suo tempore facienda insinuat: sicut in præceptis cærimonialibus veteris legis, quæ modo ad litteram mortifera essent, sed tempore legis utiliter observari volebant. Unde Apostolus: Littera, inquit, occidit, spiritus autem vivificat.
paras.en: The second rule is that holy Scripture sometimes speaks at once of the mystical body of Christ that truly belongs to Christ, and of the mystical body that belongs to him in name only, as the reprobate do: as when it is said, [[Ps 77:34|When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned, and came to him early in the morning|Quum occideret eos, quærebant eum, et revertebantur, et diluculo veniebant ad eum]]. For in such a saying Scripture seems to speak of the same men, when in fact it speaks of different ones: for some were slain, and others, seeking God, returned. The third rule is that sacred Scripture sometimes, under the same wording, points literally to something to be done in its own time, and from this the Spirit suggests to us other things to be done in their own time: as in the ceremonial precepts of the old law, which would now be deadly if kept to the letter, but in the time of the law were to be observed with profit. Hence the Apostle: [[2 Cor 3:6|the letter|Littera]], he says, [[2 Cor 3:6|killeth: but the spirit quickeneth|occidit, spiritus autem vivificat]].

paras.t: Quarta regula est, quod divina Scriptura nonnunquam quasi sub eadem voce ac pari sententia, transit de genere ad speciem, de toto ad partem, et econverso: talisque modus loquendi, in Prophetis est maxime generalis, ut quando sub comminatione unius gentis seu regni, intendunt Prophetæ prædicere ea quæ omnibus generaliter sunt futura. Sicut dum Isaias de Babylone et Tyro vaticinatur, intendit similia esse ventura omnibus eadem mala agentibus in communi. Unde et Christus in Evangelio ait: Quod vobis dico, omnibus dico. Quinta regula est, quum totum per partem, vel partem per totum Scriptura designat, sicut de triduo dominicæ sepulturæ. Tales modi loquendi, per synecdochen excusantur. Ad hunc autem modum referuntur omnes numerorum ac temporum defectus atque excessus: sicut dum ponitur præteritum pro futuro, vel aliquid minus de integro numero: tunc namque quod modicum est, pro nihilo reputatur.
paras.en: The fourth rule is that divine Scripture sometimes, as it were under the same wording and with the same meaning, passes from the genus to the species, from the whole to the part, and the other way about. And this manner of speaking is most common in the Prophets, as when under the threatening of one nation or kingdom the Prophets mean to foretell what is to come upon all in general: as when Isaias prophesies of Babylon and of Tyre, he means that like things will come upon all who do the same evils in common. Hence Christ too says in the Gospel: [[Mark 13:37|what I say to you, I say to all|Quod vobis dico, omnibus dico]]. The fifth rule is when Scripture signifies the whole by the part, or the part by the whole, as with the three days of the Lord's burial [counted as three days, though he lay in the tomb only part of the first and of the third]. Such ways of speaking are justified by synecdoche. And to this manner are referred all the shortfalls and excesses in numbers and times: as when the past is put for the future, or something less than the whole number is given; for then what is small is reckoned as nothing.

paras.t: Sexta regula est de recapitulatione et anticipatione, ut quum Scriptura redit ad ea quæ præterierat, quatenus aliquid addat, vel convenientius recitet: quemadmodum in Genesi postquam commemoravit Scriptura filios Noe divisos per linguas et gentes, postmodum subdit, Et erat populus unus et labium unum: quod utique ante divisionem prædictum fuit. Simili modo, quod postea factum est, per anticipationem aliquando antea narratur. Talia ergo per hanc regulam verificantur et excusantur. Septima regula est, de diabolo et corpore ejus, sicut dum ea quæ dæmonis sunt, reprobis adscribuntur, vel vice versa: ut in Isaia offendimus, quod sub persona regis Babylonis, fit sermo de Lucifero, qui caput est omnium malorum. Unde sic legitur: Quomodo cecidisti, Lucifer, qui mane oriebaris? Similiter in Ezechiele, sub persona regis Tyri, fit sermo de casu diaboli. Et Christus in Evangelio de Juda proditore dixit: Unus ex vobis diabolus est. Hæc autem memoriter retinenda sunt, propter intelligentiam futurorum.
paras.en: The sixth rule is of recapitulation and anticipation: as when Scripture goes back to what it had passed over, in order to add something or to tell it more fittingly. So in Genesis, after Scripture has recorded the sons of Noe divided by tongues and nations, it afterwards adds: And there was one people and one tongue[[Gen 11:6||]] [the margin gives Gen. xi; Denis's words join 11:1, “the earth was of one tongue”, and 11:6, “it is one people, and all have one tongue”]: which surely belongs to the time before the division. In like manner, what was done afterwards is sometimes told beforehand by anticipation. Such things, therefore, are shown true and justified by this rule. The seventh rule is of the devil and his body: as when what is the demon's is ascribed to the reprobate, or the other way about. So we find in Isaias that under the person of the king of Babylon[[Is 14:4||]] Lucifer is spoken of, who is the head of all the wicked. Hence we read there: [[Is 14:12|How art thou fallen|Quomodo cecidisti]], [[Is 14:12|O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning|Lucifer, qui mane oriebaris]]? Likewise in Ezechiel, under the person of the king of Tyre, the fall of the devil is spoken of[[Ezech 28:12||]] [the margin seems to read Ezech. xxvii, 12 et seq.; the lament over the king of Tyre begins at 28:12]. And Christ in the Gospel said of Judas the traitor: [[John 6:71|one of you is a devil|Unus ex vobis diabolus est]]. These things are to be kept in memory, for the understanding of what follows.

1.title: De titulo et auctore, ac varia translatione libri Psalmorum
1.title_en: Of the title and the author, and the various translations, of the book of Psalms
1.note: One of Denis's introductory articles to his commentary on the Psalter; it expounds no verse of Psalm 1.

paras.t: Nunc de titulo libri Psalmorum videndum est. Est igitur titulus talis: Incipit liber Hymnorum, seu Soliloquiorum Prophetæ de Christo. Hic titulus a catholicis doctoribus diversimode valde exponitur. Id tamen in quo omnes concordant, primo tangendum est. Dicitur igitur liber iste, liber Hymnorum, quoniam hymnus est laus Dei cum cantico. Canticum vero est exsultatio mentis de bonis æternis concepta, in vocem prorumpens. Quoniam itaque liber iste docet nos Deum laudare cum exsultatione habita de æternis non solum corde, sed etiam voce, idcirco congrue dicitur liber Hymnorum. Sunt vero hi hymni in Hebræo metrice scripti: quod in translatione servari difficile fuisset. — Additur autem in titulo: Seu Soliloquiorum: et hoc ideo, quoniam David ex sola Spiritus Sancti inspiratione, ac intellectuali revelatione, sine omni exteriori adminiculo, psalmos edidit; sicque inter ipsum et Spiritum Sanctum, quasi quoddam soliloquium fuisse videtur. Vel ideo, quoniam liber iste de solo Christo principaliter tractat et loquitur. Vel ideo, quia devota mens psalmos decantando, cum Deo quoddam soliloquium habet: quod utique tanto suavius, affectuosius, ardentius, atque sincerius est, quanto anima virtutem ac sensum psalmorum profundius clariusque cognoscit et sapit.
paras.en: Now we must look at the title of the book of Psalms. The title, then, is this: Here begins the book of Hymns, or of Soliloquies, of the Prophet, concerning Christ. This title is expounded in very different ways by the Catholic doctors. But that in which all agree is to be touched on first. This book, then, is called the book of Hymns, because a hymn is the praise of God with song. And song is the exultation of the mind, conceived from eternal goods, breaking out into the voice. Since, then, this book teaches us to praise God with exultation over eternal things, not only with the heart but also with the voice, it is fittingly called the book of Hymns. These hymns are written in metre in the Hebrew: which it would have been hard to keep in translation. — Next the title adds: Or of Soliloquies: and this because David gave forth the psalms by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost alone, and by intellectual revelation, without any outward aid; and so there seems to have been a kind of soliloquy between him and the Holy Ghost. Or because this book treats and speaks principally of Christ alone. Or because the devout mind, in singing the psalms, holds a kind of soliloquy with God: one that is all the sweeter, more loving, more ardent and more sincere, the more deeply and clearly the soul knows and tastes the power and the sense of the psalms.

paras.t: Sequitur autem in titulo: Prophetæ. Omnes namque concordant in hoc, quod universi psalmi ex divina inspiratione conscripti sunt ab aliquo Prophetarum. Sed an ab uno dumtaxat, vel certe a pluribus, de hoc varia exstat opinio, sicut infra patebit. — Sequitur quoque in titulo: De Christo. Ecce materia seu subjectum libri Psalmorum. Est enim de Christo, non utique de sola Christi persona, sed de toto Christo, hoc est de ipso et ad eum pertinentibus, nempe de Sponso et Sponsa, seu capite et mystico corpore. Interdum enim agit de capite, id est de ipso Christo secundum se; interdum de corpore ejus, id est Ecclesia. Interdum vero agit de Christo secundum utrumque. Denique, de Christo secundum se agit tripliciter. Primo secundum ejus divinitatem, ut ibi: Ego hodie genui te. Secundo, quoad ejus humanitatem, ut ibi: Ego sum vermis. Tertio transumptive, sicut dum Christus utitur voce membrorum, ut ibi: Deus, tu scis insipientiam meam.
paras.en: Then follows in the title: Of the Prophet. For all agree in this, that all the psalms were written by divine inspiration by one of the prophets. But whether by one only, or by several, there are various opinions on this, as will be seen below. — There follows also in the title: Concerning Christ. Here is the matter or subject of the book of Psalms. For it is about Christ: not, indeed, about the person of Christ alone, but about the whole Christ, that is, about him and what belongs to him, namely about the Bridegroom and the Bride, or the head and the mystical body. For sometimes it treats of the head, that is, of Christ himself in himself; sometimes of his body, that is, the Church. And sometimes it treats of Christ in respect of both. Further, it treats of Christ in himself in three ways. First, according to his divinity, as where it says: [[2:7|this day have I begotten thee|Ego hodie genui te]]. Secondly, as to his humanity, as where it says: [[21:7|I am a worm|Ego sum vermis]]. Thirdly, by transference [*transumptive*: by a figure in which one speaks in another's person], as when Christ uses the voice of his members, as where it says: [[68:6|O God, thou knowest my foolishness|Deus, tu scis insipientiam meam]].

paras.t: Nunc considerandum est, in quo doctores dissentiant exponendo titulum istum. Primo ergo discordant in hoc quod dicitur, Incipit liber. Quidam enim dicunt quinque esse libros Psalmorum, propter quinque distinctiones quæ fiunt in libro isto per Fiat, fiat. Alii autem asserunt unum tantummodo esse librum, quoniam postea dicitur, In capite libri scriptum est de me. Et in Actibus Apostolorum dicitur, Sicut scriptum est in libro Psalmorum. Non dicitur, In libris; sed, In libro. Verumtamen videtur, salvo meliori judicio, quod utraque positio posset verificari, ut videlicet dicatur unus liber totalis, et plures libri partiales, quemadmodum et liber Regum unus vocatur, qui tamen in quatuor libros partitur. Liber quoque duodecim Prophetarum dicitur unus, quem constat dividi posse in duodecim libros partiales, præsertim quum Nahum propheta, cujus vaticinium pene brevissimum est, in prophetiæ suæ exordio dicat, Liber visionis Nahum.
paras.en: Now we must consider in what the doctors disagree in expounding this title. First, then, they disagree about the words: Here begins the book. For some say there are five books of Psalms, because of the five divisions made in this book by "So be it, so be it" [*Fiat, fiat*, the close of the doxologies that end each of the five books]. Others assert that there is only one book, since later it is said: [[39:8|In the head of the book it is written of me|In capite libri scriptum est de me]]. And in the Acts of the Apostles it is said: As [[Acts 1:20|it is written in the book of Psalms|scriptum est in libro Psalmorum]]. It does not say: In the books; but: In the book. Yet it seems, saving a better judgment, that both positions could be true: namely that it may be called one book as a whole, and several books as parts; just as the book of Kings is called one, yet it is divided into four books. The book of the Twelve Prophets too is called one, though it is plain that it can be divided into twelve partial books, especially since the prophet Nahum, whose prophecy is almost the shortest, says at the opening of his prophecy: [[Nah 1:1|The book of the vision of Nahum|Liber visionis Nahum]].

paras.t: Secundo discordant circa hoc quod dicitur, Prophetæ, videlicet in auctore psalmorum. Quidam enim affirmant omnes psalmos a David compositos, nempe Augustinus, Cassiodorus, Glossator, et alii multi. Alii vero contra tenent oppositum, puta Hieronymus, Hilarius, Chrysostomus, quos sequitur Nicolaus de Lyra, asserentes Hebræorum doctores affirmare multos esse auctores psalmorum. Quid autem horum sit verius, certitudinaliter discernere nequeo.
paras.en: Secondly, they disagree about the words "of the Prophet", that is, about the author of the psalms. For some affirm that all the psalms were composed by David: namely Augustine, Cassiodorus, the Glossator, and many others. But others hold the opposite, such as Jerome, Hilary and Chrysostom, whom Nicholas of Lyra follows, asserting that the Hebrew doctors affirm that the psalms have many authors. Which of these is the truer, I cannot discern with certainty.

paras.t: Verumtamen sicut Gregorius primo libro Moralium super Job, supervacuum esse testatur multum inquirere quis fuerit auctor libri Job, quando certissimum est librum ipsum a Spiritu Sancto, sicut a principali auctore editum; sic etiam modo videtur supervacuum curiose scrutari aut multum contendere, an solus David ediderit psalmos, quum utique planum sit omnes psalmos revelatione Spiritus Sancti esse conscriptos. Nihilo minus probabilius veriusque opinor, a solo David librum Psalmorum esse compositum. Alias namque verum non appareret, omnes psalmos ex anagogica Spiritus Sancti revelatione, id est sine omni exteriori adminiculo imaginariarum formarum, et corporalium specierum sensibiliumque signorum, fuisse revelatos ac editos. Vel certe David dici non poterit eximius Prophetarum, tanquam qui solus anagogica et non symbolica revelatione prophetavit. Præterea, quæ a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt. Quum ergo, ut pene omnes concorditer adstruunt, Esdras Spiritu Sancto revelante ac disponente, psalmos reparaverit, ac in unum collegerit, non videtur quod tam diversorum auctorum seu Prophetarum psalmos tam confuse misceret, ac inordinate disponeret, nunc unius, nuncque alterius psalmum describens: quasi liber iste esset rapiarius quidam, sive quoddam ex dictis diversorum collectum. Et mirum videtur, cur psalmos David non redegerit in librum specialem, quum certum sit, majorem partem psalmorum ab ipso compositam, præsertim quum in reparatione aliorum Prophetarum, talem formam servaverit. Quamvis enim duodecim Prophetarum vaticinia in unum collegerit librum, singulorum tamen scripta seorsum posuit, cuilibetque Prophetæ specialem ac partialem deputans librum, non obstante quod nonnulli eorum in materia multum concordent, et aliqui valde breves sint. Attamen, si non solus David edidit psalmos, tunc utique ista commixtio psalmorum non est inordinata dicenda, neque confusa, sed ex certa ratione facta: quam quia invenire non valeo, id quod modo dixi, probabilius puto, quamvis nihil determinative affirmo.
paras.en: Nevertheless, as Gregory, in the first book of the Morals on Job, testifies that it is needless to inquire much who was the author of the book of Job, since it is most certain that the book itself was put forth by the Holy Ghost as its principal author; so too it seems needless now to search curiously or to dispute much whether David alone put forth the psalms, since it is quite plain that all the psalms were written by the revelation of the Holy Ghost. Nonetheless I think it more probable and truer that the book of Psalms was composed by David alone. For otherwise it would not appear true that all the psalms were revealed and put forth by an anagogical revelation of the Holy Ghost, that is, without any outward aid of imaginary forms, bodily images and sensible signs. Or at least David could not be called the foremost of the prophets, as the one who alone prophesied by anagogical and not symbolic revelation. Besides, the things that are from God are ordered[[Rom 13:1||]]. Since, then, as almost all agree, Esdras, by the revelation and disposing of the Holy Ghost, restored the psalms and gathered them into one, it does not seem that he would have mixed up the psalms of so many different authors or prophets so confusedly and arranged them so disorderly, copying now one man's psalm and now another's: as though this book were a kind of scrapbook [*rapiarius*: a notebook of extracts], or something collected from the sayings of various men. And it seems strange that he did not gather David's psalms into a book of their own, since it is certain that the greater part of the psalms was composed by him, especially since he kept such a form in restoring the other prophets. For although he gathered the prophecies of the Twelve Prophets into one book, yet he set the writings of each apart, assigning each prophet a book of his own, a part of the whole, even though some of them agree closely in matter and some are very short. Yet if David did not put forth the psalms alone, then this mixing of the psalms is surely not to be called disorderly or confused, but made for some definite reason: and since I cannot find that reason, I think what I have just said the more probable, though I affirm nothing as settled.

paras.t: Advertendum autem est, quod S. Hieronymus ter transtulit librum Psalmorum. Primo, secundum Septuaginta interpretes: quod appellatur Psalterium Romanum, quoniam Ecclesia sancti Petri utitur eo. Secundo, ad instantiam Paulæ et Eustochii fecit aliam translationem, non multum a prima differentem, licet Hebraico magis vicinam: et dicitur Psalterium Gallicanum, quia Damasus Papa ad preces Hieronymi fecit illud in ecclesiis Gallicanis cantari; et ista translatio apud Latinos communior est. Tertio, transtulit librum hunc pure juxta Hebraicum, ad instantiam cujusdam sancti episcopi nomine Sophronii, qui cum Judæis frequenter disputabat. Unde indiguit textu per omnia simili Psalterio, quod in Hebræo habetur: nam illud solum a Judæis recipitur.
paras.en: But it should be noted that St Jerome translated the book of Psalms three times. First, according to the Seventy translators: this is called the Roman Psalter, because the church of St Peter uses it. Secondly, at the request of Paula and Eustochium he made another translation, not much different from the first, though nearer the Hebrew: and it is called the Gallican Psalter, because Pope Damasus, at Jerome's prayers, had it sung in the churches of Gaul; and this translation is the more common among the Latins. Thirdly, he translated this book purely according to the Hebrew, at the request of a certain holy bishop named Sophronius, who often disputed with the Jews. Hence he needed a text in all things like the Psalter that is found in the Hebrew: for that alone is received by the Jews.

paras.t: Intentio vero libri Psalmorum est, Christi mysteria pandere, sicque genus humanum in veteri Adam lapsum ac deformatum, in novo homine Christo erigere, reformare, ac beatificare.
paras.en: And the purpose of the book of Psalms is to lay open the mysteries of Christ, and so to raise up, reform and make blessed in the new man, Christ, the human race that fell and was disfigured in the old Adam.

1.title: De virtute psalmorum, et de modo orandi atque psallendi
1.title_en: Of the power of the psalms, and of the manner of praying and of singing psalms
1.note: One of Denis's introductory articles to his commentary on the Psalter; it expounds no verse of Psalm 1.

paras.t: Quoniam igitur psalmodia est quoddam soliloquium Spiritus Sancti cum pia devotaque anima, constat neminem posse virtutem psalmorum vere et experimentaliter cognoscere, nisi eum qui puro et stabilito ac libero animo, sacratissima psalmorum verba decantat, munda ac fixa mente Deo intendens, sensumque verborum cum ingenti attentione advertens, et velut ex proprio affectu ea formans atque pronuntians. Hoc enim (ut ait Basilius) est psallere sapienter, quatenus cum intellectuali dulcedine et interno sapore verba Spiritus Sancti promamus, cum omni reverentia et cordis custodia nosmetipsos ante Dei conspectum, qui vere ubilibet præsens est, statuendo, ac recolendo quod scriptum est: Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper. Et iterum: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto hodie. Illud quoque Jeremias: Maledictus homo qui facit opus Dei negligenter.
paras.en: Since, then, psalmody is a kind of soliloquy of the Holy Ghost with a pious and devout soul, it is plain that no one can truly and by experience know the power of the psalms except one who sings the most sacred words of the psalms with a pure, steady and free mind, attending to God with a clean and fixed mind, heeding the sense of the words with great attention, and forming and uttering them as it were from his own affection. For this (as Basil says) is to sing psalms wisely: that we bring forth the words of the Holy Ghost with intellectual sweetness and inward savour, setting ourselves, with all reverence and guard of the heart, before the sight of God, who is truly present everywhere, and calling to mind what is written: [[18:15|the meditation of my heart always in thy sight|Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper]]. And again: [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth|Vivit Dominus]], [[3 Kings 17:1|in whose sight I stand|in cujus conspectu sto]] this day[[3 Kings 18:15||]]. And that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully|Maledictus homo qui facit opus Dei negligenter]] [Denis reads *negligenter*, "negligently", where the Vulgate has *fraudulenter*, "deceitfully"].

paras.t: Nam Spiritus Sanctus qui est ignis innocue ardens, ac ardentissima caritas, affectuosissima verba in psalmis deprompsit, omnique generi hominum convenientes sermones descripsit: nunc ea proponens quæ perfectos respiciunt, et ex magno caritatis fervore canenda sunt; nunc vero proponens quæ pœnitentes et imperfectos concernunt. Imo omni virtuoso affectui apta cantica exhibet. Interdum enim proponit quæ in persona Christi dicenda sunt, interdum quæ in persona Ecclesiæ, interdum quæ in persona peccatoris ac pœnitentis, interdum quæ in persona efficaciter proficientis, interdum quæ in persona perfecti et fervide diligentis, interdum quæ in persona justi et cum Deo æquitatem zelantis, interdum quæ in persona gratias agentis. Unde qui psalmos cum perfecta devotione cantare seu legere cupit, necessario indiget ut suum affectum sensui psalmorum conformet, omniumque prædictarum personarum similitudinem sibi assumat, prout psalmorum sententia exigit. Ait namque Dionysius tertio Cœlestis hierarchiæ capitulo, quod psalmi per modum divinæ laudis, includunt et continent quidquid sacra Pagina comprehendit.
paras.en: For the Holy Ghost, who is a fire that burns without harm and a most ardent charity, has brought forth the most loving words in the psalms, and has set down discourses fitting for every kind of men: now putting forward what concerns the perfect and is to be sung with great fervour of charity; now putting forward what concerns penitents and the imperfect. Indeed, he offers songs fit for every virtuous affection. For sometimes he puts forward what is to be said in the person of Christ, sometimes in the person of the Church, sometimes in the person of a sinner and penitent, sometimes in the person of one making good progress, sometimes in the person of one perfect and loving fervently, sometimes in the person of a just man zealous for justice together with God, sometimes in the person of one giving thanks. Hence whoever wishes to sing or read the psalms with perfect devotion must needs conform his affection to the sense of the psalms, and take on himself the likeness of all the persons mentioned, as the meaning of the psalms requires. For Dionysius says, in the third chapter of the Celestial Hierarchy, that the psalms, by way of divine praise, include and contain whatever the sacred Page comprises.

paras.t: Idcirco verissime dictum est, quod nullus mortalium potest vel mente concipere, vel verbis exprimere virtutem psalmorum. Omnium enim vitiorum eradicationem, omnium virtutum adeptionem, omnisque perfectionis plenitudinem docent; fidem illuminant, spem roborant, caritatem inflammant, humilitatem instruunt, mansuetudinem specialissime commendant, patientiam ceterasque virtutes erudiunt, mentem devote psallentis vehementer oblectant, omnem vitiosam sæculique tristitiam auferunt. Et qui in continua psalmorum decantatione lætatur, cœliformem atque angelicam vitam in hoc sæculo nequam ducit, carnales delectationes fastidit, vanos et infructuosos sermones, sæculares rumores ac temporis amissionem vehementer abhorret, ab humano colloquio separari satagit, cum Deo sermocinari conatur, omniumque gratiarum splendore incessabiliter adornatur. Insuper in psalmis ignitissimæ et affectuosissimæ orationes continentur, et jucundissima gratiarum actio, humillima peccatorum confessio, excellentissima Dei laudatio, omnis boni commendatio, omnis mali detestatio, et præclara ac sublimissima ad Deum mentis erectio. In psalmis quoque descripta sunt impiorum tormenta, electorum merces et gaudia, incipientium rudimenta, proficientium progressio, perfectorum plenitudo, vita activorum, speculatio contemplativorum.
paras.en: Therefore it has been most truly said that no mortal can either conceive in mind or express in words the power of the psalms. For they teach the uprooting of all vices, the gaining of all virtues, and the fulness of all perfection; they enlighten faith, strengthen hope, inflame charity, instruct humility, commend meekness most especially, train patience and the other virtues, greatly delight the mind of one who sings them devoutly, and take away all sinful sadness and the sadness of the world. And whoever rejoices in the continual singing of the psalms leads a heavenly and angelic life in this wicked world, loathes carnal delights, utterly abhors vain and fruitless talk, worldly gossip and the loss of time, takes pains to be separated from human conversation, strives to converse with God, and is unceasingly adorned with the splendour of all graces. Besides, in the psalms are contained the most fiery and loving prayers, and the most joyful thanksgiving, the humblest confession of sins, the most excellent praise of God, the commendation of every good, the detestation of every evil, and a glorious and most sublime raising of the mind to God. In the psalms too are described the torments of the wicked, the reward and joys of the elect, the first lessons of beginners, the advance of those making progress, the fulness of the perfect, the life of those in the active life, and the contemplation of contemplatives.

paras.t: De modo autem psallendi quid aptius potest doceri, quam quod devotissimus atque dulcissimus ille Bernardus inducit? Moneo, inquiens, vos, dilectissimi fratres, strenue laudibus interesse divinis, ut sicut reverenter, ita et alacriter Domino adsistatis, non pigri, non somnolenti, non oscitantes, non parcentes vocibus, non verba dimidia præscindentes, non integra transilientes, non fractis et remissis vocibus muliebre quiddam balbe de naribus resonantes; sed virili, ut dignum est, sono atque affectu voces Sancti Spiritus depromentes, nec aliud quam quod canitur cogitantes. Spiritus enim Sanctus gratum non habet, quidquid ei obtuleris, neglecto eo ad quod teneris. Nempe, ut ait Basilius, Deus orandus est atque laudandus, non vaga et huc illucque discurrente anima; sed in spiritu sollicito ac timorato adorare oportet, et ante orationem animam præparare, varias et impertinentes occupationes abjiciendo, ac aliquid salutare interioribus imprimendo, et magno serio inchoando, ne modicus error in principio, augeatur in prosecutione, magnusque fiat in fine.
paras.en: As for the manner of singing psalms, what more fitting thing can be taught than what that most devout and most sweet Bernard brings forward [in his Sermons on the Canticle, as the margin notes]?
