I warn you, he says, dearest brethren, to take part in the divine praises with vigour, so that you stand before the Lord with eagerness as well as reverence: not sluggish, not sleepy, not yawning, not sparing your voices, not clipping words in half, not skipping whole ones, not sounding something womanish through the nose in broken and feeble tones and a stammer; but bringing forth the words of the Holy Ghost with a manly sound and feeling, as is fitting, and thinking of nothing but what is being sung. For the Holy Ghost does not hold acceptable whatever you offer him while you neglect what you are bound to. Indeed, as Basil says, God is to be prayed to and praised not with a wandering soul running hither and thither; but we must adore him in a careful and fearful spirit, and prepare the soul before prayer[[Ecclus 18:23||]], casting away various and irrelevant occupations, and impressing something wholesome on our inward parts, and beginning in great earnest, lest a small error at the beginning grow as we go on and become great at the end.

paras.t: Sed sic orare et psallere, multa requirit et sanctam conversationem efflagitat, quatenus homo ante orationem ita se habeat, ut possit per gratiam Dei in ipsa oratione ac laudis tempore, stabili mentis intuitu atque ardenti affectu Deo intendere, ac sensum perpendere, divinorum eloquiorum virtutem gustare. Omnino enim oportet aggravantem vitare tristitiam, resolventem odio habere lætitiam, inordinatum timorem, immoderatam sollicitudinem, omnemque irrefrenatam concupiscentiam, et irrationabilem animæ passionem expellere: et quanto poterimus animam nostram ab omnium inferiorum virium operationibus magis suspendere, et a sensibilium memoria et amore magis abstrahere; tanto poterimus divinis præconiis sanctisque precibus, affectuosius, dulcius atque salubrius intendere ac vacare. Spiritus enim est Deus, et eos qui adorant eum, in spiritu oportet adorare.
paras.en: But to pray and sing psalms in this way requires many things and demands a holy way of life, so that a man so conducts himself before prayer that, by the grace of God, in the prayer itself and at the time of praise, he can attend to God with a steady gaze of the mind and an ardent affection, weigh the sense, and taste the power of the divine words. For we must altogether avoid the sadness that weighs down, hate the gladness that dissipates, and drive out inordinate fear, immoderate anxiety, all unbridled desire, and every unreasonable passion of the soul: and the more we can hold our soul back from the workings of all the lower powers and draw it away from the memory and love of the things of sense, the more lovingly, sweetly and wholesomely we shall be able to attend to and give ourselves to the divine praises and holy prayers. For [[John 4:24|God is a spirit: and they that adore him|Spiritus enim est Deus, et eos qui adorant eum]] [[John 4:24|must adore him in spirit|in spiritu oportet adorare]] [Denis leaves out "and in truth"].

paras.t: Denique in cantu omnis curiositas, omnis dissolutio, omnis discordia, summe vitandæ sunt; et summopere satagendum, ne alicui placere intendamus, nisi Altissimo, in eo dumtaxat spiritualiter gloriantes, ab eo solo videri, audiri, ac præmiari optantes, sensui verborum semper et Deo magis quam cantui et modo cantandi intendentes, illud dictum B. Augustini pensando: Dum mihi contingit, ut me cantus magis quam res quæ canitur, moveat, pœna committere digna me profiteor, et tunc mallem non audire cantantem. Conemur ergo, ut id in mente nostra versetur, quod ore profertur. Et si quispiam tantæ scientiæ non est, ut Scripturas sanctas intelligat, et proinde psalmodiæ sensum mente considerare nequeat; vel certe si id quod canitur, quantum ad superficiem atque historicum sensum, tale sit, ut nullam vel modicam videatur devotionem includere, cujusmodi est illud, Etenim passer invenit sibi domum, et turtur nidum sibi, ubi ponat pullos suos: tunc studere debemus, ut mentem nostram cum cordiali affectu ad Deum levemus, pensantes nos ante Dei conspectum adstare, et summo universorum Dominatori ac Judici ministrare. Sicque divinam majestatem aut aliud aliquid divinum considerantes, poterimus cum magna devotione Deo adsistere.
paras.en: Lastly, in singing, all affectation, all slackness, all discord are to be avoided above all; and we must take the greatest pains not to aim at pleasing anyone but the Most High, glorying spiritually in him alone, desiring to be seen, heard and rewarded by him alone, attending always to the sense of the words and to God rather than to the chant and the manner of singing, and weighing that saying of blessed Augustine [Confessions X, 33]: When it happens to me that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I commit a sin deserving punishment, and then I would rather not hear the singer. Let us strive, then, that what is uttered by the mouth may dwell in our mind. And if someone has not so much learning that he understands the holy Scriptures, and so cannot consider in his mind the sense of the psalmody; or if what is sung is such, as to its surface and historical sense, that it seems to contain no devotion or little, as is that verse, [[83:4|For the sparrow hath found herself a house, and the turtle a nest for herself where she may lay her young ones|Etenim passer invenit sibi domum, et turtur nidum sibi, ubi ponat pullos suos]]: then we ought to strive to lift up our mind to God with heartfelt affection, considering that we stand in God's sight and minister to the supreme Lord and Judge of all. And so, considering the divine majesty or some other divine thing, we shall be able to stand before God with great devotion.

1.title: DE INTENTIONE ET FORMA PROCEDENDI PRÆSENTIS EDITIONIS.
1.title_en: On the intention and manner of proceeding of the present work

paras.t: Quamvis autem sacra Scriptura jam a sanctis et magnis ac orthodoxis doctoribus plenissime videatur exposita, præsertim liber Psalmorum, nullusque possit David perfecte exponere, nisi Spiritus Sanctus qui per David locutus est animam ejus copiose illustraverit, docuerit atque perfecerit; nihilo minus in Dei bonitate vehementer confidens, conabor quod proprias vires prorsus excedit, nempe ipsum Psalterium utcumque elucidare, spe præmii quod Sapientia pollicetur, dicens: Qui elucidant me, vitam æternam habebunt. Et iterum: Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates. Quod de iis intelligere congruit, quorum vita seu conversatio doctrinæ concordat. Peccatori autem dixit Deus: Quare tu enarras justitias meas? Imo sicut B. Thomas super quartum Sententiarum ostendit, qui non implet quod alios docet, eo ipso quo sibi docendi onus assumit, mortaliter peccat: quoniam quantum in se est, intentionem sacræ Scripturæ evacuat. Porro cujus vita ad docendum idonea est, profecto aureolam promeretur, etiam si nunquam ore populo prædicet, sed sacram Scripturam exponendo, seu de theologia codices componendo, universis qui eos legerint, ad eruditionem loquatur.
paras.en: Now although sacred Scripture seems already to have been most fully expounded by holy, great and orthodox doctors, above all the book of Psalms, and no one can expound David perfectly unless the Holy Ghost, who spoke through David, has abundantly enlightened, taught and perfected his soul; nevertheless, trusting greatly in the goodness of God, I will attempt what altogether exceeds my own strength, namely to throw some light, as best I can, on the Psalter itself, in hope of the reward which Wisdom promises, saying: [[Ecclus 24:31|They that explain me shall have life everlasting|Qui elucidant me, vitam æternam habebunt]] [*elucidant*: “throw light on me”, the word Denis has just used of his own work]. And again: [[Dan 12:3|they that instruct many to justice|Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam]], [[Dan 12:3|shall shine|fulgebunt]] [[Dan 12:3|as stars for all eternity|quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]]. This is fittingly understood of those whose life or conduct agrees with their teaching. For [[Ps 49:16|to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices|Peccatori autem dixit Deus: Quare tu enarras justitias meas?]]? Indeed, as blessed Thomas shows on the fourth book of the Sentences [In IV Sent., dist. 19, q. 2, a. 3, as the margin notes], one who does not fulfil what he teaches others sins mortally by the very fact that he takes on himself the burden of teaching, since, as far as in him lies, he makes void the intention of sacred Scripture. But one whose life is fit for teaching surely merits the aureole [the special crown of glory given to doctors, as to virgins and martyrs], even if he never preaches to the people by word of mouth, but by expounding sacred Scripture, or by writing books of theology, speaks for the instruction of all who read them.

paras.t: Sed ne quis opus istud omnino superfluum putet, intendo speciali quodam modo librum Psalmorum exponere: sic tamen speciali, ut dictis Sanctorum concordet, nec proprio sensui credam. Intendo ergo Psalterium secundum multiplicem intellectum, prout Dominus dederit, explanare: videlicet litteraliter, allegorice, tropologice et anagogice, quantum textus ipse permittit, et mihi possibile fuerit, ejusdem litteræ nunc plures, nunc pauciores expositiones tangendo, prout materia exigit. Postremo, quemadmodum a Superioribus meis mihi injunctum est, propono stili colorem, loquendi difficultatem, et impertinentes subtilitates vitare, et plano ac simplici modo procedere.
paras.en: But lest anyone should think this work altogether superfluous, I intend to expound the book of Psalms in a certain special way: yet special in such a way that it agrees with the sayings of the Saints, and that I do not trust to my own sense. I intend, then, to explain the Psalter according to its manifold understanding, as the Lord shall grant: namely literally, allegorically, tropologically and anagogically, as far as the text itself allows and as shall be possible for me, touching now more, now fewer expositions of the same letter, as the matter requires. Lastly, as my Superiors have enjoined on me, I purpose to avoid ornament of style [*stili colorem*: the “colours” of rhetoric], difficulty of speech and subtleties beside the point, and to proceed in a plain and simple manner.

paras.t: Quod ut digne ac fructuose exsequi possim, ad superbenedictæ et supergloriosissimæ Trinitatis honorem, omniumque legentium ac audientium utilitatem, totis præcordiis oro et invoco benignitatem Spiritus Sancti copiosam et incessantem: quia sicut in libro Job habetur, Spiritus est in hominibus, et inspiratio Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam. Nam de Spiritu Sancto loquens Christus discipulis: Paracletus, ait, Spiritus Sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, et suggeret vobis omnia quæcumque dixero vobis.
paras.en: That I may carry this out worthily and fruitfully, to the honour of the superblessed and most superglorious Trinity, and for the profit of all who read and hear, I pray with my whole heart and call upon the abundant and unceasing kindness of the Holy Ghost: because, as we have it in the book of Job, [[Job 32:8|there is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth understanding|Spiritus est in hominibus, et inspiratio Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam]]. For Christ, speaking to his disciples of the Holy Ghost: [[John 14:26|the Paraclete|Paracletus]], he says, [[John 14:26|the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring all things to your mind, whatsoever I shall have said to you|Spiritus Sanctus, quem mittet Pater in nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, et suggeret vobis omnia quæcumque dixero vobis]].

1.title: De prima (videlicet litterali) expositione psalmi primi: Beatus vir qui non abiit
1.title_en: Of the first (that is, the literal) exposition of the first psalm: Blessed is the man who hath not walked

paras.t: Esdras, scriba velox, qui et prophetico spiritu fulsit, libros canonicos veteris Testamenti a Babyloniis combustos, Spiritu Sancto revelante, dicitur reparasse, præter Pentateuchum, id est quinque libros Moysis, quos apud Samaritanos invenit. Ipse ergo Psalterium reparavit, et hunc primum psalmum per modum præfationis seu prologi, libro Psalmorum præmisit, sicut vulgariter dicitur. Unde nec psalmo huic titulum præsignavit, quum psalmus iste sit quasi titulus libri sequentis: quoniam continet summam atque materiam totius libri, tractatque de his in generali, de quibus in toto hoc libro tractatur in speciali.
paras.en: Esdras, the ready scribe, who also shone with the prophetic spirit, is said to have restored, by the revelation of the Holy Ghost, the canonical books of the Old Testament burnt by the Babylonians, except the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses, which he found among the Samaritans. He therefore restored the Psalter, and set this first psalm before the book of Psalms by way of a preface or prologue, as is commonly said. Hence he did not set a title before this psalm either, since this psalm is as it were the title of the book that follows: for it contains the sum and matter of the whole book, and treats in general of the things that are treated in particular in the whole of this book.

paras.t: Denique psalmus iste ad litteram de quolibet homine virtuoso intelligi potest. Et quæ sequuntur de impiis et de vanitate atque tormentis ipsorum, de omnibus malis possunt exponi. Ait ergo auctor præsentis psalmi: Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum. Consilium est actus prudentiæ. Sed sicut prudentia duplex est, scilicet vera et falsa; ita consilium, aliud verum, aliud falsum. Verum consilium ad eos pertinet, qui diligenter inquirunt quibus viis ac mediis ad veram felicitatem pertingant. Falsum vero consilium horum est, qui vias excogitant quibus desideratam malitiam ad effectum perducant. Itaque ait: Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum. Dupliciter aliquis abit in consilio impiorum: primo, aliis malum consilium dando; secundo, perverso consilio consentiendo seu acquiescendo. Igitur, Beatus vir qui non abiit, id est, a Deo non recessit, in consilio impiorum, per hoc quod aliis male ac false consuluit, vel aliorum fallaci consilio acquievit. Qui enim aliis male consulit, causa et princeps est omnium malorum quæ ex suo perverso consilio fiunt. Abit autem homo seu recedit a Deo in consilio impiorum: non loco, quoniam Deus ubique est, et omnia penetrat, omnibusque æque immediatus est, secundum Dionysium; sed dissimilitudine, quoniam per consilium impiorum facit se homo dissimilem Deo, qui justus est, et iniqua consilia odit, gratiamque abeunti in consilio impiorum aufert, et pietatis suæ præsentiam nobis subtrahit. Per nihil enim abimus a Deo, nisi per id quo separamur et elongamur ab ipso. Nil vero separat nos a Domino Deo nostro, nisi vitia nostra, quemadmodum Isaias testatur: Peccata, inquiens, vestra diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos. Nihil quoque unit ac retinet nos in Deo, nisi virtutes, quarum est peccata auferre. Et ideo Isaias iterum ait: Hic est omnis fructus, ut deleatur iniquitas.
paras.en: Now this psalm can be understood literally of any virtuous man. And what follows about the wicked, and their vanity and torments, can be expounded of all the wicked. The author of this psalm therefore says: [[1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]] [*abiit*, literally "has gone away"]. Counsel is an act of prudence. But as prudence is twofold, namely true and false, so counsel is one true, another false. True counsel belongs to those who search carefully by what ways and means they may attain true happiness. False counsel is that of those who devise ways by which to bring their desired malice into effect. So he says: [[1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]]. One walks in the counsel of the ungodly in two ways: first, by giving bad counsel to others; second, by consenting or yielding to perverse counsel. Therefore, [[1:1|Blessed is the man|Beatus vir]] [[1:1|who hath not walked|qui non abiit]], that is, has not gone away from God, [[1:1|in the counsel of the ungodly|in consilio impiorum]], by counselling others badly and falsely, or by yielding to the deceitful counsel of others. For he who counsels others badly is the cause and author of all the evils that are done through his perverse counsel. Now a man goes away or withdraws from God in the counsel of the ungodly not in place, since God is everywhere, and pierces all things, and is equally immediate to all, according to Dionysius; but by unlikeness, since through the counsel of the ungodly a man makes himself unlike God, who is just and hates wicked counsels, and takes away his grace from one who walks in the counsel of the ungodly, and withdraws from us the presence of his loving-kindness. For we go away from God by nothing but that by which we are separated and removed from him. And nothing separates us from the Lord our God but our vices, as Isaias testifies: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Peccata, inquiens, vestra diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos]]. And nothing unites and keeps us in God but the virtues, whose work it is to take away sins. And so Isaias says again: [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Hic est omnis fructus, ut deleatur iniquitas]].

paras.t: Denique, quid est dicere, Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, nisi, Beatus vir qui permansit in consilio piorum, tam aliis recte consulendo, quam aliorum recto consilio consentiendo? Ideo enim in Proverbiis Salomon ait: Salus, ubi multa consilia. Et Tobias filium instruens: Consilium, inquit, semper a sapiente require. Præterea, quid aliud est, Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum, nisi, Infelix seu miser, qui abiit in consilio impiorum, vel male consulendo, vel male consulenti se conformando? Hinc namque sacratissimus Isaias ex Dei persona fatetur: Væ, filii desertores, ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me; et ordiremini telam, et non per Spiritum meum.
paras.en: Further, what is it to say, [[1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]], but: Blessed is the man who has remained in the counsel of the godly, both by counselling others rightly and by consenting to the right counsel of others? For that is why Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 11:14|there is safety where there is much counsel|Salus, ubi multa consilia]]. And Tobias, instructing his son: [[Tob 4:19|Seek counsel|Consilium]], he says, [[Tob 4:19|always of a wise man|semper a sapiente require]]. Again, what else is [[1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]], but: Unhappy or wretched is he who has walked in the counsel of the ungodly, either by counselling badly or by conforming himself to one who counsels badly? For hence the most holy Isaias declares in the person of God: [[Is 30:1|Woe to you, apostate children|Væ, filii desertores]], [[Is 30:1|that you would take counsel, and not of me: and would begin a web, and not by my spirit|ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me; et ordiremini telam, et non per Spiritum meum]].

paras.t: Est autem homo beatus dupliciter, scilicet in spe, et in re. In spe vero est aliquis beatus dupliciter: primo, secundum dispositionem remotam seu potentiam, quemadmodum pueros bonæ indolis appellamus beatos; secundo, quantum ad dispositionem propinquam ac habitualem, sicut ait Salvator: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Porro in re beatus est, qui Deo perfecte jam fruitur. Beatitudo ergo in spe, viatoribus competit, et de ea nunc loquimur.
paras.en: Now a man is blessed in two ways, namely in hope and in reality. And in hope one is blessed in two ways: first, by a remote disposition or capacity, as we call boys of good disposition blessed; secondly, as to a near and habitual disposition, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart|Beati mundo corde]], for [[Matt 5:8|they shall see God|ipsi Deum videbunt]]. But he is blessed in reality who already enjoys God perfectly. Blessedness in hope, then, belongs to wayfarers [*viatores*: those still on the way, in this life], and it is of this that we now speak.

paras.t: Per id quoque quod ait, Beatus vir, non existimemus mulierem exclusam. Vir namque hoc loco vocatur, non a proprietate sexus, sed ratione virtutis: qui nec prosperis elevatur, nec adversis deprimitur: qui non est sicut arundo vento agitata, sed fixus in Domino, regia via incedit: qualis exstitit nobilis ille Josue, qui non declinavit a dextris vel sinistris a lege Moysis. Sed hoc modo exsistere virum, feminis etiam competit, illis utique quæ tales sunt, qualis est illa de qua Salomon ait: Mulierem fortem quis inveniet? Et iterum: Accinxit fortitudine lumbos suos. Nonne hoc modo vir dici valet Virgo mater, de qua Dominus ad diabolum sub appellatione serpentis dixit, Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, ipsa conteret caput tuum? Et hanc utique virilem Mulierem quædam viriles feminæ præcesserunt figurative: sicut sanctissima illa Esther, quæ in omni regali suo decore atque incomparabili excellentia temporali, nunquam exaltata est; fortissima quoque illa Judith, quæ crudelissimum Holofernem tam viriliter interfecit.
paras.en: And by his saying [[1:1|Blessed is the man|Beatus vir]], let us not think woman excluded. For he is here called a man [*vir*: a man, as opposed to a woman; Denis plays on *vir* and *virtus*] not from the property of his sex but by reason of virtue: one who is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity: who is not as a reed shaken by the wind, but, fixed in the Lord, walks the king's highway: such as was that noble Josue, who did not turn aside to the right hand or the left from the law of Moses[[Jos 1:7||]]. But to be a man in this way belongs to women also, to those namely who are such as she of whom Solomon says: [[Prov 31:10|Who shall find a valiant woman?|Mulierem fortem quis inveniet]] And again: [[Prov 31:17|She hath girded her loins with strength|Accinxit fortitudine lumbos suos]]. Cannot the Virgin Mother be called a man in this way, of whom the Lord said to the devil under the name of the serpent: [[Gen 3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman|Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem]], [[Gen 3:15|she shall crush thy head|ipsa conteret caput tuum]]? And certain manly women went before this manly Woman as figures of her: such as that most holy Esther, who amid all her royal beauty and her incomparable worldly excellence was never lifted up; and that most valiant Judith too, who slew the most cruel Holofernes so manfully[[Jdt 13:10||]].

paras.t: Et in via peccatorum non stetit. Ex malo consilio oritur operatio prava. Operatio autem via vocatur, quia per eam ad terminum pervenitur. Nam operatio bona ducit ad jucunditatem æternam; operatio mala, ad sempiternam miseriam. Beatus ergo, qui in via peccatorum non stetit: qui in operatione iniqua non permansit, nec male agentibus acquievit, qui non gloriatur quum male fecerit, neque exsultat in rebus pessimis. De hac via ait Salomon: Est via quæ videtur homini bona: et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem. Et rursus: Via impiorum tenebrosa: nesciunt ubi corruant. Quocontra de viis Domini scriptum est: Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ: et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ.
paras.en: [[1:1|nor stood in the way of sinners|Et in via peccatorum non stetit]]. From bad counsel springs wicked working. And working is called a way, because by it one comes to an end. For good working leads to eternal joy; evil working to everlasting misery. Blessed, then, is he who has not [[1:1|stood in the way of sinners|in via peccatorum non stetit]]: who did not remain in wicked working, nor yield to evildoers, who does not glory when he has done evil, nor rejoice in the most wicked things[[Prov 2:14||]]. Of this way Solomon says: [[Prov 14:12|There is a way which seemeth just to a man|Est via quæ videtur homini bona]] [Denis reads *bona*, "good", where the Vulgate has *recta*]: [[Prov 14:12|but the ends thereof lead to death|et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem]]. And again: [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|Via impiorum tenebrosa: nesciunt ubi corruant]]. Whereas of the ways of the Lord it is written: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable|Viæ ejus, viæ pulchræ: et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ]].

paras.t: Et in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedit. Pestilentia est morbus infectivus. Cathedra vero est sedes doctoris vel judicis. Unde in cathedra pestilentiæ sedere, est alios falsa doctrina, aut malo exemplo corrumpere vel scandalizare, et fratribus offendiculum ponere. Quod quam damnabile sit, Salvator manifestat: Qui scandalizaverit, inquiens, unum ex his pusillis, expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, et demergatur in profundum maris. Et iterum: Væ homini per quem scandalum venit. Unde et Apostolus: Non ergo judicemus amplius; sed hoc judicate potius, ne ponatis offendiculum fratribus vel scandalum. Ille utique, qui nec dicto nec facto aliis occasionem peccandi præbet, in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedet, et tali merito vocatur beatus.
paras.en: [[1:1|nor sat in the chair of pestilence|Et in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedit]]. A pestilence is an infectious disease. And a chair is the seat of a teacher or a judge. Hence to sit in the chair of pestilence is to corrupt or scandalize others by false teaching or bad example, and to put a stumbling-block before the brethren. How damnable this is the Saviour shows: [[Matt 18:6|he that shall scandalize one of these little ones|Qui scandalizaverit, inquiens, unum ex his pusillis]], he says, [[Matt 18:6|it were better for him that a millstone should be hanged about his neck, and that he should be drowned in the depth of the sea|expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, et demergatur in profundum maris]]. And again: [[Matt 18:7|woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh|Væ homini per quem scandalum venit]]. Hence the Apostle too: [[Rom 14:13|Let us not therefore judge one another any more|Non ergo judicemus amplius]]. [[Rom 14:13|But judge this rather, that you put not a stumblingblock or a scandal|sed hoc judicate potius, ne ponatis offendiculum fratribus vel scandalum]]. Surely he who gives others no occasion of sin by word or deed does not sit in the chair of pestilence, and by such merit is called blessed.

paras.t: Triplex autem peccatum in hoc primo versu tangitur, et vitandum docetur, videlicet peccatum iniquæ cogitationis, peccatum injustæ actionis, et peccatum perversæ instructionis. Primo quoque peccato adjungitur hoc verbum, Abiit, quod motum designat. Secundo vero adjungitur, Stetit: et tertio, Sedit: quæ ambo quietem designant. Sed major est quies seu fixio in sedente, quam stante: quoniam qui sola cogitatione peccat, faciliter revocatur: qui vero ad opus procedit, difficilius redit: sed qui jam habituatur in malo, et alios inficit, difficillime emendatur.
paras.en: Now a threefold sin is touched on in this first verse and taught to be avoided: namely the sin of wicked thought, the sin of unjust action, and the sin of perverse teaching. And to the first sin is joined the word [[1:1|hath not walked|abiit]], which signifies motion. To the second is joined [[1:1|stood|stetit]]: and to the third [[1:1|sat|sedit]]: both of which signify rest. But the rest or fixedness is greater in one sitting than in one standing: since he who sins by thought alone is easily called back; he who goes on to the deed returns with more difficulty; but he who is already habituated to evil, and infects others, is amended with the greatest difficulty.

paras.t: Denique, quia non sufficit mala non facere, sed oportet etiam bona peragere, sicut Salvator testatur, dicens, Omnis arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur: propterea in versu sequenti ostendit, quid boni pertineat ad virum beatum, prædicta mala vitantem. Ait ergo: Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus, id est, desiderium cordis ejus et tota mentis suæ affectio tendit ad hoc, ut legem Dei adimpleat, et secundum altissimam Dei voluntatem, omnem suam conversationem gubernet. Debemus enim divinis mandatis sponte et prompte, non coacte aut pigre, obtemperare, et ex filiali amore potius quam ex servili timore, cuncta implere, ut dicere Deo possimus: Domine, ante te omne desiderium meum. Hoc namque hortatur Paulus, dicens: Probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, beneplacens, et perfecta. Et iterum: Non accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba (Pater). Hinc quoque David dixit: Tu autem, fili mi, scito Deum patris tui, et servi ei corde perfecto et animo voluntario. Sed quia voluntas de se cæca est, et amoris impetum, affectionisque impulsum sequi solet, idcirco rationis directione indiget, quatenus rationale obsequium Deo exhibeat.
paras.en: Further, since it is not enough not to do evil, but one must also do good, as the Saviour testifies, saying: [[Matt 7:19|Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire|Omnis arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur]][[Matt 3:10||]]: therefore in the next verse he shows what good belongs to the blessed man who avoids the evils just named. He says, then: [[1:2|But his will is in the law of the Lord|Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus]], that is, the desire of his heart and the whole affection of his mind tends to this, that he fulfil the law of God and govern all his conduct according to the most high will of God. For we ought to obey the divine commandments willingly and promptly, not by force or sluggishly, and to fulfil all things from filial love rather than servile fear, so that we may say to God: [[37:10|Lord, all my desire is before thee|Domine, ante te omne desiderium meum]]. For to this Paul exhorts us, saying: [[Rom 12:2|that you may prove what is the good and the acceptable and the perfect will of God|Probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei bona, beneplacens, et perfecta]]. And again: [[Rom 8:15|you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear: but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, whereby we cry: Abba (Father|Non accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba (Pater]]. Hence too David said: [[1 Par 28:9|thou my son Solomon, know the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart, and a willing mind|Tu autem, fili mi, scito Deum patris tui, et servi ei corde perfecto et animo voluntario]]. But since the will is blind of itself, and is wont to follow the rush of love and the drive of affection, it therefore needs the direction of reason, so that it may offer God a reasonable service[[Rom 12:1||]].

paras.t: Talem ergo rationis directionem ac discussionem ad virum beatum pertinere consequenter declaratur, dum subditur: Et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte, examinando quid Deo complaceat, quid ei displiceat, quid præcepit, quid prohibuit, qualiter homo compendiosius proficere possit, quanta beneficia Deus hominibus præstitit, quanta bona in futuro promisit, quanta est cæcitas ingratorum, quanta tormenta reproborum. Ista atque similia fideliter contemplari, est in lege Domini meditari.
paras.en: That such direction and weighing by reason belongs to the blessed man is next declared, when it is added: [[1:2|and on his law he shall meditate day and night|Et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte]], examining what pleases God, what displeases him, what he has commanded, what he has forbidden, how a man may make progress by the shortest way, how great are the benefits God has bestowed on men, how great the goods he has promised in the future, how great is the blindness of the ungrateful, how great the torments of the reprobate. To contemplate these and like things faithfully is to meditate on the law of the Lord.

paras.t: Sed quomodo hoc modo potest homo meditari in lege Domini die ac nocte? Nonne vicissim dormire, ac aliis necessitatibus hujus miserabilis vitæ vacare oportet? Et respondendum, quod homo justus in lege Domini meditari debet die ac nocte, non quod quolibet horæ spatio, singulisque momentis, possit actualem habere divinæ legis memoriam, vel incessabiliter speculari divina; sed quia quolibet tempore debito ac opportuno facit hoc. Sic quippe semper dicitur aliquis aliquid facere, quoniam nunquam negligit id facere quando debet: quemadmodum dicimus, Iste semper scribit, Iste semper frequentat ecclesiam. Secundum hunc sensum dicit Apostolus: Sine intermissione orate. Et Moyses: Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo, et narrabis ea filiis tuis; meditaberis in eis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens. Aliter etiam dici potest, quod aliquis dicitur orare et meditari dupliciter: primo, quoniam actus tales exercet; secundo, quia secundum actus tales operatur et vivit: sicque incessanter die ac nocte in lege Domini meditatur et orat, qui totam vitam suam secundum tenorem præceptorum divinæ legis gubernat, quemadmodum docet Apostolus: Omne, inquiens, quodcumque facitis in verbo aut opere, omnia in nomine Domini Jesu Christi facite.
paras.en: But how can a man in this way meditate on the law of the Lord day and night? Must he not sleep in turn, and give time to the other needs of this wretched life? And the answer is that the just man ought to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, not in the sense that at every space of an hour and every moment he can have actual remembrance of the divine law or contemplate divine things without ceasing; but because he does this at every due and fitting time. For thus someone is said always to do something because he never neglects to do it when he ought: as we say, This man is always writing, That man always goes to church. In this sense the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:17|Pray without ceasing|Sine intermissione orate]]. And Moses: [[Deut 6:6|these words which I command thee this day, shall be in thy heart|Erunt verba Domini in corde tuo]], [[Deut 6:7|And thou shalt tell them to thy children|et narrabis ea filiis tuis]]; [[Deut 6:7|thou shalt meditate upon them sitting in thy house, and walking on thy journey, sleeping and rising|meditaberis in eis sedens in domo tua, et ambulans in itinere, et dormiens atque consurgens]]. It can also be said otherwise, that someone is said to pray and meditate in two ways: first, because he performs such acts; secondly, because he works and lives according to such acts: and so he meditates and prays unceasingly, day and night, in the law of the Lord, who governs his whole life according to the tenor of the precepts of the divine law, as the Apostle teaches, saying: [[Col 3:17|All whatsoever you do in word or in work, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ|Omne, inquiens, quodcumque facitis in verbo aut opere, omnia in nomine Domini Jesu Christi facite]].

paras.t: Porro, quia connaturale est nobis, ut ex similitudine sensibilium rerum ad spiritualium rerum notitiam perducamur, idcirco in versu sequenti comparat Scriptura sacra justitiam viri beati ligno juxta aquas plantato. Vel comparat virum beatum ac justum ligno hujusmodi, ratione justitiæ, ita quod virtus justitiæ quæ est spirituale bonum, est causa formalis comparationis istius. Ideo subditur: Et erit tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suum dabit in tempore suo. Lignum juxta decursus aquarum seu aquas fluentes plantatum, convenienti tempore floret, et fructum producit, quoniam radix ejus ex fluentibus aquis attrahit alimentum, videlicet humorem. Unde in Evangelio Christus dicit, quod semen natum aruit, quia non habebat humorem. Sic est homo virtuosus. Quia enim in Deo confidit, et ei adhæret, manens in Christo, sicut palmes in vite, ideo rorem gratiæ Dei et humorem conservationis a Spiritu Sancto sortitur, proficiens de virtute in virtutem, et crescens in caritate de die in diem.
paras.en: Further, since it is natural to us to be led from the likeness of sensible things to the knowledge of spiritual things[[Rom 1:20||]], in the next verse holy Scripture compares the justice of the blessed man to a tree planted by the waters. Or it compares the blessed and just man to such a tree by reason of his justice, so that the virtue of justice, which is a spiritual good, is the formal cause of this comparison. So it is added: [[1:3|And he shall be like a tree which is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit, in due season|Et erit tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suum dabit in tempore suo]]. A tree planted by the running of waters, that is, by flowing waters, flowers and bears fruit at the fitting time, since its root draws its nourishment, namely moisture, from the flowing waters. Hence Christ says in the Gospel that the seed [[Luke 8:6|as soon as it was sprung up, it withered away, because it had no moisture|natum aruit, quia non habebat humorem]]. So it is with the virtuous man. For since he trusts in God and cleaves to him, abiding in Christ as the branch in the vine, he receives from the Holy Ghost the dew of God's grace and the moisture of preservation, going on [[83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]], and growing in charity from day to day.

paras.t: Et propterea folium ejus non defluet: id est, sermo ejus a rectitudine legis divinæ non cadit, quoniam implet illud Apostoli: Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus, id est discretione ornatus. Non enim est procax ad loquendum, sed moderatur labia sua. Et omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur. Scimus enim (teste Apostolo) quoniam diligentibus Deum, omnia cooperantur in bonum. Omnia itaque quæ faciet homo, prædicto modo beatus ac justus, prosperabuntur, id est, omnes operationes suæ proficient sibi ad veram beatitudinem, seu vitam æternam. Nam et mala quæ fortasse committit, occasionaliter cooperantur sibi in bonum, eo quod cautior surgat, custoditior fiat, humilius pœniteat, imo et ardentius diligat: quoniam teste Salvatore, Cui plus dimittitur, plus diligit. Propter quod et Apostolus ait: Ubi abundavit delictum, superabundavit et gratia. Ideo etiam de viro electo inferius dicitur: Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam.
paras.en: And therefore [[1:3|his leaf shall not fall off|folium ejus non defluet]]: that is, his speech does not fall away from the uprightness of the divine law, since he fulfils that saying of the Apostle: [[Col 4:6|Let your speech be always in grace seasoned with salt|Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus]], that is, adorned with discretion. For he is not forward in speaking, but [[Prov 10:19|refraineth his lips|moderatur labia sua]]. [[1:3|and all whatsoever he shall do shall prosper|Et omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur]]. For we know (as the Apostle testifies) [[Rom 8:28|that to them that love God all things work together unto good|quoniam diligentibus Deum, omnia cooperantur in bonum]]. So all things that the man who is blessed and just in the way described shall do shall prosper: that is, all his works will profit him for true blessedness, or eternal life. For even the evils he may perhaps commit work together for his good by occasion, in that he rises more careful, becomes more watchful, repents more humbly, and indeed loves more ardently: since, as the Saviour testifies, he to whom more is forgiven loves more[[Luke 7:47||]]. That is why the Apostle too says: [[Rom 5:20|where sin abounded, grace did more abound|Ubi abundavit delictum, superabundavit et gratia]]. And so it is said below of the chosen man: [[36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him|Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]].

paras.t: Considerandum vero, quod sermo comparatus est folio, et operatio fructui. Sicut enim floritio arboris inutilis est et inanis, quando fructus nullus subsequitur; sic pulcher sermo atque magna seu decora verborum prolatio vana est, dum vita verbis non consonat. Ideo enim Dominus maledixit ficulneæ folia habenti, non fructus.
paras.en: But it should be considered that speech is compared to the leaf, and working to the fruit. For as the flowering of a tree is useless and empty when no fruit follows; so fair speech and a great or elegant flow of words is vain when the life does not agree with the words. That is why the Lord cursed the fig tree that had leaves and not fruit[[Mark 11:13||]][[Mark 11:14||]].

paras.t: Consequenter in isto psalmo agitur de vanitate impiorum, et differentia eorum a justis, dum subditur: Non sic impii, non sic; id est, ita non erit de impiis sicut de justis prædictum est. Nam non possunt comparari ligno juxta decursus aquarum plantato, sed arido ligno et sterili palmiti, membroque a capite separato. Non enim habent radicem cordis fixam in Deo, nec Christo per gratiam uniuntur, nec stabili fundamento innituntur: propterea pulveri comparantur, sicut subjungitur: Sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ: id est, tales sunt impii sicut pulvis a vento jactatus. Sicut enim pulvis omni vento circumfertur, sic impii variis passionibus commoventur, et a recta ratione discedunt; nec Deo stabili mente adhærent, sed propter amorem rerum temporalium a divina dilectione recedunt, creaturas Creatori præponentes.
paras.en: Next this psalm treats of the vanity of the wicked and of their difference from the just, when it is added: [[1:4|Not so the wicked, not so|Non sic impii, non sic]]; that is, it will not be with the wicked as was said of the just. For they cannot be compared to a tree planted by the running waters, but to a dry tree and a barren branch, and a member cut off from the head. For they have not the root of the heart fixed in God, nor are they united to Christ by grace, nor do they rest on a firm foundation: therefore they are compared to dust, as is added: [[1:4|but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth|Sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]]: that is, the wicked are like dust tossed by the wind. For as dust is carried about by every wind, so the wicked are stirred by various passions and depart from right reason; nor do they cleave to God with a steady mind, but for love of temporal things withdraw from the love of God, setting creatures before the Creator.

paras.t: Quid vero ex hoc consequatur, sequens versus explanat. Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio. Hoc dupliciter intelligi potest: Primo, de judicio discretionis, quo quotidie homines justi et vere pœnitentes se ipsos examinant, et conscientias suas discernunt, atque omne vitiosum quod in se inveniunt, dijudicant, reprobant, damnant, deflent, et vindicant, sicut scriptum est: Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum; levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlos. De hoc salubri judicio ait Apostolus: Quod si nosmetipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Hoc modo judicantes se ipsos, adversa æquanimiter ferunt, illud dicentes: Et nos ergo non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur; sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem nostram evenisse credamus. Secundo, intelligitur de futuro extremo judicio, in quo impii non resurgent, quantum ad beatam immortalitatem atque felicem immutationem, sed quantum ad damnationem majorem. Omnes enim (ut ait Apostolus) resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur. Sed prima expositio magis concordat verbis sequentibus. Additur enim: Neque peccatores in consilio justorum. Consilium justorum est, ut præterita mala corrigant et deplangant, atque de cetero ad cavendum futura solliciti ac timorati exsistant. Huic consilio non se conformant peccatores, et ideo a vitiis suis non resurgunt in consilio justorum, consilio justorum acquiescendo, et dignos pœnitentiæ fructus agendo.
paras.en: What follows from this the next verse explains: [[1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio]]. This can be understood in two ways. First, of the judgment of discernment, by which just and truly penitent men examine themselves daily and sift their consciences, and judge, reprove, condemn, bewail and punish whatever sinful thing they find in themselves, as it is written: [[Lam 3:40|Let us search our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord|Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum]]: [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlos]]. Of this wholesome judgment the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:31|But if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Quod si nosmetipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. Judging themselves in this way, they bear adversity with an even mind, saying that word: [[Jdt 8:26|As for us therefore let us not revenge ourselves for these things which we suffer|Et nos ergo non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur]]: [[Jdt 8:27|But esteeming these very punishments to be less than our sins deserve, let us believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment|sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem nostram]]. Secondly, it is understood of the future last judgment, in which the wicked will not rise again as to blessed immortality and a happy change, but as to greater damnation. For (as the Apostle says) [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed|resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur]]. But the first exposition agrees better with the words that follow. For it adds: [[1:5|nor sinners in the council of the just|Neque peccatores in consilio justorum]] [Denis reads *consilio*, "counsel", for the Vulgate's *concilio*, "council"]. The counsel of the just is that they correct and bewail past evils, and for the rest be careful and fearful in avoiding those to come. To this counsel sinners do not conform themselves, and therefore they do not rise from their vices in the counsel of the just, by yielding to the counsel of the just and bringing forth fruits worthy of penance[[Matt 3:8||]].

paras.t: Postremo ostenditur causa prædictæ distinctionis inter justos et impios. Quoniam novit Dominus viam justorum, id est, quoniam Deus notitia approbationis novit atque acceptat viam, id est operationem seu vitam justorum. Idcirco impii separabuntur a bonis secundum modum prædictum, et opera impiorum non prosperabuntur, id est, ad veram beatitudinem non perducentur, nec felicem exitum sortientur. Et ideo subditur: Et iter impiorum peribit, id est, vita, actio et delectatio eorum destruentur, quia post temporales delicias habebunt æternam tristitiam. Unde in die novissimo, dum videbunt se errasse, sero pœnitebunt, et dicent: Erravimus a via veritatis, et lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis.
paras.en: Lastly the cause of the distinction just described between the just and the wicked is shown: [[1:6|For the Lord knoweth the way of the just|Quoniam novit Dominus viam justorum]], that is, because God knows with the knowledge of approval [*notitia approbationis*: knowing as approving, not mere knowledge] and accepts the way, that is, the working or the life, of the just. Therefore the wicked will be separated from the good in the way described, and the works of the wicked will not prosper, that is, they will not be brought to true blessedness, nor have a happy end. And so it is added: [[1:6|and the way of the wicked shall perish|Et iter impiorum peribit]], that is, their life, action and delight will be destroyed, since after temporal delights they will have eternal sadness. Hence on the last day, when they see that they have erred, they will repent too late, and will say: [[Wis 5:6|we have erred from the way of truth|Erravimus a via veritatis]], [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction|et lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis]].

1.title: EXPOSITIO EJUSDEM PRIMI PSALMI SECUNDUM ALLEGORICUM INTELLECTUM, VIDELICET DE CHRISTO.
1.title_en: Exposition of the same first Psalm according to the allegorical understanding, that is, of Christ

paras.t: Sicut ostensum est, allegorice sacra Scriptura exponitur, dum ea quæ in lege et Prophetis et Psalmis scripta sunt, de Christo exponuntur: quod intelligendum est de illis Scripturis, quæ de Christo ad litteram non exponuntur. Hic ergo psalmus, qui litteraliter de quolibet viro justo et impiis in communi intelligi potest, de Christo allegorice multum convenienter exponitur.
paras.en: As has been shown, sacred Scripture is expounded allegorically when what is written in the law and the Prophets and the Psalms is expounded of Christ: which is to be understood of those Scriptures that are not expounded of Christ according to the letter. This psalm, then, which can be understood literally of any just man, and of the wicked in general, is very fittingly expounded allegorically of Christ.

paras.t: Ait enim: Beatus vir, videlicet Christus, qui a primo instanti suæ conceptionis in Virgine matre, fuit vir perfectus atque beatus: perfectus quidem non ratione ætatis, sed propter plenitudinem gratiæ, eminentiamque virtutum, ac sapientiæ perfectionem: in quibus omnibus perfecta creata est anima Christi; nec profecit in istis quantum ad habitum, sed quantum ad exercitium. Unde scriptum est: Novum creabit Dominus super terram: Mulier circumdabit virum, id est, Virgo præelecta in utero habebit puerum ætate, sed virum perfectione. Fuit etiam Christus ab exordio maternæ conceptionis beatus, propter perfectissimam Divinitatis fruitionem, et clarissimam ejus beatificamque visionem: quia tam clare, tamque beate vidit anima Christi Deum a primo creationis suæ momento, sicut et modo; nec unquam profecit in essentiali præmio Beatorum. Quoniam enim humanæ naturæ Christi, a primo suæ creationis exordio, datum est esse unitum Verbo personali seu hypostatica unione, hoc est subsistere in eodem esse personali, in quo Unigenitus Dei æternaliter subsistit, quum sit assumpta ad esse increatum Filii Dei; multo clarius patet, quod animæ Christi a sui principio concessa est beatifica Dei visio, prout Damascenus testatur et Thomas. Minus est enim Deum beatifice contemplari, quam ei personaliter uniri. Sic ergo est Christus beatus vir. Dicitur quoque vir, quoniam a vera fortitudine nunquam defecit, sed in omnibus virtuosissime egit.
paras.en: For it says: [[1:1|Blessed is the man|Beatus vir]], namely Christ, who from the first instant of his conception in his Virgin mother was a man perfect and blessed: perfect, not by reason of age, but because of the fullness of grace, the eminence of the virtues and the perfection of wisdom, in all of which the soul of Christ was created perfect; nor did he advance in these as to the habit, but only as to their exercise [that is, he did not grow in the virtues themselves, but showed them more and more in act]. Hence it is written: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN|Novum creabit Dominus super terram: Mulier circumdabit virum]]: that is, the chosen Virgin shall have in her womb one who is a child in age but a man in perfection. Christ was also blessed from the beginning of his conception in his mother, because of his most perfect fruition of the Godhead and his most clear and beatific vision of it: for the soul of Christ saw God as clearly and as blessedly from the first moment of its creation as it does now, nor did it ever advance in the essential reward of the Blessed. For since it was given to the human nature of Christ, from the first beginning of its creation, to be united to the Word by a personal or hypostatic union, that is, to subsist in the same personal being in which the Only-begotten of God subsists eternally, since it was taken up into the uncreated being of the Son of God; much more plainly is it clear that the beatific vision of God was granted to the soul of Christ from its beginning, as Damascene and Thomas testify [the margin cites Damascene, De fide orthodoxa, book III, and Thomas, Summa III, q. 10]. For it is less to contemplate God beatifically than to be united to him in person. In this way, then, Christ is the blessed man. And he is called a man [*vir*, which Denis connects with *virtus*, strength and virtue] because he never fell short of true fortitude, but acted most virtuously in all things.

paras.t: Beatus itaque vir, scilicet Christus, qui non abiit in consilio impiorum: quia tentatori præcipitium et sui adorationem consulenti non acquievit, neque Scribarum ac Pharisæorum malignis consiliis favit; sed consilio, quod est unum septem donorum Spiritus Sancti, plenissimus fuit. Et in via peccatorum non stetit: quia ab omni peccato immunissimus fuit. Detrahibiles enim defectus non assumpsit, sed naturales atque pœnales, ut sunt fames, sitis, timor, dolor et mors. Et in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedit. Nulli enim malum exemplum præbuit, neque perversa dogmata protulit, quamvis Judæi frequenter scandalizabantur ex verbis et actibus ejus: tale enim scandalum non erat nisi ex malignitate vel infirmitate ipsorum. Porro vita Christi, totius sanctitatis ac perfectionis exemplar fuit: et omnis ejus actio, nostra instructio est, sicut et ipsemet ait: Ego sum lux mundi; qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris. Christus quoque saluberrimam mundo doctrinam advexit, legalibusque præceptis evangelica consilia, universæ perfectionis plenitudinem continentia, addidit. Non enim venit solvere legem, sed adimplere.
paras.en: [[1:1|Blessed is the man|Beatus itaque vir]], then, namely Christ, [[1:1|who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]]: because he did not give way to the tempter when he counselled him to cast himself down[[Matt 4:6||]] and to adore him[[Matt 4:9||]], nor did he favour the malicious counsels of the Scribes and Pharisees; but he was most full of counsel, which is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]. [[1:1|nor stood in the way of sinners|Et in via peccatorum non stetit]]: because he was wholly free of all sin. For he did not take on the defects that bring reproach [*detrahibiles defectus*: defects such as ignorance or an inclination to sin, which would detract from his perfection], but the natural and penal ones, such as hunger, thirst, fear, pain and death. [[1:1|nor sat in the chair of pestilence|Et in cathedra pestilentiæ non sedit]]. For he gave no one a bad example, nor did he put forward perverse teachings, although the Jews were often scandalized at his words and deeds[[Matt 15:12||]] [the margin is half unreadable ('… th, 12'); Matt 15:12, the Pharisees scandalized at his word, is the likeliest reading]: for such scandal came only from their own malice or weakness. Further, the life of Christ was the pattern of all holiness and perfection, and his every action is our instruction, as he himself says: [[John 8:12|I am the light of the world. He that followeth me walketh not in darkness|Ego sum lux mundi; qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris]]. Christ also brought the world a most wholesome doctrine, and added to the precepts of the law the counsels of the Gospel, which contain the fullness of all perfection. For he came not [[Matt 5:17|to destroy the law|solvere legem]], but [[Matt 5:17|to fulfil|adimplere]].

paras.t: Tanguntur hic tria, per quæ Christus a protoplasto parente distinguitur. Adam namque in consilium impiorum abiit, quando serpentis et Evæ instigationi consensit. Et in via peccatorum stetit, dum de prohibiti ligni fructu comedit. Et in cathedra pestilentiæ sedit, quum proprium crimen excusavit, illudque in mulierem, imo Creatorem quodammodo retorquere sategit: Mulier, inquiens, quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi. Horum autem nullum in Christo fuisse jam patuit.
paras.en: Three things are touched on here by which Christ is set apart from our first-formed parent. For Adam [[1:1|walked in the counsel of the ungodly|in consilium impiorum abiit]] when he consented to the urging of the serpent and of Eve. And he [[1:1|stood in the way of sinners|in via peccatorum stetit]] when he ate of the fruit of the forbidden tree. And he [[1:1|sat in the chair of pestilence|in cathedra pestilentiæ sedit]] when he excused his own crime and took pains to turn it back upon the woman, nay, in a manner upon the Creator, saying: [[Gen 3:12|The woman|Mulier]], he says, [[Gen 3:12|whom thou gavest me to be my companion, gave me of the tree, and I did eat|quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi]]. And it has already been made clear that none of these was in Christ.

paras.t: Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus. Hoc Christo singulariter et perfectissime convenit. Nam ipse solus præceptum caritatis divinæ perfecte implevit in hac vita, et multo perfectius quam aliquis Beatorum in patria ipsum potuerit adimplere. Nam toto corde, tota mente, ex omni fortitudine, et tota anima semper actualiter ferebatur in Deum, ipsum contemplando, diligendo, honorando, atque in omnibus sibi obediendo, quemadmodum in Evangelio ipsemet de Patre loquens, testatur: Quia quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper. Et denuo: Ego, ait, non quæro gloriam meam, sed honorifico Patrem meum. Et ergo passioni jam proximus, dixit ad Patrem: Non quod ego volo, sed quod tu. Id quoque quod sequitur, solus Christus ut homo in hac vita perfecte actualiterque implevit: Et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte, id est omni tempore et omni momento. Intellectualis enim operatio Christi, impediri non potuit nec interrumpi per somnum vel actum exteriorem, aut per sensitivum appetitum, neque per aliquid aliud. Sed omnia quæ in ipso fuerunt, ordinatissima erant, semperque inferius deservivit superiori, et secundum illius movebatur imperium. Sic itaque anima Christi meditabatur divina sine interruptione. Nam et omnia quæ sunt, fuerunt, et erunt, et præsertim ea quæ ad mysterium humanæ redemptionis pertinent, cognovit et semper actualiter vidit in Verbo, sicut et modo.
paras.en: [[1:2|But his will is in the law of the Lord|Sed in lege Domini voluntas ejus]]. This befits Christ singularly and most perfectly. For he alone perfectly fulfilled the precept of divine charity in this life, and much more perfectly than any of the Blessed in the fatherland could fulfil it. For with his whole heart, his whole mind, with all his strength and his whole soul, he was always actually borne towards God, contemplating him, loving him, honouring him and obeying him in all things: as he himself testifies in the Gospel, speaking of the Father: [[John 8:29|For I do always the things that please him|Quia quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]]. And again: [[John 8:50|I seek not my own glory|non quæro gloriam meam]], he says, [[John 8:49|but I honour my Father|sed honorifico Patrem meum]]. And so, when his passion was already near, he said to the Father: [[Mark 14:36|not what I will, but what thou wilt|Non quod ego volo, sed quod tu]] [the margin gives Matt. xxvi, 39; Denis's words are those of Mark 14:36]. What follows, too, Christ alone as man fulfilled perfectly and actually in this life: [[1:2|and on his law he shall meditate day and night|Et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte]], that is, at every time and every moment. For the intellectual working of Christ could not be hindered or interrupted by sleep or by outward action, or by the sensitive appetite, or by anything else. But all that was in him was most perfectly ordered, and the lower always served the higher and was moved at its command. So the soul of Christ meditated on divine things without interruption. For all things that are, have been and will be, and above all those which belong to the mystery of man's redemption, he knew and always actually saw in the Word, as he does now.

paras.t: Et erit tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suum dabit in tempore suo. Hic designatur Christi fecunditas atque utilitas per comparationem ad lignum, juxta aquarum fluenta plantatum. Tale enim lignum tempore suo floret, et fructus producit, sicque delectabile est intuenti, utile manducanti, honestum possidenti. Ita Christus, qui est speciosus forma præ filiis hominum, in quem desiderant angeli prospicere, delectabilis est ipsum sinceriter contemplanti, utilis spiritualiter manducanti, honestissimum quoque bonum, ipsum per caritatem et gratiam possidenti. Quemadmodum etiam arbor fertilis copiosum fructum producit, et plurimos reficit, sic Christus multum fructum attulit, dum pretiosissimo suo sanguine genus humanum redemit, totque poma produxit, quot animas electorum sua morte salvavit. Unde ad passionem jam transiens, et crucem sibi bajulans, semetipsum viridi ligno comparavit, dum mulieribus ipsum plangentibus dixit: Nolite flere super me; sed super vos ipsas flete et super filios vestros: quia si in viridi ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet?
paras.en: [[1:3|And he shall be like a tree which is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit, in due season|Et erit tanquam lignum quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suum dabit in tempore suo]]. Here the fruitfulness and usefulness of Christ is signified by comparison with a tree planted beside flowing waters. For such a tree flowers in its season and brings forth fruit, and so it is delightful to the one who looks at it, useful to the one who eats of it, and a worthy possession to the one who owns it. So Christ, who is [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]], [[1 Pet 1:12|on whom the angels desire to look|in quem desiderant angeli prospicere]], is delightful to one who contemplates him sincerely, useful to one who eats him spiritually, and a most worthy good to one who possesses him through charity and grace. And as a fertile tree brings forth abundant fruit and refreshes very many, so Christ bore much fruit when he redeemed the human race with his most precious blood, and brought forth as many apples as the souls of the elect he saved by his death. Hence, as he was going to his passion and carrying his cross, he compared himself to a green tree, when he said to the women who were lamenting him: [[Luke 23:28|weep not over me; but weep for yourselves and for your children|Nolite flere super me; sed super vos ipsas flete et super filios vestros]]: [[Luke 23:31|For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?|quia si in viridi ligno hæc faciunt, in arido quid fiet?]]

paras.t: Potest quoque istud exponi de ligno vitæ in paradiso plantato, cui idcirco Christus comparatur, quoniam sicut homo semper vixisset, si de ligno illo edere potuisset, ita qui Christum digne manducat, non morietur in æternum. Potest etiam per lignum intelligi ipsa sapientia, de qua Salomon ait, quod sit lignum vitæ omnibus apprehendentibus eam. Christus vero est sapientia Dei Patris. Sapientia autem juxta decursus aquarum plantata, est unigenitus Dei Filius, veraciter incarnatus, et inter homines peccatores, qui comparantur fluentibus aquis, sine macula conversatus. Secundum hunc igitur sensum innuitur incarnatio Verbi Dei; et hæc vox, Tanquam, non solum dicit similitudinem, sed etiam exprimit veritatem, quoniam hoc modo ipsemet Christus est ipsum lignum juxta aquarum decursus plantatum.
paras.en: This can also be expounded of the tree of life planted in paradise[[Gen 2:9||]], to which Christ is compared for this reason: that as man would always have lived if he could have eaten of that tree, so he who eats Christ worthily shall not die for ever[[John 6:52||]] [the margin gives Joann. vi, 53; the verse meant seems to be 6:52, “he shall live for ever”]. By the tree may also be understood wisdom itself, of which Solomon says that it is [[Prov 3:18|a tree of life to them that lay hold on her|lignum vitæ omnibus apprehendentibus eam]]. And Christ is [[1 Cor 1:24|the wisdom of God|sapientia Dei]] the Father. Now the wisdom planted [[1:3|near the running waters|juxta decursus aquarum]] is the only-begotten Son of God, truly incarnate, who lived without stain among sinful men, who are compared to flowing waters[[Bar 3:38||]]. According to this sense, then, the incarnation of the Word of God is hinted at; and this word *like* not only expresses a likeness but also states a truth, since in this way Christ himself is the very tree planted near the running waters.

paras.t: Et folium ejus non defluet, quia Christi sermo, prædicatio atque oratio non erunt inanes, neque peribunt, nec cassabuntur, sed fructificabunt in cordibus electorum, et verificabuntur in finem, quemadmodum ipsemet ait: Cœlum et terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt. Et omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur. Omnis operatio Christi meritoria fuit: imo quidquid cogitavit, dixit et fecit, in quantum viator, meritorium exstitit. Unde semper actualiter meruit. Sed quia ipse etiam ut homo, habens humanitatem Verbo unitam, perfectissimus comprehensor fuit, quantum ad superiorem animæ partem, idcirco sibi ipsi de præmio essentiali nil meruit, nec in illo unquam profecit. Nihilo minus tota vita ejus essentialis præmii meritoria fuit: quoniam quidquid cogitavit, dixit et fecit, ex excellentissimo divinæ caritatis fervore processit. Cui ergo essentiale præmium meruit, nisi membris suis seu corpori mystico, quod est Ecclesia? Nobis igitur tota vita Christi meritoria fuit. Sicque omnia quæcumque Christus fecit, prosperabuntur, id est, ad æternam vitam proficient prædestinatis, quibus per sacramenta Ecclesiæ, et fidem ac caritatem meritum Christi applicatur, et cooperatur ad felicitatem æternam. Hoc est quod per Isaiam Dominus ait: Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum; et non revertetur ad me vacuum, sed faciet quæcumque volui, et prosperabitur in his ad quæ misi illud.
paras.en: [[1:3|And his leaf shall not fall off|Et folium ejus non defluet]]: because the word, preaching and prayer of Christ will not be empty, nor will they perish or come to nothing, but they will bear fruit in the hearts of the elect and be proved true to the end, as he himself says: [[Matt 24:35|Heaven and earth shall pass: but my words shall not pass|Cœlum et terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt]]. [[1:3|and all whatsoever he shall do shall prosper|Et omnia quæcumque faciet, prosperabuntur]]. Every working of Christ was meritorious: indeed, whatever he thought, said and did, in so far as he was a wayfarer [*viator*: one still on the way to the fatherland, as opposed to a *comprehensor*, one who already possesses God], was meritorious. Hence he was always actually meriting. But because, even as man, having his humanity united to the Word, he was a most perfect comprehensor as to the higher part of his soul, he merited nothing of the essential reward for himself, nor did he ever advance in it. Nevertheless his whole life was meritorious of the essential reward, since whatever he thought, said and did proceeded from the most excellent fervour of divine charity. For whom, then, did he merit the essential reward, if not for his members, or mystical body, which is the Church? For us, therefore, the whole life of Christ was meritorious. And so all whatsoever Christ did shall prosper: that is, it will profit unto eternal life the predestined, to whom the merit of Christ is applied through the sacraments of the Church and through faith and charity, and it works with them towards eternal happiness. This is what the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 45:23|the word of justice shall go out of my mouth|Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum]]; [[Is 55:11|it shall not return to me void, but it shall do whatsoever I please, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it|et non revertetur ad me vacuum, sed faciet quæcumque volui, et prosperabitur in his ad quæ misi illud]] [the margin gives Is. lv, 11; the first words, “the word of justice shall go out of my mouth”, are from Is 45:23].

paras.t: Consequenter agit Scriptura de his qui Christo non uniuntur, nec ejus vestigia imitantur. Ait namque: Non sic impii, non sic. Nullus Sanctorum potest Christo esse æqualis, sed similis. Nam Christus, in quantum Deus, omnes in infinitum excedit in omni perfectione; sed ut homo, etiam major ac dignior, Deoque carior est, quam tota universitas electorum, angelorum simul ac hominum. Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum homini Christo. Boni ergo fideles, qui Christum regem fideliter assequuntur, quemadmodum scriptum est, Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare: hi tales Christo in prædictis bonis aliquo modo assimilantur, non abeundo in consilio impiorum, nec stando in via peccatorum, nec sedendo in cathedra pestiferorum, sed in lege Domini voluntas eorum. Sed impii non sic. Ipsi enim nullo modo sunt similes Christo, similitudine virtutis et gratiæ, nec amantur ab ipso secundum præsentem justitiam amore caritatis gratifico, quum similitudo sit causa amoris; imo perfecto odio odit eos. Propterea quales sint, statim ostenditur.
paras.en: Next, Scripture treats of those who are not united to Christ and do not follow in his footsteps. For it says: [[1:4|Not so the wicked, not so|Non sic impii, non sic]]. None of the Saints can be equal to Christ, but only like him. For Christ, as God, exceeds all infinitely in every perfection; but even as man he is greater and worthier, and dearer to God, than the whole company of the elect, angels and men together. For [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|Non enim ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum]] to the man Christ. The good faithful, then, who faithfully follow Christ their king, as it is written, [[1 John 2:6|He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also to walk even as he walked|Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare]] [Denis reads “abideth in Christ” for “abideth in him”]: such as these are in some way made like Christ in the good things spoken of, not walking in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standing in the way of sinners, nor sitting in the chair of the pestilent, but their will is in the law of the Lord. [[1:4|but like the dust|Sed impii non sic]]. For they are in no way like Christ by likeness of virtue and grace, nor are they loved by him, according to their present justice, with the gracious love of charity, since likeness is the cause of love; rather, he hates them with a perfect hatred[[Ps 138:22||]]. Therefore what they are like is shown at once.

paras.t: Sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ. Quemadmodum enim ventus projicit pulverem de loco suo: sic sermo Christi projiciet impios de superficie terræ, de congregatione justorum, de societate Sanctorum, quando separabit agnos ab hædis; quando purgabit aream suam, mittens triticum in horreum suum, et paleas inexstinguibili igne comburens; quando dicturus est his qui a sinistris erunt, verbum illud asperrimum, Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum.
paras.en: [[1:4|but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth|Sed tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]]. For as the wind drives the dust from its place, so the word of Christ will drive the wicked from the face of the earth, from the congregation of the just, from the fellowship of the Saints: when he shall separate the lambs from the goats[[Matt 25:32||]]; when he shall purge his floor, putting the wheat into his barn and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire[[Luke 3:17||]]; when he shall speak to those on his left hand that harshest word: Go, [[Matt 25:41|you cursed, into everlasting fire|maledicti, in ignem æternum]] [Denis reads *Ite*, “Go”, for *Discedite a me*, “Depart from me”].

paras.t: Ideo non resurgent impii in judicio: quia a Christo divisi sunt, et omni gratia destituti, idcirco non resurgunt in judicio. Quod intelligi potest tam de judicio discretionis, quo boni se ipsos dijudicant, (de quo Propheta, Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, utique facere judicium; et Job, Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius; et, Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest?) quam de judicio beatæ remunerationis, ut supra proximo articulo explanatum est. Neque peccatores in consilio justorum resurgent. Consilium proprie appellatur inquisitio rationis de agendis vel omittendis. Justorum ergo consilium est, ut Deum præ omnibus diligant, ut ei reverenter deserviant, ut in caritate et gratia ejus quotidie crescant, atque de perpetratis malis digne pœniteant. In tali autem consilio impii non resurgunt, sed manent in fæcibus vitiorum et sordibus passionum. Non audiunt Paulum clamantem: Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Et iterum: Quæ sursum sunt sapite.
paras.en: [[1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgent impii in judicio]]: because they are divided from Christ and bereft of all grace, therefore they do not rise again in judgment. This can be understood both of the judgment of discernment, by which the good judge themselves (of which the Prophet says, [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good|Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum]], [[Mich 6:8|Verily to do judgment|utique facere judicium]]; and Job, [[Job 34:4|Let us choose to us judgment, and let us see among ourselves what is the best|Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius]]; and, [[Job 34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment?|Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest?]]), and of the judgment of blessed reward, as was explained above in the last article. [[1:5|nor sinners in the council of the just|Neque peccatores in consilio justorum]] [Denis reads *consilio*, “counsel”, which he goes on to explain, where the Vulgate has *concilio*, “council”] shall rise again. Counsel is properly the name for reason's inquiry into what is to be done or left undone. The counsel of the just, then, is that they love God above all things, serve him reverently, grow daily in his charity and grace, and do worthy penance for the evils they have committed. But in such counsel the wicked do not rise again: they stay in the dregs of vices and the filth of passions. They do not hear Paul crying out: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. And again: [[Col 3:2|Mind the things that are above|Quæ sursum sunt sapite]].

paras.t: Quoniam novit Dominus viam justorum: id est, ea quæ nunc de differentia impiorum atque justorum prædicta sunt, veritatem habent: quoniam Dominus Jesus Christus, qui est Rex regum et Dominus dominantium, Judex quoque vivorum et mortuorum, novit viam justorum, id est, acceptam habet operationem bonorum, quorum utique et capilli capitis numerati sunt. Et iter impiorum peribit. Non enim ad ultimum finem, qui est Deus benedictus, pervenient.
paras.en: [[1:6|For the Lord knoweth the way of the just|Quoniam novit Dominus viam justorum]]: that is, what has now been said of the difference between the wicked and the just holds true: for the Lord Jesus Christ, who is [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]], and also the Judge of the living and the dead[[Heb 12:23||]] [the margin reads Hebr. xii, verse unread; 12:23, “God the judge of all”, is the likeliest], [[1:6|knoweth the way of the just|novit viam justorum]], that is, holds as acceptable the working of the good, whose very hairs of the head are numbered[[Luke 12:7||]]. [[1:6|and the way of the wicked shall perish|Et iter impiorum peribit]]. For they will not come to their last end, which is God the blessed.

1.title: EXPLANATIO EJUSDEM PRIMI PSALMI JUXTA SENSUM TROPOLOGICUM.
1.title_en: Explanation of the same first Psalm according to the tropological sense

paras.t: Recordandum est autem, quoniam, sicut ostensum est, tropologicus seu sensus moralis Scripturæ est, quando ea quæ de Christo vel de Sanctis scribuntur aut recitantur, ad singulorum moralem eruditionem trahuntur. Quæcumque enim de Christo capite nostro scripta sunt, ad nostram eruditionem scripta sunt. Nec solum quæ de Christo scribuntur, sed etiam quæ de Sanctis ejus leguntur, ad imitationem trahenda sunt, secundum Augustinum. Denique utilissimum est sacram Scripturam tropologice intelligere, quatenus sic Christum et Sanctos, sacram Scripturam commemorando seu proferendo, laudemus, ut ea quæ scripta sunt, ad propriam informationem trahamus: et sic imperfectum nostrum cognoscendo, salubriter doleamus, eorumque perfectionem quos laudamus, imitari studeamus.
paras.en: Now it is to be remembered that, as has been shown, the tropological or moral sense of Scripture is when what is written or told of Christ or of the Saints is drawn to the moral instruction of each one. For [[Rom 15:4|what things soever were written|Quæcumque enim]] of Christ our head [[Rom 15:4|were written for our learning|ad nostram eruditionem scripta sunt]]. And not only what is written of Christ, but also what we read of his Saints, is to be drawn to imitation, according to Augustine. Moreover, it is most useful to understand sacred Scripture tropologically, so that, while we praise Christ and the Saints by recalling or reciting sacred Scripture, we may draw what is written to our own forming; and so, knowing our own imperfection, we may grieve over it to our profit, and strive to imitate the perfection of those whom we praise.

paras.t: Tropologica autem expositio hujus psalmi, non differt a prima ac litterali expositione, nisi quod sicut illa expositio docet quid factum sit, sic ista instruit quid sit faciendum. Et est sensus omnino idem, sed ad diversa refertur. Unde secundum istum sensum, scilicet tropologicum, dicit Scriptura, Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum: ut scilicet hortetur ac doceat unumquemque fidelem, ne malignis consiliis acquiescat, et ne stet in via peccatorum male agendo, et ne in cathedra pestilentiæ sedeat malum exemplum præbendo, seu falsam doctrinam introducendo. Sicque omnia quæ sequuntur legenda sunt, quatenus omnia convertat et trahat devotus quilibet ad animæ suæ spiritualem doctrinam. Nam si ea quæ dicit, legit vel audit, ad impiorum tormenta vel derelictionem pertinent: potest ex his sanctum timorem concipere, ne et ipse similia patiatur; aut gratiarum actionem et amoris inflammationem, quia miserante Deo a talibus præservatum se videt; seu bonam tristitiam, si se talia mala pro quibus torqueri ac deseri meruit, incidisse considerat. Si vero quæ dicit vel audit, ad perfectionem beatitudinemque justorum pertinent, potest ad imitandum succendi, et ad sperandum roborari.
paras.en: The tropological exposition of this psalm does not differ from the first and literal exposition, except that, as that exposition teaches what was done, so this one instructs us in what is to be done. And the sense is altogether the same, but it is referred to different things. Hence according to this sense, namely the tropological, Scripture says, [[1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]]: that is, so as to exhort and teach each of the faithful not to give way to malicious counsels, and not to stand in the way of sinners by doing evil, and not to sit in the chair of pestilence by giving a bad example or bringing in false doctrine. And so everything that follows is to be read in such a way that each devout person may turn and draw it all to the spiritual instruction of his own soul.
