For it is well known to anyone who knows the Scriptures how, as is told, Absalom, greedy for the kingdom, wished to kill his father, holy David, so that once he was dead he himself might reign; and having gathered an army he meant to besiege Jerusalem[[2 Kings 15:1||]] [the margin's numerals are hard to read; it seems to give II Reg. xv; the story runs through 2 Kings 15–18]. When David heard of it he fled with his men; and in the end his army defeated and routed the army of Absalom. Joab too, the captain of the host, killed Absalom as he hung from an oak. It was in this persecution, then, that David made this psalm, which can be understood literally of him, though it is more truly and more forcefully expounded of Christ.

paras.t: Loquens ergo David de se ipso ad Deum: Domine, inquit, quid multiplicati sunt qui tribulant me? id est ob quam causam? quasi dicat: Non est rationabilis causa, sed conjuratio valida. Quamvis enim David peccavit, adulterium et homicidium committendo, quia Bethsabee cognovit, et virum ejus Uriam interfici ordinavit, tamen vehementer pœnituit: et tamen in pœnam tanti peccati, permisit Dominus sibi hanc fieri persecutionem; sed persequentes movebantur injuste, putantes eum omnino reprobatum a Deo. Multi, scilicet omnes Absaloni faventes, insurgunt adversum me, volentes me de regno expellere atque occidere.
paras.en: So David, speaking of himself to God, says: [[3:2|Why, O Lord|Domine]], he says, [[3:2|are they multiplied that afflict me|quid multiplicati sunt qui tribulant me]]? that is, for what cause? as if to say: There is no reasonable cause, only a strong conspiracy. For although David had sinned, committing adultery and murder, since he knew Bethsabee and ordered her husband Urias to be killed[[2 Kings 11:4||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the story is told in 2 Kings 11], yet he repented vehemently; and still, in punishment of so great a sin, the Lord allowed this persecution to befall him; but his persecutors were moved unjustly, thinking him utterly rejected by God. [[3:2|many|Multi]], namely all who favoured Absalom, [[3:2|rise up against me|insurgunt adversum me]], wishing to drive me out of the kingdom and kill me.

paras.t: Multi dicunt animæ meæ, id est, multi loquuntur de anima mea: Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus, id est, omnino maledicta et reprobata est propter scelerum ejus enormitatem, scilicet homicidii et adulterii. Unde Achitophel et alii multi persuaserunt populo, quod Deus abjecisset David, et ergo sine peccato persequerentur eum, et Absaloni adhærerent.
paras.en: [[3:3|Many say to my soul|Multi dicunt animæ meæ]], that is, many speak of my soul: [[3:3|There is no salvation for him in his God|Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus]], that is, it is altogether accursed and rejected because of the enormity of its crimes, namely murder and adultery. Hence Achitophel and many others persuaded the people that God had cast David off, and that they could therefore persecute him without sin and cleave to Absalom.

paras.t: Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es. Hæc sunt verba David consolantis se ipsum, et amorose atque gratanter ad Deum loquentis, quasi dicat: Illi ita desperant de me; tu autem, Domine, susceptor es animæ meæ, id est miserator meus, recipiens pœnitentiam meam, et precem meam exaudiens; gloria mea, id est objectum et causa gloriæ meæ, quia in te solo glorior, et gratiam hujus sanctæ gloriationis tu mihi infundis. Et ideo sequitur: et exaltans caput meum, id est erigens mentem meam ad te, dansque fiduciam elevandi oculos meos ad te.
paras.en: [[3:4|But thou, O Lord, art my protector|Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es]]. These are the words of David consoling himself and speaking to God lovingly and gratefully, as if to say: They despair of me in this way; [[3:4|but thou, O Lord|tu autem, Domine]], art the [[3:4|protector|susceptor]] of my soul [*susceptor*: literally one who takes up or receives], that is, the one who has mercy on me, receiving my repentance and hearing my prayer; [[3:4|my glory|gloria mea]], that is, the object and cause of my glory, because I glory in thee alone[[2 Cor 10:17||]], and thou pourest into me the grace of this holy glorying. And so there follows: [[3:4|and the lifter up of my head|et exaltans caput meum]], that is, raising my mind to thee and giving me confidence to lift up my eyes to thee.

paras.t: Idcirco, Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi, petens liberari ab eo a malo pœnæ et culpæ, et ejus voluntati me totum committens. Nec frustra, nam sequitur: et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo, id est de sublimi throno solii sui, vel de excelsa ac summa clementia sua.
paras.en: Therefore, [[3:5|I have cried to the Lord with my voice|Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi]], asking to be freed by him from the evil of punishment and of guilt, and committing myself wholly to his will. Nor in vain, for there follows: [[3:5|and he hath heard me from his holy hill|et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo]], that is, from the lofty throne of his seat, or from his high and supreme clemency.

paras.t: Ego dormivi, et soporatus sum. Ad litteram, somnus valet ad mitigationem tristitiæ, sicut et balnea. David ergo dormiendo relevamen suæ tristitiæ sumpsit, tam ex causa naturali, scilicet somni, quam ex infusione consolationis divinæ. Propterea ait: et exsurrexi, quia Dominus suscepit me, id est, per gratiam et misericordiam suam adjunxit me sibi, et roboravit cor meum in se.
paras.en: [[3:6|I have slept and have taken my rest|Ego dormivi, et soporatus sum]]. Literally, sleep serves to soften sadness, as do baths too [so St Thomas, who asks whether sorrow is eased by sleep and baths]. So David by sleeping took relief from his sadness, both from a natural cause, namely sleep, and from the infusion of divine consolation. Therefore he says: [[3:6|and I have risen up, because the Lord hath protected me|et exsurrexi, quia Dominus suscepit me]], that is, by his grace and mercy he joined me to himself and strengthened my heart in him.

paras.t: Unde subjungit: Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me, id est, nullam multitudinem contra me insurgentem verebor; et ut in hac fortitudine animi stabilis perseverem, exsurge, Domine, non de loco surgendo, sed succurrendo et modum exsurgentis te habendo; salvum me fac, Deus meus.
paras.en: Hence he adds: [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]], that is, I will fear no multitude rising up against me; and that I may persevere steadfast in this strength of mind, [[3:7|arise, O Lord|exsurge, Domine]], not by rising from a place, but by coming to my help and bearing thyself as one who rises up; [[3:7|save me, O my God|salvum me fac, Deus meus]].

paras.t: Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa. Hic redditur causa, non ejus quod dictum est, sed ejus quod sequitur: non enim ideo oravit David salvari a Deo, quoniam Deus percussit omnes adversantes sibi, nam illa percussio orationem ejus secuta est. Sed quia Dominus percussit adversarios David, vel terrendo, vel lædendo, vel interficiendo eos qui Absaloni favebant; ideo dentes peccatorum contrivit, id est, ora obloquentium ipsi David clausit, et verba eorum maligna repressit. Ideo subdit: dentes peccatorum contrivisti.
paras.en: [[3:8|For thou hast struck all them who are my adversaries without cause|Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]]. Here a cause is given, not of what has been said but of what follows: for David did not pray to be saved by God because God had struck all his adversaries, since that striking followed his prayer. But because the Lord struck David's adversaries, by terrifying, or hurting, or killing those who favoured Absalom, therefore he broke the teeth of sinners, that is, he shut the mouths of those who spoke against David and held back their malicious words. Therefore he adds: [[3:8|thou hast broken the teeth of sinners|dentes peccatorum contrivisti]].

paras.t: Verum quoniam omnis ista victoria a Deo collata est David, ideo addit: Domini est salus, id est, liberatio ab adversariis a Deo confertur, et ipsi recte adscribitur. Consequenter David mutat personam, per figuram quæ dicitur metaplasmus; et loquens ad Dominum, ait: et super populum tuum benedictio tua, id est collatio munerum tuorum, protectio atque redemptio: quia exercitus David, quamvis modicus esset in comparatione exercitus Absalonis, tamen Deo auxiliante prævaluit.
paras.en: But since all this victory was granted to David by God, he therefore adds: [[3:9|Salvation is of the Lord|Domini est salus]], that is, deliverance from adversaries is bestowed by God and is rightly ascribed to him. Then David changes the person, by the figure called metaplasm [Denis's name for the change from speaking of the Lord to speaking to him]; and speaking to the Lord he says: [[3:9|and thy blessing is upon thy people|et super populum tuum benedictio tua]], that is, the bestowal of thy gifts, protection and redemption: for David's army, though small in comparison with the army of Absalom, yet prevailed with God's help.

3.title: Expositio ejusdem psalmi tertii allegorica
3.title_en: Allegorical exposition of the same third psalm

paras.t: Doctores catholici, Augustinus, Cassiodorus et alii, exponunt hunc psalmum ad litteram de Christo; qui vero eum litteraliter de David exponunt, ipsum allegorice de Christo intelligunt. Sed quidquid dicatur, de Christo convenienter exponitur. Titulus tamen mystice exponendus est. David enim (sicut ostensum est) ratione interpretationis, figura est Christi. Absalon vero, qui interpretatur pax patris, typus est Judæ traditoris, de quo postea dicitur, Etenim homo pacis meæ in quo speravi; qui etiam in Evangelio filius Christi seu Sponsi inter ceteros discipulos nuncupatur, ubi Christus ait: Non possunt filii sponsi, quamdiu cum illis est sponsus, jejunare. Sensus ergo tituli est: Psalmus David, quum fugeret a facie Absalon filii sui, id est, psalmus loquens de Christo, quum fugeret a mente Judæ quondam discipuli sui. Tunc enim Christus recessit a corde Judæ, quando post buccellam introivit in eum Satanas.
paras.en: The Catholic doctors, Augustine, Cassiodorus and others, expound this psalm literally of Christ; and those who expound it literally of David understand it allegorically of Christ. But whatever is said, it is fittingly expounded of Christ. The title, however, is to be expounded mystically. For David (as has been shown) is a figure of Christ by reason of the meaning of his name. And Absalom, which is interpreted "peace of the father", is a type of Judas the traitor, of whom it is said later: [[40:10|even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted|Etenim homo pacis meæ in quo speravi]]; who is also called in the Gospel a son of Christ, the Bridegroom, among the other disciples, where Christ says: The sons of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them[[Matt 9:15||]] [the margin gives Matt 9:15; Denis's words are nearer Mark 2:19]. The sense of the title, then, is: [[3:1|The psalm of David when he fled from the face of his son Absalom|Psalmus David, quum fugeret a facie Absalon filii sui]], that is, a psalm speaking of Christ when he fled from the mind of Judas, once his disciple. For Christ withdrew from the heart of Judas when, [[John 13:27|after the morsel, Satan entered into him|post buccellam introivit in eum Satanas]].

paras.t: Sic igitur Christus ad Deum Patrem, vel etiam ad totam supersanctissimam Trinitatem loquendo, vel certe Christus ut homo, loquens ad se ipsum ut est Deus: Domine, inquit, id est, o Deus Pater; vel, o Deus trine ac simplex, qui es omnium Dominus; vel, o Verbum ac Fili Dei, qui meam humilitatem ad tuam personalitatem assumpsisti; quid, id est quo meo demerito, multiplicati sunt, qui tribulant me, id est, qui quærunt occidere me, et obloquuntur, convitianturque mihi? quasi dicat, Nullo: non enim Christus fecit peccatum pro quo pati meruit. Multi insurgunt adversum me, illi scilicet qui tribulant me, scilicet Pharisæi et Scribæ, cum principibus sacerdotum ac populo. Multi dicunt animæ meæ: Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus. Tales erant prædicti infideles Judæi, qui Christum reputabant blasphemum, voratorem, dæmoniacum, et insanum, sicut in Evangelio sæpe habetur.
paras.en: So, then, Christ, speaking to God the Father, or to the whole most holy Trinity, or Christ as man speaking to himself as he is God, says: [[3:2|O Lord|Domine]], that is, O God the Father; or, O God three and simple, who art Lord of all; or, O Word and Son of God, who hast taken my lowliness into thy Person; [[3:2|Why|quid]], that is, for what fault of mine, [[3:2|are they multiplied that afflict me?|multiplicati sunt, qui tribulant me]] that is, who seek to kill me, and speak against me and revile me? As if to say: For none: for Christ committed no sin for which he deserved to suffer. [[3:2|many are they who rise up against me|Multi insurgunt adversum me]], namely those who afflict me, the Pharisees and Scribes, with the chief priests and the people. [[3:3|Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God|Multi dicunt animæ meæ: Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus]]. Such were the unbelieving Jews just mentioned, who held Christ a blasphemer[[Mark 2:7||]], a glutton[[Matt 11:19||]], possessed by a devil, and mad[[John 10:20||]], as we often find in the Gospel.

paras.t: Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es: id est, tu, Verbum atque Unigenite Dei secundum divinam naturam, susceptor meus es quantum ad naturam humanam. Christus enim ut Deus, suscepit atque assumpsit in unitate personæ naturam humanam. Gloria mea, id est objectum beatitudinis meæ: quia gloria humanitatis Christi consistit in unione ac speculatione propriæ deitatis. Unde subjungitur: et exaltans caput meum, id est, elevans intellectum meum creatum, sive humanum, ad claram ac beatificam divinæ essentiæ visionem, quam Christus ut homo, vidit a primo instanti suæ conceptionis in Virgine matre, ut dictum est. — Vel sic: Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es: id est, tu, Deus Pater, vel tota Trinitas, susceptor meus es, id est exauditor et conservator meus, a cujus amore et beneplacito separari nec volo nec valeo; gloria mea, id est causa et ratio omnis lætitiæ meæ: et exaltans caput meum, id est, honorans atque glorificans me in signis et virtutibus, quibus hominibus innotescere potest me esse verum Christum ac Filium tuum, imo et verum Deum. Sicque per caput intelligi potest Christi divinitas: caput enim Christi Deus, secundum Apostolum. Et hanc Deus Pater, seu Deus Trinitas exaltavit, quando per Spiritum hominibus revelavit Christum esse Deum ac hominem, non in una natura, sed in una persona. Unde Christus ait: Clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum, claritate quam habui antequam mundus fieret: non quod Christus claritatem, quam ante mundi constitutionem habuit, unquam amisit; sed oravit ut vera sui cognitio hominibus innotesceret. Unde iterum ait: Pater, venit hora, clarifica Filium tuum, ut Filius tuus clarificet te: ubi, nisi in cordibus hominum?
paras.en: [[3:4|But thou, O Lord, art my protector|Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es]] [*susceptor*, literally "one who takes up"]: that is, thou, Word and Only-begotten of God according to the divine nature, art he who takes me up as to the human nature. For Christ as God took up and assumed the human nature into the unity of his Person. [[3:4|my glory|Gloria mea]], that is, the object of my blessedness: for the glory of Christ's humanity consists in its union with, and contemplation of, its own Godhead. Hence it is added: [[3:4|and the lifter up of my head|et exaltans caput meum]], that is, raising my created or human intellect to the clear and beatific vision of the divine essence, which Christ as man saw from the first instant of his conception in the Virgin Mother, as has been said. — Or thus: [[3:4|But thou, O Lord, art my protector|Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es]]: that is, thou, God the Father, or the whole Trinity, art my protector, that is, he who hears and keeps me, from whose love and good pleasure I neither will nor can be separated; [[3:4|my glory|gloria mea]], that is, the cause and reason of all my joy: [[3:4|and the lifter up of my head|et exaltans caput meum]], that is, honouring and glorifying me in the signs and miracles by which it can be made known to men that I am the true Christ and thy Son, and indeed true God. And so by the head can be understood the Godhead of Christ: for [[1 Cor 11:3|the head of Christ is God|caput enim Christi Deus]], according to the Apostle. And this God the Father, or God the Trinity, exalted when he revealed to men through the Spirit[[Matt 3:16||]][[Matt 3:17||]] that Christ is God and man, not in one nature but in one Person. Hence Christ says: [[John 17:5|glorify thou me, O Father, with thyself, with the glory which I had, before the world was|Clarifica me tu, Pater, apud temetipsum, claritate quam habui antequam mundus fieret]]: not that Christ ever lost the glory he had before the foundation of the world; but he prayed that the true knowledge of himself might be made known to men. Hence again he says: [[John 17:1|the hour is come. Glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee|Pater, venit hora, clarifica Filium tuum, ut Filius tuus clarificet te]]: where, if not in the hearts of men?

paras.t: Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi. Sicut Evangelistæ testantur, Christus erat pernoctans in oratione Dei, et passione instante, ter Patrem oravit: nec frustra, quoniam subditur, et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo, id est de excelso habitaculo suo, vel de sublimi justitia sua. Infra enim habetur: Justitia tua sicut montes Dei. De hac ergo justitia exaudivit Deus Christum, quoniam divina dictante justitia, decuit Christum in omni oratione a Deo exaudiri, sicut et ipse Deo in omnibus obedientissimus fuit. Nam orationem illam quam ante passionem effudit, dicens, Transeat a me calix iste, Deus implevit. Non enim absolute oravit a passione liberari, sed hoc finaliter desideravit atque oravit ut Patris impleretur voluntas, dicens: Non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua. Quare ad Hebræos de Christo Apostolus: Exauditus est, inquit, pro sua reverentia. Christus quoque dicit ad Patrem: Pater, gratias ago tibi, quoniam exaudisti me; ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis.
paras.en: [[3:5|I have cried to the Lord with my voice|Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi]]. As the Evangelists testify, Christ [[Luke 6:12|passed the whole night in the prayer of God|erat pernoctans in oratione Dei]], and when his passion was at hand he prayed to the Father three times[[Matt 26:44||]]: and not in vain, since it is added: [[3:5|and he hath heard me from his holy hill|et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo]], that is, from his lofty dwelling, or from his sublime justice. For we find below: [[35:7|Thy justice is as the mountains of God|Justitia tua sicut montes Dei]]. From this justice, then, God heard Christ, since, as divine justice dictated, it was fitting that Christ be heard by God in every prayer, as he too was most obedient to God in all things. For the prayer he poured out before his passion, saying: [[Matt 26:39|let this chalice pass from me|Transeat a me calix iste]], God fulfilled. For he did not pray absolutely to be freed from the passion; but what he finally desired and prayed for was that the Father's will be fulfilled, saying: [[Luke 22:42|not my will, but thine be done|Non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua]]. That is why the Apostle says of Christ to the Hebrews: [[Heb 5:7|was heard for his reverence|Exauditus est, inquit, pro sua reverentia]]. Christ too says to the Father: [[John 11:41|Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me|Pater, gratias ago tibi, quoniam exaudisti me]]; [[John 11:42|And I knew that thou hearest me always|ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis]].

paras.t: Consequenter Christus loquitur de sua passione, sepultura, ac resurrectione, dicens: Ego dormivi, somno mortis in cruce; et soporatus sum, tribus diebus ac noctibus jacens in tumulo. Mors quippe Sanctorum, somnus vocatur, quia ad vitam immortalem a Deo suscitabuntur. Et sepelitio Christi, bene soporatio appellatur, quia tam cito (utpote tertia die) suscitabatur. Unde subjungitur, et exsurrexi, de clauso sepulcro, sicut egressus sum de clauso Virginis utero; quia Dominus suscepit me, id est, de numero mortuorum reduxit me.
paras.en: Next Christ speaks of his passion, burial and resurrection, saying: [[3:6|I have slept|Ego dormivi]], with the sleep of death on the cross; [[3:6|and have taken my rest|et soporatus sum]], lying three days and nights in the tomb. For the death of the saints is called sleep, because they will be raised by God to immortal life. And Christ's burial is well called a taking of rest, because he was raised so soon (namely on the third day). Hence it is added: [[3:6|and I have risen up|et exsurrexi]], from the closed tomb, as I came forth from the closed womb of the Virgin; [[3:6|because the Lord hath protected me|quia Dominus suscepit me]], that is, brought me back from the number of the dead.

paras.t: Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me. Hæc possunt esse verba Christi post resurrectionem, quoniam surgens a mortuis, jam non moritur, quia immortalis surrexit. Et ideo de cetero non timebo millia populi, id est quamcumque multitudinem mihi resistere cupientem, vel me circumdantem: non quod post resurrectionem valuerint adversarii Christi ipsum circumdare, quoniam inter impios post mortem conversatus non est, neque injustis apparuit, sed testibus præordinatis a Deo; sed ideo dicit, Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me, id est, qui tempore passionis circumdedit me (illos enim post passionem non timuit), quia impassibiliter resurrexit. — Possunt et hæc verba de Christo intelligi ante passionem. Quamvis enim naturalem timorem sponte admisit, quando passione instante cœpit contristari ac mœstus esse, pavere atque tædere, et quando factus est sudor ejus sicut guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram; tamen ab oratione surgens, turbis impiorum intrepidus obviavit, et dixit: Quem quæritis? Sic itaque ait, Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me; et ut non formidem, oro, o Domine, exsurge, subveniendo; salvum me fac, Deus meus, a morte, non deserendo me in sepulcro, nec derelinquendo animam meam in inferno, sed ad cœlos recipiendo me.
paras.en: [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]]. These can be words of Christ after the resurrection, since [[Rom 6:9|rising again from the dead, dieth now no more|surgens a mortuis, jam non moritur]], because he rose immortal. And therefore from now on [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people|non timebo millia populi]], that is, any multitude wishing to resist me or surrounding me: not that after the resurrection Christ's adversaries were able to surround him, since after his death he did not go about among the wicked nor appear to the unjust, but [[Acts 10:41|to witnesses preordained by God|testibus præordinatis a Deo]]; but he says, [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]], that is, the people who surrounded me at the time of the passion (for after the passion he did not fear them), because he rose again beyond suffering. — These words can also be understood of Christ before the passion. For although he willingly admitted natural fear, when, with the passion at hand, [[Matt 26:37|he began to grow sorrowful and to be sad|cœpit contristari ac mœstus esse]], [[Mark 14:33|to fear and to be heavy|pavere atque tædere]], and when [[Luke 22:44|his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground|factus est sudor ejus sicut guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram]]; yet, rising from prayer, he went fearlessly to meet the crowds of the wicked, and said: [[John 18:4|Whom seek ye?|Quem quæritis]] So, then, he says: [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]]; and that I may not fear, I pray: [[3:7|arise, O Lord|exsurge]], by coming to my help; [[3:7|save me, O my God|salvum me fac, Deus meus]], from death, not deserting me in the tomb, nor [[15:10|leave my soul in hell|derelinquendo animam meam in inferno]], but taking me up to heaven.

paras.t: Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa. Sæpe in Prophetis ponitur tempus præteritum seu præsens pro futuro, propter certitudinem prophetiæ. Ita hic ponitur præteritum pro futuro: quod tamen modo impletum videmus. Quoniam tu percussisti, id est quia percuties, omnes adversantes mihi sine causa, id est persecutores ac crucifixores meos, incredulosque Judæos, qui æterna pœna percussi sunt, et posteri eorum usque in præsens capti sunt, expulsi, et multis miseriis involuti, illis exceptis qui pœnituerunt. Dentes peccatorum contrivisti, id est, blasphemias, irrisiones et oblocutiones eorum qui mihi in vita et in morte atque post mortem illudebant et detrahebant, conteres, ostendendo falsitatem eorum, et digna eos pœna torquendo. Domini est salus, id est, a Deo est ista mea salvatio de manibus iniquorum; et super populum tuum, id est super eos qui in me credunt, et mea vestigia insequuntur, benedictio tua, id est collatio gratiarum tuarum, o Domine Pater. Hæc enim sunt verba Christi ad Deum.
paras.en: [[3:8|For thou hast struck all them who are my adversaries without cause|Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]]. In the prophets the past or present tense is often put for the future, because of the certainty of prophecy. So here the past is put for the future: which, however, we now see fulfilled. [[3:8|For thou hast struck|Quoniam tu percussisti]], that is, for thou wilt strike, [[3:8|all them who are my adversaries without cause|omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]], that is, my persecutors and crucifiers, and the unbelieving Jews, who have been struck with eternal punishment, and whose descendants down to the present have been taken captive, driven out, and wrapped in many miseries, except those who repented. [[3:8|thou hast broken the teeth of sinners|Dentes peccatorum contrivisti]], that is, thou wilt crush the blasphemies, mockeries and slanders of those who mocked and disparaged me in life, in death and after death, by showing their falsehood and tormenting them with fitting punishment. [[3:9|Salvation is of the Lord|Domini est salus]], that is, this my deliverance from the hands of the wicked is from God; [[3:9|and thy blessing is upon thy people|et super populum tuum benedictio tua]], that is, upon those who believe in me and follow my footsteps, is thy blessing, that is, the bestowal of thy graces, O Lord Father. For these are words of Christ to God.

3.title: TROPOLOGICA EJUSDEM PSALMI TERTII EXPLANATIO.
3.title_en: Tropological explanation of the same third Psalm

paras.t: Insuper exponendus est psalmus iste de quolibet justo seu tota militante Ecclesia, quatenus ex his quæ de prioribus justis ac Sancto Sanctorum Domino nostro Jesu Christo scripta sunt, accipiamus moralem doctrinam, et instruamur quid nobis agendum sit, dum talia nobis eveniunt, qualia antiquis Sanctis, Deique Filio contigerunt.
paras.en: Further, this psalm is to be expounded of any just man, or of the whole Church militant, so that from what is written of the just of old and of the Holy of Holies, our Lord Jesus Christ, we may take moral teaching, and be instructed in what we must do when such things befall us as befell the Saints of old and the Son of God.

paras.t: David enim non solum Christi, sed et cujuslibet justi atque Ecclesiæ tenet figuram, quia Ecclesia per virtutem sponsi sui Christi Jesu, quilibet quoque fidelis, est David, id est manu fortis et desiderabilis adspectu. Absalon vero typus est mundi, et horum qui justos persequuntur ac tentant. Unde secundum tropologiam, sensus tituli hujus psalmi est: Psalmus David, quum fugeret a facie Absalon filii sui, id est, canticum Ecclesiæ omniumque justorum, quum se per bonam conversationem abstrahunt a consortio mundi ac impiorum, qui sunt filii Ecclesiæ potentia, non actu; nomine, non re.
paras.en: For David bears the figure not only of Christ but also of any just man and of the Church, because the Church, by the power of her spouse Christ Jesus, and every one of the faithful too, is David, that is, strong of hand and desirable to behold. And Absalom is a type of the world, and of those who persecute and tempt the just. Hence according to tropology the sense of the title of this psalm is: [[3:1|The psalm of David when he fled from the face of his son Absalom|Psalmus David, quum fugeret a facie Absalon filii sui]], that is, the song of the Church and of all the just, when by good living they withdraw from the company of the world and of the wicked, who are sons of the Church in potency, not in act; in name, not in reality.

paras.t: Dicat ergo Ecclesia, dicat et quælibet rationalis creatura, variis tentationibus, multis tribulationibus atque miseriis pulsata, pressa ac fatigata: Domine, id est, o Deus æterne, omnipotens, adorande; vel, Domine, id est, o Jesu Christe; quid multiplicati sunt qui tribulant me? scilicet mundus, caro et diabolus, quia tres sunt inimici justorum. Multi insurgunt adversum me, utpote homines sæculares, concupiscentiæ carnales, et aereæ potestates: hi enim infestant et tribulant justos. Multi dicunt, id est, verbo vel opere asserunt, animæ meæ: Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus. Mundani ac impii vitam justorum putant insaniam, et finem illorum sine honore: et ideo habent eos in derisum et in similitudinem improperii.
paras.en: Let the Church say, then, and let every rational creature say, when buffeted, pressed and wearied by various temptations, many tribulations and miseries: [[3:2|O Lord|Domine]], that is, O God eternal, almighty, to be adored; or, [[3:2|O Lord|Domine]], that is, O Jesus Christ; [[3:2|Why|quid]] [[3:2|are they multiplied that afflict me?|multiplicati sunt qui tribulant me?]] namely the world, the flesh and the devil, for the enemies of the just are three. [[3:2|many are they who rise up against me|Multi insurgunt adversum me]], such as worldly men, carnal lusts and the powers of the air: for these harass and afflict the just. [[3:3|Many say|Multi dicunt]], that is, assert by word or deed, [[3:3|to my soul|animæ meæ]]: [[3:3|There is no salvation for him in his God|Non est salus ipsi in Deo ejus]]. The worldly and the wicked think the life of the just madness[[Wis 5:4||]], [[Wis 5:4|and their end without honour|et finem illorum sine honore]]: and therefore they hold them [[Wis 5:3|in derision, and for a parable of reproach|in derisum et in similitudinem improperii]].

paras.t: Deinde sequitur verbum dulcissimum, atque consolatio optima: quod verbum unicuique in tribulatione ac tentatione constituto, cum magna et amorosa fiducia ad Deum dicendum est. Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es, ad quem in adversis confugio; gloria mea, ad quam in omni mœrore propero et respiro; et exaltans caput meum, id est, ab omni dejectione eripiens animam meam. Unde scriptum: Quum ignoremus quid facere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te.
paras.en: Then follows a most sweet word and the best of consolations, a word which everyone set in tribulation and temptation should say to God with great and loving confidence: [[3:4|But thou, O Lord, art my protector|Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es]], to whom I flee in adversity; [[3:4|my glory|gloria mea]], to which I hasten in every sorrow and find breath again; [[3:4|and the lifter up of my head|et exaltans caput meum]], that is, delivering my soul from all dejection. Hence it is written: [[2 Par 20:12|as we know not what to do, we can only turn our eyes to thee|Quum ignoremus quid facere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te]].

paras.t: Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi. Hoc versu docetur omnis fidelis, quid tempore tribulationis sibi agendum sit. Debet enim voce sua clamare, id est vehementi et alto cordis affectu clamare, ad Dominum: et tunc Dominus exaudiet eum, ita ut se relevatum sentiens, dicat, Et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo. Sed perseveranter orare oportet, imo sine intermissione.
paras.en: [[3:5|I have cried to the Lord with my voice|Voce mea ad Dominum clamavi]]. In this verse every one of the faithful is taught what he must do in time of tribulation. For he should cry with his voice, that is, cry with a vehement and deep affection of the heart, to the Lord: and then the Lord will hear him, so that, feeling himself relieved, he may say, [[3:5|and he hath heard me from his holy hill|Et exaudivit me de monte sancto suo]]. But one must pray perseveringly, nay, [[1 Thess 5:17|without ceasing|sine intermissione]].

paras.t: Ego, scilicet Ecclesia seu quilibet justus, dormivi, id est, tribulationibus opprimebar, ut tæderet animam meam vitæ meæ, et præ tædio dormitarem; et soporatus sum, per tempus perseverando in tali angustia; et exsurrexi, id est, consolationem recepi, atque prævalui, non viribus aut meritis meis, sed quia Dominus suscepit me, id est, misericordia ejus amplexata est me et precem meam admisit. Vel sic: Ego dormivi, id est, in peccatis prostratus fui et jacui; et soporatus sum, id est, in peccatorum delectatione permansi, et propter pigritiam a bonis operibus cessavi. Peccatori autem clamat Apostolus: Surge, qui dormis. Et Salomon: Usquequo, piger, dormies? Dormit enim qui nec contemplatur cœlestia, nec verba Dei audit, nec alicujus spiritualis sensus operationem exercet. Et exsurrexi, quia Dominus suscepit me, id est, a vitiis desii, et juste vivere cœpi, quia Dominus misertus est mei, indulgentiam gratiamque præstando.
paras.en: [[3:6|I|Ego]], namely the Church or any just man, [[3:6|have slept|dormivi]], that is, I was weighed down by tribulations, so that [[Job 10:1|My soul is weary of my life|tæderet animam meam vitæ meæ]], and I slumbered for weariness[[Ps 118:28||]]; [[3:6|and have taken my rest|et soporatus sum]], by remaining for a time in such distress; [[3:6|and I have risen up|et exsurrexi]], that is, I received consolation and prevailed, not by my own strength or merits, but [[3:6|because the Lord hath protected me|quia Dominus suscepit me]], that is, his mercy embraced me and admitted my prayer. Or thus: [[3:6|I have slept|Ego dormivi]], that is, I lay prostrate in sins; [[3:6|and have taken my rest|et soporatus sum]], that is, I remained in the delight of sins, and through sloth ceased from good works. But to the sinner the Apostle cries: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest|Surge, qui dormis]]. And Solomon: [[Prov 6:9|How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?|Usquequo, piger, dormies?]] For he sleeps who neither contemplates heavenly things, nor hears the words of God, nor exercises the working of any spiritual sense. [[3:6|and I have risen up, because the Lord hath protected me|Et exsurrexi, quia Dominus suscepit me]], that is, I left off my vices and began to live justly, because the Lord had mercy on me, granting me pardon and grace.

paras.t: Unde subdit: Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me, id est, nullam adversariorum catervam verebor. Cor enim in Deo firmatum nihil timet præter Deum: quia si timet hominem, hoc est propter Deum. Justus enim, quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit. Et, Qui timet hominem, cito corruet. Sed quia fortitudinem non habet aliquis a se ipso, ideo additur: Exsurge, Domine; salvum me fac, Deus meus. Oportet enim ut Deus in nobis bona inchoet, continuet, et consummet: ideoque incessabiliter ad ipsum clamare debemus.
paras.en: Hence it adds: [[3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]], that is, I will dread no band of adversaries. For a heart made firm in God fears nothing but God: because if it fears man, this is for God's sake. For [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Justus enim, quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]. And: [[Prov 29:25|He that feareth man shall quickly fall|Qui timet hominem, cito corruet]] [the margin reads Ibid. xxi, 25; the words are those of Prov 29:25]. But since no one has strength of himself, it is added: [[3:7|arise, O Lord; save me, O my God|Exsurge, Domine; salvum me fac, Deus meus]]. For God must begin, continue and complete good things in us; and therefore we ought to cry to him unceasingly.

paras.t: Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa. Christus in Evangelio discipulis dixit: Confidite, ego vici mundum. Ipse quoque superavit principem hujus mundi. Sic ergo Ecclesia et unusquisque devotus ad Christum dicere potest: Quoniam tu percussisti, id est, superasti ac reprobasti, omnes adversantes mihi sine causa, id est mundum seu homines sæculares ac dæmones, qui mihi adversantur conando me a te summo bono avertere, et vitiis implicare. Dentes peccatorum contrivisti, id est, sermones seu ora eorum qui vitam bonorum diffamant, et famam ipsorum honestam dilacerant, contrivisti, saltem per prohibitionem. Potest autem exponi hic versus, accipiendo præteritum pro futuro, modo locutionis propheticæ. […] Domine Jesu Christe, omnium judex, percuties in die judicii, omnes adversantes mihi sine causa, id est eos qui modo me injuste vexant ac tribulant: et tunc dentes peccatorum, id est verba detractorum ac invidorum, contrivisti, id est, conteres, retundes, damnabis.
paras.en: [[3:8|For thou hast struck all them who are my adversaries without cause|Quoniam tu percussisti omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]]. Christ said to his disciples in the Gospel: [[John 16:33|But have confidence. I have overcome the world|Confidite, ego vici mundum]]. He also overcame the prince of this world. So, then, the Church and every devout soul can say to Christ: [[3:8|For thou hast struck|Quoniam tu percussisti]], that is, overcome and rejected, [[3:8|all them who are my adversaries without cause|omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]], that is, the world, or worldly men, and the demons, who are my adversaries in trying to turn me away from thee, the highest good, and to entangle me in vices. [[3:8|thou hast broken the teeth of sinners|Dentes peccatorum contrivisti]], that is, thou hast broken the speech or the mouths of those who defame the life of the good and tear apart their good name, at least by forbidding it. This verse can also be expounded by taking the past for the future, in the manner of prophetic speech: […] [a line of the page is unreadable in the OCR] O Lord Jesus Christ, judge of all, thou wilt strike in the day of judgment [[3:8|all them who are my adversaries without cause|omnes adversantes mihi sine causa]], that is, those who now unjustly vex and afflict me; and then [[3:8|the teeth of sinners|dentes peccatorum]], that is, the words of detractors and the envious, [[3:8|thou hast broken|contrivisti]], that is, thou wilt break, blunt and condemn.

paras.t: Hunc igitur psalmum decantet, qui tentationibus tribulationibusque pulsatur: et si eum attente cantaverit, magnum utique elevamen experietur, sentietque quam vere atque salubriter Jacobus in […] consulat: Tristatur aliquis vestrum? […] æquo animo, et psallat.
paras.en: Let him, then, sing this psalm who is buffeted by temptations and tribulations: and if he sings it attentively, he will surely feel a great relief, and will find how truly and wholesomely James counsels in […]: [[Jas 5:13|Is any of you sad?|Tristatur aliquis vestrum?]] […] with an even mind, and let him sing [the OCR is lost here; James says, “Is any of you sad? Let him pray. Is he cheerful in mind? Let him sing”].

paras.t: Precatio. Voce nostra ad te, Domine Deus noster, oratione clamantes, exaudi nos de monte sancto tuo: exsurge in adjutorium nostrum, ut tua opitulatione salutem et æternam benedictionem consequamur.
paras.en: Prayer. Crying to thee in prayer with our voice, O Lord our God, hear us from thy holy hill: arise to our help, that by thy aid we may obtain salvation and eternal blessing.

4.title: Expositio quarti psalmi: Cum invocarem, etc.
4.title_en: Exposition of the fourth psalm: When I called upon him, etc.

paras.t: Porro psalmus iste talem habet titulum: In finem, psalmus cantici David: id est, tractatus iste, qui ad bene operandum hortatur, est psalmus cantici, id est spiritualem jucunditatem includens, et de æternis bonis gaudere nos faciens; David, id est factus ab ipso; in finem, id est dirigens nos ad Christum, qui est omnium rerum Alpha et Omega, principium et finis. Est enim duplex finis, videlicet consumens, sicut de candela jam igne consumpta dicimus, Finita est candela; et est finis consummans seu perficiens, ut de domo jam completa asserimus, Finita est domus. Et hoc secundo modo Christus est omnium rerum finis, quoniam ipse est consummata perfectio atque felicitas nostra. Continet igitur psalmus iste spiritualem doctrinam seu informationem moralem, spei inflammationem et internam lætitiam.
paras.en: Now this psalm has this title: [[4:1|Unto the end|In finem]], a psalm of a canticle of David [Denis's text of the title reads *psalmus cantici David*; the Vulgate has *in carminibus. Psalmus David*]: that is, this treatise, which exhorts to good works, is a psalm of a canticle, that is, containing spiritual joy and making us rejoice in eternal goods; of David, that is, made by him; [[4:1|unto the end|in finem]], that is, directing us to Christ, who is of all things [[Apoc 1:8|Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end|Alpha et Omega, principium et finis]][[Apoc 22:13||]]. For the end is twofold: one that consumes, as we say of a candle already consumed by the fire, The candle is finished; and the end that consummates or perfects, as we say of a house now completed, The house is finished. And in this second way Christ is the end of all things, since he is our consummate perfection and happiness. This psalm, then, contains spiritual doctrine or moral instruction, the kindling of hope, and inward joy.

paras.t: Loquens itaque Propheta in persona Ecclesiæ seu cujuslibet justi: Quum invocarem, inquit, exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ: id est, quum intus Deum rogarem, quum ex interno affectu ad ipsum clamarem, dum tota mentis occupatione in Deum versante ac fixa orarem; exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ, id est, a quo omne est bonum quod habeo, omnis justitia quam exerceo. Et in hoc Propheta instruit nos, ut Deum intime invocemus in omni nostra angustia. Per id vero quod addit, Exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ, inflammat atque confortat spem nostram, ut fiducialiter invocemus, quasi diceret: Quemadmodum Deus me invocantem exaudivit, sic vos quoque exaudiet, si pure, perseveranter et sine omni hæsitatione deprecati fueritis, non in vestris justitiis, sed in Dei miserationibus confidentes. In tribulatione dilatasti mihi: id est, in ipsa spiritus mei afflictione, seu corporis infirmitate interius consolatus es me, dando patientiam veram, per quam cuncta adversa lætanter sustineo, et æquanimiter fero, ita ut cor meum ex mentali et sancta lætitia dilatetur in semetipso. Per tristitiam namque cor constringitur et coarctatur, sed per lætitiam dilatatur seu amplificatur. Unde Apostolus, ex discipulorum suorum memoria exhilaratus: Cor, inquit, nostrum dilatatum est. Verum, quoniam homo semper debet esse timoratus atque sollicitus quamdiu in præsenti versatur exsilio, nec sic propter adeptam a Deo gratiam et consolationem securus sit, quin semper sit de periculis futuris anxius, quemadmodum scriptum est, Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus; ideo subditur: Miserere mei, compatiendo mihi ne in futura pericula incidam, ne susceptam gratiam perdam, ne tibi ingratus inveniar; et exaudi orationem meam. Per hoc inflammatur, et quasi recalescit affectus, desiderando ut Deus misereatur ipsius.
paras.en: So the Prophet, speaking in the person of the Church or of any just man, says: [[4:2|When I called upon him|Quum invocarem]], [[4:2|the God of my justice heard me|exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ]]: that is, when I besought God inwardly, when I cried to him from inward affection, while I prayed with my whole mind turned and fixed on God; [[4:2|the God of my justice heard me|exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ]], that is, he from whom is all the good I have and all the justice I practise. And in this the Prophet teaches us to call upon God inwardly in all our distress. And by adding [[4:2|the God of my justice heard me|Exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ]], he kindles and strengthens our hope, so that we may call upon him with confidence; as if to say: As God heard me when I called upon him, so he will hear you too, if you pray purely, perseveringly and without any hesitation, trusting not in your own righteousness but in God's mercies. [[4:2|when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me|In tribulatione dilatasti mihi]]: that is, in the very affliction of my spirit, or the sickness of my body, thou hast consoled me inwardly, giving me true patience, by which I bear all adversity gladly and endure it with an even mind, so that my heart is enlarged within itself by a holy joy of the mind. For by sadness the heart is constricted and narrowed, but by joy it is enlarged or widened. Hence the Apostle, cheered by the memory of his disciples, says: [[2 Cor 6:11|our heart is enlarged|Cor, inquit, nostrum dilatatum est]]. But since a man ought always to be fearful and anxious so long as he lives in this present exile, and should not, because of the grace and consolation he has received from God, be so secure as not to be always anxious about dangers to come, as it is written: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]]; therefore it is added: [[4:2|Have mercy on me|Miserere mei]], by having compassion on me lest I fall into dangers to come, lest I lose the grace I have received, lest I be found ungrateful to thee; [[4:2|and hear my prayer|et exaudi orationem meam]]. By this the affection is kindled and as it were grows warm again, desiring that God have mercy on it.

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam caritas fraterna exigit, ut homo gratiam sibi divinitus impertitam, proximis suis communicare desideret, orando, docendo, aut exemplariter conversando: sicut in prima sua Canonica gloriosissimus apostolici ordinis princeps hortatur, Unusquisque, inquiens, sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei: idcirco Ecclesia seu quilibet justus, postquam coram Domino cor suum orando effudit, ad aliorum se informationem convertit, et ait: Filii hominum. In Hebræo habetur, Filii Adam. Adam enim apud Hebræos non solum est nomen proprium, sed etiam appellativum, designans idem quod homo. Itaque, Filii hominum, filii Adam, filii primorum parentum, qui portatis imaginem terreni, non cœlestis, id est, qui imitamini prævaricationem Adæ, non obedientiam Christi, usquequo gravi corde? id est, quamdiu habebitis cor deorsum? quousque in rebus transitoriis affectum demergitis, non quærentes quæ sursum sunt? Ut quid diligitis vanitatem, id est temporalia ista vanissima? quæ dum plus amantur quam Deus, vanissima sunt, quia mentem a summo bono avertunt, et vilissimis consolationibus implicant; et quæritis mendacium, decipiendo mutuo vosmetipsos? Vel, Ut quid quæritis mendacium, id est sensibilia bona, atque carnalia oblectamenta? quæ satietatem et felicitatem quamdam promittunt amanti; sed fallunt, quoniam desiderium non quiescit in ipsis: imo amori et delectationi carnali multæ admiscentur miseriæ, angustiæ, tristitiæ atque malitiæ.
paras.en: Further, since brotherly charity requires that a man desire to share with his neighbours the grace given him by God, by praying, teaching, or living as an example, as the most glorious prince of the apostolic order exhorts in his first Epistle: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace|Unusquisque, inquiens, sicut accepit gratiam]], he says, [[1 Pet 4:10|ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God|in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]]: therefore the Church, or any just man, after pouring out his heart before the Lord in prayer, turns to the instruction of others and says: [[4:3|O ye sons of men|Filii hominum]]. In the Hebrew it is: Sons of Adam. For among the Hebrews Adam is not only a proper name but also a common noun, meaning the same as man. So: [[4:3|O ye sons of men|Filii hominum]], sons of Adam, sons of our first parents, who bear the image of the earthly, not of the heavenly[[1 Cor 15:49||]], that is, who imitate the transgression of Adam, not the obedience of Christ, [[4:3|how long will you be dull of heart?|usquequo gravi corde]] that is, how long will you have your heart downwards? how long will you sink your affection in passing things, not seeking the things that are above? [[4:3|why do you love vanity|Ut quid diligitis vanitatem]], that is, these most vain temporal things? which, when they are loved more than God, are most vain, since they turn the mind away from the highest good and entangle it in the vilest consolations; [[4:3|and seek after lying?|et quæritis mendacium]] by deceiving one another? Or: [[4:3|why do you|Ut quid]] [[4:3|seek after lying?|quæritis mendacium]] that is, the goods of sense and carnal delights, which promise the lover a kind of fulness and happiness, but deceive him, since desire does not rest in them: indeed, with carnal love and delight are mingled many miseries, straits, sorrows and wickednesses.

paras.t: Consequenter ponit Scriptura considerationem, quæ peccatores merito debet a terrenis avertere, et ad Dei obsequium inflammare. Et scitote, id est, sapienter pensate, quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum, id est, mirabiliter adornavit et exaltavit sanctum suum, id est quemlibet sibi perfecte et pure ministrantem, vel per gratiam excellentem in præsenti, vel per gloriam jam in cœlo, vel per divina miracula, per quæ Deus ostendit hominibus quam accepta sit sibi vita sanctorum. Vel sic: Scitote quoniam Dominus, id est Deus Pater, mirificavit Sanctum suum, id est Jesum Christum, qui in evangelio Marci dicitur Sanctus Dei: quem mirificavit ante nativitatem, prædicendo per Prophetas eum nasciturum; in nativitate, educendo eum ex clauso Virginis alvo; post nativitatem, quoniam angeli ejus nativitatem pastoribus nuntiabant; atque in deserto, dum erat cum bestiis, et angeli sibi ministrabant; in morte quoque, per solis supernaturalem eclipsim; atque post mortem, per resuscitationem, ascensionem, ac Spiritus Sancti missionem. Dominus exaudiet me, quum clamavero ad eum. Hoc est verbum bonæ spei, quæ ex amore ad Deum nascitur. Nam qui diligit Deum, firmiter sperat, nihil eorum quæ ad veram salutem spectant, sibi a Deo fore negandum. In hoc quoque verbo, præstatur nobis spes adipiscendi gratiam Domini, per quam efficiamur sancti, et mirificemur ab ipso.
paras.en: Next Scripture sets down a consideration which ought rightly to turn sinners away from earthly things and kindle them to the service of God. [[4:4|Know ye also|Et scitote]], that is, weigh wisely, [[4:4|that the Lord hath made his holy one wonderful|quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum]], that is, has wonderfully adorned and exalted his holy one, that is, anyone who serves him perfectly and purely: either by excellent grace in the present, or by glory now in heaven, or by divine miracles, by which God shows men how acceptable to him is the life of the saints. Or thus: Know ye that the Lord, that is, God the Father, hath made wonderful his Holy One, that is, Jesus Christ, who in the gospel of Mark is called [[Mark 1:24|the Holy One of God|Sanctus Dei]]: whom he made wonderful before his birth, by foretelling through the prophets that he would be born; in his birth, by bringing him forth from the closed womb of the Virgin; after his birth, since angels announced his birth to the shepherds[[Luke 2:9||]]; and in the desert, when [[Mark 1:13|he was with beasts: and the angels ministered to him|erat cum bestiis, et angeli sibi ministrabant]][[Matt 4:11||]]; in his death too, by the supernatural eclipse of the sun[[Luke 23:45||]]; and after his death, by his raising, his ascension, and the sending of the Holy Ghost. [[4:4|the Lord will hear me when I shall cry unto him|Dominus exaudiet me, quum clamavero ad eum]]. This is the word of a good hope, which is born of love for God. For he who loves God hopes firmly that nothing of what concerns true salvation will be denied him by God. In this word too we are given the hope of obtaining the grace of the Lord, by which we may be made holy and made wonderful by him.

paras.t: Irascimini, et nolite peccare. Quædam est ira procedens ex zelo justitiæ, et rationem sequens ac sponte assumpta, quatenus homo per eam opus virtuosum fortius exsequatur. Hæc autem ira est bona, nisi fortasse excessive fervescat seu accendatur, vel graviorem pœnam exposcat, quam culpa meretur. De hac igitur ira exhortando dicitur: Irascimini, scilicet contra vitia, contra diabolum, contra negligentias vestras; et nolite peccare, id est permittere ut iræ commotio ita crescat, ut ratio perturbetur, vel immoderata ultio appetatur. Denique alia est ira per vitium, quæ rationem præcedit, et ei frequenter resistit, cujus tamen primi motus sunt veniales: et de ista ira intelligi potest quod dicitur, Irascimini; sed tunc dicitur hoc, non exhortando ut irascamur, sed remedium atque consilium exhibendo, quid nobis agendum sit quando motus iræ insurgit. Unde subjungitur, Et nolite peccare, id est, reprimite iram, ne per verba aut gestus aliis innotescat, aut certe in opus procedat: et hoc verba sequentia planius pandunt. Quæ dicitis in cordibus vestris, id est, in animo cogitatis, in cubilibus vestris compungimini, id est, in secreto mentis vestræ pœnitentiam agite de peccato cogitationum vestrarum, ne suggestioni illicitæ consentiatis. Corda enim sunt quasi cogitationum cubilia.
paras.en: [[4:5|Be ye angry, and sin not|Irascimini, et nolite peccare]]. There is a certain anger that proceeds from zeal for justice, follows reason and is taken up willingly, so that by it a man may carry out a virtuous work more vigorously. And this anger is good, unless perhaps it boils or is kindled to excess, or demands a heavier punishment than the fault deserves. Of this anger, then, it is said by way of exhortation: [[4:5|Be ye angry|Irascimini]], namely against vices, against the devil, against your own negligences; [[4:5|and sin not|et nolite peccare]], that is, do not let the stirring of anger grow so that reason is disturbed or immoderate vengeance is sought. Further, there is another anger, through vice, which goes before reason and often resists it, though its first motions are venial: and of this anger the word [[4:5|Be ye angry|Irascimini]] can be understood; but then it is said not to exhort us to be angry, but to give a remedy and counsel as to what we must do when a motion of anger rises. Hence it is added: [[4:5|and sin not|Et nolite peccare]], that is, keep down your anger, so that it is not made known to others by words or gestures, or at least does not go on into deed: and the words that follow show this more plainly. [[4:5|the things you say in your hearts|Quæ dicitis in cordibus vestris]], that is, what you think in your mind, [[4:5|be sorry for them upon your beds|in cubilibus vestris compungimini]], that is, do penance in the secret of your mind for the sin of your thoughts, lest you consent to an unlawful suggestion. For hearts are as it were the beds of the thoughts.

paras.t: Quia vero non sufficit a vitiis abstinere, ideo subditur: Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ. Sacrificium appellatur, quod Deo offertur. Externum autem sacrificium, signum est sacrificii interioris, quo spiritus se ipsum Deo offert per sanctam devotionem, veram caritatem, ac intimam humilitatem, se ipsum et omnia sua Deo adscribens, ejusque venerationi impendens quidquid est, potest, et agit. Itaque, Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ, id est, omnia opera vestra interiora et exteriora ad Dei honorem exercete; et ut Deo grata sint, satagite laudabiliter conversari, justeque vivere. Sed quia ex tali conversatione posset aliquis se ipsum extollere, et quasi de propriis meritis gloriari atque confidere, ideo addit: et sperate in Domino: non in vestris justitiis, sed in misericordia ejus, a quo est omnis sufficientia vestra. Ignorantes enim Dei justitiam, et suam volentes constituere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti.
paras.en: But since it is not enough to abstain from vices, it is added: [[4:6|Offer up the sacrifice of justice|Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ]]. That is called a sacrifice which is offered to God. And the outward sacrifice is a sign of the inward sacrifice, by which the spirit offers itself to God through holy devotion, true charity and deep humility, ascribing itself and all its own to God, and spending in his worship whatever it is, can and does. So: [[4:6|Offer up the sacrifice of justice|Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ]], that is, do all your works, inward and outward, for the honour of God; and that they may be pleasing to God, take care to live praiseworthily and justly. But since from such a life someone might exalt himself, and as it were glory and trust in his own merits, he therefore adds: [[4:6|and trust in the Lord|et sperate in Domino]]: not in your own righteousness, but in his mercy, from whom is all your sufficiency[[2 Cor 3:5||]]. For [[Rom 10:3|not knowing the justice of God|Ignorantes enim Dei justitiam]] [[Rom 10:3|and seeking to establish their own|et suam volentes constituere]] [Denis reads *volentes*, "wishing", for *quærentes*], [[Rom 10:3|have not submitted themselves to the justice of God|justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti]].

paras.t: Multi dicunt: Quis ostendit nobis bona? Hæc est quæstio malignorum, qui vel providentiam Dei negant, vel esse aliam vitam post istam non putant. De quibus Malachias dicit: Prævaluerunt super me verba vestra, dicit Dominus, et dixistis: Vanus est qui servit Domino; et quod emolumentum, quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et ambulavimus tristes coram Domino? Hi itaque dicunt: Quis ostendit nobis bona? id est, quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat, et an sit vita in qua unicuique justa retributio fiat? Potest quoque verbum istud aliter introduci. Multi namque, videlicet Academici, asserebant non posse hominem aliquid certo scire: unde de omnibus dubitabant, et solum opinative loquebantur. De his ergo ait Propheta: Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona? id est, quis facit veritatem certo cognoscere? Ad hanc vero quæstionem respondet Propheta:
paras.en: [[4:6|many say, Who sheweth us good things?|Multi dicunt: Quis ostendit nobis bona]] This is the question of the wicked, who either deny the providence of God or do not think there is another life after this one. Of whom Malachias says: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me, saith the Lord|Prævaluerunt super me verba vestra, dicit Dominus]], and you have said: [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God|Vanus est qui servit Domino]]; [[Mal 3:14|and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances, and that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord|et quod emolumentum, quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et ambulavimus tristes coram Domino?]]? So these say: [[4:6|Who sheweth us good things?|Quis ostendit nobis bona]] that is, [[Eccles 3:21|Who knoweth if the spirit of the children of Adam ascend|quis novit si spiritus filiorum Adam ascendat]], and whether there is a life in which a just reward is given to each? This word can also be brought in otherwise. For many, namely the Academics, asserted that man cannot know anything for certain: hence they doubted everything and spoke only as a matter of opinion. Of these, then, the Prophet says: [[4:6|many say, Who sheweth us good things?|Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona]] that is, who makes us know the truth for certain? And the Prophet answers this question:

paras.t: Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine: id est, animæ nostræ impressa est quædam participatio luminis vultus tui, hoc est divini intellectus; et in claritate hujus lucis ostenduntur nobis bona, id est, intellectualiter videmus animæ immortalitatem, divinam providentiam, justam omnium præmiationem, et certitudinaliter rerum veritates agnoscimus. Hoc autem lumen signatum super nos, quamvis dici posset naturale lumen intellectus humani, per quod philosophi multa de prædictis veraciter cognoverunt; melius tamen intelligitur supernaturale lumen, videlicet fides et splendor gratiæ Dei, reformans in nobis imaginem beatissimæ Trinitatis, seu donum sapientiæ atque scientiæ. Dedisti lætitiam in corde meo: id est, o Domine, ex hoc quod scio esse signatum super me lumen vultus tui, spiritualiter gaudeo, et vehementer exsulto: quod utique gaudium, ne ingratus exsistam, tibi adscribo.
paras.en: [[4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]]: that is, there is impressed on our soul a certain share in the light of thy countenance, that is, of the divine intellect; and in the brightness of this light good things are shown us: that is, we see with the intellect the immortality of the soul, divine providence, the just rewarding of all, and we know the truths of things with certainty. And this light signed upon us, though it could be called the natural light of the human intellect, by which the philosophers truly knew much about the things just mentioned, is better understood as a supernatural light, namely faith and the splendour of God's grace, which reforms in us the image of the most blessed Trinity, or the gift of wisdom and knowledge. [[4:7|thou hast given gladness in my heart|Dedisti lætitiam in corde meo]]: that is, O Lord, because I know that the light of thy countenance is signed upon me, I rejoice spiritually and exult greatly: and this joy I ascribe to thee, lest I be ungrateful.

paras.t: A fructu frumenti, vini et olei sui, id est ex abundantia temporalium rerum, multiplicati sunt, id est, ab illo summo uno, quod solum necessarium est, multipliciter aversi sunt, miserabiliter vagantes atque distracti. Qui? nisi de quibus jam dixit, Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona? id est, homines sæculares, mundi divitiis et carnis deliciis obtenebrati: qui cor suum in Deo nequaquam simplex esse sinunt, sed in caducis bonis ipsum dispergunt. De quibus Osee ait: Divisum est cor eorum; nunc interibunt. Et apostolus Judas in sua Canonica: Hi sunt qui segregant semetipsos, animales, spiritum non habentes. Verumtamen est quoddam frumentum et quoddam vinum, a quorum fructu bonum est multiplicari, hoc est fecunditate ac numero augeri. De quibus Zacharias: Quid bonum Domini, et quid pulchrum ejus, nisi frumentum electorum, et vinum germinans virgines? Quod melius exponi non potest, nisi de Sacramento corporis ac sanguinis Christi. Similiter de quodam oleo postea dicitur: Impinguasti in oleo caput meum. Sed ista non sunt frumentum, vinum, et oleum eorum de quibus nunc ait Scriptura, sed electorum: et ideo addidit, Sui.
paras.en: [[4:8|By the fruit of their corn, their wine, and oil|A fructu frumenti, vini et olei sui]], that is, by the abundance of temporal things, [[4:8|they are multiplied|multiplicati sunt]], that is, they are turned away in many ways from that highest One which alone is necessary[[Luke 10:42||]], wandering and distracted to their misery. Who? Who but those of whom he has just said: [[4:6|many say, Who sheweth us good things?|Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona]] that is, worldly men, darkened by the riches of the world and the delights of the flesh, who do not let their heart be single in God, but scatter it among perishing goods. Of whom Osee says: [[Osee 10:2|Their heart is divided: now they shall perish|Divisum est cor eorum; nunc interibunt]]. And the apostle Jude in his Epistle: [[Jude 1:19|These are they who separate themselves, sensual men, having not the Spirit|Hi sunt qui segregant semetipsos, animales, spiritum non habentes]]. But there is a certain corn and a certain wine by whose fruit it is good to be multiplied, that is, increased in fruitfulness and number. Of which Zacharias says: [[Zach 9:17|what is the good thing of him, and what is his beautiful thing, but the corn of the elect, and wine springing forth virgins?|Quid bonum Domini, et quid pulchrum ejus, nisi frumentum electorum, et vinum germinans virgines?]] Which cannot be better expounded than of the Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. Likewise of a certain oil it is said later: [[22:5|Thou hast anointed my head with oil|Impinguasti in oleo caput meum]]. But these are not the corn, wine and oil of those of whom Scripture now speaks, but of the elect: and therefore it added [[4:8|their|sui]].

paras.t: Hi ergo jam dicti, sic multiplicati, sunt instabiles, vagi, distracti; sed ego (dicit Ecclesia vel quilibet justus), In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam. Pax est tranquillitas bonæ ordinationis, seu quies a perturbatione: sicut dum caro obedit spiritui, sensualitas rationi, et ratio Deo. Id ipsum vero, est Deus sublimis et benedictus, apud quem non est transmutatio nec vicissitudinis obumbratio, quia semper et invariabiliter æque perfectus, æque beatus, et æque gloriosus exsistit. Itaque, In pace, id est in vera mentis tranquillitate ac stabili ordinatione, in id ipsum, id est in Deum æternum qui semper idem ipse est, dormiam, id est, ab exteriori occupatione, a sensibilium attrectatione cessabo, et requiescam, id est, in divinæ dulcedinis degustatione, in divinæ bonitatis contemplatione, in divini amoris ardore suaviter repausabo, nunc quidem inchoative per gratiam, in futuro autem consummative per gloriam: et hæc ob id, o Domine Deus, dicere audeo, Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me. Quamvis siquidem de nullo desperandum sit in vita præsenti, sed omnibus dederit Deus spem posse adipisci ea, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit; tamen homines justos constituit Deus singulariter in spe, quia ex receptione præsentium munerum certa fit eis exspectatio futurorum. Ipsa etiam divina consolatio in præsenti experta, quid aliud est, nisi pignus et arrha felicitatis futuræ, gaudiique cœlestis prælibatio quædam? Justus igitur beneficia Dei sibi collata considerans, atque ex divinæ pietatis contemplatione, specialem et magnam ad Deum fiduciam mente concipiens, secure ac amorose dicat Altissimo: Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me.
paras.en: These just mentioned, then, multiplied in this way, are unstable, wandering, distracted; but I (says the Church or any just man) [[4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam]]. Peace is the tranquillity of good order, or rest from disturbance: as when the flesh obeys the spirit, sensuality reason, and reason God. And the Self-same is God, most high and blessed, [[Jas 1:17|with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration|apud quem non est transmutatio nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]], since he is always and unchangeably equally perfect, equally blessed and equally glorious. So: [[4:9|In peace|In pace]], that is, in true tranquillity of mind and settled order, [[4:9|in the self same|in id ipsum]], that is, in the eternal God, who is always the selfsame, [[4:9|I will sleep|dormiam]], that is, I will cease from outward business and from handling the things of sense, [[4:9|and I will rest|et requiescam]], that is, I will repose sweetly in tasting the divine sweetness, in contemplating the divine goodness, in the ardour of divine love: now indeed in its beginning by grace, but in the future in its fulness by glory: and this, O Lord God, I dare to say because [[4:10|For thou, O Lord, singularly hast settled me in hope|Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me]]. For although no one is to be despaired of in this present life, and God has given to all the hope of being able to obtain the things which [[1 Cor 2:9|eye hath not seen, nor ear heard|nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit]], yet God has settled just men singularly in hope, since from the receiving of present gifts the expectation of things to come becomes certain for them. And the divine consolation itself, experienced in the present, what else is it but a pledge and earnest of future happiness and a kind of foretaste of heavenly joy? Let the just man, then, considering the benefits God has bestowed on him, and conceiving in his mind from the contemplation of the divine loving-kindness a special and great confidence in God, say securely and lovingly to the Most High: [[4:10|For thou, O Lord, singularly hast settled me in hope|Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me]].

4.title: QUOMODO PSALMUS ISTE QUARTUS MULTIPLICITER POSSIT EXPONI; ET SPECIALITER DE EXPOSITIONE EJUS IN PERSONA CHRISTI.
4.title_en: How this fourth Psalm can be expounded in many ways; and in particular, its exposition in the person of Christ

paras.t: Quoniam quidem psalmus iste jam ad litteram expositus est de ipsa Ecclesia et quolibet homine justo, certum est ipsum litteraliter posse exponi de David, qui auctor est psalmi istius, eo quod ipse in numero contineatur Sanctorum: et ipse veraciter a Deo sæpe exauditus est quum invocaret, et in tribulationibus suis Dominus contulit ei patientiam magnam, ita ut dilataretur cor ejus, quia agnovit in spiritu, quod postea evidenter Apostolus docuit, quod non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam. Hoc quoque quod sequitur, Et scitote quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum, de David litteraliter verum est. Nam de manu Saulis, ac multis periculis, et variis persecutionibus, mirabiliter valde a Deo præservatus salvatusque fuit; et ipse leonem ac ursum occidit, quemadmodum in libris Regum scribitur; et spiritu prophetiæ impletus est, viditque angelum Domini percutientem populum Israel.
paras.en: Since this psalm has already been expounded according to the letter of the Church herself and of any just man, it is certain that it can be expounded literally of David, who is the author of this psalm, since he is numbered among the Saints: and he was truly often heard by God when he called upon him, and in his tribulations the Lord gave him great patience, so that his heart was enlarged, because he knew in spirit what the Apostle afterwards plainly taught, that [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|non sunt condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]]. What follows, too, [[4:4|Know ye also that the Lord hath made his holy one wonderful|Et scitote quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum]], is literally true of David. For he was most wonderfully preserved and saved by God from the hand of Saul[[1 Kings 19:1||]][[1 Kings 21:1||]] and from many dangers and various persecutions; and he killed a lion and a bear, as is written in the books of Kings[[1 Kings 17:34||]]; and he was filled with the spirit of prophecy, and saw the angel of the Lord striking the people of Israel[[2 Kings 24:17||]][[1 Par 21:16||]].

paras.t: Porro secundum hanc expositionem litteralem de David vel Synagoga, exponeretur hic psalmus de quolibet homine justo vel Ecclesia secundum tropologiam; sed quia nunc psalmus iste de Ecclesia ac quolibet justo expositus est, alia expositione non eget. Sed diligenter pensandum est omni devoto hunc psalmum legenti, ut intente advertat propria verba, sicque conversari conetur, ut in propria persona hunc psalmum vere possit proferre. Quod utique fiet, si semper assuescat orare, si in omni causa et necessitate fiducialiter recurrat ad Deum, sicut ad unicum Salvatorem, fidelissimum adjutorem, spemque singularem: tunc enim non solum credet, sed experimentaliter sentiet, se frequenter exaudiri a Domino; sicque cum magna gratiarum actione concinet: Quum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ. Insuper, tanta gratia implebit eum Dominus, ut non solum dura et aspera quæ sibi contingunt, lætanter sustineat; sed paratus erit pro Dei amore et peccatorum suorum emundatione semper graviora perferre. Et hoc est vere in tribulationibus dilatari, habere animum ad duriora paratum, exemplo sancti David, qui quum fugeret a facie Absalon, dixit: Si inveni gratiam in oculis Domini, reducet me; si autem dixerit, Non places, præsto sum, faciat quod bonum est coram se, id est, de regno expellat me, vel si ei placet, occidat me.
paras.en: Further, according to this literal exposition of David or of the Synagogue, this psalm would be expounded of any just man or of the Church according to tropology; but since this psalm has now been expounded of the Church and of any just man, it needs no other exposition. But every devout person who reads this psalm must ponder carefully, so as to pay close heed to the very words, and strive so to live that he can truly utter this psalm in his own person. And this will surely come about if he makes a habit of always praying, if in every cause and need he runs back with confidence to God as to his only Saviour, most faithful helper and singular hope: for then he will not only believe, but will feel by experience, that he is often heard by the Lord; and so with great thanksgiving he will sing: [[4:2|When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me|Quum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ]]. Moreover, the Lord will fill him with such grace that he will not only bear gladly the hard and harsh things that befall him, but will always be ready to endure heavier things for the love of God and the cleansing of his sins. And this is truly to be enlarged in tribulations: to have a mind ready for harder things, after the example of holy David, who, when he fled from the face of Absalom, said: [[2 Kings 15:25|if I shall find grace in the sight of the Lord, he will bring me again|Si inveni gratiam in oculis Domini, reducet me]]; [[2 Kings 15:26|But if he shall say to me: Thou pleasest me not: I am ready, let him do that which is good before him|si autem dixerit, Non places, præsto sum, faciat quod bonum est coram se]]: that is, let him drive me out of the kingdom, or, if it please him, kill me.

paras.t: Potest etiam psalmus hic specialiter satis de Christo exponi, eritque expositio talis allegorica, si de David litteraliter exponatur. Verumtamen de nullo tam proprie potest exponi sicut de Christo, solam litteram assequendo. Christus igitur ratione naturæ assumptæ, vel Propheta in persona Christi loquens, ait: Quum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ, id est Deus unus ac trinus, vel ipsummet Verbum ac Filius Dei, qui meam humanitatem assumpsit. Jam enim superius dictum est, quod Christus semper exaudiebatur a Deo pro sua reverentia. In tribulatione dilatasti mihi. Hoc Christo potissime competit, quoniam in omni persecutione et passione, quam ab hora nativitatis usque ad mortem crucis sustinuit, nunquam inordinate tristatus est; sed omnia pro mundi salute libentissime atque affectuosissime pertulit, paratus semper ad duriora, si Patri placuisset. Iterum illud convenit Christo, quia in omni sua adversitate et pœna habuit gaudium beatificæ fruitionis, et ita Deus spiritualiter dilatavit et lætificavit mentem ipsius. Oravit quoque Christus sibi a Deo misereri, non propter propriæ culpæ remissionem, sed vel propter Ecclesiæ culpam, vel propter corporis sui a morte resuscitationem et glorificationem.
paras.en: This psalm can also quite fittingly be expounded specially of Christ; and such an exposition will be allegorical if it is expounded of David literally. Yet it can be expounded of no one so properly as of Christ, following the letter alone. Christ, then, by reason of the nature he assumed, or the Prophet speaking in the person of Christ, says: [[4:2|When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me|Quum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus justitiæ meæ]], that is, God one and three, or the very Word and Son of God, who assumed my humanity. For it has already been said above that Christ was always heard by God [[Heb 5:7|for his reverence|pro sua reverentia]]. [[4:2|when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me|In tribulatione dilatasti mihi]]. This befits Christ above all, since in every persecution and suffering which he bore from the hour of his birth to the death of the cross he was never inordinately saddened, but bore all things most willingly and lovingly for the salvation of the world, always ready for harder things, had it pleased the Father. This fits Christ in another way too: because in all his adversity and pain he had the joy of beatific fruition, and so God spiritually enlarged and gladdened his mind. Christ also prayed God to [[4:2|Have mercy on me|misereri]] [Denis: *sibi a Deo misereri*, to be shown mercy by God], not for the remission of any fault of his own, but either for the fault of the Church, or for the raising of his body from death and its glorification.

paras.t: Et scitote quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum. Quomodo hoc competat Christo, in præcedenti expositione tactum est; et nunc adjiciendum, quod Deus benedictus et sanctus Filium suum mirificavit per totum mundum, dando Apostolis aliisque sanctissimis Christi ministris gratiam miraculorum, spiritum prophetiæ, genera linguarum, excellentiam vitæ, idololatriæ exstirpationem; et hactenus non cessat mirificare Filium suum dilectum, et glorificare fidem ipsius per magna prodigia, appendens sigillum testimonii sui Evangelio Christi.
paras.en: [[4:4|Know ye also that the Lord hath made his holy one wonderful|Et scitote quoniam mirificavit Dominus sanctum suum]]. How this befits Christ was touched on in the preceding exposition; and now it must be added that God, blessed and holy, made his Son wonderful throughout the whole world, by giving the Apostles and the other most holy ministers of Christ the grace of miracles, the spirit of prophecy, kinds of tongues[[Mark 16:17||]], excellence of life and the rooting out of idolatry; and to this day he does not cease to make his beloved Son wonderful, and to glorify his faith by great wonders, setting the seal of his own testimony to the Gospel of Christ.

paras.t: Irascimini, et nolite peccare. Hoc est verbum Christi ad Judæos incredulos, tanquam dicat: Si oritur in vobis aliquis motus iracundiæ contra me, dum auditis me dicere quod Christus sim, judex mundi et Filius Dei, eo quod videatis me carnis infirmitati ac mortalitati subjectum, nolite peccare, id est, nolite consentire, nolite blasphemare, nolite esse increduli, qui videtis me talia facere, qualia alius nullus facere valet. Opera enim quæ dedit mihi Pater, testimonium perhibent de me.
paras.en: [[4:5|Be ye angry, and sin not|Irascimini, et nolite peccare]]. This is Christ's word to the unbelieving Jews, as if to say: If any movement of anger against me arises in you when you hear me say that I am the Christ, the judge of the world and the Son of God, because you see me subject to the weakness and mortality of the flesh, [[4:5|sin not|nolite peccare]], that is, do not consent, do not blaspheme, do not be unbelieving, you who see me doing such things as no other can do[[John 15:24||]]. For [[John 5:36|the works which the Father hath given me|Opera enim quæ dedit mihi Pater]] [[John 10:25|give testimony of me|testimonium perhibent de me]] [Denis joins John 5:36 to John 10:25; the margin seems to read Joann. x].

paras.t: Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ. Hoc est verbum Domini Salvatoris ad […] Ecclesiam, imo ad omnes qui post Evangelii promulgationem salvari desiderant, quasi dicat: Cessate a sacrificiis veteris legis, quæ non possunt auferre peccatum, nec accedentem perficere, quia non continent gratiam, sed figurant. Unde Isaias: Qui immolat bovem, quasi qui interficiat virum: qui mactat pecus, quasi qui excerebret canem.
