Ab his ergo sacrificiis tempore novæ legis cessate, et sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ, id est Sacramentum altaris, quod est finis et consummatio, ac veritas omnium sacrificiorum legalium. Hoc, inquam, sacrificate, id est, Deo offerte, vel celebrando, vel celebranti adstando.
paras.en: [[4:6|Offer up the sacrifice of justice|Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ]]. This is the word of the Lord our Saviour to […] Church, nay, to all who after the promulgation of the Gospel desire to be saved, as if to say: Cease from the sacrifices of the old law, which cannot take away sin[[Heb 10:4||]] nor make him perfect who comes to them[[Heb 10:1||]], because they do not contain grace but only figure it. Hence Isaias: [[Is 66:3|He that sacrificeth an ox, is as if he slew a man: he that killeth a sheep in sacrifice, as if he should brain a dog|Qui immolat bovem, quasi qui interficiat virum: qui mactat pecus, quasi qui excerebret canem]]. Cease, then, from these sacrifices in the time of the new law, and [[4:6|Offer up the sacrifice of justice|sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ]], that is, the Sacrament of the altar, which is the end and consummation, and the truth, of all the sacrifices of the law. This, I say, offer up, that is, offer to God, either by celebrating or by assisting the one who celebrates.

paras.t: A fructu frumenti, vini et olei sui, multiplicati sunt. Quamvis istud superius de malis expositum sit, potest tamen de bonis exponi, sicut et S. Thomas in cantu de festo Corporis Christi intelligit, ubi ex verbis istis talem antiphonam sumpsit: A fructu frumenti, vini et olei multiplicati fideles, in pace Christi requiescunt. Est igitur sensus: Fideles multiplicati sunt fide et merito, a fructu frumenti, vini, id est ab effectu et gratia corporis et sanguinis Christi, et olei sui, id est a fructu spiritualis consolationis, quam in Eucharistiæ communione percipiunt.
paras.en: [[4:8|By the fruit of their corn, their wine, and oil, they are multiplied|A fructu frumenti, vini et olei sui, multiplicati sunt]]. Although this was expounded above of the wicked, it can also be expounded of the good, as St Thomas too understands it in the office of the feast of Corpus Christi, where he took from these words this antiphon: The faithful, multiplied by the fruit of corn, wine and oil, rest in the peace of Christ. The sense, then, is: The faithful are multiplied in faith and merit [[4:8|By the fruit of their corn, their wine|a fructu frumenti, vini]], that is, by the effect and grace of the body and blood of Christ, [[4:8|and oil|et olei sui]], that is, by the fruit of the spiritual consolation which they receive in the communion of the Eucharist.

paras.t: In pace in idipsum dormiam et requiescam. Hoc Christus de sua morte ac sepultura affirmat. Dormivit enim in cruce et requievit in monumento, nec in aliquo horum interior mentis suæ tranquillitas concussa est, turbata, vel diminuta, sed in omni sua pœnali angustia constans, solidus atque in Deo immobilis mansit. Denique aliter exponi potest. Anima enim Christi semper videbat faciem Dei Patris, quia viatrix non erat: sicque a primo suæ creationis momento, in summa ac tranquillissima pace fuit: et in Deo ab omni distractione atque aversione dormivit, et in ipso ab omni inquietudine immobiliter requievit. Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me. Verba sunt Christi, ut homo est, ad Deum. Christus autem quia purus viator non exstitit, ideo nec fidem habebat, nec spem, prout spes est virtus theologica, habens Deum pro immediato objecto, sicut quum dicimus, quod spes est exspectatio futuræ beatitudinis. Nunquam enim beatitudo, futura vel absens fuit animæ Christi. Sed prout spes est quæcumque exspectatio boni futuri, sic Christus habuit spem. Exspectabat enim resuscitari a morte, et glorificari in corpore. Ob hanc exspectationem ait ad Patrem: In pace dormiam, etc., quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe, videlicet resurrectionis et glorificationis, constituisti me. Quamvis enim omnes fideles habeant spem resurgendi et glorificandi in die novissimo, Christus tamen ut homo, constitutus fuit in spe resurgendi ac glorificandi singulari modo, quoniam die tertia speravit in corpore impassibili et glorioso resurgere.
paras.en: [[4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in idipsum dormiam et requiescam]]. Christ says this of his death and burial. For he slept on the cross and rested in the tomb; and in neither of these was the inner calm of his mind shaken, troubled or lessened, but in all his painful distress he remained steadfast, firm and immovable in God. It can also be expounded otherwise. For the soul of Christ always saw the face of God the Father, since it was not a wayfarer [*viatrix*: still on the way, not yet possessing God]: and so from the first moment of its creation it was in the highest and most tranquil peace, and in God it slept from all distraction and turning away, and in him it rested immovably from all disquiet. [[4:10|For thou, O Lord, singularly hast settled me in hope|Quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter in spe constituisti me]]. These are the words of Christ, as he is man, to God. Now since Christ was not simply a wayfarer, he had neither faith nor hope, taking hope as the theological virtue that has God for its immediate object, as when we say that hope is the expectation of future beatitude. For beatitude was never future or absent to the soul of Christ. But taking hope as any expectation of a future good, Christ had hope. For he expected to be raised from death and glorified in his body. Because of this expectation he says to the Father: [[4:9|In peace|In pace]] [[4:9|I will sleep|dormiam]], etc., [[4:10|For thou, O Lord, singularly|quoniam tu, Domine, singulariter]] [[4:10|in hope|in spe]], namely of resurrection and glorification, [[4:10|hast settled me|constituisti me]]. For although all the faithful have the hope of rising again and being glorified on the last day, yet Christ as man was settled in the hope of rising again and being glorified in a singular manner, since he hoped to rise again on the third day[[Matt 16:21||]][[Matt 20:19||]][[Mark 9:30||]] in a body impassible and glorious.

paras.t: Cetera autem quæ nunc exposita non sunt, ex dictis in præcedenti expositione plana sunt.
paras.en: The rest, which has not been expounded now, is plain from what was said in the preceding exposition.

paras.t: Precatio. Da, quæsumus, omnipotens Deus, lætitiam Spiritus tui in corde nostro: ut sacrificantes sacrificium justitiæ, ac jugiter in te sperantes, instante termino vitæ, in pace Christi dormiamus, et in ejus regno perenniter requiescamus.
paras.en: Prayer. Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, the gladness of thy Spirit in our heart: that, offering the sacrifice of justice and hoping in thee always, we may, when the end of life is at hand, sleep in the peace of Christ, and rest for ever in his kingdom.

paras.t: Est autem titulus psalmi hujus: In finem pro ea quæ hæreditatem consequitur. In Genesi legitur, quemadmodum Abraham duas habebat uxores: quarum una videlicet Sara, cum Isaac filio suo mansit in domo, et hæreditatem obtinuit; altera, videlicet Agar, cum filio Ismaele expulsa est. Posset ergo hic psalmus ad litteram explanari secundum istam historiam, quod psalmus iste conscriptus sit pro Sara et filio ejus; sed multo convenientius exponitur de re significata, videlicet de Ecclesia, quæ significatur per Saram; Synagoga, quæ significatur per Agar, dimissa ac reprobata. Est igitur sensus: Psalmus iste dirigens nos in finem, id est in Christum vel in hæreditatem cælestem seu vitam æternam, est pro ea, scilicet Ecclesia, quæ consequitur hæreditatem, id est Deum vel Dei fruitionem. Deus namque appellatur nostra hæreditas, quoniam ipse alit et continet nos; nos quoque dicimur hæreditas Dei, quia colit et regit nos, et sanguine suo redemit nos.
paras.en: The title of this psalm is: [[5:1|Unto the end, for her that obtaineth the inheritance|In finem pro ea quæ hæreditatem consequitur]]. We read in Genesis how Abraham had two wives[[Gen 21:1||]]: one of them, namely Sara, stayed in the house with her son Isaac and obtained the inheritance; the other, namely Agar, was cast out with her son Ismael. So this psalm could be explained literally according to that history, as written for Sara and her son; but it is far more fittingly expounded of the thing signified, namely of the Church, which is signified by Sara, the Synagogue, which is signified by Agar, being sent away and rejected[[Gal 4:22||]]. So the sense is: This psalm, directing us [[5:1|unto the end|in finem]], that is, to Christ, or to the heavenly inheritance or eternal life, is [[5:1|for her|pro ea]], namely the Church, [[5:1|that obtaineth the inheritance|quæ consequitur hæreditatem]], that is, God or the enjoyment of God. For God is called our inheritance because he feeds and holds us; and we are called God's inheritance because he tends and rules us and has redeemed us with his blood.

paras.t: Loquens Propheta in persona Ecclesiæ, pro se suisque membris orantis, primo proponit orationem, et ait: Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine; intellige clamorem meum. Intende voci orationis meæ. Eumdem cordis affectum ter explicavit, quatenus desiderium cordis tanto interius arderet calidius, quanto verbis exprimeretur frequentius. Quanto namque verba cordis affectum significantia sæpius iterantur, tanto affectio cordis amplius inflammatur, et ita oratio citius effectum sortitur. Unde modus Scripturæ est in his quæ affectum respiciunt, idem sæpe repetere, ut accendatur affectus.
paras.en: The Prophet, speaking in the person of the Church praying for herself and her members, first sets out the prayer and says: [[5:2|Give ear, O Lord, to my words, understand my cry|Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine; intellige clamorem meum]]. [[5:3|Hearken to the voice of my prayer|Intende voci orationis meæ]]. He has expressed the same affection of the heart three times, so that the heart's desire might burn the more hotly within the more often it was put into words. For the more often words signifying the heart's affection are repeated, the more the heart's affection is inflamed, and so the prayer the sooner obtains its effect. Hence it is the way of Scripture, in things that concern the affections, to repeat the same thing often, so that the affection may be kindled.

paras.t: Posset tamen inter hæc assignari distinctio, ut dicatur: Verba mea, id est orationem vocalem, auribus percipe, Domine; et intellige clamorem meum, id est cordis affectum. Per clamorem enim intelligit sacra Scriptura spiritualem clamorem. Aures Domini sunt sapientia ejus et bonitas. Per sapientiam quippe cuncta cognoscit ac percipit. Per bonitatem vero dona naturæ et munera gratiæ præstat, dans omnibus affluenter, et non improperans. Dicit quoque ad Deum, Intellige clamorem meum: non quod Deus possit aliquid non intelligere: omnia enim aperta et nuda sunt oculis ejus; sed, Intellige, inquit, id est, per approbationem agnosce, per affectum adverte, per sapientiam tuam succurre.
paras.en: Yet a distinction could be drawn between them, so that it is said: [[5:2|Give ear, O Lord, to my words|Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine]], that is, to my spoken prayer; and [[5:2|understand my cry|intellige clamorem meum]], that is, the affection of my heart. For by a cry holy Scripture understands a spiritual cry. The ears of the Lord are his wisdom and goodness. For by his wisdom he knows and perceives all things; and by his goodness he bestows the gifts of nature and the gifts of grace, giving [[Jas 1:5|to all men abundantly and upbraideth not|omnibus affluenter, et non improperans]]. He also says to God, [[5:2|understand my cry|Intellige clamorem meum]]: not that God could fail to understand anything, for [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open to his eyes|omnia enim aperta et nuda sunt oculis ejus]]; but [[5:2|understand|Intellige]], he says, that is, acknowledge it by approving it, attend to it with love, come to my help by thy wisdom.

paras.t: Rex meus, ratione gubernationis, et Deus meus, ratione creationis. Sed quum Deus sit omnium rex et Deus, cur dicit, Rex meus et Deus meus, nisi propter specialem providentiam, qua providet suis electis, et dirigit eos in vitam æternam, a malis præservans, a periculis eruens? Sic dicit: Deus meus, quia te specialiter colo, tibi soli adhæreo, me totum tibi committo. Hoc dicere nequeunt, quorum deus venter est, aurum, vel aliquid tale.
paras.en: [[5:3|O my King|Rex meus]], by reason of governing, [[5:3|and my God|et Deus meus]], by reason of creating. But since God is the king and God of all, why does he say [[5:3|O my King and my God|Rex meus et Deus meus]], if not because of the special providence with which he provides for his elect and directs them to eternal life, keeping them from evils and rescuing them from dangers? So he says [[5:3|my God|Deus meus]] because I worship thee specially, cleave to thee alone, commit myself wholly to thee. This cannot be said by those [[Phil 3:19|whose God is their belly|quorum deus venter est]], or gold, or some such thing.

paras.t: Quoniam ad te orabo, Domine, mane exaudies vocem meam: id est, quia orabo, o Domine, ad te, dirigendo affectum ad te, vel ad te adipiscendum atque fruendum, ut possideam te in patria in æternum; vel, Ad te, id est, ordinans precem meam ad honorem et gloriam nominis tui. Quoniam ergo ita orabo ad te, ideo mane exaudies vocem meam, id est cito et festinanter; vel, Mane, id est, quum lucem miserationum tuarum effuderis super me; vel, Mane, id est initio operationum bonarum. Et antequam finiatur oratio mea, exaudies me: nam sicut per Isaiam testatus es, Adhuc, inquiens, illis loquentibus, ego dicam, Adsum. Et dicit, Mane exaudies, non præsumendo, sed sperando, et misericordiam provocando.
paras.en: [[5:4|For to thee will I pray: O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice|Quoniam ad te orabo, Domine, mane exaudies vocem meam]]: that is, because I will pray to thee, O Lord, directing my affection to thee, or to obtaining and enjoying thee, so that I may possess thee in the fatherland for ever; or, [[5:4|to thee|Ad te]], that is, ordering my prayer to the honour and glory of thy name. Since then I will pray to thee in this way, therefore [[5:4|in the morning thou shalt hear my voice|mane exaudies vocem meam]], that is, quickly and in haste; or, [[5:4|in the morning|Mane]], that is, when thou hast poured out upon me the light of thy mercies; or, [[5:4|in the morning|Mane]], that is, at the beginning of good works. And before my prayer is ended thou wilt hear me: for as thou hast testified by Isaias, saying: [[Is 65:24|as they are yet speaking|Adhuc, inquiens, illis loquentibus]], I will say: Here I am [the margin gives Is. lxv, 24; Denis ends the verse with words like those of Is 58:9, “he shall say, Here I am”]. And he says [[5:4|in the morning thou shalt hear|Mane exaudies]] not presuming, but hoping, and calling forth mercy.

paras.t: Mane, id est quum Christus, qui est sol justitiæ et splendor lucis æternæ, illuminaverit animam meam sedentem in tenebris, atque ejecerit a me ignorantiæ cæcitatem et vitiorum caliginem; adstabo tibi, offerendo tibi cor meum, ad ministrandum ac obediendum affectuose paratum: et videbo, id est, splendide contemplabor, et certo cognoscam, quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es: imo omnis iniquitas et omnis impuritas culpæ displicet tibi; nec vis eam effective, sed permissive.
paras.en: [[5:5|In the morning|Mane]], that is, when Christ, who is the sun of justice and [[Wis 7:26|the brightness of eternal light|splendor lucis æternæ]][[Heb 1:3||]], has enlightened my soul sitting in darkness, and has cast out of me the blindness of ignorance and the fog of vices, [[5:5|I will stand before thee|adstabo tibi]], offering thee my heart, lovingly ready to serve and obey; [[5:5|and I will see|et videbo]], that is, I will contemplate clearly and know with certainty, [[5:5|because thou art not a God that willest iniquity|quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es]]: rather, all iniquity and all impurity of guilt displeases thee; nor dost thou will it effectively, but only permissively [that is, God does not cause sin, but allows it].

paras.t: Neque habitabit juxta te malignus: id est, non erit tibi conjunctus, nec moram faciet prope te malignus, id est, qui aliis cupit nocere: non quod spatio locorum distabit a te, qui ubique es et omnia penetras; sed quia propter dissimilitudinem peccati recedit a te, sancto justoque Deo: nec unitur tibi per gratiam in præsenti, neque per gloriam in futuro: quemadmodum scriptum est, Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei. Neque permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos, id est ante præsentiam majestatis tuæ, ante conspectum miserationis tuæ. Vel sic: Non permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos, id est, non agnoscentur a te per approbationis notitiam. Unde inferius dicitur: Deleantur de libro viventium. Et alibi: Nescio vos. Oculus autem Dei, est intellectus ipsius.
paras.en: [[5:6|Neither shall the wicked dwell near thee|Neque habitabit juxta te malignus]]: that is, he will not be joined to thee nor stay near thee, [[5:6|the wicked|malignus]], that is, he who desires to harm others: not that he will be distant from thee in space, who art everywhere and penetratest all things, but because through the unlikeness of sin he goes away from thee, the holy and just God: he is not united to thee by grace in the present, nor by glory in the future; as it is written: Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God[[Is 26:10||]] [the margin gives Is. xxvi, 10, according to the Septuagint; the Vulgate reads differently there]. [[5:6|nor shall the unjust abide before thy eyes|Neque permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos]], that is, before the presence of thy majesty, before the sight of thy mercy. Or thus: [[5:6|nor shall the unjust abide before thy eyes|Non permanebunt injusti ante oculos tuos]], that is, they will not be known by thee with the knowledge of approval. Hence it is said further on: [[Ps 68:29|Let them be blotted out of the book of the living|Deleantur de libro viventium]]. And elsewhere: [[Matt 25:12|I know you not|Nescio vos]][[Luke 13:25||]]. Now the eye of God is his understanding.

paras.t: Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Odium, prout est passio animæ, non competit Deo, nisi transumptive, quemadmodum ira. Sed prout est detestatio voluntatis malum volentis, sic potest competere Deo: et ita Deus odit male agentes, quia detestatur et abjicit eos a se. Odit autem eos non ratione naturæ, sed culpæ. Unde Sapiens dicit: Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti. Nihilo minus in eodem libro habetur: Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus. Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium, id est, æternaliter condemnabis mentientes, nisi pœniteant. Propter quod in libro Sapientiæ scriptum est: Os quod mentitur, occidit animam. Quæ de mendacio pernicioso intelligenda sunt, quod fit intentione fallendi atque nocendi, et ex malignitate procedit, estque Deo contrarium et mortale peccatum, quum Deus sit ipsa veritas. Est autem mendacium officiosum, quod pro alicujus salute aut commodo dicitur. Et est mendacium jocosum, quod ex levitate procedit, et causa solatii dicitur. Ista vero duo mendacii genera non sunt peccata mortalia, sed venialia. Virum sanguinum, id est homicidam, re vel affectu: nam qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est, secundum Joannem. Itaque, Virum sanguinum, et dolosum, id est bilinguem, simulatorem, falsum doctorem, atque hypocritam, abominabitur Dominus, despiciens eum, et expellens a consortio electorum.
paras.en: [[5:7|Thou hatest all the workers of iniquity|Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]. Hatred, as it is a passion of the soul, does not belong to God except by transference [that is, in a figurative sense], as anger does. But as it is the detestation by the will of one who wills evil, so it can belong to God: and thus God hates evildoers, because he detests them and casts them away from himself. Yet he hates them not by reason of their nature, but of their guilt. Hence the Wise Man says: [[Wis 11:25|For thou lovest all things that are, and hatest none of the things which thou hast made|Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti]]. Nevertheless in the same book we have: [[Wis 14:9|But to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful alike|Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus]]. [[5:7|thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie|Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium]], that is, thou wilt condemn liars eternally unless they repent. For which reason it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]]. This is to be understood of the pernicious lie, which is told with the intention of deceiving and harming, proceeds from malice, and is contrary to God and a mortal sin, since God is truth itself. There is also the officious lie [that is, a lie told to help someone or avert harm, not a malicious one], which is told for someone's safety or advantage; and there is the jocose lie, which proceeds from levity and is told for amusement. These two kinds of lie are not mortal sins, but venial. [[5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man|Virum sanguinum]], that is, a murderer, in deed or in desire: for, according to John, [[1 John 3:15|Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer|qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est]]. So, [[5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man|Virum sanguinum, et dolosum]], that is, the double-tongued, the dissembler, the false teacher and the hypocrite, [[5:7|the Lord will abhor|abominabitur Dominus]], despising him and driving him out of the company of the elect.

paras.t: Deinde Ecclesia seu quilibet justus ad Deum convertens sermonem, ait: Ego autem in multitudine misericordiæ tuæ, supple, a prædictis peccatis et pœnis eripiar, in tua gratia perseverabo, et beato fine concludar. Et hoc est verbum bonæ spei, vel potest intelligi per modum orationis. Introibo in domum tuam, id est in Jerusalem cælestem seu triumphantem Ecclesiam post præsentis vitæ exsilium, ut ædificentur ex me muri Jerusalem; interim vero introibo quotidie per affectum, cupiens dissolvi et esse cum Christo. Adorabo ad templum sanctum tuum: id est, in omni oratione et adoratione dirigam intentionem meam, et figam desiderium meum ad civitatem cælestem, ut ad eam pervenire promerear. Adorabo autem, non intimorate vagaque mente, sed adorabo in timore tuo: quia cum magna reverentia et ingenti cordis custodia decet te, Dominum majestatis altissimum, adorare.
paras.en: Then the Church, or any just man, turning his words to God, says: [[5:8|But as for me in the multitude of thy mercy|Ego autem in multitudine misericordiæ tuæ]], supply: I shall be rescued from the sins and punishments just named, shall persevere in thy grace, and be brought to a blessed end. And this is a word of good hope, or it can be understood as a prayer. [[5:8|I will come into thy house|Introibo in domum tuam]], that is, into the heavenly Jerusalem or the Church triumphant after the exile of the present life, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up out of me; meanwhile I will come in daily by desire, [[Phil 1:23|having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ|cupiens dissolvi et esse cum Christo]]. [[5:8|I will worship towards thy holy temple|Adorabo ad templum sanctum tuum]]: that is, in every prayer and act of worship I will direct my intention and fix my desire on the heavenly city, so that I may deserve to reach it. And I will worship, not with an unfearing and wandering mind, but [[5:8|I will worship|adorabo]] [[5:8|in thy fear|in timore tuo]]: for it befits us to worship thee, the most high Lord of majesty, with great reverence and a great guard upon the heart.

paras.t: Denique, quatenus ad prædictam beatitudinem tandem perducar, oro nunc, o Domine, Deduc me in justitia tua: id est, da gratiam ambulandi in via recta perveniendi ad te, ut scilicet tuis præceptis obediam, et in omni sancta operatione tuæ legi obtemperem. Deduc me ne errem, ne passiones et vitia intellectum obnubilent et corruam in conspectu adversariorum meorum: sed esto tu dux meus, ostendendo mihi per illuminationem Spiritus Sancti, quomodo caute ambulem, de virtute in virtutem proficiam, atque feliciter cursum meum consummem. Propter inimicos meos dirige in conspectu meo viam tuam: id est, quia vides, o Domine Deus, me in medio laqueorum jam positum, et inimicis meis, qui sunt caro, mundus atque aeris potestates, undique circumvallatum; idcirco dirige, id est pone, et clare memoriterque propone, in conspectu meo, id est in consideratione intellectus mei, viam tuam, id est legem mandatorum tuorum, ne unquam obliviscar eorum quæ mihi mandasti, et quæ tibi accepta sunt.
paras.en: Lastly, so that I may at length be brought to the blessedness just spoken of, I now pray, O Lord: [[5:9|Conduct me, O Lord, in thy justice|Deduc me in justitia tua]]: that is, give me the grace to walk in the right way of coming to thee, so that I may obey thy precepts and in every holy work be obedient to thy law. [[5:9|Conduct me|Deduc me]], lest I go astray, lest passions and vices cloud my understanding and I fall in the sight of my adversaries: but be thou my guide, showing me by the enlightening of the Holy Spirit how to walk warily, to go forward from virtue to virtue, and to finish my course happily. [[5:9|because of my enemies|Propter inimicos meos]] direct in my sight thy way [Denis reads *in conspectu meo viam tuam*, “in my sight thy way”; the margin gives the reading *tuo … meam*, as in the Douay-Rheims, “direct my way in thy sight”]: that is, because thou seest, O Lord God, that I am already set in the midst of snares, and surrounded on every side by my enemies, who are the flesh, the world and the powers of the air; therefore [[5:9|direct|dirige]], that is, set and put clearly and memorably before me, in my sight, that is, in the consideration of my understanding, thy way, that is, the law of thy commandments, so that I may never forget what thou hast commanded me and what is pleasing to thee.

paras.t: Quoniam non est in ore eorum, scilicet inimicorum meorum, veritas, sed dolus. Cor eorum vanum est, id est a summo bono, ab incommutabili Deo, ab æterna veritate aversum, et ad caduca inaniaque conversum.
paras.en: [[5:10|For there is no truth in their mouth|Quoniam non est in ore eorum veritas]], that is, in the mouth of my enemies, but deceit. [[5:10|their heart is vain|Cor eorum vanum est]], that is, turned away from the highest good, from the unchangeable God, from the eternal truth, and turned towards perishable and empty things.

paras.t: Sepulcrum patens est guttur eorum, id est simile aperto sepulcro, in quo homo facile labitur, et ex quo cito inficitur. Sic guttur impiorum se habet, quia mortua atque pestifera verba ex ipso procedunt; et sermo ipsorum cadere facit, ac inficit innocentes ac simplices, nisi Deus provideat. Linguis suis dolose agebant, proponendo mala sub specie boni, ut magis decipiant.
paras.en: [[5:11|Their throat is an open sepulchre|Sepulcrum patens est guttur eorum]], that is, like an open grave, into which a man easily slips and by which he is soon infected. So it is with the throat of the wicked, for dead and pestilent words come out of it; and their speech makes the innocent and simple fall and infects them, unless God provides. [[5:11|they dealt deceitfully with their tongues|Linguis suis dolose agebant]], putting forward evil under the appearance of good, the better to deceive.

paras.t: Judica illos Deus. Hoc dicit Propheta seu quilibet justus, non optando vindictam, sed prænuntiando veritatem, vel conformando se divinæ justitiæ. Itaque, Judica illos Deus, id est, justo tuo judicio eos condemna. Decidant a cogitationibus suis: id est, non obtineant quod adipisci nituntur, sed apprehende astutos in astutia ipsorum: simulatores enim et callidi provocant iram Dei, quemadmodum in Job habetur. Secundum multitudinem impietatum eorum expelle eos: id est, secundum gravitatem scelerum suorum projice eos a te in justa tormenta, quatenus quantum glorificaverunt se in malis, tantum recipiant in tormentis.
paras.en: [[5:11|judge them, O God|Judica illos Deus]]. The Prophet, or any just man, says this not wishing for vengeance, but foretelling the truth, or conforming himself to the divine justice. So, [[5:11|judge them, O God|Judica illos Deus]], that is, condemn them by thy just judgment. [[5:11|Let them fall from their devices|Decidant a cogitationibus suis]]: that is, let them not obtain what they strive to gain, but catch the crafty in their own craftiness: for [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|simulatores enim et callidi provocant iram Dei]], as we have in Job. [[5:11|according to the multitude of their wickednesses cast them out|Secundum multitudinem impietatum eorum expelle eos]]: that is, according to the gravity of their crimes cast them away from thee into just torments, so that as much as they have glorified themselves in evil, so much they may receive in torments[[Apoc 18:7||]] [the margin gives Apoc. xvii; the words are those of Apoc 18:7].

paras.t: Quoniam irritaverunt te, Domine, id est, ad iracundiam et indignationem provocaverunt: non quod invariabilis ac tranquillissimus Deus veraciter irritetur, amaricetur, aut provocetur, sicut Jeremias ait: Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant? dicit Dominus; nonne se ipsos in confusione vultus sui? Dicitur ergo Deus ad iracundiam provocari et irritari propter similitudinem operis, quia tanquam irritatus se habet, dum impios terribiliter torquet. Et in hoc verbo, Irritaverunt, notatur quam enorme sit Deum offendere, quamque horrendum sit in manus Dei viventis incidere.
paras.en: [[5:11|for they have provoked thee, O Lord|Quoniam irritaverunt te, Domine]], that is, they have provoked thee to anger and indignation: not that the unchanging and most tranquil God is truly provoked, embittered or stirred, as Jeremias says: [[Jer 7:19|Do they provoke me to anger, saith the Lord? is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own countenance?|Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant? dicit Dominus; nonne se ipsos in confusione vultus sui?]] God is said, then, to be provoked and stirred to anger by a likeness of effect, because he behaves as one provoked when he terribly torments the wicked. And in this word, [[5:11|they have provoked|Irritaverunt]], it is shown how enormous a thing it is to offend God, and how fearful a thing it is [[Heb 10:31|to fall into the hands of the living God|in manus Dei viventis incidere]].

paras.t: Et lætentur omnes qui sperant in te, id est, in interiori et sancta hilaritate exsultent, qui totam spem suam fixerunt in tua clementia. In æternum exsultabunt; quia nunc temporaliter consolantur a te, et tandem regnabunt in æternum apud te; et habitabis in eis per caritatem et gratiam. Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos, ait Apostolus. Unde Salvator dicit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum; et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus.
paras.en: [[5:12|But let all them be glad that hope in thee|Et lætentur omnes qui sperant in te]], that is, let them exult with an inward and holy gladness who have fixed all their hope on thy clemency. [[5:12|they shall rejoice for ever|In æternum exsultabunt]], because now they are comforted by thee in time, and at length they will reign for ever with thee; [[5:12|and thou shalt dwell in them|et habitabis in eis]] by charity and grace. [[1 Cor 3:17|For the temple of God is holy, which you are|Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos]], says the Apostle. Hence the Saviour says: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him and we will come to him and will make our abode with him|Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum; et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus]].

paras.t: Et gloriabuntur in te omnes qui diligunt nomen tuum. Caritas Dei otiosa esse non valet, sed semper, ut potest, procedit in actum tam interiorem quam exteriorem. Actus autem caritatis sunt, dilecto bonum velle, de ejus perfectione lætari, ejus beatitudini congratulari. Propterea, qui vere diligit Deum, de immensa ejus perfectione summe lætatur, et ejus felicitati cordialiter conjucundatur: et talis gloriatio est divinissima, ac Deo gratissima, summeque meritoria. Ideo autem diligentes te, Domine, gloriabuntur in te, quoniam tu benedices, id est, gratiam tribues, et copiosa munera dabis justo: imo faciem tuam ei ostendes, in cujus contemplatione totius lætitiæ plenitudo consistit: sicut postea dicitur, Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo. Unde in Evangelio: Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum.
paras.en: [[5:12|And all they that love thy name shall glory in thee|Et gloriabuntur in te omnes qui diligunt nomen tuum]]. The charity of God cannot be idle, but always, as far as it can, goes forth into act, inward as well as outward. Now the acts of charity are to will good to the beloved, to rejoice in his perfection, to rejoice with him in his beatitude. Therefore he who truly loves God rejoices supremely in his immense perfection and is glad with all his heart at his happiness: and such glorying is most divine, most pleasing to God, and supremely meritorious. And those who love thee, O Lord, will glory in thee because [[5:13|thou wilt bless|tu benedices]], that is, thou wilt give grace and bestow abundant gifts on [[5:13|the just|justo]]: nay, thou wilt show him thy face, in the contemplation of which the fullness of all joy consists; as is said later on: [[Ps 15:11|thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance|Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo]]. Hence in the Gospel: [[John 14:21|he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him and will manifest myself to him|Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum]].

paras.t: Domine, ut scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ coronasti nos: id est, o Domine, coronasti nos, id est, genus regium et sacerdotale fecisti nos, dando nobis potestatem filios Dei fieri, et de adversariis triumphandi, ornando nos variis donis Spiritus Sancti, atque omnia subjiciendo sub pedibus nostris. Quomodo autem coronavit nos, pandit, quum addit: Ut scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ, id est tegumento benignissimæ pietatis tuæ. Quasi dicat: Sic coronasti nos, id est, undique gratia tua ornasti ac sublimasti nos, ac si essemus scuto quodam operti atque protecti: imo scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ, id est ipsamet bona seu pia voluntate tua, quæ est nobis ut scutum, coronasti nos, præveniendo per gratiam, conservando per misericordiam, et beatitudinem promittendo per consummationem.
paras.en: [[5:13|O Lord, thou hast crowned us, as with a shield of thy good will|Domine, ut scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ coronasti nos]]: that is, O Lord, [[5:13|thou hast crowned us|coronasti nos]], that is, thou hast made us a kingly and priestly race[[1 Pet 2:9||]], giving us [[John 1:12|power to be made the sons of God|potestatem filios Dei fieri]], and to triumph over our adversaries, adorning us with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, and subjecting [[Ps 8:8|all things under|omnia subjiciendo sub pedibus]] our feet. And how he has crowned us he shows when he adds: [[5:13|as with a shield of thy good will|Ut scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ]], that is, with the covering of thy most kind loving-kindness. As if to say: Thou hast so crowned us, that is, adorned and exalted us on every side with thy grace, as if we were covered and protected by a shield: nay, [[5:13|as with a shield of thy good will|scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ]], that is, by thy good and loving will itself, which is to us as a shield, [[5:13|thou hast crowned us|coronasti nos]], going before us by grace, keeping us by mercy, and promising beatitude by bringing all to completion.

5.title: Quomodo psalmus iste quintus specialiter et congruenter exponi possit de Christo
5.title_en: How this fifth psalm can be expounded especially and fittingly of Christ

paras.t: Porro, quum titulus libri istius sit talis, Incipit liber Hymnorum Prophetæ de Christo, debemus in hoc sacratissimo libro omnia pro posse ad Christum referre. Potest ergo non solum hic psalmus, sed etiam titulus ejus convenienter de Christo exponi, ut sit tituli sensus: In finem pro ea quæ consequitur hæreditatem, id est, psalmus iste dirigens nos in finem, id est felicitatem æternam, est pro ea quæ consequitur hæreditatem, id est, tractat de Christi humana natura, quæ unita est hypostatica unione Verbo Dei, sicque tam specialiter, tamque eminenter consecuta est hæreditatem, id est omnium divinorum charismatum plenitudinem atque felicissimam Dei fruitionem, ut per eam totum genus humanum perducatur ad vitam beatam: quia de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes gratiam pro gratia, sicut Joannes ait.
paras.en: Now, since the title of this book is: Here begins the book of Hymns of the Prophet concerning Christ, we ought in this most sacred book to refer everything to Christ as far as we can. Not only this psalm, then, but its title too can fittingly be expounded of Christ, so that the sense of the title is: [[5:1|Unto the end, for her that obtaineth the inheritance|In finem pro ea quæ consequitur hæreditatem]]: that is, this psalm, directing us to the end, that is, eternal happiness, is for her that obtaineth the inheritance, that is, it treats of the human nature of Christ, which is united to the Word of God by hypostatic union, and so has obtained the inheritance so specially and so eminently, that is, the fulness of all divine gifts and the most happy enjoyment of God, that through it the whole human race is brought to the blessed life: for [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received: and grace for grace|de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes gratiam pro gratia]], as John says.

paras.t: Christus ergo ratione humanæ naturæ orans, ait ad Patrem seu totam Trinitatem, vel ad se ipsum, secundum quod Deus est: Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine. Quæ sunt verba, quæ Christus a Deo exaudiri precatur, nisi orationes illæ quas pro membris suis, id est pro nobis, effudit? De quibus in Evangelio Joannis legitur: Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his quos dedisti mihi de mundo. Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo. Et denuo: Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut et nos. Alibi quoque ad Petrum: Ego, inquit, rogavi pro te, Petre, ut non deficiat fides tua. Rogavi, inquit, pro te, id est, pro tota Ecclesia. Unde rursus ad Patrem dicit: Non pro his, scilicet Apostolis, rogo tantum, sed pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me, ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu, Pater, in me, et ego in te, ut omnes sint consummati in unum. Insuper addit: Intellige clamorem meum. Quis est iste clamor Filii Dei, quem cupit a Patre intelligi? nisi oratio quam pendens in cruce emisit, dum dixit, Pater, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt; et iterum, quando clamans voce magna, dixit, Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum: et rursus, Sitio, id est, hominum salutem desidero.
paras.en: Christ, then, praying by reason of his human nature, says to the Father, or to the whole Trinity, or to himself as he is God: [[5:2|Give ear, O Lord, to my words|Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine]]. What are the words which Christ prays to be heard by God, but those prayers which he poured out for his members, that is, for us? Of which we read in the Gospel of John: [[John 17:9|I pray not for the world, but for them whom thou hast given me|Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his quos dedisti mihi]] out of the world. [[John 17:15|I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil|Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo]]. And again: [[John 17:11|Holy Father, keep them in thy name whom thou hast given me: that they may be one, as we also are|Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut et nos]]. And elsewhere to Peter: [[Luke 22:32|I have prayed for thee|Ego, inquit, rogavi pro te]], Peter, he says, [[Luke 22:32|that thy faith fail not|ut non deficiat fides tua]]. I have prayed for thee, he says, that is, for the whole Church. Hence again he says to the Father: [[John 17:20|not for them only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me|Non pro his, scilicet Apostolis, rogo tantum, sed pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me]]: [[John 17:21|That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee|ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu, Pater, in me, et ego in te]], [[John 17:23|that they may be made perfect in one|ut omnes sint consummati in unum]] [Denis: "that all may be made perfect in one"]. Moreover he adds: [[5:2|understand my cry|Intellige clamorem meum]]. What is this cry of the Son of God which he wishes the Father to understand, but the prayer he uttered hanging on the cross, when he said: [[Luke 23:34|Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do|Pater, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt]]; and again, when, crying with a loud voice, he said: [[Luke 23:46|Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit|Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum]]: and again: [[John 19:28|I thirst|Sitio]], that is, I desire the salvation of men.

paras.t: Intende voci orationis meæ, Rex meus: omnium quidem rex, sed specialiter rex meus, quoniam ita rexisti me Filium tuum incarnatum, quod nunquam peccavi, nunquam a via recta erravi, nunquam imperfecte me habui; et Deus meus: omnium quidem Deus, sed singulariter Deus meus, quoniam ego solus, in quantum sum homo, magis te diligo, magisque colo ac veneror, quam omnes simul intellectuales creaturæ.
paras.en: [[5:3|Hearken to the voice of my prayer, O my King|Intende voci orationis meæ, Rex meus]]: King of all indeed, but especially my King, since thou hast so ruled me, thy Son incarnate, that I have never sinned, never strayed from the right way, never been in any way imperfect; [[5:3|and my God|et Deus meus]]: God of all indeed, but singularly my God, since I alone, as man, love thee more, and worship and revere thee more, than all intellectual creatures together.

paras.t: Quoniam ad te orabo, Domine. Hoc competit Christo, quoniam diabolo dicenti, Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si procidens adoraveris me, ipse respondit: Vade retro, Satana; Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies. Mane exaudies vocem meam, id est cito. Quomodo enim Filio suo carissimo, in quo sibi complacuit, aliquid denegaret Pater cœlestis? Mane adstabo tibi, et videbo, quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es. Mane, id est primo omnium et ante omnem aliam occupationem; adstabo tibi: quemadmodum scriptum est, Primum quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus. Istud Christo specialissime competit, quoniam ipse a Deo constitutus est justorum impiorumque judex. Et ideo adstat Deo tanquam ex ejus commissione judicans, et ejus justitiæ summe concordans, voluntatique ejus semper plene consentiens: et ita videt, id est, clare cognoscit, quoniam Deus qui est judex per auctoritatem, non vult iniquitatem. Neque habitabit juxta te malignus, etc. Quumque sit ita, ideo, o Deus Pater, judicabo sicut te sentire cognosco, separando bonos a malis; et bonos in palatio gloriæ tuæ recolligam, malos autem in ignem æternum projiciam.
paras.en: [[5:4|For to thee will I pray: O Lord|Quoniam ad te orabo, Domine]]. This befits Christ, since when the devil said: [[Matt 4:9|All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me|Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si procidens adoraveris me]], he answered: [[Matt 4:10|Begone, Satan|Vade retro, Satana]]: [[Matt 4:10|The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve|Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies]][[Deut 6:13||]]. [[5:4|in the morning thou shalt hear my voice|Mane exaudies vocem meam]], that is, quickly. For how could the heavenly Father deny anything to his most dear Son, in whom he is well pleased[[Matt 3:17||]][[Matt 17:5||]]? [[5:5|In the morning I will stand before thee, and I will see: because thou art not a God that willest iniquity|Mane adstabo tibi, et videbo, quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es]]. [[5:5|In the morning|Mane]], that is, first of all, and before any other occupation; [[5:5|I will stand before thee|adstabo tibi]]: as it is written: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice|Primum quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus]]. This befits Christ most especially, since he has been appointed by God judge of the just and the wicked[[Acts 10:42||]]. And therefore he stands before God as judging by his commission, agreeing supremely with his justice and always consenting fully to his will: and so he sees, that is, clearly knows, that God, who is judge by authority, does not will iniquity. [[5:6|Neither shall the wicked dwell near thee|Neque habitabit juxta te malignus]], etc. And since this is so, therefore, O God the Father, I will judge as I know thee to judge, separating the good from the wicked; and the good I will gather into the palace of thy glory, but the wicked I will cast into everlasting fire[[Matt 25:32||]][[Matt 25:46||]].

paras.t: Ego autem in multitudine misericordiæ tuæ: id est, ego Filius tuus magna et multa misericordia tua præventus sum, in quantum homo: quoniam sola divina dignatione et misericordia unita est humanitas mea Verbo tuo, omni gratia adimpleta, sine præviis meritis ab omni culpa præservata, et in omni bono completa. Merito ergo dico me esse in multitudine misericordiæ tuæ. Introibo in domum tuam, scilicet in die ascensionis, quando reversus sum in domum cœlestem. Vel, In domum tuam, id est in templum tibi in Jerusalem consecratum: in quo Christus prædicavit atque miracula fecit, et de quo vendentes et ementes ejecit, dicens, Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur. In hoc enim templum Dominum Christum fuisse introiturum, Aggæus propheta ita prædixit: Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus, et implebo domum istam gloria, dicit Dominus. In hoc quoque templo Christus adoravit in timore Domini: quia replevit eum spiritus timoris Domini, juxta Isaiæ oraculum. De Christo etiam ad dexteram Patris jam residente ait Apostolus, quia interpellat pro nobis.
paras.en: [[5:8|But as for me in the multitude of thy mercy|Ego autem in multitudine misericordiæ tuæ]]: that is, I thy Son have been prevented [*præventus*: forestalled, gone before] by thy great and abundant mercy, as man: since by divine condescension and mercy alone my humanity was united to thy Word, filled with all grace, preserved from all fault without any previous merits, and made complete in all good. Rightly, then, do I say that I am in the multitude of thy mercy. [[5:8|I will come into thy house|Introibo in domum tuam]], namely on the day of the ascension, when I returned into the heavenly house. Or: [[5:8|into thy house|In domum tuam]], that is, into the temple consecrated to thee in Jerusalem: in which Christ preached and worked miracles, and from which he cast out the sellers and buyers, saying: [[Matt 21:13|My house shall be called the house of prayer|Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur]]. For that the Lord Christ would enter this temple the prophet Aggeus foretold thus: [[Agg 2:8|AND THE DESIRED OF ALL NATIONS SHALL COME|Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus]]: [[Agg 2:8|and I will fill this house with glory: saith the Lord|et implebo domum istam gloria, dicit Dominus]]. In this temple too Christ worshipped in the fear of the Lord: since [[Is 11:3|he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord|replevit eum spiritus timoris Domini]], according to the oracle of Isaias. And of Christ now seated at the right hand of the Father the Apostle says that he [[Rom 8:34|maketh intercession for us|interpellat pro nobis]].

paras.t: Domine, deduc me in justitia tua. Hanc orationem facit Christus pro corpore suo mystico, quod est Ecclesia. Ipse enim non oravit duci in via Dei, quia confirmatus erat in bono, neque mereri potuit sibi, neque proficere, quoniam comprehensor fuit perfectus. Oravit tamen interdum pro se, scilicet pro corporis sui glorificatione, vel aliquo simili.
paras.en: [[5:9|Conduct me, O Lord, in thy justice|Domine, deduc me in justitia tua]]. Christ makes this prayer for his mystical body, which is the Church. For he did not pray for himself to be led in the way of God, since he was confirmed in good, and could neither merit for himself nor make progress, since he was a perfect comprehensor [one already in full possession of the vision of God]. Yet he sometimes prayed for himself, namely for the glorifying of his body, or something of the kind.

paras.t: Cetera hujus psalmi patent ex dictis in præcedenti explanatione.
paras.en: The rest of this psalm is plain from what was said in the preceding explanation.

paras.t: Quomodo autem hic psalmus moraliter possit exponi, jam satis ostensum est, nec est difficultas in hoc. Docemur vero ex psalmo isto, quatenus cum magna attentione oremus. Qualiter enim Deo dicere possumus, Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine, si nos ipsi non percipiamus auribus cordis quid loquamur? Et quomodo dicimus ei, Intellige clamorem meum, si non mentaliter, sed vocaliter solum clamamus? Denique, quid apparentiæ habet, ut Deus voci orationis nostræ intendat, si nos ipsi inattenti ac vagi corde fuerimus? Et ideo scriptum est: Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo tentans Deum. Docet enim nos hic psalmus diligenter pensare, quam enorme atque damnabile sit Deo non obedire, nec juste conversari, eo quod Deus impios odio habeat, et æternaliter separet eos a se, tradens eos æternis suppliciis. Postremo, docemur in Deo sperare, sperando lætari, lætando diligere, diligendo quiescere.
paras.en: How this psalm can be expounded morally has been shown well enough already, and there is no difficulty in it. But we are taught by this psalm to pray with great attention. For how can we say to God: [[5:2|Give ear, O Lord, to my words|Verba mea auribus percipe, Domine]], if we ourselves do not perceive with the ears of the heart what we are saying? And how do we say to him: [[5:2|understand my cry|Intellige clamorem meum]], if we cry not with the mind but only with the voice? Lastly, what likelihood is there that God will attend to the voice of our prayer if we ourselves are inattentive and wandering in heart? And therefore it is written: [[Ecclus 18:23|Before prayer prepare thy soul: and be not as a man that tempteth God|Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo tentans Deum]]. For this psalm teaches us to weigh carefully how enormous and damnable it is not to obey God nor to live justly, since God hates the wicked[[Wis 14:9||]], and separates them from himself eternally, handing them over to eternal punishments[[Matt 25:41||]]. Lastly, we are taught to hope in God, in hoping to rejoice, in rejoicing to love, in loving to rest.

paras.t: Precatio. Rex et Deus noster, deduc nos in justitia tua propter inimicos nostros, et dirige in conspectu tuo viam nostram: ut in nobis scuto bonæ voluntatis tuæ coronatis, in æternum exsultes et habites.
paras.en: Prayer. Our King and our God, lead us in thy justice because of our enemies, and direct our way in thy sight: that in us, crowned with the shield of thy good will, thou mayest exult and dwell for ever.

6.title: EXPLANATIO SEXTI PSALMI: DOMINE, NE IN FURORE, ETC.
6.title_en: Explanation of the sixth Psalm: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, etc.

paras.t: Præscribitur autem psalmo huic titulus iste: In finem, psalmus David, pro octava. Cujus sensus est: Psalmus iste a sancto David compositus est, et dirigit nos in finem seu Christum, qui est terminus peregrinationis nostræ; pro octava, id est, scriptus ac editus est timore extremi judicii, quod fiet in die novissimo, quæ vocatur octava, quoniam sequitur tempus sæculi hujus, quod septem diebus evolvitur.
paras.en: This title is set before this psalm: [[6:1|Unto the end|In finem]], [[6:1|a psalm for David, for the octave|psalmus David, pro octava]]. Its sense is: This psalm was composed by holy David, and it directs us to the end, that is, to Christ, who is the goal of our pilgrimage; [[6:1|for the octave|pro octava]], that is, it was written and set forth for fear of the last judgment, which will take place on the last day, which is called the octave because it follows the time of this world, which runs its course in seven days.

paras.t: Denique verba sunt signa eorum quæ versantur in mente. Unde secundum diversas animæ affectiones, et diversa formantur verba orationis ac laudis. Interdum enim afficitur anima vehementi timore, interdum ardenti amore, interdum delectatione insolita, interdum vero ingenti tristitia: et secundum hoc variantur sermones forinsecus. Clarum est quoque, ex vehementiori affectu verba affectuosiora procedere.
paras.en: Now words are signs of what is in the mind. Hence according to the different affections of the soul, different words of prayer and praise are formed. For the soul is sometimes moved by vehement fear, sometimes by burning love, sometimes by unwonted delight, and sometimes by great sadness: and outward speech varies accordingly. It is clear, too, that more affectionate words proceed from a more vehement affection.

paras.t: Igitur anima fidelis ac timorata deliquisse se pensans, atque futuri judicii districtionem considerans, quasi vehementer perterrita, et Judicem suum interim mitigare affectans, talem precem effundit: Domine, inquit, ne in furore tuo arguas me: id est, o Domine, ne ita in præsenti vita relinquas me impœnitentem, inemendatum, incastigatum, ut in die judicii arguas me in furore tuo, id est secundum districtissimum zelum justitiæ tuæ, quando jam pœnitentiæ locus non erit, nec misericordia miseris fiet, sed summa justitia omnibus impendetur. Et ideo tunc quasi furiosus, quantum ad reprobos, apparebis per examinis districtionem sive asperitatem, et supplicii acerbitatem: et iste effectus tuæ justitiæ, furor vocatur. Sed modo da gratiam deplangendi peccata, vitandi pericula, faciendi opera virtuosa, ne tunc in furore tuo arguas me. Non enim bis vindicabis in id ipsum. Neque in ira tua corripias me: id est, nec ita modo permittas me indultum pœnitentiæ tempus negligere, ut in hora particularis judicii mei, quando scilicet anima mea egredietur a corpore, et tuo tribunali præsentanda est, corripias me in ira tua, id est in severitate æquitatis divinæ, condemnando animam meam in infernum, donec in die novissimo corpori reunita, simul cum illo sortiatur duplicem pœnam. Duplex constat esse judicium, scilicet universale, quod fiet in fine sæculi, quando omnes homines simul judicabuntur. Aliud est judicium particulare, quo singuli judicantur, quum moriuntur. Universale autem judicium terribilius est particulari judicio, quia in illo anima et corpus simul damnabuntur, et judex tunc terribilior apparebit; multaque alia erunt, quæ illud judicium horribilissimum facient, ut ardens mundus, hians infernus, dæmones accusantes, angeli adstantes, coram omnibus angelis, hominibus, atque dæmonibus accusari, reprobari, confundi, damnari: quoniam singulorum peccata singulis innotescent, ut omnes cognoscant judicem esse justissimum. Unde furor, qui sonat aliquid majus quam ira, ad universale judicium pertinet; ira vero, ad particulare judicium.
paras.en: So the faithful and God-fearing soul, weighing that it has sinned, and considering the strictness of the judgment to come, as it were greatly terrified, and seeking meanwhile to appease its Judge, pours out such a prayer as this: [[6:2|O Lord|Domine]], it says, [[6:2|rebuke me not in thy indignation|ne in furore tuo arguas me]]: that is, O Lord, do not so leave me in this present life unrepentant, unamended, unchastised, that in the day of judgment thou rebuke me in thy indignation, that is, according to the strictest zeal of thy justice, when there will no longer be place for repentance, nor will mercy be shown to the wretched, but the highest justice will be dealt out to all. And therefore then, as regards the reprobate, thou wilt appear as one in fury, by the strictness or harshness of the examination and the bitterness of the punishment: and this effect of thy justice is called fury [*furor*, here rendered “indignation”]. But now give me the grace to bewail my sins, to avoid dangers, and to do virtuous works, lest then thou rebuke me in thy indignation. For thou wilt not punish twice for the same thing[[Nah 1:9||]] [the saying is drawn from Nahum 1:9, which the margin gives; the Vulgate there reads “there shall not rise a double affliction”]. [[6:2|nor chastise me in thy wrath|Neque in ira tua corripias me]]: that is, do not now so allow me to neglect the time of repentance granted me, that in the hour of my particular judgment, namely when my soul shall go forth from the body and is to be presented at thy tribunal, thou chastise me in thy wrath, that is, in the severity of divine equity, condemning my soul to hell, until on the last day, reunited to the body, it receive together with it a double punishment. It is certain that there is a twofold judgment: namely the universal, which will take place at the end of the world, when all men will be judged together; the other is the particular judgment, by which each is judged when he dies. And the universal judgment is more terrible than the particular judgment, because in it soul and body will be condemned together, and the judge will then appear more terrible; and there will be many other things to make that judgment most dreadful, such as the burning world, gaping hell, accusing demons, angels standing by, and to be accused, rejected, confounded and condemned before all angels, men and demons: since the sins of each will be made known to each, so that all may know that the judge is most just. Hence indignation [*furor*], which sounds something greater than wrath [*ira*], belongs to the universal judgment, and wrath to the particular judgment.

paras.t: Potest etiam aliter explanari quod dicitur, ut sit sensus: Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, id est, ne in æternum condemnes me; neque in ira tua corripias me, id est, neque in purgatorio torqueas me: sed nunc quotidie purga me paternaliter corrigendo, dulciter inflammando me tuo sancto amore, quoniam caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum; et secundum mansuetudinem tuam fac mecum. Ideo enim sanctus Job orat: Dimitte me, Domine, ut plangam paululum dolorem meum, antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine. Jeremias insuper futuri judicii furorem se ferre non posse perpendens, sic orat: Corripe me, Domine, verumtamen in judicio et non in furore tuo, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me.
paras.en: What is said can also be explained otherwise, so that the sense is: [[6:2|O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation|Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me]], that is, do not condemn me for ever; [[6:2|nor chastise me in thy wrath|neque in ira tua corripias me]], that is, do not torment me in purgatory: but now purge me daily by correcting me as a father, by sweetly inflaming me with thy holy love, since [[1 Pet 4:8|charity covereth a multitude of sins|caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum]]; and deal with me according to thy gentleness. For this is why holy Job prays: [[Job 10:20|Suffer me|Dimitte me]], O Lord, [[Job 10:20|that I may lament my sorrow a little|ut plangam paululum dolorem meum]], [[Job 10:21|Before I go and return no more, to a land that is dark and covered with the mist of death|antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine]]. Jeremias, moreover, weighing that he could not bear the fury of the judgment to come, prays thus: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord, but yet with judgment: and not in thy fury, lest thou bring me to nothing|Corripe me, Domine, verumtamen in judicio et non in furore tuo, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me]].

paras.t: Peccator ergo vere pœnitens, et de se Deo respondere ac satisfacere non posse adspiciens, oret, et dicat quod sequitur: Miserere mei, Domine, compatiendo miseriæ meæ, id est per modum compatientis te habendo, videlicet succurrendo mihi in omni angustia et indigentia; quoniam infirmus sum, quia ex me ipso nil possum, sed tota sufficientia mea ex te est, ex gratia tua dependet, ex misericordia tua emanat. Infirmus sum, non possum tibi respondere unum pro mille; non possum, imo nec opto resistere vultui tuo: et ideo sana me, Domine, id est, a peccatis quæ sunt vulnera animæ meæ, purga et eripe me, non solum culpam, sed etiam pœnam relaxando; quoniam conturbata sunt ossa mea, id est, virtutes animæ meæ concussæ et motæ sunt. Adversitates namque, passiones et vitia, actum virtutum frequenter impediunt atque commaculant, atque per hoc ipsi habitus virtuosi debilitantur. Et ideo propter admixtionem imperfectionum nostrarum cum actu virtutum, omnes nostræ justitiæ, sunt tanquam pannus menstruatæ. Unde ad removendum impedimenta virtutum, indigemus donis Spiritus Sancti, quæ a virtutibus distinguuntur, et in adjutorium earum præstantur.
paras.en: Let the truly penitent sinner, then, seeing that of himself he cannot answer God or make satisfaction, pray and say what follows: [[6:3|Have mercy on me, O Lord|Miserere mei, Domine]], by pitying my misery, that is, by behaving as one who has compassion, namely by helping me in every distress and need; [[6:3|for I am weak|quoniam infirmus sum]], because of myself I can do nothing, but all my sufficiency is from thee[[2 Cor 3:5||]], depends on thy grace, flows from thy mercy. [[6:3|I am weak|Infirmus sum]]: I cannot answer thee [[Job 9:3|one for a thousand|unum pro mille]]; I cannot, nay, I do not wish to, resist thy face: and therefore [[6:3|heal me, O Lord|sana me, Domine]], that is, cleanse me and deliver me from sins, which are the wounds of my soul, remitting not only the guilt but also the punishment; [[6:3|for my bones are troubled|quoniam conturbata sunt ossa mea]], that is, the virtues of my soul are shaken and disturbed. For adversities, passions and vices often hinder and stain the act of the virtues, and by this the virtuous habits themselves are weakened. And therefore, because of the mingling of our imperfections with the act of the virtues, [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|omnes nostræ justitiæ, sunt tanquam pannus menstruatæ]]. Hence, to remove the hindrances to the virtues, we need the gifts of the Holy Ghost, which are distinct from the virtues and are given to help them.

paras.t: Et anima mea turbata est valde, scilicet recordatione præteritorum malorum, consideratione futurarum pœnarum, contemplatione divinæ justitiæ, et propter difficultatem perveniendi ad veram perfectionem, quam vehementer desiderat. Sed tu, Domine, usquequo? id est, quamdiu in tanta tribulatione relinquis me? quousque non subvenis exaudiendo, et desideratam gratiæ plenitudinem infundendo?
paras.en: [[6:4|And my soul is troubled exceedingly|Et anima mea turbata est valde]], namely by the remembrance of past evils, the consideration of punishments to come, the contemplation of divine justice, and because of the difficulty of coming to the true perfection which it vehemently desires. [[6:4|but thou, O Lord, how long?|Sed tu, Domine, usquequo?]] that is, how long dost thou leave me in such tribulation? how long dost thou not come to my help by hearing me, and by pouring in the fullness of grace that I desire?

paras.t: Convertere, Domine, id est, converte me ad te; vel, Convertere, ut qui gratiam subtrahendo propter peccata mea recessisti a me, per gratiæ infusionem revertaris ad me; convertere ab ultione ad indulgentiam, a rigore justitiæ ad suavitatem clementiæ; et eripe animam meam, ab omni periculo, a sterilitate et tædio proficiendi in bonis, et a turbatione præmissa. Salvum me fac, nunc per gratiam, et in futuro per gloriam: et hoc non propter meam justitiam, sed propter misericordiam tuam. Scio enim, o Domine, te per sanctum Ezechielem dixisse: Non propter vos ego faciam, dicit Dominus, notum sit vobis, sed propter nomen sanctum meum.
paras.en: [[6:5|Turn to me, O Lord|Convertere, Domine]], that is, turn me to thee; or, [[6:5|Turn|Convertere]], so that thou who, by withdrawing grace because of my sins, didst depart from me, mayest return to me by the pouring in of grace; turn from vengeance to pardon, from the rigour of justice to the sweetness of clemency; [[6:5|and deliver my soul|et eripe animam meam]] from every danger, from barrenness and weariness in advancing in good things, and from the trouble spoken of. [[6:5|O save me|Salvum me fac]], now by grace and hereafter by glory: and this not for my own justice, but [[6:5|for thy mercy's sake|propter misericordiam tuam]]. For I know, O Lord, that thou didst say through holy Ezechiel: [[Ezech 36:32|It is not for your sakes that I will do this|Non propter vos ego faciam]], [[Ezech 36:32|saith the Lord God, be it known to you|dicit Dominus, notum sit vobis]], [[Ezech 36:22|but for my holy name's sake|sed propter nomen sanctum meum]] [Denis joins Ezech 36:32 and 36:22, as the margin notes].

paras.t: Quoniam non est in morte qui memor sit tui: id est, nullus in peccato mortali exsistens, memor est tui memoria meritoria: et ideo peto gratiam mihi infundi, ut opera mea meritoria fiant. Vel, Non est in morte, id est post mortem, qui memor sit tui memoria salutari: et hoc verum est de his qui sine caritate et gratia mortui sunt. Nam qui in purgatorio sunt, Dei sunt memores: alias non sperarent liberari a pœnis. In inferno autem quis confitebitur tibi? quasi dicat, Nullus: quoniam nec confessio laudis divinæ, neque confessio propriæ culpæ in inferno invenitur. His consonat autem quod Salomon ait: Quodcumque potest facere manus tua, instanter operare: quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas.
paras.en: [[6:6|For there is no one in death, that is mindful of thee|Quoniam non est in morte qui memor sit tui]]: that is, no one who is in mortal sin is mindful of thee with a meritorious remembrance: and therefore I ask that grace be poured into me, so that my works may become meritorious. Or, [[6:6|there is no one in death|Non est in morte]], that is, after death, [[6:6|that is mindful of thee|qui memor sit tui]] with a saving remembrance: and this is true of those who have died without charity and grace. For those who are in purgatory are mindful of God: otherwise they would not hope to be freed from their pains. [[6:6|and who shall confess to thee in hell?|In inferno autem quis confitebitur tibi?]] as if to say, No one: since neither the confession of divine praise nor the confession of one's own guilt is found in hell. And with this agrees what Solomon says: [[Eccles 9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly: for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening|Quodcumque potest facere manus tua, instanter operare: quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas]].

paras.t: Hucusque beatissimus David in persona veraciter pœnitentis loquens, ostendit quomodo a peccatore pœnitentiam agente orandus sit Judex cœlestis. Nunc insuper proprio exemplo docet quid pœnitens agere debeat, ut non solum verbo, sed etiam opere Deum conciliet. Ait enim: Laboravi in gemitu meo: id est, sic interius de peccatis meis contritus sum, quod exteriores pœnitentiæ actus et satisfactionis labores non omisi, sed flendo, abstinendo, sacris vigiliis insistendo, me ipsum afflixi. Peccatum namque, quoniam delectationem habet annexam, per laborem cui adjuncta est quædam afflictio, indulgetur. Hoc quoque quod dicitur, Laboravi in gemitu meo, de interiori labore accipi potest, imo interior labor exteriorem excedit, sicut et dolor interior exteriorem. Sic igitur, Laboravi in gemitu meo, id est, in interiori cordis tristitia laboravi, interius meditando, me ipsum spernendo, Deum mentaliter exorando. Nam, ut ait Agathon anachoreta, Non est labor tam grandis, ut Deum intente orare. Laboriosum est enim cor diu servare in summo, propter fragilitatem et instabilitatem mentis humanæ.
paras.en: Thus far most blessed David, speaking in the person of one truly penitent, has shown how the heavenly Judge is to be prayed to by a sinner doing penance. Now he further teaches by his own example what the penitent ought to do, so as to win God over not only by word but also by deed. For he says: [[6:7|I have laboured in my groanings|Laboravi in gemitu meo]]: that is, I was so contrite within for my sins that I did not leave out the outward acts of penance and the labours of satisfaction, but afflicted myself by weeping, fasting and keeping holy vigils. For sin, since it has delight joined to it, is pardoned through labour, to which a certain affliction is joined. What is said, [[6:7|I have laboured in my groanings|Laboravi in gemitu meo]], can also be taken of inward labour; nay, inward labour exceeds outward, as inward pain exceeds outward. So, then: [[6:7|I have laboured in my groanings|Laboravi in gemitu meo]], that is, I laboured in the inward sadness of the heart, meditating within, despising myself, praying to God in my mind. For, as Agathon the anchorite says, There is no labour so great as to pray to God intently. For it is laborious to keep the heart long on high, because of the frailty and instability of the human mind.

paras.t: Lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum. Qui hoc ad litteram posset implere, vere pœnitens probaretur; nec videtur impossibile hoc ipsum litteraliter adimplere, si sane intelligatur, ut sit sensus: Lavabo per singulas noctes, id est aliquo tempore singularum noctium, lectum meum, id est aliquam partem lecti, sic quod præ abundantia lacrimarum non tantum facies mea, sed etiam pars lecti vultui proxima humectetur. Debet enim se homo in lecto quasi in tumulo ponere, et peccatorum suorum ac mortis atque divini judicii recordari; sicque adspirare ad Deum, et vultum et lectum sanctis lacrimis lavare: et ideo additur, Lacrimis meis stratum meum rigabo: et hoc est explanatio ejus quod dictum est. Possumus tamen per noctes, intelligere peccata; et per lectum, conscientiam seu delectationem malam; et per stratum, consuetudinem pravam. Ut sit sensus: Lavabo, seu mundabo, per singulas noctes, id est per singula vitia, gemendo pro singulis memoriæ occurrentibus et magis ponderandis, lectum meum, id est conscientiam meam, ea abjiciendo de quibus remorsum conscientiæ habeo; vel, Lectum meum, id est delectationem malam, in qua tanquam in lecto prostratus jacui et quievi, hanc lavabo, pro ea me ipsum castigando, atque ab ea me de cetero subtrahendo. Stratum meum, id est consuetudinem pessimam, lacrimis meis rigabo, id est, copiose deplangam, nec cessabo donec ipsam funditus exstirpavero, habitumque virtutis ei oppositum adeptus exstitero: quod utique magno et longo eget labore.
paras.en: [[6:7|every night I will wash my bed|Lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum]]. One who could fulfil this according to the letter would be proved truly penitent; and it does not seem impossible to fulfil it literally, if it is soundly understood, so that the sense is: [[6:7|every night I will wash|Lavabo per singulas noctes]], that is, at some time of each night, [[6:7|my bed|lectum meum]], that is, some part of the bed, so that from the abundance of tears not only my face but also the part of the bed nearest my face is wetted. For a man ought to lay himself in bed as in a tomb, and remember his sins, and death, and the divine judgment; and so to aspire to God, and wash both face and bed with holy tears: and therefore it is added, [[6:7|I will water my couch with my tears|Lacrimis meis stratum meum rigabo]]; and this is the explanation of what was said. Yet we can understand by the nights sins; by the bed, conscience or evil delight; and by the couch, wicked habit. So that the sense is: [[6:7|I will wash|Lavabo]], or cleanse, [[6:7|every night|per singulas noctes]], that is, every vice, groaning over each as it comes to mind and is to be weighed more deeply, [[6:7|my bed|lectum meum]], that is, my conscience, by casting away the things for which I have remorse of conscience; or, [[6:7|my bed|Lectum meum]], that is, the evil delight in which I lay prostrate and took my rest as in a bed: this I will wash by chastising myself for it and withdrawing myself from it for the future. [[6:7|my couch|Stratum meum]], that is, my most wicked habit, [[6:7|I will water my couch with my tears|lacrimis meis rigabo]], that is, I will bewail it abundantly, and will not cease until I have rooted it out completely and acquired the habit of virtue opposed to it: which surely needs great and long labour.

paras.t: Turbatus est a furore oculus meus: id est, consideratio mentis meæ turbata est, concussa seu perterrita, a furore, id est a districtione judicii Dei, seu propter gravem vindictam divinæ justitiæ. Vel sic: Turbatus est a furore oculus meus, id est, intellectus meus inquietatus est et intranquillus effectus a furore, id est ex vehementi ira seu indignatione, quam concepi contra me ipsum, propter enormitatem peccatorum meorum. Passiones quippe quamvis sint bonæ et sponte assumptæ, solent tamen rationem aliqualiter perturbare, secundum Thomam in prima secundæ. Hujus vero turbationis causa subjungitur: Inveteravi, id est, animo vetus factus sum, et prope interitum factus, in vitiis jacens sordidus, et a spirituali juventute, quæ est reformatio mentis per gratiam, elongatus: et hoc, inter omnes inimicos meos, id est inter omnes qui me a summo bono conantur avertere, qui sunt mundus, diabolus, vitia, et concupiscentiæ carnis. Inter hos inveteravi, ipsorum suggestionibus consentiendo, atque ipsorum operibus me conformando. Non acquievi divino Apostolo exhortanti: Exspoliate veterem hominem cum actibus suis, et induite novum, qui secundum Deum creatus est, qui renovatur de die in diem in agnitione ejus qui creavit eum.
paras.en: [[6:8|My eye is troubled through indignation|Turbatus est a furore oculus meus]]: that is, the consideration of my mind is troubled, shaken or terrified, [[6:8|through indignation|a furore]], that is, by the strictness of God's judgment, or because of the heavy vengeance of divine justice. Or thus: [[6:8|My eye is troubled through indignation|Turbatus est a furore oculus meus]], that is, my understanding has been disquieted and made restless [[6:8|through indignation|a furore]], that is, from the vehement anger or indignation which I have conceived against myself because of the enormity of my sins. For passions, even when they are good and freely taken up, are wont to disturb reason somewhat, according to Thomas in the Prima Secundæ [the margin gives I-II, q. 22 and following]. The cause of this trouble is added: [[6:8|I have grown old|Inveteravi]], that is, I have become old in mind, and near to perishing[[Heb 8:13||]], lying filthy in vices, and far from spiritual youth, which is the reforming of the mind by grace: and this [[6:8|amongst all my enemies|inter omnes inimicos meos]], that is, amongst all who try to turn me away from the highest good, who are the world, the devil, vices and the lusts of the flesh. Among these [[6:8|I have grown old|inveteravi]], consenting to their suggestions and conforming myself to their works. I did not heed the divine Apostle exhorting us: [[Col 3:9|stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds|Exspoliate veterem hominem cum actibus suis]], [[Col 3:10|And putting on the new|et induite novum]], [[Eph 4:24|who according to God is created|qui secundum Deum creatus est]], [[2 Cor 4:16|is renewed day by day|qui renovatur de die in diem]] [[Col 3:10|unto knowledge, according to the image of him that created him|in agnitione ejus qui creavit eum]] [Denis joins Col 3:9–10, which the margin gives, with words from Eph 4:24 and 2 Cor 4:16].

paras.t: Nunc autem obedire cupio ei qui ait: Abjiciamus opera tenebrarum: et ergo Discedite a me, id est, nolite me ad peccandum inducere; discedite consilio, similitudine, vita, affectu, omnes qui operamini iniquitatem: qui mecum pœnitere non vultis. Nolo enim vestro consentire consilio, nolo vobis similis esse, nolo imitari vestram vitam neque affectum. Et hoc ideo, quoniam exaudivit Dominus vocem fletus mei, id est interiorem affectum, ex quo vox et fletus oriuntur, et propter quem exaudiri dicuntur. Non enim clamor, sed amor, non fletus oculi, sed cordis contritio, penetrant cœlos, et in aures Dei introeunt.
paras.en: But now I desire to obey him who says: [[Rom 13:12|Let us, therefore cast off the works of darkness|Abjiciamus opera tenebrarum]]; and so, [[6:9|Depart from me|Discedite a me]], that is, do not lead me into sin; depart in counsel, likeness, life and affection, [[6:9|all ye workers of iniquity|omnes qui operamini iniquitatem]], who will not do penance with me. For I will not consent to your counsel, I will not be like you, I will not imitate your life or your affection. And this [[6:9|for the Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping|quoniam exaudivit Dominus vocem fletus mei]], that is, the inward affection from which voice and weeping arise, and for whose sake they are said to be heard. For it is not clamour but love, not the weeping of the eye but the contrition of the heart, that pierces the heavens and enters the ears of God.

paras.t: Denique hanc suam exauditionem bis repetit, ad ostendendum quam gratus sit Deo, quamque jucundus in Domino pro beneficiis ejus. Ait enim: Exaudivit Dominus deprecationem meam, indulgentiam donans; Dominus orationem meam suscepit, gratiam præstans. Nunquam enim peccatum mortale dimittitur, nisi simul gratia gratum faciens infundatur.
paras.en: Further, he repeats this hearing of his twice, to show how grateful he is to God, and how glad in the Lord for his benefits. For he says: [[6:10|The Lord hath heard my supplication|Exaudivit Dominus deprecationem meam]], granting pardon; [[6:10|the Lord hath received my prayer|Dominus orationem meam suscepit]], bestowing grace. For mortal sin is never forgiven unless sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*: the grace that makes one pleasing to God] is poured in at the same time.

paras.t: Sed quoniam piæ amorosæque mentis est, ut eamdem gratiam aliis optet ac oret, quam sibi divinitus datam cognoscit, idcirco pro aliis orans veraciter pœnitens, Erubescant, inquit, id est, de malis culpæ verecundentur, et conturbentur vehementer ea conturbatione, qua ego turbatus sum, scilicet commotione ad bonum, omnes inimici mei, id est, qui me odiunt, quia me a Deo avertere cupiunt; sed ego diligo eos propter bonum naturæ, quo beatitudinis sunt capaces: nisi enim diligerem eos et essent amici mei, nequaquam orarem pro eis. Convertantur a vanis atque caducis ad verum et incommutabile bonum, et erubescant. Repetitio verbi, est affectionis indicium. Erubescant igitur valde velociter, quia periculum est in mora. Unde scriptum est: Non tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem, et dicas, Miseratio Dei magna est: subito enim veniet ira ejus, et in die qua non speras, disperdet te.
