paras.en: But since it belongs to a devout and loving mind to wish and pray for others the same grace which it knows has been given it by God, the truly penitent man, praying for others, says: [[6:11|Let all my enemies be ashamed|Erubescant]], that is, let them be abashed at the evils of their guilt, [[6:11|and be very much troubled|et conturbentur vehementer]] with that trouble with which I was troubled, namely a stirring towards good, [[6:11|all my enemies|omnes inimici mei]], that is, those who hate me because they desire to turn me away from God; but I love them because of the good of their nature, by which they are capable of beatitude: for unless I loved them, and they were my friends, I would not pray for them at all. [[6:11|let them be turned back|Convertantur]] from vain and perishable things to the true and unchangeable good, [[6:11|and be ashamed|et erubescant]]. The repetition of the word is a sign of affection. Let them be ashamed, then, [[6:11|very speedily|valde velociter]], because there is danger in delay. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 5:8|Delay not to be converted to the Lord, and defer it not from day to day|Non tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem]], and say, [[Ecclus 5:6|The mercy of the Lord is great|Miseratio Dei magna est]]: [[Ecclus 5:9|For his wrath shall come on a sudden|subito enim veniet ira ejus]], and on a day when thou dost not look for it he will destroy thee [the margin gives Eccli. v, 8, 6, 9; Denis's last words differ from 5:9, “in the time of vengeance he will destroy thee”].

paras.t: Postremo certum est, psalmum hunc ad litteram posse exponi de David, quoniam ipse non solum peccator ac pœnitens fuit, sed magna quoque peccata commisit, et omnium pœnitentium spes atque exemplar effectus est, efficacissime pœnitendo, plenissimam indulgentiam consequendo, et excellentissimam gratiam acquirendo. Creditur etiam frequenter ad litteram implevisse quod dictum est: Laboravi in gemitu meo; lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum. Si igitur sic intelligeretur de David, tunc allegorice exponeretur de quolibet efficaciter pœnitente, sicut et modo expositus est. Sed quoniam expositiones istæ non differunt, nisi quod una docet quid sit factum, alia quid sit faciendum, idcirco unica ista expositio sufficit.
paras.en: Lastly, it is certain that this psalm can be expounded literally of David, since he was not only a sinner and a penitent, but also committed great sins, and became the hope and pattern of all penitents, by repenting most effectively, obtaining the fullest pardon and acquiring the most excellent grace. He is also believed often to have fulfilled literally what was said: [[6:7|I have laboured in my groanings, every night I will wash my bed|Laboravi in gemitu meo; lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum]]. If, then, it were understood thus of David, it would be expounded allegorically of anyone who repents effectively, as it has just been expounded. But since these expositions differ only in that one teaches what was done and the other what is to be done, this single exposition suffices.

paras.t: Est autem hic psalmus primus inter pœnitentiales psalmos: qui omnes cum summa diligentia perscrutandi et intelligendi atque legendi sunt, quia in eis tanquam in libro ac speculo docetur peccator se ipsum respicere, peccatorum suorum enormitatem pensare, divinum judicium formidare, devotissimas quoque et affectuosissimas, imo et efficacissimas orationes ad Dominum fundere, quæ cito exaudiri merentur, si tamen cum gustu cordis ac præcordiali contritione fundantur. Considera ergo, o peccator ac pœnitens, sanctum David; labora cum eo in gemitu cordis tui; non des requiem tibi, donec reconcilies tibi Judicem tuum; lava per singulas noctes lectum tuum, quemadmodum Jeremias desiderat, Deducant, inquiens, oculi mei lacrimas per diem et noctem, et non taceant. Unde et sanctus Job ait: Antequam comedam, suspiro; et quasi inundantis aquæ sic rugitus meus. Non tantum emundat et ornat candidissimum pannum ex incuria maculatum lotio aquæ, quantum purgat et ornat rationalem animam pœnitentialis profusio lacrimarum.
paras.en: This psalm is the first among the penitential psalms, all of which are to be searched, understood and read with the greatest care, because in them, as in a book and a mirror, the sinner is taught to look at himself, to weigh the enormity of his sins, to dread the divine judgment, and to pour out to the Lord most devout and affectionate, nay, most effective prayers, which deserve to be quickly heard, provided they are poured out with relish of heart and heartfelt contrition. Consider, then, O sinner and penitent, holy David; labour with him in the groaning of thy heart; give thyself no rest until thou reconcile thy Judge to thee; wash thy bed every night, as Jeremias desires, saying: [[Jer 14:17|Let my eyes shed down tears night and day, and let them not cease|Deducant, inquiens, oculi mei lacrimas per diem et noctem, et non taceant]] [Denis reads “by day and night”]. Hence holy Job too says: [[Job 3:24|Before I eat I sigh: and as overflowing waters, so is my roaring|Antequam comedam, suspiro; et quasi inundantis aquæ sic rugitus meus]]. The washing of water does not so cleanse and adorn a very white cloth soiled by carelessness as the penitential pouring out of tears cleanses and adorns the rational soul.

paras.t: Precatio. Piissimam clementiam tuam, omnipotens Deus, suppliciter imploramus: ut qui assiduis excessibus te offendimus, non in furore tuo arguas, neque in ira tua corripias; sed converte et ab æterna damnatione eripe animas nostras, et salvos nos fac propter misericordiam tuam.
paras.en: Prayer. We humbly implore thy most loving clemency, almighty God: that thou rebuke not in thy indignation, nor chastise in thy wrath, us who offend thee by constant transgressions; but turn us, and deliver our souls from eternal damnation, and save us for thy mercy's sake.

7.title: Explanatio litteralis septimi psalmi: Domine Deus meus, in te speravi
7.title_en: Literal explanation of the seventh psalm: O Lord, my God, in thee have I put my trust

paras.t: Præponitur demum psalmo huic hic titulus: In finem, psalmus David, quem cantavit Domino pro verbis Chusi filii Jemini. Titulus iste variis modis exponitur, secundum quod psalmus iste diversimode explanatur. Secundum litteralem ergo intelligentiam psalmi istius, sensus tituli facilis est. Legitur enim in libro Regum, quemadmodum David persecutionem Absalon fugiens, remisit amicum suum Chusi ad Absalon, quatenus ejus consilia exploraret, et regi David continuo nuntiaret: quod et factum est. Itaque, verborum occasione quæ Chusi intimaverat David, edidit sanctus David hunc psalmum. Qui licet convenientius exponatur de re significata, quam de significante figura, potest tamen exponi de ipsa re gesta ac significante. Unde sic primo exponendus est, sed breviter valde atque cursorie, eo quod talis expositio sit minus fructuosa seu dulcis, et devotioribus fratribus parum suavis ac placens.
paras.en: Next, this title is set before this psalm: Unto the end, [[7:1|The psalm of David, which he sung to the Lord, for the words of Chusi, the son of Jemini|psalmus David, quem cantavit Domino pro verbis Chusi filii Jemini]] [Denis's text has *In finem*, "Unto the end", before the title]. This title is expounded in various ways, according as this psalm is explained in different ways. According to the literal understanding of this psalm, then, the sense of the title is easy. For we read in the book of Kings how David, fleeing the persecution of Absalom, sent his friend Chusi back to Absalom to spy out his counsels and report them at once to King David[[2 Kings 15:34||]]: which was done. So holy David put forth this psalm on the occasion of the words which Chusi had made known to David. And though it is more fittingly expounded of the thing signified than of the figure that signifies, yet it can be expounded of the event itself, the signifying one. So it is first to be expounded thus, but very briefly and in passing, since such an exposition is less fruitful or sweet, and little pleasing or agreeable to the more devout brethren.

paras.t: David igitur ab insidiis, quas sibi Absalon ex consilio Achitophel præparavit, cupiens liberari, sic orat: Domine Deus meus, in te speravi: et ita quodammodo merui exaudiri, quoniam scio quod non deseris sperantes in te: propter quod fiducialiter ad te confugio et exoro; salvum me fac ex omnibus persequentibus me, et libera me; Nequando, id est ne unquam seu aliquo tempore, inimicus meus rapiat animam meam, id est, exstinguat vitam meam, ut leo, qui animalia mansueta decidit: ne, inquam, sic rapiat, dum non est qui redimat, neque qui salvum faciat, id est, quia non est qui redimat et salvet, nisi tu redimas, salvumque facias.
paras.en: David, then, wishing to be delivered from the snares which Absalom laid for him on the counsel of Achitophel, prays thus: [[7:2|O Lord, my God, in thee have I put my trust|Domine Deus meus, in te speravi]]: and so in a manner I have deserved to be heard, since I know that thou dost not forsake those who hope in thee: wherefore I flee to thee with confidence and pray: [[7:2|save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me|salvum me fac ex omnibus persequentibus me, et libera me]]; [[7:3|Lest at any time|Nequando]], that is, lest ever or at any time my enemy [[7:3|seize upon my soul|rapiat animam meam]], that is, put out my life, [[7:3|like a lion|ut leo]], which kills gentle beasts: lest, I say, he so seize it, [[7:3|while there is no one to redeem me, nor to save|dum non est qui redimat, neque qui salvum faciat]], that is, since there is none to redeem and save unless thou redeem and save.

paras.t: Consequenter excusat se David a peccato, quod adversarii sui ei impingebant, asserentes se juste persequi eum, quemadmodum in expositione tertii psalmi plenius dictum est. Ait igitur: Domine Deus meus, si feci istud, quod mihi imponitur, et si est iniquitas in manibus meis, de qua jam non sum contritus; si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, id est, si reddidi malum pro malo: si, inquam, aliquod horum in me est, decidam merito, id est, juste cadam et vincar, ab inimicis meis inanis, id est vanus et a gratia vacuus. David enim puerum Absalon servari præcepit, ne occideretur, et Sauli aliisque suis æmulis benefecit. Denique clarius istud prosequitur: Persequatur inimicus meus, scilicet Absalon et omnis ei adhærens, animam meam, et comprehendat, id est, me ipsum vel vitam meam corporalem exstinguat, et me captivet seu perimat; et conculcet in terra vitam meam, eam penitus exstinguendo, et gloriam meam in pulverem deducat, id est, regia potestate me privet.
paras.en: Next David clears himself of the sin which his adversaries charged him with, claiming that they persecuted him justly, as was said more fully in the exposition of the third psalm. He says, then: [[7:4|O Lord, my God, if I have done this thing|Domine Deus meus, si feci istud]], which is laid to my charge, [[7:4|if there be iniquity in my hands|si est iniquitas in manibus meis]], of which I have not yet repented; [[7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils|si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala]], that is, if I have rendered evil for evil: if, I say, any of these is in me, [[7:5|let me deservedly fall|decidam merito]], that is, let me justly fall and be overcome, [[7:5|empty before my enemies|ab inimicis meis inanis]], that is, vain and void of grace. For David commanded that the young man Absalom be spared and not killed[[2 Kings 18:5||]], and did good to Saul[[1 Kings 24:7||]][[1 Kings 26:9||]] and his other rivals. Next he pursues this more clearly: [[7:6|Let the enemy pursue|Persequatur inimicus]] me, namely Absalom and all who cleave to him, [[7:6|my soul, and take it|animam meam, et comprehendat]], that is, let him put out me or my bodily life, and take me captive or slay me; [[7:6|and tread down my life, on the earth|et conculcet in terra vitam meam]], putting it out altogether, [[7:6|and bring down my glory to the dust|et gloriam meam in pulverem deducat]], that is, deprive me of royal power.

paras.t: Sed quia ita non est, propterea Exsurge, Domine, auxiliando, in ira tua pugnando pro me, et impios juste corripiendo in præsenti, ne æternaliter pereant; et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum, id est, triumpha et prævale in loco et terra adversantium mihi, dando mihi victoriam contra eos, ut desinant dominari in terra, in qua violenter dominium obtinent. Et exsurge, id est, ad actum justitiamque procede, Domine Deus meus, in præcepto quod mandasti; id est, per ipsum tuum legis præceptum ostende impietatem adversariorum meorum. Lex enim præcepit ut filii honorarent parentes, et subditi regem: contra quod faciebant Absalon et ejus fautores, David de regno expellentes. Et synagoga populorum, id est congregatio bonorum atque fidelium, circumdabit te, id est, ex omni parte convolabit ad te, adhærendo tibi, et tuam justitiam approbando. Et propter hanc, id est propter salutem et informationem synagogæ seu populi tui, in altum regredere, id est, majestatem justitiæ tuæ declara, impios et superbos dejiciendo, humiles vero ac pios sublimando. Vel, Regredere, id est, redi in altum, id est in summum justitiæ tuæ, ut qui malos permisisti ad tempus regnare, nunc juste reprimas eos, ne diutius præsidendo, gravius condemnentur. Dominus judicat, id est, discernit, ac juste remunerat, populos, dando unicuique secundum opera sua. Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam, id est secundum exigentiam meritorum meorum, et secundum innocentiam meam super me: id est, secundum abstinentiam meam a malo, restitue mihi, faciendo mihi sicut ego feci proximis meis: quatenus sicut ego illis non nocui, ita nec tu noceas mihi. Istud est verbum hominum perfectorum: et beatus qui tuta conscientia de se ita loqui potest ad Deum omnia cognoscentem.
paras.en: But since it is not so, therefore [[7:7|Rise up, O Lord|Exsurge, Domine]], by helping me, [[7:7|in thy anger|in ira tua]], by fighting for me and justly chastising the wicked in the present, lest they perish eternally; [[7:7|and be thou exalted in the borders of my enemies|et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum]], that is, triumph and prevail in the place and land of those who oppose me, giving me victory over them, so that they cease to rule in the land in which they hold dominion by violence. [[7:7|And arise|Et exsurge]], that is, go forth to the act of justice, [[7:7|O Lord, my God, in the precept which thou hast commanded|Domine Deus meus, in præcepto quod mandasti]]; that is, by that very precept of thy law show the wickedness of my adversaries. For the law commanded that children honour their parents[[Ex 20:12||]], and subjects their king: against which Absalom and his supporters were acting in driving David from the kingdom. [[7:8|And a congregation of people shall surround thee|et synagoga populorum circumdabit te]], that is, the congregation of the good and faithful, that is, will flock to thee from every side, cleaving to thee and approving thy justice. [[7:8|And for their sakes|Et propter hanc]], that is, for the salvation and instruction of the congregation, thy people, [[7:8|return thou on high|in altum regredere]], that is, make known the majesty of thy justice by casting down the wicked and proud and raising up the humble and godly. Or: [[7:8|return thou|Regredere]], that is, go back on high, that is, to the height of thy justice, so that thou, who hast allowed the wicked to reign for a time, mayest now justly restrain them, lest by ruling longer they be more heavily condemned. [[7:9|The Lord judgeth|Dominus judicat]], that is, discerns and justly rewards, [[7:9|the people|populos]], giving to each according to his works[[Rom 2:6||]]. [[7:9|Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice|Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam]], that is, according to what my merits require, [[7:9|and according to my innocence in me|et secundum innocentiam meam super me]] [*super me*, literally "upon me"]: that is, according to my abstaining from evil, repay me, doing to me as I have done to my neighbours: so that as I have not harmed them, neither mayest thou harm me. This is the word of perfect men: and blessed is he who with a safe conscience can speak so of himself to God who knows all things.

paras.t: Consumetur, id est, finem accipiat, nequitia peccatorum, ne addant peccata peccatis, et thesaurizent sibi iram divinæ vindictæ; et diriges justum, id est, in rectam viam deduces, atque perficere facies justum, scrutans corda et renes, Deus, id est, discutiens et intime videns cogitationes, et concupiscentias seu delectationes examinans. Justum adjutorium meum a Domino, qui salvos facit rectos corde. Quia enim superius dixit, Si est iniquitas in manibus meis, etc.; et, Judica me secundum justitiam meam: ideo sequitur, ut juste mereatur adjuvari a Domino, cujus est rectos corde seu justos salvare. Deus judex omnium infallibilis, justus, apud quem non est personarum acceptio, fortis, cujus sententiæ nemo resistere potest, et patiens, id est longanimiter sustinens; numquid irascitur, id est, ulciscitur et juste remunerat, per singulos dies, id est tam cito ut mali merentur? quasi dicat: Non; sed diu et æquanimiter tolerat impios, ut convertantur.
paras.en: [[7:10|The wickedness of sinners shall be brought to nought|Consumetur nequitia peccatorum]], that is, let it come to an end, lest they add sins to sins and treasure up for themselves the wrath of God's vengeance[[Rom 2:5||]]; [[7:10|and thou shalt direct the just|et diriges justum]], that is, thou wilt lead the just into the right way and make him reach perfection, [[7:10|the searcher of hearts and reins is God|scrutans corda et renes, Deus]], that is, sifting and seeing inwardly the thoughts, and examining the desires or delights. [[7:10|Just|Justum]] [[7:11|Is my help from the Lord; who saveth the upright of heart|adjutorium meum a Domino, qui salvos facit rectos corde]]. For since he said above: [[7:4|if there be iniquity in my hands|Si est iniquitas in manibus meis]], etc.; and [[7:9|Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice|Judica me secundum justitiam meam]]: therefore it follows that he justly deserves to be helped by the Lord, whose part it is to save the upright of heart, or the just. [[7:12|God is a just judge|Deus judex omnium infallibilis, justus]], judge of all, infallible, just, with whom there is no respect of persons[[Rom 2:11||]], [[7:12|strong|fortis]], whose sentence no one can resist, [[7:12|and patient|et patiens]], that is, bearing long; [[7:12|is he angry|numquid irascitur]], that is, does he avenge and justly repay, [[7:12|every day?|per singulos dies]] that is, as soon as the wicked deserve? As if to say: No; but he bears with the wicked long and evenly, that they may be converted.

paras.t: Verumtamen, o impii, ne dilatio iræ Dei vos pigros et intimoratos, securosque reddat, ideo dico vobis: Nisi conversi fueritis ad pœnitentiam salutarem, gladium suum vibrabit, id est, manifestam vindictam exercebit, præsertim in futuro, id est universali judicio, quando videbit omnis caro Christum judicem. Arcum suum tetendit, id est, occultam ultionem minatus est impiis, quoniam subtrahit gratiam suam ac paternam correctionem: quæ est occulta atque dirissima pœna divinæ justitiæ; et paravit illum, scilicet arcum ad sagittandum, id est letaliter et æternaliter condemnandum ingratos et duros. Et in eo, scilicet in arcu suo, paravit vasa mortis, id est in effusione ultionis suæ mortiferas pœnas, imo et æterna tormenta. Sagittas suas, id est inflictiones pœnarum, ardentibus effecit, id est, in illicitæ concupiscentiæ ardorem resolutis paravit.
paras.en: Nevertheless, O ye wicked, lest the delay of God's anger make you slothful, fearless and secure, I say to you therefore: [[7:13|Except you will be converted|Nisi conversi fueritis]] to saving penance, [[7:13|he will brandish his sword|gladium suum vibrabit]], that is, he will execute open vengeance, especially in the future, that is, the universal judgment, when all flesh will see Christ the judge[[Matt 25:31||]]. [[7:13|he hath bent his bow|Arcum suum tetendit]], that is, he has threatened the wicked with a hidden vengeance, since he withdraws his grace and fatherly correction: which is the hidden and most dreadful punishment of the divine justice; [[7:13|and made it ready|et paravit illum]], namely the bow for shooting, that is, for condemning mortally and eternally the ungrateful and hard. [[7:14|And in it|Et in eo]], namely in his bow, [[7:14|he hath prepared to instruments of death|paravit vasa mortis]], that is, in the outpouring of his vengeance, deadly punishments, and indeed eternal torments. [[7:14|his arrows|Sagittas suas]], that is, the inflicting of punishments, he hath made ready [[7:14|for them that burn|ardentibus effecit]], that is, he has prepared them for those melted in the heat of unlawful desire.

paras.t: Ecce parturiit injustitiam, id est, impius suggerente diabolo operatus est contra divinum præceptum; concepit dolorem, id est animum inordinatum ac malum propositum: animus enim inordinatus sibi ipsi est pœna; et peperit iniquitatem, id est, ad effectum perduxit quod animo cogitavit. Lacum aperuit, id est, non solum in se ipsum peccavit, sed aliis quoque occasionem peccandi exhibuit: lacum aperuit, id est, malum exemplum seu falsum consilium ministravit proximis; et effodit eum, id est, lacum hunc quantum in se fuit, foris ad operationem malam eduxit; vel, Effodit, id est, profunde in cordibus aliorum eum infixit; vel, Effodit, id est, industriose et penetrative cogitavit quomodo lacum hunc aliis aperiret, eosque in ipsum induceret; et incidit in foveam quam fecit, id est, fraudem et malum seu laqueum quem aliis præparavit, ipsemet incidit. Uniuscujusque iniquitas in proprium redundat auctorem, et ipsi primo atque præcipue nocet; imo dum alium decipere cupit, ipse a dæmone fallitur; et dum alii parat malum pœnæ seu temporalia damna, ipse incidit malum culpæ ac pœnas æternas. Istud in Absalone impletum est, qui alios ad patris sui persecutionem ac mortem induxit; sed incidit in foveam quam fecit, quoniam in fugam conversus est, et laqueo arboris irretitus, tandem a Joab tribus lanceis est transfixus. Convertetur dolor ejus in caput ejus, id est, malitia impii in se ipsum et in rationem ejus revertatur, et noceat ei, habeatque conscientia vermem de vitiis suis; et in verticem ipsius, id est in intellectum ipsius, qui est summa potentia animæ, iniquitas ejus descendet, seu redundabit. Hoc ait, non desiderando, sed prophetando; vel certe desiderando ut temporaliter puniatur a Domino, ne æternaliter crucietur.
paras.en: [[7:15|Behold he hath been in labour with injustice|Ecce parturiit injustitiam]], that is, the wicked man, at the devil's suggestion, has acted against the divine precept; [[7:15|he hath conceived sorrow|concepit dolorem]], that is, a disordered mind and an evil purpose: for a disordered mind is its own punishment; [[7:15|and brought forth iniquity|et peperit iniquitatem]], that is, he has brought into effect what he planned in his mind. [[7:16|He hath opened a pit|Lacum aperuit]], that is, he has not only sinned in himself, but has also given others occasion of sin: [[7:16|He hath opened a pit|lacum aperuit]], that is, he has offered his neighbours bad example or false counsel; [[7:16|and dug it|et effodit eum]], that is, so far as in him lay he has brought this pit out into evil working; or, dug it, that is, fixed it deep in the hearts of others; or, dug it, that is, thought out busily and searchingly how to open this pit to others and lead them into it; [[7:16|and he is fallen into the hole he made|et incidit in foveam quam fecit]], that is, he himself has fallen into the fraud and evil, or the snare, which he prepared for others. Each man's wickedness falls back on its own author, and harms him first and chiefly; indeed, while he wishes to deceive another, he himself is deceived by the devil; and while he prepares for another the evil of punishment, or temporal losses, he himself falls into the evil of guilt and eternal punishments. This was fulfilled in Absalom, who led others to persecute his father and seek his death[[2 Kings 15:10||]]; but he fell into the hole he made, since he was put to flight, caught in the snare of a tree, and at last pierced by Joab with three lances[[2 Kings 18:9||]][[2 Kings 18:14||]]. [[7:17|His sorrow shall be turned on his own head|Convertetur dolor ejus in caput ejus]], that is, let the wicked man's malice turn back upon himself and his reason, and harm him, and let his conscience have the worm for his vices; [[7:17|and his iniquity shall come down upon his crown|et in verticem ipsius iniquitas ejus descendet]], that is, upon his intellect, which is the highest power of the soul, his iniquity will come down, or fall back. He says this not as desiring it but as prophesying; or at least desiring that he be punished by the Lord in time, lest he be tormented eternally.

paras.t: Confitebor Domino, confessione laudis, id est, laudabo Dominum, et laudem ejus cantabo, secundum justitiam ejus, id est, prout justitia ejus declarat eum omni laude dignissimum, eo quod unicuique reddat quemadmodum meruit; et psallam nomini Domini altissimi, id est ipsimet Domino, cujus nomen est super omne nomen: sumit enim nomen pro nomine nominato, non pro voce nominante.
paras.en: [[7:18|I will give glory to the Lord|Confitebor Domino]] with the confession of praise [*confiteri*: both to confess and to praise], that is, I will praise the Lord and sing his praise, [[7:18|according to his justice|secundum justitiam ejus]], that is, as his justice shows him most worthy of all praise, since he renders to each as he has deserved; [[7:18|and will sing to the name of the Lord the most high|et psallam nomini Domini altissimi]], that is, to the Lord himself, whose name is above every name[[Phil 2:9||]]: for it takes *name* for the thing named, not for the word that names.

7.title: EXPLANATIO TROPOLOGICA PSALMI ISTIUS SEPTIMI.
7.title_en: Tropological explanation of this seventh Psalm

paras.t: Insuper, juxta tropologicam expositionem, talis est sensus tituli psalmi istius: In finem, psalmus David, id est, psalmus iste dirigens nos in finem, id est in Christum, attribuitur David, id est fideli, cui facta est revelatio mysteriorum Christi: quem psalmum ille fidelis cantavit Domino, id est ad laudem Dei, pro verbis Chusi, id est pro manifestatione alti silentii, quo Christus dimicavit contra Judæos, occultans eis mysterium suæ passionis.
paras.en: Further, according to the tropological exposition, the sense of the title of this psalm is this: Unto the end, [[7:1|The psalm of David|psalmus David]] [Denis's title has *In finem*, “Unto the end”, which the Vulgate lacks here]: that is, this psalm, directing us to the end, that is, to Christ, is ascribed to David, that is, to one of the faithful to whom the revelation of the mysteries of Christ has been made; which psalm that faithful man [[7:1|sung to the Lord|cantavit Domino]], that is, to the praise of God, [[7:1|for the words of Chusi|pro verbis Chusi]], that is, for the making known of the deep silence with which Christ fought against the Jews, hiding from them the mystery of his passion [*Chusi* is interpreted “silence”].

paras.t: Fidelis igitur Deum cupiens exorare, primo prætendit meritum, dicens: Domine Deus meus, in te speravi: quatenus aures divinæ pietatis tali præludio attrahat, et in se ipso majorem fiduciam exauditionis concipiat. Sperans enim in Domino, meretur exaudiri ab ipso. Itaque, Domine universorum; Deus meus, propter singularem affectum, et cordis fervorem in te; in te speravi. Nam maledictus qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum. Idcirco speravi in te, quia tu solus potes salvare me. Sed vide, o serve Dei, ut ista tibi vere conveniant; vide ut is qui est omnium Dominus, sit specialiter Deus tuus, ita ut tota et pura ac integra mente ei adhæreas, omnem affectionem a summi boni amore elongantem abjicias: quoniam unum est necessarium. Beatus homo qui hoc modo Domino dicere potest: Deus meus. Non est hoc omnium, sed perfectorum dumtaxat. Sacratissimus enim ille atque divinissimus Dionysius in libris suis scribit: Deus, et si fas est dicere, meus. Non audebat absolute dicere, Deus meus: quod tamen verissime dicere potuit, quia instar ferri candentis atque carbonis igniti, in Dei amore mirabiliter æstuabat.
paras.en: The faithful man, then, desiring to entreat God, first puts forward his merit, saying: [[7:2|O Lord, my God, in thee have I put my trust|Domine Deus meus, in te speravi]]: so as to draw the ears of the divine goodness by such a prelude, and to conceive in himself greater confidence of being heard. For one who hopes in the Lord merits to be heard by him. So: [[7:2|O Lord|Domine]] of all things; [[7:2|my God|Deus meus]], because of my singular affection and fervour of heart towards thee; [[7:2|in thee have I put my trust|in te speravi]]. For [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm|maledictus qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum]]. Therefore I have hoped in thee, because thou alone canst save me. But see, O servant of God, that these words truly fit thee; see that he who is Lord of all be in a special way thy God, so that thou cleave to him with a whole, pure and undivided mind, and cast away every affection that draws thee away from the love of the highest good: for [[Luke 10:42|one thing is necessary|unum est necessarium]]. Blessed is the man who can say to the Lord in this way: My God. This belongs not to all, but only to the perfect. For that most sacred and most divine Dionysius writes in his books: God, and, if it is lawful to say so, mine. He did not dare to say outright, My God: which yet he could most truly have said, because, like glowing iron and a burning coal, he burned wonderfully in the love of God.

paras.t: Salvum me fac ex omnibus persequentibus me, ne tentationibus dæmonum vincar, vel carnis illecebris maculer, aut a mundo seducar; et libera me a vinculis peccatorum, et a malis futuris. Nequando rapiat persecutor ac hostis ut leo animam meam, alliciendo eam ad consensum peccati, aut alio modo eam fallendo. Unde in prima Petri docemur: Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret: cui resistite fortes in fide.
paras.en: [[7:2|save me from all them that persecute me|Salvum me fac ex omnibus persequentibus me]], lest I be overcome by the temptations of demons, or stained by the allurements of the flesh, or led astray by the world; [[7:2|and deliver me|et libera me]] from the bonds of sins and from evils to come. [[7:3|Lest at any time he seize|Nequando rapiat]], the persecutor and enemy, [[7:3|upon my soul like a lion|ut leo animam meam]], by enticing it to consent to sin or deceiving it in some other way. Hence we are taught in the first Epistle of Peter: [[1 Pet 5:8|Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]: [[1 Pet 5:9|Whom resist ye, strong in faith|cui resistite fortes in fide]].

paras.t: Domine Deus meus, si feci istud quod sequitur, nempe, si est iniquitas in manibus meis, id est in operationibus et conversatione mea: non quod nunquam peccaverim, vel ab omni peccato immunis sim (si enim dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nosmetipsos seducimus; et nemo mundus a sorde, etiamsi unius diei sit vita ejus super terram); sed ideo dico, Non est iniquitas in manibus meis, quoniam non intendo alicui nocere, et tibi, o Domine, propono fideliter obedire, et de malis præteritis doleo: sicque me ab omni peccato mortali purum confido, præsertim propter id quod sequitur. Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, id est, si vindicavi me ipsum, si non indulsi proximis meis, si non implevi illud Apostoli, Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum: decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis, id est, tunc merito prævalebit adversarius meus in me. Si namque invenitur iniquitas in manibus meis, id est consensus peccandi, propositumque nocendi, et si me ipsum ulciscor, tunc merear non exaudiri a te: et ita destitutus ope et gratia tua, protinus cadam atque deficiam. Hoc autem quod dicitur, Decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis, et, Persequatur, etc., non dicitur imprecando vel desiderando, sed veritatem pandendo.
paras.en: [[7:4|O Lord, my God, if I have done this thing|Domine Deus meus, si feci istud]] which follows, namely, [[7:4|if there be iniquity in my hands|si est iniquitas in manibus meis]], that is, in my doings and conduct: not that I have never sinned, or am free from all sin (for [[1 John 1:8|If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves|si enim dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nosmetipsos seducimus]]; and no one is clean from stain, even if his life upon earth be of one day[[Job 14:4||]] [the margin gives Job 14:4 “in the old version”, that is, the Old Latin made from the Greek; the Vulgate reads differently]); but I say, There is no iniquity in my hands, because I do not intend to harm anyone, and I purpose, O Lord, to obey thee faithfully, and I grieve over past evils: and so I trust that I am clean of all mortal sin, above all because of what follows. [[7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils|Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala]], that is, if I have avenged myself, if I have not forgiven my neighbours, if I have not fulfilled that saying of the Apostle, [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]: [[7:5|let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies|decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis]], that is, then my adversary will deservedly prevail against me. For if iniquity is found in my hands, that is, consent to sin and the purpose of harming, and if I take vengeance for myself, then I shall deserve not to be heard by thee; and so, bereft of thy help and grace, I shall at once fall and fail. And what is said, [[7:5|let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies|Decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis]], and, Let the enemy pursue, etc., is not said by way of curse or wish, but by way of declaring the truth.

paras.t: Si, inquam, reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, persequatur inimicus animam meam, et comprehendat: id est, quia tunc utique merui ut hanc persecutionem patiar. Persequatur inimicus, id est tentator, scilicet dæmon vel mundus seu fomes peccati, animam meam, conando eam ad culpam inducere; et comprehendat, id est eam in lege peccati captivam obtineat; et conculcet in terra vitam meam, id est, affectum animæ meæ temporalibus terrenisque rebus subjiciat, et operationes meas infimis ac vilibus rebus agglutinet: quemadmodum Jeremias ad Dominum ait, Recedentes a te, in terra scribentur; et gloriam meam in pulverem deducat, id est intellectualem animæ meæ portionem, per quam a bestiis separor, ac summæ Trinitatis imagine ornor, ita obtenebret, ut tanquam irrationabilis existimer, et jumentis insipientibus comparer.
paras.en: [[7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils|Si, inquam, reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala]], I say, [[7:6|Let the enemy pursue my soul, and take it|persequatur inimicus animam meam, et comprehendat]]: that is, because then I shall surely have deserved to suffer this persecution. [[7:6|Let the enemy pursue|Persequatur inimicus]], that is, the tempter, namely the devil or the world or the tinder of sin [*fomes peccati*: the inclination to sin left by original sin], [[7:6|my soul|animam meam]], by trying to lead it into guilt; [[7:6|and take it|et comprehendat]], that is, hold it captive in the law of sin; [[7:6|and tread down my life, on the earth|et conculcet in terra vitam meam]], that is, subject the affection of my soul to temporal and earthly things, and glue my doings fast to the lowest and basest things: as Jeremias says to the Lord, [[Jer 17:13|they that depart from thee, shall be written in the earth|Recedentes a te, in terra scribentur]]; [[7:6|and bring down my glory to the dust|et gloriam meam in pulverem deducat]], that is, so darken the intellectual part of my soul, by which I am set apart from the beasts and adorned with the image of the most high Trinity, that I be thought as one without reason and compared to senseless beasts.

paras.t: Ex his autem docetur et commendatur nobis patientiæ virtus, ne alicui vel noceamus vel nocere optemus, nullam exigendo vindictam, nec zelum amarum gerendo ad aliquem, sed cordialiter remittendo: quia nec aliter a Domino exaudiri possumus; sed omnibus insidiis inimicorum nostrorum nos ipsos exponimus atque patefacimus, quemadmodum Sapiens inquit: Qui vindicari vult, a Deo inveniet vindictam. Homo homini reservat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam? In hominem sibi similem non habet misericordiam: quis exorabit pro peccatis illius? Sunt quoque patientiæ tres gradus. Primus est, pro culpa commissa illatam pœnam æquanimiter ferre. Secundus est, pœnam injuste illatam sine tristitia sustinere. Tertius est, non solum illata gaudenter tolerare, sed etiam pro malis reddere bona. Horum patientiæ graduum primus est infimus, et de necessitate salutis: de quo ait Salvator, In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Secundus est altior: de quo Petrus in prima sua Canonica asserit, Hæc est gratia, si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias patiens injuste. Tertius vero gradus est summus: quem imitari christianæ perfectionis est.
paras.en: From these words the virtue of patience is taught and commended to us: that we should neither harm anyone nor wish to harm, demanding no vengeance and bearing no bitter zeal towards anyone, but forgiving from the heart: since otherwise we cannot be heard by the Lord, but lay ourselves open and exposed to all the snares of our enemies, as the Wise man says: [[Ecclus 28:1|He that seeketh to revenge himself, shall find vengeance from the Lord|Qui vindicari vult, a Deo inveniet vindictam]]. [[Ecclus 28:3|Man to man reserveth anger, and doth he seek remedy of God?|Homo homini reservat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam?]] [[Ecclus 28:4|He hath no mercy on a man like himself|In hominem sibi similem non habet misericordiam]]: [[Ecclus 28:5|who shall obtain pardon for his sins?|quis exorabit pro peccatis illius?]] [the margin gives Eccli. xxviii, 1, 3, 4; the last words are from 28:5]. There are also three degrees of patience. The first is to bear with an even mind the punishment inflicted for a fault committed. The second is to endure without sadness punishment unjustly inflicted. The third is not only to bear gladly what is inflicted, but also to return good for evil. Of these degrees of patience the first is the lowest, and necessary for salvation: of it the Saviour says, [[Luke 21:19|In your patience you shall possess your souls|In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras]]. The second is higher: of it Peter asserts in his first canonical Epistle, [[1 Pet 2:19|For this is thankworthy: if, for conscience towards God, a man endure sorrows, suffering wrongfully|Hæc est gratia, si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias patiens injuste]]. But the third degree is the highest: to imitate it belongs to Christian perfection.

paras.t: Post hæc orat fidelis pro resurrectione Christi, quæ sibi divinitus occulte est revelata. Et poterat ista esse oratio antiquorum Sanctorum, dicentium: Exsurge, Domine, o Christe et rex Messia, a mortuis, in ira tua, juste derelinquendo obstinatos incredulos, misericorditerque vocando ad fidem electos; et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum. Hoc in præcedenti expositione satis tractatum est. Potest quoque aliter iste locus exponi: Exsurge, Domine, id est, mihi succurre, et fac me exsurgere a torpore pigritiæ, ab omnique vitio: et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum, id est, per caritatem ac fidem regna et habita in corpore meo, et in omnibus membris meis, in quibus viget lex peccati, atque in viribus animæ meæ, in quibus amplius dominatur originalis culpæ infectio seu fomes. Hæ autem vires sunt appetitus concupiscibilis et irascibilis, ratio atque voluntas, in quibus sunt quatuor vulnera animæ: nam in concupiscibili est concupiscentia; in irascibili, infirmitas; in ratione, ignorantia; et in voluntate, malitia. In his ergo, o Domine, exaltare et regna, vitia expellendo, corpus spiritui subjiciendo, vires naturales virtutibus adornando, ne ultra sint fines inimicorum meorum, id est, ne de cetero regnet in eis dæmon et vitium.
paras.en: After this the faithful man prays for the resurrection of Christ, which has been secretly revealed to him by God. And this could have been the prayer of the Saints of old, saying: [[7:7|Rise up, O Lord|Exsurge, Domine]], O Christ and king Messias, from the dead, [[7:7|in thy anger|in ira tua]], justly forsaking the obstinate unbelievers and mercifully calling the elect to faith; [[7:7|and be thou exalted in the borders of my enemies|et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum]]. This has been treated sufficiently in the preceding exposition. This passage can also be expounded otherwise: [[7:7|Rise up, O Lord|Exsurge, Domine]], that is, help me, and make me rise up from the torpor of sloth and from every vice: [[7:7|and be thou exalted in the borders of my enemies|et exaltare in finibus inimicorum meorum]], that is, by charity and faith reign and dwell in my body and in all my members, in which the law of sin is strong[[Rom 7:23||]], and in the powers of my soul, in which the infection of original guilt, or the tinder, rules the more. These powers are the concupiscible and irascible appetites, reason and will, in which are the four wounds of the soul: for in the concupiscible is concupiscence; in the irascible, weakness; in reason, ignorance; and in the will, malice. In these, then, O Lord, be exalted and reign, by driving out vices, subjecting the body to the spirit and adorning the natural powers with virtues, so that they be no longer the borders of my enemies, that is, so that the devil and vice may reign in them no more.

paras.t: Et exsurge, Domine Deus meus, me exaudiendo et adjuvando in præcepto quod mandasti, id est, dando virtutem exsequendi ac implendi præceptum, quo mandasti nos a carnalibus desideriis abstinere, et sobrie, juste ac sancte ac pie incedere. Et synagoga populorum circumdabit te: id est, si dederis mihi hanc gratiam tam sancte vivendi, profecto multi exemplo mei ædificabuntur, et convertentur ad te: sicque congregatio populi convolabit ad te gratiam deprecando, ut dones eis vitam talem qualem mihi dedisti. Et ideo subditur: Et propter hanc, id est synagogæ seu populi fidelis salutem, in altum regredere, id est, in supremo animæ meæ principare ac præside, omnia opera mea dirigendo secundum divinæ legis ac rectæ rationis imperium.
paras.en: [[7:7|And arise, O Lord, my God|Et exsurge, Domine Deus meus]], by hearing and helping me, [[7:7|in the precept which thou hast commanded|in præcepto quod mandasti]], that is, by giving the strength to carry out and fulfil the precept by which thou hast commanded us to abstain [[1 Pet 2:11|from carnal desires|a carnalibus desideriis]], and to walk soberly, justly, holily and piously[[Tit 2:12||]]. [[7:8|And a congregation of people shall surround thee|Et synagoga populorum circumdabit te]]: that is, if thou give me this grace of living so holily, surely many will be edified by my example and will be converted to thee: and so the gathering of the people will flock to thee, praying for grace, that thou give them such a life as thou hast given me. And therefore it is added: [[7:8|And for their sakes|Et propter hanc]], that is, for the salvation of the congregation or of the faithful people, [[7:8|return thou on high|in altum regredere]], that is, rule and preside in the highest part of my soul, directing all my works according to the command of the divine law and of right reason.

paras.t: Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam. Hæc est oratio viri perfecti de sua perfectione non elati, sed Domino grati, scientis sua merita esse Dei dona: atque bona sua commemorantis non ad propriam laudem, sed ad Creatoris honorem. Itaque ait: Judica me, Domine, id est, discerne ac segrega me a societate malorum, ne eis actu aut voto communicem. Quamvis enim modo cum eis localiter habitem, in vita tamen futura separabis me ab eis loco et gloria, secundum justitiam meam, qua bona commisi, et secundum innocentiam meam, qua a malo declinavi. Consumetur nequitia peccatorum, id est, non diu duret, sed finem accipiat omnis persecutio, atque tentatio malignorum qui opprimunt justos. Breve enim est omne quod nos modo affligit; sed æterna sunt gaudia, quæ justis reposita sunt; æterna quoque tormenta impiis restant. Et diriges justum: id est, cogitationes ejus, affectus, verba et opera ordinabis; et recte perduces ad te, qui es omnium rerum ultimus finis. Cetera autem quæ restant, exponenda sunt sicut ante exposita sunt.
paras.en: [[7:9|Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice|Judica me, Domine, secundum justitiam meam]]. This is the prayer of a perfect man who is not puffed up over his perfection, but grateful to the Lord, knowing that his merits are God's gifts, and recalling his good deeds not for his own praise but for the honour of the Creator. So he says: [[7:9|Judge me, O Lord|Judica me, Domine]], that is, discern and separate me from the company of the wicked, lest I share with them in deed or desire. For though I now dwell with them in place, yet in the life to come thou wilt separate me from them in place and in glory, [[7:9|according to my justice|secundum justitiam meam]], by which I have done good, [[7:9|and according to my innocence|et secundum innocentiam meam]], by which I have turned aside from evil. [[7:10|The wickedness of sinners shall be brought to nought|Consumetur nequitia peccatorum]], that is, let it not last long, but let all the persecution and temptation of the wicked who oppress the just come to an end. For all that afflicts us now is brief[[Rom 8:18||]] [the margin reads Rom. viii, verse unread]; but eternal are the joys laid up for the just, and eternal too the torments that await the wicked. [[7:10|and thou shalt direct the just|Et diriges justum]]: that is, thou wilt order his thoughts, affections, words and works, and lead him aright to thee, who art the last end of all things. The rest that remains is to be expounded as it was expounded before.

paras.t: Sed attende tibi, o frater, quum psalmum hunc cantas vel legis, ne os tuum condemnet te, videlicet si sit iniquitas, id est mala voluntas, et cor impœnitens, in manibus tuis, id est in viribus operativis; et ne velis male facientibus malefacere, sed redde bonum pro malo. Et dimitte si quid habes adversus aliquem, ut et Pater cœlestis tibi ignoscat. Patientia nempe nobis summe necessaria est: et qui eam non habet, nunquam vel raro quietus erit.
paras.en: But take heed to thyself, O brother, when thou singest or readest this psalm, lest thy own mouth condemn thee: namely if there be iniquity, that is, an evil will and an unrepentant heart, in thy hands, that is, in thy working powers; and do not wish to do evil to those who do evil, but render good for evil[[1 Thess 5:15||]][[Rom 12:17||]][[1 Pet 3:9||]]. And forgive, [[Mark 11:25|if you have aught against any man|si quid habes adversus aliquem]], that thy heavenly Father too may pardon thee. For patience is supremely necessary to us: and he who has it not will never, or seldom, be at peace.

paras.t: Precatio. Domine Deus noster, in quem speramus, libera fideles tuos ex omnibus se persequentibus inimicis visibilibus, ut te protectore securitate accepta, sine timore jugiter psallamus nomini tuo benedicto.
paras.en: Prayer. O Lord our God, in whom we hope, deliver thy faithful from all the visible enemies that persecute them, that, having received security under thy protection, we may sing without fear for ever to thy blessed name.

44.title: EXPOSITIO PSALMI QUADRAGESIMI QUARTI : ERUCTAVIT COR MEUM.
44.title_en: Exposition of the forty-fourth psalm: My heart hath uttered.

paras.t: Psalmus jam elucidandus, tali titulo prænotatur : In finem, pro his qui commutabuntur filiis Core, ad intellectum, canticum pro dilecto. Psalmus iste gloriosus ac nobilis, de duplici Christi natura, ac divina generatione ipsius, et de unitate personæ ipsius, de conjunctione quoque Christi sponsi et sponsæ suæ Ecclesiæ, seu Virginis gloriosæ, aut fidelis animæ, excellenter evidenterque tractat : et ideo appellatur epithalamium, id est carmen thalami, nuptias Sponsi ac Sponsæ collaudans.
paras.en: The psalm now to be explained is headed with this title: [[44:1|Unto the end|In finem]], [[44:1|for them that shall be changed|pro his qui commutabuntur]], [[44:1|for the sons of Core|filiis Core]], [[44:1|for understanding|ad intellectum]], [[44:1|A canticle for the Beloved|canticum pro dilecto]]. This glorious and noble psalm treats excellently and plainly of the two natures of Christ and of his divine generation, and of the unity of his person, and also of the union of Christ the bridegroom with his bride, the Church, or the glorious Virgin, or the faithful soul: and therefore it is called an epithalamium, that is, a bridal song [*carmen thalami*, literally "song of the bridal chamber"], praising the marriage of the Bridegroom and the Bride.

paras.t: Sensus ergo tituli talis est : Canticum, in finem, id est psalmus iste, qui dicitur canticum, tendens in Christum, qui est principium nostræ creationis, et finis nostræ recreationis : canticum, inquam, scriptum pro his qui commutabuntur, id est pro electis, qui non solum resurgent, sed etiam immutabuntur, id est, beatam immortalitatem adipiscentur, videlicet pro filiis Core, id est imitatoribus Christi in loco Calvariæ crucifixi. Core enim interpretatur Calvaria. Pro dilecto : id est, canticum istud etiam scriptum est pro Christo, ad quem Pater dixit : Tu es Filius meus carissimus. Sic ergo canticum istud est pro Christo et fidelibus ejus, id est, de Sponso Ecclesiæ et ipsa Ecclesia loquitur. Ad intellectum, id est, quatenus Christi fideles sapienter intelligant Christum, et ejus mysteria, scilicet incarnationem, et conjunctionem cum Ecclesia, fideliter contemplentur. Hieronymus autem in translatione sua juxta Hebræum, ponit hunc titulum : Victori, pro liliis filiorum Core, eruditionis canticum amantissimum : et redit in idem cum titulo præinducto. Per lilia enim intelliguntur fidelia Christi membra, quæ sunt filii Sponsæ.
paras.en: The sense of the title, then, is this: [[44:1|A canticle|Canticum]], [[44:1|unto the end|in finem]], that is, this psalm, which is called a canticle, tending towards Christ, who is the beginning of our creation and the end of our re-creation: a canticle, I say, written [[44:1|for them that shall be changed|pro his qui commutabuntur]], that is, for the elect, who will not only rise again but will also be changed, that is, will attain blessed immortality; namely [[44:1|for the sons of Core|pro filiis Core]], that is, for the imitators of Christ crucified in the place of Calvary. For *Core* is interpreted *Calvary* [the name was taken to mean "baldness", whence Calvary, the bare "place of the skull"]. [[44:1|for the Beloved|Pro dilecto]]: that is, this canticle was also written for Christ, to whom the Father said: [[Luke 3:22|Thou art my beloved Son|Tu es Filius meus carissimus]][[Matt 3:17||]][[Matt 17:5||]][[Luke 9:35||]] [the margin gives Matt. iii, 17; xxii, 5; Luke ii, 22; ii, 35, evidently for Matt 3:17 and 17:5, Luke 3:22 and 9:35; Denis has *carissimus*, "dearest", for *dilectus*, "beloved"]. So this canticle is for Christ and for his faithful, that is, it speaks of the Bridegroom of the Church and of the Church herself. [[44:1|for understanding|Ad intellectum]], that is, so that the faithful of Christ may wisely understand Christ, and faithfully contemplate his mysteries, namely his incarnation and his union with the Church. Jerome, however, in his translation from the Hebrew, gives this title: To the victor, for the lilies of the sons of Core, a most loving canticle of instruction; and it comes to the same as the title given above. For by the lilies are understood the faithful members of Christ, who are the sons of the Bride.

paras.t: Porro exordium psalmi hujus, videlicet primi duo versus, dupliciter exponuntur. Primo, ut sint verba Dei Patris, in cujus persona loquens Propheta, ait : Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum : id est, mens mea paterna, seu ego ipse qui aliud nihil sum nisi mens paterna simplicissima atque purissima, vel intellectus meus æternus, sive memoria mea fecunda, de plenitudine suæ infinitæ fecunditatis ac bonitatis, et de ipso fonte meæ essentiæ infinitis divitiis pleno, intellectualiter protuli, æternaliter dixi, vereque genui unicum Filium mihi consubstantialem, qui est Verbum bonum. De quo scriptum est : Fons sapientiæ Verbum Dei in excelsis ; et, In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum. De quo superius dictum est : Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt. Sapiens quoque : Dum quietum silentium tenerent omnia, et nox in suo cursu medium iter haberet, omnipotens sermo tuus, Domine, de cœlo exsiliens, a regalibus sedibus venit. Dico ego, Pater æternus, opera mea, id est quæcumque ago, regi, id est Christo Filio meo amantissimo, qui est Rex regum et Dominus dominantium. Hoc est quod Christus ait : Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit. Quidquid enim Pater in se ipso cognoscit, hoc in Verbo suo exprimit, ita ut quidquid in Patris essentia continetur, hoc plane resplendet in Filio. Ipse namque Unigenitus, est mentis paternæ Verbum æternum, intelligentiæ dictio, et sapientiæ ejus plena expressio. Denique quidquid Pater in ordine rerum a principio condidit, hoc æternaliter in Verbo suo dixit, atque per ipsum congruo tempore fecit. Propter quod Joannes testatur : Omnia per ipsum facta sunt ; et iterum, Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat.
paras.en: Now the opening of this psalm, namely its first two verses [in this edition's count; both fall within v. 2 as numbered here], is expounded in two ways. First, so that they are the words of God the Father, in whose person the Prophet speaks and says: [[44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]] [*eructavit*, literally "hath belched forth", that is, has poured out from its fullness]: that is, my fatherly mind, or I myself, who am nothing else but the most simple and most pure fatherly mind, or my eternal intellect, or my fruitful memory, out of the fullness of its infinite fruitfulness and goodness, and from the very fountain of my essence, full of infinite riches, have brought forth intellectually, have spoken eternally, and have truly begotten an only Son consubstantial with me, who is the good Word. Of whom it is written: [[Ecclus 1:5|The word of God on high is the fountain of wisdom|Fons sapientiæ Verbum Dei in excelsis]]; and, [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God.|In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum]] Of whom it was said above: [[Ps 32:6|By the word of the Lord the heavens were established|Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt]]. And the Wise Man too: [[Wis 18:14|while all things were in quiet silence, and the night was in the midst of her course|Dum quietum silentium tenerent omnia, et nox in suo cursu medium iter haberet]], [[Wis 18:15|thy Almighty word|omnipotens sermo tuus]], O Lord, [[Wis 18:15|leaped down from heaven from thy royal throne|de cœlo exsiliens, a regalibus sedibus venit]]. [[44:2|I speak|Dico ego]], the eternal Father, [[44:2|my works|opera mea]], that is, whatever I do, [[44:2|to the king|regi]], that is, to Christ, my most beloved Son, who is [[Apoc 19:16|King of kings and Lord of lords|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]]. This is what Christ says: [[John 5:20|the Father loveth the Son and sheweth him all things which himself doth|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit]]. For whatever the Father knows in himself, he expresses in his Word, so that whatever is contained in the Father's essence shines forth plainly in the Son. For the Only-begotten is the eternal Word of the fatherly mind, the utterance of his understanding, and the full expression of his wisdom. Lastly, whatever the Father created in the order of things from the beginning, he spoke eternally in his Word, and made through him at the fitting time. Wherefore John testifies: [[John 1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]; and again, [[John 1:3|that was made|Quod factum est]], [[John 1:4|In him was life|in ipso vita erat]] [Denis follows the old reading "What was made, in him was life", joining the last words of v. 3 to v. 4].

paras.t: Deinde ait Pater æternus : Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis : id est, intellectus meus similis est stilo hominis cito scribentis. Et hoc propter duo. Primo, quoniam sicut verbum quod stilo scribitur, non est sonans ac transiens, sed silens, firmum ac permanens ; sic Verbum Dei Patris non est transiens, sonans atque instabile, sed secretum, firmum, immobile et æternum. Secundo, quoniam sicut stilus velociter scribentis, sine labore ac mora notabili verbum exarat ; sic intellectus divinus ad intra loquens, vel Deus Pater, sine motu, labore et mora Verbum suum produxit in ipso æternitatis momento, quemadmodum Sapientia æterna, quæ est Verbum ac Filius Dei, ait : Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio ; ab æterno ordinata sum. Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram.
paras.en: Then the eternal Father says: [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis]]: that is, my intellect is like the pen of a man who writes quickly. And this for two reasons. First, because as a word that is written with a pen is not sounding and passing, but silent, firm and lasting, so the Word of God the Father is not passing, sounding and unstable, but hidden, firm, unmoved and eternal. Second, because as the pen of one who writes swiftly traces a word without labour or noticeable delay, so the divine intellect speaking within [*ad intra*, that is, within the Godhead itself], or God the Father, brought forth his Word without movement, labour or delay, in the very instant of eternity; as eternal Wisdom, who is the Word and Son of God, says: [[Prov 8:22|The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning|Dominus possedit me in initio viarum suarum, antequam quidquam faceret a principio]]; [[Prov 8:23|I was set up from eternity|ab æterno ordinata sum]]. [[Prov 8:24|The depths were not as yet, and I was already conceived|Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram]].

paras.t: Secundo exponi potest hic locus, ut sint verba Prophetæ ; eritque sensus : Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum : id est, ex plenitudine divinæ illuminationis, et ex abundantia prophetalis notitiæ, intellectus meus protulit, intra se dixit et ore expressit psalmum præsentem, qui est verbum bonum et salubre, ac optimus sermo. Dico ego opera mea regi : id est, scripturam istam et alia cuncta quæ ago, dico, canto, et scribo ad gloriam regis Messiæ, de cujus nuptiis in hoc psalmo tractabo. Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis : id est, lingua oris mei in scribendo hunc psalmum fuit calamus, stilus, penna, seu graphium scriptoris cito scribentis, id est mei ipsius, qui psalmum istum sine proprio studio scripsi et sine labore, secundum quod Spiritus Sanctus me docuit. Lingua enim Prophetæ fuit instrumentum animæ suæ, quemadmodum penna instrumentum est manus scribentis. Scripsitque Propheta hunc psalmum velociter, sicut apud Jeremiam habetur : Dixit Baruch ad principes Juda : Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos ad me, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento. Vel sic : Lingua mea calamus fuit scribæ velociter scribentis, id est Spiritus Sancti, qui quos ad scribendum inspirat, velociter scribere facit. Nescit enim tarda molimina Spiritus Sancti gratia, teste Ambrosio. Et huic sensui consonat quod David alio loco fatetur : Spiritus Domini locutus est per me, et sermo ejus per linguam meam.
paras.en: Second, this passage can be expounded so that they are the words of the Prophet; and the sense will be: [[44:2|My heart hath uttered a good word|Eructavit cor meum verbum bonum]]: that is, out of the fullness of divine enlightenment and the abundance of prophetic knowledge, my intellect has brought forth, has spoken within itself and expressed with the mouth, the present psalm, which is a good and wholesome word, and an excellent discourse. [[44:2|I speak my works to the king|Dico ego opera mea regi]]: that is, this writing and all the other things that I do, I speak, sing and write to the glory of the king Messias, of whose marriage I shall treat in this psalm. [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus scribæ velociter scribentis]]: that is, the tongue of my mouth, in writing this psalm, was the reed, the stylus, the pen or the graver of a writer who writes quickly, that is, of myself, who wrote this psalm without study of my own and without labour, as the Holy Ghost taught me. For the Prophet's tongue was the instrument of his soul, as the pen is the instrument of the hand that writes. And the Prophet wrote this psalm swiftly, as is found in Jeremias: [[Jer 36:18|Baruch said|Dixit Baruch]] to the princes of Juda: [[Jer 36:18|With his mouth he pronounced all these words as if he were reading to me: and I wrote in a volume with ink|Ex ore suo loquebatur Jeremias, quasi legens omnes sermones istos ad me, et ego scribebam in volumine atramento]]. Or thus: [[44:2|My tongue is the pen of a scrivener that writeth swiftly|Lingua mea calamus fuit scribæ velociter scribentis]], that is, of the Holy Ghost, who makes those whom he inspires to write, write swiftly. For the grace of the Holy Ghost knows no slow labours, as Ambrose witnesses. And with this sense agrees what David confesses in another place: [[2 Kings 23:2|The spirit of the Lord hath spoken by me and his word by my tongue.|Spiritus Domini locutus est per me, et sermo ejus per linguam meam]]

paras.t: Prima autem expositio horum versuum, melior est atque profundior, et ei concordat quod per Isaiam ait Deus Pater, Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum, et non revertetur ; illud quoque Ecclesiastici, Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Non solum autem dixit, Eructavit cor meum verbum ; sed, Verbum bonum : ad insinuandum quod Verbum istud sit verus Deus. Nam Christo testante : Nemo bonus nisi Deus. Ipse enim Deus est naturaliter atque quomodolibet bonus ; et secundum Dionysium, natura ejus est bonitas ; primumque Dei nomen est, bonum.
paras.en: But the first exposition of these verses is the better and the deeper, and with it agrees what God the Father says through Isaias: [[Is 45:23|the word of justice shall go out of my mouth, and shall not return|Egredietur de ore meo justitiæ verbum, et non revertetur]]; and that word of Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi primogenita ante omnem creaturam]]. And he did not say only, [[44:2|My heart hath uttered|Eructavit cor meum]] a word, but [[44:2|a good word|Verbum bonum]]: to suggest that this Word is true God. For Christ testifies: [[Mark 10:18|None is good but one, that is God|Nemo bonus nisi Deus]]. For he is God, good by nature and in every way; and according to Dionysius his nature is goodness, and the first name of God is Good.

paras.t: Consequenter prorumpit Propheta in laudem regis istius, et primo commendat eum propter pulchritudinem, dicens : Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum. Triplex speciositas in Christo fuit. Una æterna, divina et infinita : quæ convenit ei ratione divinæ naturæ, estque essentialiter idem cum divina essentia, atque in tribus Personis una ac indivisa. Et de hac pulchritudine Christi, qui est sapientia Patris, scriptum est : Sapientia emanatio quædam est omnipotentis Dei sincera. Candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius. Et Apostolus : Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus, sedet ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis. Unde sanctus Hilarius appropriata divinarum personarum designans : Æternitas, inquit, est in Patre, species in imagine, usus in munere. Quid autem est, Species in imagine, nisi, Pulchritudo convenit Filio tanquam per omnia simili Deo Patri? Propter quod Filius contestatur : Qui videt me, videt et Patrem. Hoc enim ait, non propter identitatem personæ, ut asserebat inimicus sanctæ Trinitatis Sabellius, sed propter omnimodam similitudinem utriusque, secundum quod ait Apostolus : Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ. De hac increata pulchritudine Dei Dionysius pulcherrime loquitur. Propter hanc quoque speciositatem ait de Christo Petrus apostolus : In quem desiderant angeli prospicere.
paras.en: Next the Prophet breaks out into the praise of this king, and first he commends him for his beauty, saying: [[44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]] [literally "beautiful in form"; Denis's word for this beauty is *speciositas*]. There was a threefold beauty in Christ. One is eternal, divine and infinite: it belongs to him by reason of the divine nature, and is essentially the same as the divine essence, and is one and undivided in the three Persons. And of this beauty of Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father, it is written: Wisdom is [[Wis 7:25|a certain pure emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|emanatio quædam est omnipotentis Dei sincera]]. [[Wis 7:26|For she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of God's majesty, and the image of his goodness.|Candor est enim lucis æternæ, et speculum sine macula Dei majestatis, et imago bonitatis illius]] And the Apostle: [[Heb 1:3|Who being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance|Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ et figura substantiæ ejus]], [[Heb 1:3|sitteth on the right hand of the majesty on high|sedet ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis]]. Hence Saint Hilary, setting out the appropriations of the divine Persons [that is, attributes common to all three but ascribed to one of them for a likeness to what is proper to him], says: Eternity is in the Father, beauty [*species*] in the Image, use [*usus*, that is, enjoyment] in the Gift. And what does "beauty in the Image" mean, if not that beauty belongs to the Son as being in all things like God the Father? Wherefore the Son testifies: [[John 14:9|he that seeth me seeth the Father also|Qui videt me, videt et Patrem]]. He says this not because of identity of person, as Sabellius, the enemy of the Holy Trinity, asserted, but because of the complete likeness of each to the other, according to what the Apostle says: [[Col 1:15|Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature|Qui est imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus omnis creaturæ]]. Of this uncreated beauty of God Dionysius speaks most beautifully. Because of this beauty also the apostle Peter says of Christ: [[1 Pet 1:12|on whom the angels desire to look|In quem desiderant angeli prospicere]].

paras.t: Alia est speciositas Christi creata et spiritualis, quæ consistit in perfectione suæ sapientiæ, in excellentia gratiæ, et in eminentia suæ caritatis atque virtutum. Et ista speciositas Christi, summa et incomparabilis fuit, imo et major quam omnium simul electorum : quia scriptum est, Non ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum, subintelligendum est, Christo homini.
paras.en: Another beauty of Christ is created and spiritual, which consists in the perfection of his wisdom, the excellence of his grace, and the eminence of his charity and virtues. And this beauty of Christ was supreme and beyond compare, indeed greater than that of all the elect together: for it is written, [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|Non ad mensuram dat Deus spiritum]]; and we must understand: to Christ as man.

paras.t: Tertia autem speciositas Christi, fuit creata et corporalis, quæ consistit in debita proportione, situ et quantitate membrorum, et in congrua superfusione vivacis coloris. Et ista pulchritudo Christi magna ac vehemens fuit. Primo, quoniam nulla naturalis perfectio defuit ei. Secundo, quia decebat ut anima illa sanctissima atque pulcherrima proportionatum sibi corpus, utpote pulchrum ac nitidum, sortiretur. Tertio, quoniam corpus Christi sumptum erat ex purissima materia, scilicet ex mundissimis sanguinibus dignissimæ Virginis. Quarto, quia formatum compactumque fuit ab agente infallibili, non errante, puta a Spiritu Sancto. Verum an ista corporalis speciositas Christi fuerit simpliciter major, quam aliqua unquam alterius hominis speciositas fuerit, de hoc diversimode dicitur. Ego autem pie credo quod Dominus meus Jesus Christus, etiam quantum ad corporalem pulchritudinem, ceteros omnes, imo et Absalonem excesserit, propter rationes prædictas. Non tamen semper (ut arbitror) æque pulcher in vultu apparuit, quoniam ea quæ pulchritudinem corporalem ornant atque conservant, non curavit, sed sprevit. Pulchritudo autem ejus spiritualis semper æqualis fuit, quia in gratia non profecit. Pulchritudo vero corporis sui, tempore passionis in tantum evanuit, ut de ipso ab Isaia dictum sit : Non est ei species, neque decor ; et vidimus eum, et non erat ei adspectus. De hac autem multiplici pulchritudine Sponsi cœlestis ac regis Messiæ, ait Sponsa : Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus, electus ex millibus ; et, Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus. Sic ergo, o Christe, tu speciosus es forma præ filiis hominum. Quod enim id ipsum ad litteram de Christo dicatur, patet ex translatione Chaldaica, apud Hebræos authentica, quæ sic habet : Pulchritudo tua, rex Messia, major quam filiorum hominum.
paras.en: The third beauty of Christ was created and bodily, which consists in the due proportion, position and size of the members, and in a fitting overspreading of lively colour. And this beauty of Christ was great and striking. First, because no natural perfection was lacking to him. Second, because it was fitting that that most holy and most beautiful soul should receive a body proportioned to it, that is, beautiful and bright. Third, because the body of Christ was taken from the purest matter, namely from the most pure blood of the most worthy Virgin. Fourth, because it was formed and put together by an agent that cannot fail or err, that is, by the Holy Ghost. But whether this bodily beauty of Christ was simply greater than any beauty of any other man ever was, on this different things are said. I for my part piously believe that my Lord Jesus Christ, even in bodily beauty, surpassed all others, even Absalom[[2 Kings 14:25||]], for the reasons given. Yet he did not always (as I think) appear equally beautiful in face, since he did not care for the things that adorn and preserve bodily beauty, but despised them. His spiritual beauty, however, was always the same, because he did not advance in grace. But the beauty of his body so faded at the time of his passion that it was said of him by Isaias: [[Is 53:2|there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness: and we have seen him, and there was no sightliness|Non est ei species, neque decor ; et vidimus eum, et non erat ei adspectus]]. And of this manifold beauty of the heavenly Bridegroom and king Messias the Bride says: [[Cant 5:10|My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands|Dilectus meus candidus et rubicundus, electus ex millibus]]; and, [[Cant 1:15|Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely|Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus]]. So then, O Christ, [[44:3|thou art beautiful above the sons of men|tu speciosus es forma præ filiis hominum]]. For that this very thing is said literally of Christ is clear from the Chaldee translation, held authoritative among the Hebrews, which reads thus: Thy beauty, O king Messias, is greater than that of the sons of men.

paras.t: Porro in libris annalibus Romanorum legitur, quod Christus fuit staturæ proceræ, mediocris et spectabilis, vultum habens venerabilem, quem possent intuentes diligere et formidare ; capillos habens coloris nucis avellanæ præmaturæ, planos fere usque ad aures, ab auribus cincinnos crispos aliquantulum cæruliores et fulgentiores, ab humeris ventilantes ; discrimen habens in medio capitis juxta morem Nazaræorum, frontem planam ac serenissimam sine macula ac ruga, quam rubor moderatus venustavit ; nasi et oris nulla prorsus reprehensio : barbam habens copiosam, capillis concolorem, non longam, sed in mento parum bifurcatam, adspectum simplicem et maturum, oculis glaucis, variis et claris exsistentibus ; in increpatione terribilis, in admonitione blandus et amabilis, hilaris servata gravitate : aliquando flevit, sed nunquam risit ; statura corporis propagatus et rectus, brachia vero et manus visui delectabiles, alloquio gravis, rarus et modestus : talis utique per omnia, ut merito diceretur, Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum.
paras.en: Moreover, it is read in the annals of the Romans that Christ was of tall stature, of middling build and comely to look on, having a venerable face, such that those who looked on it could both love and fear him; having hair of the colour of a hazelnut fully ripe, smooth almost down to the ears, and from the ears in curling locks somewhat darker and more shining, waving about from the shoulders; having a parting in the middle of the head after the manner of the Nazarenes; a forehead smooth and most serene, without spot or wrinkle, graced by a moderate ruddiness; nose and mouth altogether faultless; having a full beard of the colour of his hair, not long, but a little forked at the chin; a simple and mature look, the eyes grey, changeful and clear; terrible in rebuke, gentle and lovable in admonition, cheerful while keeping his gravity; he sometimes wept, but never laughed; in stature of body tall and straight, his arms and hands a delight to see; in speech grave, sparing and modest: such indeed in all things that he might rightly be called: [[44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]] [a footnote of the edition says that earlier editions inserted here the letters of Lentulus and Pilate about Christ, which, according to the edition of 1558, are not found in the Author's original].

paras.t: Deinde Christus laudatur ab eloquentia. Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis : id est, fructuosa et efficax eloquentia data est tibi. Unde per Isaiam Christus ait : Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum. Et ipsi quoque adversarii Christi, compulsi sunt dicere : Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur. Sed et de ipso apud Lucam legitur : Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus. Efficaciam autem Christi in loquendo pandit Evangelista dum ait : Erat docens sicut virtutem habens, non sicut Pharisæi et Scribæ. Sciendum quoque, quod Christus habuit donum linguarum, sicut et ceteras gratias gratis datas : non tamen legitur usus hoc dono, quia non prædicavit nisi in Hebræo. Unde ipse ait : Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel. Denique, sicut manus est organum intellectus practici, sic lingua est organum seu instrumentum intellectus speculativi. Quemadmodum ergo Christus habuit summam sapientiam, sic decuit eum habere summam eloquentiam. Ideo de gratia labiorum Christi sponsi sui ait Sponsa : Anima mea liquefacta est, ut dilectus locutus est.
paras.en: Then Christ is praised for his eloquence. [[44:3|grace is poured abroad in thy lips|Diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis]]: that is, a fruitful and effective eloquence has been given thee. Hence Christ says through Isaias: The Lord [[Is 49:2|hath made my mouth like a sharp sword|Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum]]. And even Christ's adversaries were compelled to say: [[John 7:46|Never did man speak like this man|Nunquam sic locutus est homo, sicut hic loquitur]]. And in Luke too it is read of him that all [[Luke 4:22|wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|Mirabantur omnes in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus]]. And the Evangelist shows Christ's effectiveness in speaking when he says: [[Matt 7:29|he was teaching them as one having power, and not as the scribes and Pharisees|Erat docens sicut virtutem habens, non sicut Pharisæi et Scribæ]]. It should also be known that Christ had the gift of tongues, as he had the other graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts such as prophecy and tongues, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who has them]; yet we do not read that he used this gift, because he preached only in Hebrew. Hence he himself says: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]]. Lastly, as the hand is the organ of the practical intellect, so the tongue is the organ or instrument of the speculative intellect. As Christ, then, had the highest wisdom, so it was fitting that he should have the highest eloquence. Therefore the Bride says of the grace of the lips of Christ her Bridegroom: [[Cant 5:6|My soul melted when he spoke|Anima mea liquefacta est, ut dilectus locutus est]].

paras.t: Propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum. Benedictio Dei, est collatio seu infusio gratiæ Dei ac divinorum donorum, et multiplicatio eorumdem. Christus autem in gratia non profecit, nec sibi ipsi aliquid de essentiali præmio meruit, sicut ubertim præhabitum est. Quomodo ergo propter gratiam labiorum suorum benedictus a Deo asseritur? Et respondendum, quod benedictio ista intelligenda est quantum ad accidentale præmium Christi. Nam per prædicationem suam sanctissimam meruit sibi corporis sui glorificationem et ascensionem. Potest quoque benedictio ista referri ad fructum eloquentiæ Christi, atque ad mysticum corpus ipsius. Dicimus enim terram seu arborem benedici, dum fert copiosum fructum. Similiter quoniam per Christi doctrinam multi salutem sortiti sunt, ipse Christus ratione suæ eloquentiæ benedici asseritur.
paras.en: [[44:3|therefore hath God blessed thee for ever|Propterea benedixit te Deus in æternum]]. The blessing of God is the bestowal or infusion of the grace of God and of divine gifts, and the multiplying of them. But Christ did not advance in grace, nor did he merit for himself anything of the essential reward, as has been set out at length before. How then is he said to be blessed by God because of the grace of his lips? The answer is that this blessing is to be understood with regard to Christ's accidental reward [the joys added to the essential reward, which is the vision of God; for Christ, such as the glory of his body]. For by his most holy preaching he merited for himself the glorification of his body and his ascension. This blessing can also be referred to the fruit of Christ's eloquence, and to his mystical body. For we say that land or a tree is blessed when it bears abundant fruit. Likewise, since many have obtained salvation through Christ's teaching, Christ himself is said to be blessed by reason of his eloquence.
