And each of us ought to honour his angel with special veneration, above all by calling upon him in the morning, that he may protect and guide us the whole day, and in the evening, that through the whole night he may guard our heart and body, drive away harsh dreams, enlighten the mind, go lovingly before us as we rise, and stand by us without ceasing. And that we may deserve to obtain the divine promises set down at the end of this psalm, let us be zealous to sing this psalm at Compline with the most devout mind. If we do so, we shall often taste with the inner palate the power and sweetness of the present psalm, which truly overflows with a wonderful sweetness.

paras.t: Precatio. Deus altissime, concede nos, quæsumus, in adjutorio tuo habitare, et in tua commorari protectione : ut dextera tua avertente, non accedat ad nos malum, nec tangat nos peccatoris flagellum ; sed te mandante, ab angelis in omnibus custodiamur viis nostris.
paras.en: Prayer. O most high God, grant us, we beseech thee, to dwell in thy [[90:1|aid|adjutorio]] and to abide under thy [[90:1|protection|protectione]]: that, thy right hand turning it aside, there may [[90:10|no evil come|non accedat ad nos malum]] to us, nor the sinner's [[90:10|scourge|flagellum]] touch us; but that, at thy charge, we may be kept by the [[90:11|angels|angelis]] in all our ways.

91.title: EXPLANATIO PSALMI NONAGESIMI PRIMI : BONUM EST CONFITERI DOMINO.
91.title_en: Explanation of the ninety-first psalm: It is good to give praise to the Lord.

paras.t: Habet psalmus jam exponendus hunc titulum: Psalmus cantici, in die sabbati, id est, psalmus spiritualis lætitiæ decantandus in die sabbati, id est in sabbato mentis, videlicet in tranquillitate conscientiæ, quatenus ad sabbatum æternitatis mereamur perduci. Ad litteram psalmus iste specialiter conveniebat sabbato, et cantabatur a Judæis in eo, quoniam agit de opere creationis: ad quam commemorandam jussit Dominus diem sabbati celebrari, atque in eo ab omni actu servili cessare, eo quod Deus die septima seu sabbato requievit ab omni opere quod patrarat. Voluit namque Deus inducere homines ad cognitionem suæ æternitatis, et ad cognoscendum omnia alia esse creata. Ad hoc autem (secundum Rabbi Moysen) evidentissima atque facillima via fuit celebratio sabbati, in quo recolitur mundus de novo incepisse, seu ex tempore esse productus, ex quo clarissime constat Creatorem mundi esse æternum.
paras.en: The psalm now to be explained has this title: [[91:1|A psalm of a canticle on the sabbath day|Psalmus cantici, in die sabbati]], that is, a psalm of spiritual gladness to be sung on the sabbath day, that is, in the sabbath of the mind, namely in tranquillity of conscience, so that we may deserve to be brought to the sabbath of eternity. According to the letter, this psalm was especially suited to the sabbath, and was sung on it by the Jews, since it treats of the work of creation: in remembrance of which the Lord commanded the sabbath day to be kept, and on it men to cease from all servile work[[Ex 20:8||]] [the margin gives Exod. xx, 8–11], because God on the seventh day, or sabbath, rested from all the work which he had done[[Gen 2:2||]]. For God wished to lead men to the knowledge of his eternity, and to the knowledge that all other things are created. And for this (according to Rabbi Moses [that is, Moses Maimonides]) the most evident and easiest way was the keeping of the sabbath, on which the world is remembered to have begun anew, or to have been brought forth in time; from which it is most clearly established that the Creator of the world is eternal.

paras.t: Ait ergo sanctus Propheta: Bonum est confiteri Domino. Sicut ubertim prædictum est, duplex est confessio, scilicet: confessio laudis divinæ, de qua ait Salvator, Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ; et confessio nostræ culpæ, de qua alibi scriptum est, Confitemini alterutrum peccata vestra. Utraque autem confessio, bona est et salubris; sed prima multo melior, nobilior atque divinior, quum sit actus angelicus. Sed quoniam non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris, propterea peccatori confessio culpæ in primis magis necessaria est ac salubris, quatenus vitiis per confessionem istam deletis, dignus reddatur Domino confiteri seu Deum laudare. Nunc vero de confessione laudis loquitur psalmus. Bonum est etiam et psallere, id est publice et in sublimi psalmos ac laudes divinas cantare, nomini tuo, id est ad honorem nominis tui, o Deus altissime. Unde Tobiæ angelus Raphael ait: Benedicite Deum cœli, et coram omnibus viventibus confitemini illi, quia fecit vobiscum misericordiam suam. Idcirco nunc subditur:
paras.en: The holy Prophet therefore says: [[91:2|It is good to give praise to the Lord|Bonum est confiteri Domino]]. As has been said at length before, confession [*confessio*: the Latin *confiteri* means both to praise and to confess] is twofold: namely, the confession of divine praise, of which the Saviour says, [[Luke 10:21|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth|Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cœli et terræ]]; and the confession of our guilt, of which it is written elsewhere, [[Jas 5:16|Confess therefore your sins one to another|Confitemini alterutrum peccata vestra]]. Both kinds of confession are good and wholesome; but the first is much better, nobler and more divine, since it is an angelic act. But since [[Ecclus 15:9|Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris]], the confession of guilt is, for the sinner, first of all the more necessary and wholesome, so that, his vices being blotted out by that confession, he may be made worthy to give praise to the Lord, that is, to praise God. Here, however, the psalm speaks of the confession of praise. It is good also [[91:2|to sing|et psallere]], that is, to sing psalms and divine praises openly and aloud, [[91:2|to thy name|nomini tuo]], that is, to the honour of thy name, O God [[91:2|most High|altissime]]. Hence the angel Raphael says to Tobias: [[Tob 12:6|Bless ye the God of heaven, give glory to him in the sight of all that live, because he hath shewn his mercy to you|Benedicite Deum cœli, et coram omnibus viventibus confitemini illi, quia fecit vobiscum misericordiam suam]]. Therefore it is now added:

paras.t: Ad annuntiandum mane, id est in principio diei: de quo Isaias, De mane, inquit, vigilabo ad te; vel, Mane, id est in spirituali aurora, quando videlicet infusionem supernæ claritatis corde sentimus, ex immutatione ac novitate sanctæ devotionis; vel, Mane, id est tempore prosperitatis ac jucunditatis; misericordiam tuam, id est gratiosa beneficia tuæ piissimæ bonitatis, seu benignitatem tibi connaturalem, eam laudando ac prædicando. In quolibet mane jam dicto, annuntiare debemus misericordiam Dei, omnia bona nostra divinæ bonitati devotissime adscribendo: et bonum ac optimum est, a divina laude diem incipere, quatenus totum diem in Dei præconio expendamus, quemadmodum dictum est supra, Repleatur os meum laude, ut cantem gloriam tuam, tota die magnitudinem tuam.
paras.en: [[91:3|To shew forth|Ad annuntiandum]] [[91:3|in the morning|mane]], that is, at the beginning of the day, of which Isaias says: [[Is 26:9|in the morning early|De mane]], he says, [[Is 26:9|I will watch to thee|vigilabo ad te]]; or [[91:3|in the morning|Mane]], that is, in the spiritual dawn, namely when we feel in our heart the infusion of heavenly brightness, from the change and newness of holy devotion; or [[91:3|in the morning|Mane]], that is, in a time of prosperity and joy; [[91:3|thy mercy|misericordiam tuam]], that is, the gracious benefits of thy most loving goodness, or the kindness that is connatural to thee, by praising and proclaiming it. In every morning just named we ought to shew forth the mercy of God, most devoutly ascribing all our goods to the divine goodness; and it is good, and best of all, to begin the day with the praise of God, so that we may spend the whole day in proclaiming him, as was said above: [[Ps 70:8|Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing thy glory; thy greatness all the day long.|Repleatur os meum laude, ut cantem gloriam tuam, tota die magnitudinem tuam.]]

paras.t: Ad annuntiandum quoque et veritatem tuam, per noctem, id est certis horis nocturni temporis: sicut Jeremias hortatur, Consurge, lauda in nocte, in principio vigiliarum. Vel, Per noctem, id est tempore adversitatis, quatenus in nostra castigatione tuam laudemus justitiam, nostramque fateamur malitiam, ob quam flagellari meruimus: dicentes illud Tobiæ, Benedico te, Domine, quoniam tu castigasti me; illud quoque Job, Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut dignus eram non recepi. Vel, Per noctem mentis spiritualem, quando videlicet spiritualis consolatio tollitur, gratia Dei suspenditur, et anima propriam infirmitatem experitur. Tunc enim divinam justitiam laudare debemus, et non fieri pusillanimes, neque adulterinas consolationes desiderare, sed affectuose orare pro reditu pristinæ gratiæ, patienterque sufferre dilecti absentiam vel potius absconsionem (veraciter namque præsens est, non tamen sentitur ejus præsentia), dicentes cum Isaia, Anima mea desideravit te in nocte; cordialiterque pensantes quod apud eumdem Prophetam Dominus asserit: Ad punctum in modico dereliqui te, et in miserationibus magnis congregabo te; in momento indignationis meæ abscondi parumper faciem meam a te, et in misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui.
paras.en: To shew forth also [[91:3|and thy truth|et veritatem tuam]], that is, holy Scripture, the doctrine of Christ, or the divine justice, [[91:3|in the night|per noctem]], that is, at certain hours of the night-time, as Jeremias exhorts: [[Lam 2:19|Arise, give praise in the night, in the beginning of the watches|Consurge, lauda in nocte, in principio vigiliarum]]. Or [[91:3|in the night|Per noctem]], that is, in a time of adversity, so that in our chastisement we may praise thy justice and confess our own wickedness, for which we have deserved to be scourged, saying that word of Tobias, [[Tob 11:17|I bless thee, O Lord|Benedico te, Domine]], [[Tob 11:17|because thou hast chastised me|quoniam tu castigasti me]]; and that of Job, [[Job 33:27|I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and I have not received what I have deserved|Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut dignus eram non recepi]]. Or in the spiritual night of the mind, namely when spiritual consolation is taken away, the grace of God is withheld, and the soul experiences its own weakness. For then we ought to praise the divine justice, and not grow faint-hearted, nor desire counterfeit consolations, but pray with affection for the return of the former grace, and patiently bear the absence, or rather the hiding, of the Beloved (for truly he is present, though his presence is not felt), saying with Isaias, [[Is 26:9|My soul hath desired thee in the night|Anima mea desideravit te in nocte]]; and pondering from the heart what the Lord declares by the same Prophet: [[Is 54:7|For a small moment have I forsaken thee, but with great mercies will I gather thee.|Ad punctum in modico dereliqui te, et in miserationibus magnis congregabo te.]] [[Is 54:8|In a moment of indignation have I hid my face a little while from thee, but with everlasting kindness have I had mercy on thee|in momento indignationis meæ abscondi parumper faciem meam a te, et in misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui]].

paras.t: Et quia Hebræi cum musicis instrumentis Deum laudare solebant, sicut Ecclesia jam agit, organis utens, ideo additur: In decachordo psalterio, cum cantico in cithara. Qualiter vero psalterium decachordum (id est decem chordarum) et cithara spiritualiter exponantur, dictum est supra in elucidatione psalmi octogesimi, cujus exordium est, Exsultate Deo adjutori nostro. Breviter namque tangendo, in decachordo psalterio Deum collaudat, qui decem præcepta observat; laudat quoque in cithara, qui opera misericordiæ non omittit. Taliter conversantis vita et laus, dulcem efficit melodiam in auribus Dei, ita ut dicat illud: Sonet vox tua in auribus meis; vox enim tua dulcis.
paras.en: And because the Hebrews were wont to praise God with musical instruments, as the Church now does in using organs, therefore it is added: [[91:4|Upon an instrument of ten strings, upon the psaltery|In decachordo psalterio]]: [[91:4|with a canticle upon the harp|cum cantico in cithara]]. How the decachord psaltery (that is, of ten strings) and the harp are to be expounded spiritually was said above in the explanation of the eightieth psalm, whose opening is [[Ps 80:2|Rejoice to God our helper|Exsultate Deo adjutori nostro]]. To touch on it briefly: he praises God upon the ten-stringed psaltery who keeps the ten commandments; and he praises him upon the harp who does not leave undone the works of mercy. The life and praise of one who lives so make a sweet melody in the ears of God, so that he says that word: [[Cant 2:14|let thy voice sound in my ears: for thy voice is sweet|Sonet vox tua in auribus meis; vox enim tua dulcis]].

paras.t: Ideo autem bonum est mihi psallere nomini tuo, o Deus altissime, quia delectasti me, Domine, spirituali, interna ac pura delectatione, in factura tua, id est in consideratione ac usu creaturarum tuarum; et in operibus manuum tuarum, id est omnipotentiæ tuæ, videlicet in ordine universi, in speciebus rerum, in pulchritudine mundi, in operibus creationis, recreationis et glorificationis, in contemplatione visibilium ac invisibilium rerum, exsultabo. Unde scriptum est: Quam desiderabilia sunt omnia opera ejus! Et quis satiabitur videns gloriam ejus? In creaturis autem Dei, dupliciter delectari quis potest: primo, in ipsis creaturis secundum se; secundo, referendo omnem perfectionem earum ad Creatorem, ita quod in sapientia atque potentia Dei potius quam in rebus creatis, homo lætatur: et ista delectatio sancta est. Prima quoque mala non est secundum se, nisi quis finaliter insistat in ea, vel immoderate in ipsa occupetur, diffundatur, aut resolvatur.
paras.en: And it is good for me [[91:2|to sing to thy name, O most High|psallere nomini tuo, o Deus altissime]] for this reason: [[91:5|For thou hast given me, O Lord, a delight|quia delectasti me, Domine]], a spiritual, inward and pure delight, [[91:5|in thy doings|in factura tua]], that is, in the consideration and use of thy creatures; [[91:5|and in the works of thy hands|et in operibus manuum tuarum]], that is, of thy omnipotence, namely in the order of the universe, in the species of things, in the beauty of the world, in the works of creation, re-creation and glorification, in the contemplation of things visible and invisible, [[91:5|I shall rejoice|exsultabo]]. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 42:23|O how desirable are all his works|Quam desiderabilia sunt omnia opera ejus]]! [[Ecclus 42:26|And who shall be filled with beholding his glory?|Et quis satiabitur videns gloriam ejus?]] [the margin gives Eccli. xliii, 23, 26; the words are Ecclus 42:23 and 26]. Now a man can take delight in the creatures of God in two ways: first, in the creatures themselves, as they are in themselves; secondly, by referring all their perfection to the Creator, so that a man rejoices in the wisdom and power of God rather than in created things: and this delight is holy. Nor is the first evil in itself, unless one rests in it as in an end, or is immoderately busied with it, poured out or dissolved in it.

paras.t: Quoniam autem Deum in hac vita in se ipso, seu per speciem cernere non valemus, compellimur ex rebus creatis ad ejus cognitionem assurgere. Nam sicut in Proverbiis scribitur, Omnia propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus: quatenus scilicet divinæ naturæ perfectiones in entibus relucerent, sicut perfectio causæ splendet in suo effectu. In quantum igitur ordo specierum universi est velut scala pertingendi ad Creatoris notitiam, delectari et exsultare debemus in operibus Dei. Ex consideratione insuper rerum, videlicet ex rapidissimo ac supervelocissimo motu cœlorum ac siderum, solis ac planetarum, ex magnitudine cœlestium orbium, ex ordine, puritate ac ministerio angelorum, docemur quam sublimis sit Deus, quam reverenter sit ei ministrandum, quam prompte obediendum. Sed et in infimis rebus, puta in ape, formica, lepusculo atque similibus, innotescit ineffabilis sapientia Dei. Omnis quoque pulchritudo, ornatus, dulcedo, bonitas, harmonia atque amabilitas creaturarum, ad omnipotentis Creatoris desiderium et amorem nos provocant. Unde ad hanc contemplationem ac delectationem ab Isaia invitamur: Levate, inquit, in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc. Exsultare etiam debet homo in operibus Dei, quoniam omnia facta sunt propter nos, et ad sustentandam indigentiam nostram condidit Deus omnipotens pisces maris, volucres cœli, bestias terræ, ligna pomifera, herbas diversas.
paras.en: Now since in this life we cannot see God in himself, that is, by sight [*per speciem*: face to face, as opposed to by faith], we are compelled to rise from created things to the knowledge of him. For, as is written in Proverbs, [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|Omnia propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]]: so, namely, that the perfections of the divine nature might shine forth in the things that are, as the perfection of a cause shines in its effect. Inasmuch, then, as the order of the species of the universe is as it were a ladder for reaching the knowledge of the Creator, we ought to delight and rejoice in the works of God. Moreover, from the consideration of things, namely from the most rapid and more than swift motion of the heavens and the stars, the sun and the planets, from the greatness of the heavenly spheres, from the order, purity and ministry of the angels, we are taught how sublime God is, how reverently he is to be served, how promptly obeyed. And even in the lowest things, for instance in the bee, the ant, the little hare and the like, the ineffable wisdom of God becomes known. All the beauty, too, the adornment, sweetness, goodness, harmony and loveliness of creatures stir us to the desire and love of the almighty Creator. Hence we are invited by Isaias to this contemplation and delight: [[Is 40:26|Lift up|Levate]], he says, [[Is 40:26|your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]]. Man ought also to rejoice in the works of God because all things were made for our sake, and to sustain our need almighty God created the fishes of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts of the earth, the fruit trees and the divers herbs.

paras.t: Quam magnificata sunt opera tua, Domine! id est, valde magnifice, sapienter, potenter et inscrutabiliter sunt instituta, distincta atque ornata. Decuit namque (quemadmodum Plato affirmat) a sapientissimo, speciosissimo, optimoque opifice opus pulcherrimum, præclarissimum, excellentissimumque produci, qualis est machina mundi, qui incomparabili pulchritudine constat. Majora autem et incomprehensibiliora sunt opera recreationis et glorificationis, quam creationis. Unde quæ unigenitus Filius Dei pro nostra salute assumpsit, fecit ac pertulit, omnem magnificentiam, investigationem, sermonem transcendunt. Propter quod in Apocalypsi dicitur: Magna et mirabilia sunt opera tua, Domine Deus omnipotens. Et in Ecclesiaste: Cunctæ res difficiles, non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Sapiens quoque: Difficile æstimamus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore. Quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit?
paras.en: [[91:6|O Lord, how great are thy works!|Quam magnificata sunt opera tua, Domine!]] that is, they are very magnificently, wisely, mightily and unsearchably established, set in order and adorned. For it was fitting (as Plato affirms) that by a most wise, most beautiful and best of craftsmen a work most beautiful, most glorious and most excellent should be produced, such as is the fabric of the world, which consists of incomparable beauty. But greater and more incomprehensible are the works of re-creation [that is, of redemption] and of glorification than those of creation. Hence what the only-begotten Son of God took upon himself, did and endured for our salvation surpasses all magnificence, all searching and all speech. Wherefore it is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 15:3|Great and wonderful are thy works, O Lord God Almighty|Magna et mirabilia sunt opera tua, Domine Deus omnipotens]]. And in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word|Cunctæ res difficiles, non potest eas homo explicare sermone]]. The Wise Man also: [[Wis 9:16|And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth: and with labour do we find the things that are before us. But the things that are in heaven, who shall search out?|Difficile æstimamus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore. Quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit?]]

paras.t: Denique si subtilius contemplari desideramus, quam magnificata sunt opera Creatoris, profunde pensemus quid Dominus dicat ad sanctum Job: Ubi, inquit, eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ? Indica mihi, si habes intelligentiam. Quis posuit mensuras ejus? aut quis tetendit super eam lineam? Super quo bases ejus solidatæ sunt? Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens; quum ponerem nubem vestimentum ejus, et caligine illud quasi pannis infantiæ obvolverem? Circumdedi illud terminis meis, et posui vectem et ostia, et dixi: Usque huc venies, et non procedes amplius, et hic confringes tumentes fluctus tuos. Numquid conjungere valebis micantes stellas Pleiades, aut gyrum Arcturi poteris dissipare? Numquid nosti ordinem cœli, aut pones rationem ejus in terra? Quis posuit in visceribus hominis sapientiam? aut quis dedit gallo intelligentiam? Quis enarrabit cœlorum rationem? et concentum cœli dormire quis faciet? Sed vere quidquid de operibus supergloriosissimi Creatoris intelligere aut profari valemus, pene nullius momenti est ad id, quod in re ipsa est. Propter quod iterum in Job habetur: Ecce hæc ex parte dicta sunt viarum ejus; et quum vix parvam stillam sermonum ejus audierimus, quis poterit tonitruum magnitudinis ejus intueri? Propter quod etiam Plato testatur, quod ea quæ scimus, minima et prope nulla sunt respectu eorum quæ ignoramus. Aristoteles quoque disseruit: Quia sicut se habet oculus vespertilionis ad solis fulgorem, ita se habet intellectus humanus ad cognitionem manifestissimorum naturæ, id est ad notitiam substantiarum separatarum.
paras.en: Lastly, if we wish to contemplate more subtly how great are the works of the Creator, let us ponder deeply what the Lord says to holy Job: [[Job 38:4|Where|Ubi]], he says, [[Job 38:4|wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? tell me if thou hast understanding|eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ? Indica mihi, si habes intelligentiam]]. [[Job 38:5|Who hath laid the measures thereof|Quis posuit mensuras ejus?]] [[Job 38:5|or who hath stretched the line upon it?|aut quis tetendit super eam lineam?]] [[Job 38:6|Upon what are its bases grounded?|Super quo bases ejus solidatæ sunt?]] [[Job 38:8|Who shut up the sea with doors, when it broke forth as issuing out of the womb:|Quis conclusit ostiis mare, quando erumpebat quasi de vulva procedens]] [[Job 38:9|When I made a cloud the garment thereof, and wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands?|quum ponerem nubem vestimentum ejus, et caligine illud quasi pannis infantiæ obvolverem?]] [[Job 38:10|I set my bounds around it, and made it bars and doors:|Circumdedi illud terminis meis, et posui vectem et ostia]] [[Job 38:11|And I said: Hitherto thou shalt come, and shalt go no further, and here thou shalt break thy swelling waves.|et dixi: Usque huc venies, et non procedes amplius, et hic confringes tumentes fluctus tuos]] [[Job 38:31|Shalt thou be able to join together the shining stars the Pleiades, or canst thou stop the turning about of Arcturus?|Numquid conjungere valebis micantes stellas Pleiades, aut gyrum Arcturi poteris dissipare?]] [[Job 38:33|Dost thou know the order of heaven, and canst thou set down the reason thereof on the earth?|Numquid nosti ordinem cœli, aut pones rationem ejus in terra?]] [[Job 38:36|Who hath put wisdom in the heart of man? or who gave the cock understanding?|Quis posuit in visceribus hominis sapientiam? aut quis dedit gallo intelligentiam?]] [[Job 38:37|Who can declare the order of the heavens, or who can make the harmony of heaven to sleep?|Quis enarrabit cœlorum rationem? et concentum cœli dormire quis faciet?]] But truly, whatever we can understand or utter of the works of the supremely glorious Creator is of almost no account beside what is in the thing itself. Wherefore again it is said in Job: [[Job 26:14|Lo, these things are said in part of his ways: and seeing we have heard scarce a little drop of his word, who shall be able to behold the thunder of his greatness?|Ecce hæc ex parte dicta sunt viarum ejus; et quum vix parvam stillam sermonum ejus audierimus, quis poterit tonitruum magnitudinis ejus intueri?]] Wherefore Plato too testifies that the things we know are very few and almost nothing in respect of those we do not know. Aristotle also taught that as the eye of the bat is to the brightness of the sun, so is the human intellect to the knowledge of the things most manifest in nature, that is, to the knowledge of the separated substances [that is, the pure spirits, which are most knowable in themselves, though least so to us].

paras.t: Itaque si opera Dei tam magna et incomprehensibilia sunt, quam incomprehensibilis est Creator eorum! (Ipse enim in infinitum cuncta in omni nobilitate transcendit.) Ideo subditur: nimis profundæ factæ sunt cogitationes tuæ, id est, consilium, ratio et ordinatio sapientiæ tuæ, qua omnia certo fine fecisti, atque in numero, mensura ac pondere constituisti, valde et penitus imperscrutabilis ineffabilisque consistit. Certissime enim cognoscimus, nihil sine legitima ratione a te fieri aut permitti. Verumtamen rationem operum tuorum in speciali assignare omnino impossibile profitemur. Quis enim excogitet, cur in primordiali rerum institutione seu creatione, quando merita nulla præcesserant, ampliorem perfectionem dederis uni, quam alteri? Quis novit, cur mundum ab æterno non feceris, vel cur eum creaveris in illo instanti quo factus est, et non prius neque posterius? Quis insuper capere poterit, cur potius unum angelum, unumque hominem ab æterno ad vitam æternam elegeris, quam alium? Quum ergo omnia hæc tam incomprehensibilia sint, liquet quod cogitationes tuæ, id est sapientialis tua dispositio, universorum finem, rationem ac ordinem pensans, sit nimis profunda: idcirco scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria. Et veraciter scriptum est: Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris spiritum tuum de cœlis? Isaias quoque profunditatem cogitationum divinæ mentis declarat ex eo, quod nullus prior Deo formam agendi ostendit, sed ipse ex propriæ sapientiæ supersplendidissimo atque certissimo fonte cuncta molitus est. Ait enim: Quis adjuvit spiritum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit, et ostendit illi? Cum quo iniit consilium, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientia, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi? Huic autem prophetali eloquio consonat Apostolicus sermo: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei, etc.
paras.en: If, then, the works of God are so great and incomprehensible, how incomprehensible is their Creator! (For he infinitely surpasses all things in every nobility.) Therefore it is added: [[91:6|thy thoughts are exceeding deep|nimis profundæ factæ sunt cogitationes tuæ]], that is, the counsel, reason and ordering of thy wisdom, by which thou hast made all things for a fixed end, and established them in number, measure and weight[[Wis 11:21||]], is very greatly and wholly unsearchable and ineffable. For we know most certainly that nothing is done or permitted by thee without a just reason. Yet we confess that to assign the reason of thy works in particular is altogether impossible. For who could think out why, in the first establishment or creation of things, when no merits had gone before, thou gavest greater perfection to one than to another? Who knows why thou didst not make the world from eternity, or why thou didst create it at the instant at which it was made, and not earlier or later? Who, moreover, can grasp why from eternity thou hast chosen one angel and one man to eternal life rather than another? Since, then, all these things are so incomprehensible, it is plain that thy thoughts, that is, thy wise disposition, weighing the end, reason and order of all things, are exceeding deep: therefore [[Prov 25:27|he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria]]. And truly it is written: [[Wis 9:17|who shall know thy thought, except thou give wisdom, and send thy holy Spirit from above|Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris spiritum tuum de cœlis?]]? [the margin gives Psal. xci, 17, evidently for Sap. ix, 17] Isaias too declares the depth of the thoughts of the divine mind from this, that no one before God showed him the manner of working, but he himself framed all things from the most resplendent and most certain fountain of his own wisdom. For he says: [[Is 40:13|Who hath forwarded the spirit of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor, and hath taught him?|Quis adjuvit spiritum Domini? aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit, et ostendit illi?]] [[Is 40:14|With whom hath he consulted, and who hath instructed him, and taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and shewed him the way of understanding?|Cum quo iniit consilium, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientia, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi?]] And with this prophetic utterance the word of the Apostle agrees: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei]] etc.

paras.t: Dicuntur autem cogitationes Dei pluraliter, non quod in Deo sint distinctæ ac multæ cogitationes, quum cogitatio Dei sit ejus essentia, intellectus et sapientia: sed sicut dicuntur in Deo plures atque distinctæ ideæ, per relationem ad creata in Deo idealiter existentia, sic dicuntur in Deo plures cogitationes secundum diversitatem operationum quæ cognoscuntur a Deo.
paras.en: Now God's thoughts are spoken of in the plural, not because there are many distinct thoughts in God, since the thought of God is his essence, his intellect and his wisdom; but as many distinct ideas are said to be in God, by their relation to created things existing ideally in God, so many thoughts are said to be in God according to the diversity of the works that are known by God.

paras.t: Vir insipiens, id est illa sapientia carens quæ in malevolam animam non intrat, quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti: per quam utique sapientiam judicat homo recte de Deo, non per informem notitiam, sed per cognitionem formatam et sapidam: non cognoscet quomodo ex creaturis honorandus atque amandus sit Deus creator: de quo scriptum est, Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur. Propter quod de philosophis hujus mundi dicit Apostolus: Evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum. Et stultus, id est, qui vel vera scientia divinæ legis privatus est, vel ea quæ novit esse agenda non operatur, non intelliget hæc dicta atque dicenda, per intelligentiam salutarem ac operosam. Propter quod Dominus apud Jeremiam ait: Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor. Me non timebitis, qui posui arenam terminum mari? Et Apostolus dicit: Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Stultitia enim est illi, et non potest intelligere, scilicet mysteria Dei, præmia bonorum, et pœnas malorum.
paras.en: [[91:7|The senseless man|Vir insipiens]], that is, one lacking that wisdom which does not enter into a malicious soul, which is a gift of the Holy Ghost, by which wisdom a man judges rightly of God, not through unformed knowledge but through formed and savouring knowledge [*sapida*, "having savour", a play on *sapientia*; "formed" knowledge is knowledge quickened by charity], [[91:7|shall not know|non cognoscet]] how God the Creator is to be honoured and loved from his creatures; of whom it is written: [[Eccles 3:14|God hath made|Fecit Deus]] his works [[Eccles 3:14|that he may be feared|ut timeatur]]. Wherefore the Apostle says of the philosophers of this world: [[Rom 1:21|became vain in their thoughts. And their foolish heart was darkened|Evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum]]. [[91:7|nor will the fool|Et stultus]], that is, he who is either deprived of the true knowledge of the divine law, or does not do what he knows ought to be done, [[91:7|understand these things|non intelliget hæc]] said and still to be said, with a saving and working understanding. Wherefore the Lord says by Jeremias: [[Jer 5:21|Hear, O foolish people, and without understanding|Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor]]. [[Jer 5:22|Will not you then fear me|Me non timebitis]], who [[Jer 5:22|have set the sand a bound for the sea|posui arenam terminum mari]]? And the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him: and he cannot understand|Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Stultitia enim est illi, et non potest intelligere]], namely the mysteries of God, the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked.

paras.t: De quorum damnatione subjungitur: Quum creverint impii sicut fœnum, id est, quando iniqui cœperint consurgere, prosperari, atque florere sicut fœnum quod hodie floret et est, cras vero in clibanum mittitur, esseque desinit: quoniam sicut nunc superius dictum est, impiorum prosperitas momentanea est, statimque marcescit eorum floritio, quemadmodum viror fœni mox decidit. Unde in Isaia legitur: Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus quasi flos agri; et denuo: Vere fœnum est populus: exsiccatum est fœnum, et cecidit flos. Et apparuerint aliquid esse, seu modico tempore prævalere et gloriari, omnes qui operantur iniquitatem: quos Deus permittit ad horam in suis desideriis ambulare, quatenus æternaliter justa pœna plectantur, quemadmodum sequitur: Ut intereant, id est, spiritualiter moriantur et condemnentur, in sæculum sæculi, id est sine fine, tanquam separati a fonte omnis vitæ ac gloriæ. Unde Salomon ait: Impium operatus est Dominus ad diem malum. De quo die impiique damnatione in libro Job scriptum est: In diem perditionis servatur malus, et ad diem furoris ducetur: et de furore Omnipotentis bibet.
paras.en: Of their damnation it is added: [[91:8|When the wicked shall spring up as grass|Quum creverint impii sicut fœnum]] [Denis reads *Quum creverint impii*, "when the wicked shall grow"; the Vulgate has *Cum exorti fuerint peccatores*], that is, when the unjust begin to rise up, to prosper and to flourish like grass, which to-day flourishes and is, but [[Matt 6:30|to morrow is cast into the oven|cras vero in clibanum mittitur]], and ceases to be: since, as was said just above, the prosperity of the wicked is momentary, and their flowering withers at once, as the greenness of grass soon falls away. Hence we read in Isaias: [[Is 40:6|All flesh is grass, and all the glory thereof as the flower of the field|Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus quasi flos agri]]; and again: [[Is 40:7|Indeed the people is grass|Vere fœnum est populus]]: [[Is 40:8|The grass is withered, and the flower is fallen|exsiccatum est fœnum, et cecidit flos]]. And [[91:8|shall appear|apparuerint]] to be something, or to prevail and glory for a little time, [[91:8|all the workers of iniquity|omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]], whom God permits for an hour to walk in their own desires, so that they may be punished eternally with a just penalty, as follows: [[91:8|That they may perish|Ut intereant]], that is, die spiritually and be condemned, [[91:8|for ever and ever|in sæculum sæculi]], that is, without end, as being cut off from the fountain of all life and glory. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made|operatus est Dominus]] [[Prov 16:4|the wicked|Impium]] [[Prov 16:4|for the evil day|ad diem malum]]. Of which day, and of the damnation of the wicked, it is written in the book of Job: [[Job 21:30|the wicked man is reserved to the day of destruction, and he shall be brought to the day of wrath|In diem perditionis servatur malus, et ad diem furoris ducetur]]: [[Job 21:20|and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty|et de furore Omnipotentis bibet]] [the margin gives Job xxi, 20, which is the last clause; the first words are v. 30].

paras.t: Tu autem Altissimus in æternum, Domine: quia omnes in omnipotentia, in sapientia, in æquitate, in bonitate et felicitate incomparabiliter superas. Quod patet ex eo.
paras.en: [[91:9|But thou, O Lord, art most high for evermore|Tu autem Altissimus in æternum, Domine]]: because thou surpassest all beyond compare in omnipotence, in wisdom, in equity, in goodness and in happiness. This is plain from what follows.

paras.t: Quoniam ecce inimici tui, id est tibi rebelles, ingrati ac reprobi, Domine, quoniam ecce inimici tui peribunt, gratiam in præsenti perdendo, gloriamque regni cœlestis postmodum amittendo, atque æternæ mortis incendia in inferno ferendo. Quam horribile nimis est esse inimicum Dei! imo horribile est hoc ipsum audire: idcirco repetitur, ut amplius expavescas. Et dispergentur, id est, a grege electorum repellentur in die judicii, omnes qui operantur sine cessatione et pœnitentia iniquitatem. Tunc enim dicetur ad eos: Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum. Propterea ait Scriptura: Ruinæ impiorum erunt, et disperdam eos a facie terræ, dicit Dominus; itemque, Disperdam eos qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini, dicit Dominus, et qui Dominum non exquisierunt, nec investigaverunt eum.
paras.en: [[91:10|For behold thy enemies|Quoniam ecce inimici tui]], that is, those who are rebellious against thee, ungrateful and reprobate, [[91:10|O Lord, for behold thy enemies shall perish|Domine, quoniam ecce inimici tui peribunt]], losing grace in the present, afterwards losing the glory of the heavenly kingdom, and bearing the fires of eternal death in hell. How exceedingly horrible it is to be an enemy of God! nay, it is horrible even to hear of it: therefore it is repeated, that thou mayest be the more afraid. And [[91:10|shall be scattered|dispergentur]], that is, shall be driven out from the flock of the elect on the day of judgment, [[91:10|all the workers|omnes qui operantur]], without ceasing and without penance, [[91:10|of iniquity|iniquitatem]]. For then it shall be said to them: [[Matt 25:41|Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire|Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum]]. Therefore Scripture says: [[Soph 1:3|the ungodly shall meet with ruin|Ruinæ impiorum erunt]], [[Soph 1:3|and I will destroy|et disperdam]] them [[Soph 1:3|from off the face of the land, saith the Lord|a facie terræ, dicit Dominus]]; and again: I will destroy [[Soph 1:6|them that turn away from following after the Lord|eos qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini]], saith the Lord, [[Soph 1:6|and that have not sought the Lord, nor searched after him|et qui Dominum non exquisierunt, nec investigaverunt eum]].

paras.t: Deinde ab hac damnatione distinguuntur electi, de quorum tribulatione et gloria subditur: Et exaltabitur sicut unicornis cornu meum: id est, imperium rationis meæ, sensualitati ac animo dominantis, sublimabitur per confirmationem gratiæ Dei, sicut unicornis cornu sublimatur: quia hoc animal fortissimum est, unoque cornu ab aliorum invasione se protegit. Sic cornu meum, id est fortitudo sive dominium rationis meæ, roborabitur contra passionum, tentationum, persecutionumque universos incursus. In die autem judicii cornu hoc animæ in tantum exaltabitur in electis, ut caro nunquam concupiscat adversus spiritum, neque aliquid actum rationis impediat: quin imo corpus corruptibile nunc aggravans animam, tunc erit spirituale, immortale, animam ornans atque exhilarans. Et senectus mea, id est ætas mea ultima, erit in misericordia uberi: quia quum deficiet virtus mea, non derelinques me. Et licet is qui foris est, noster homo corrumpatur, tamen is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem in gratia Dei, secundum Apostolum. Ista sunt verba bonæ spei, non præsumptionis iniquæ; quoniam ex caritate ardenti et fiducia magna mentis in Deo, ista dicuntur ab Ecclesia seu quolibet justo.
paras.en: Next the elect are set apart from this damnation, and of their tribulation and glory it is added: [[91:11|But my horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn|Et exaltabitur sicut unicornis cornu meum]]: that is, the rule of my reason, which governs sensuality and the passions [*animo*: here the soul's lower impulses], shall be raised on high through the confirmation of the grace of God, as the horn of the unicorn is raised on high: for this animal is very strong, and with its one horn protects itself against the attack of others. So *my horn*, that is, the strength or dominion of my reason, shall be strengthened against all the assaults of passions, temptations and persecutions. And on the day of judgment this horn of the soul shall be so exalted in the elect that the flesh shall never lust against the spirit[[Gal 5:17||]], nor hinder any act of reason: nay rather, the corruptible body that now weighs down the soul[[Wis 9:15||]] shall then be spiritual and immortal, adorning and gladdening the soul. [[91:11|and my old age|Et senectus mea]], that is, my last age, shall be [[91:11|in plentiful mercy|in misericordia uberi]]: because [[Ps 70:9|when my strength shall fail|quum deficiet virtus mea]], thou wilt not forsake me [Denis turns the Psalm's prayer, *do not thou forsake me*, into a statement]. And though [[2 Cor 4:16|our outward man is corrupted|is qui foris est, noster homo corrumpatur]], yet [[2 Cor 4:16|the inward man is renewed day by day|is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem]] in the grace of God, according to the Apostle. These are words of good hope, not of wicked presumption; for they are spoken by the Church, or by any just man, out of burning charity and great confidence of mind in God.

paras.t: Et despexerit oculus meus intellectualis inimicos meos, dæmones hominesque perversos: quoniam propter spem quam habeo in Domino Deo meo, non timeo superari ab eis: sicut inferius dicitur, Dominus mihi adjutor, non timebo quid faciat mihi homo. Et rursus scriptum est: Timorem eorum ne timueritis, nec conturbemini. Inimici nostri visibiles, scilicet homines mali, in quantum sunt homines gratiæ gloriæque capaces, amandi sunt, juxta illud: Diligite inimicos vestros. In quantum vero sunt impii, et veritatis adversarii, despiciendi sunt, odiendi et vilipendendi. Unde superius de viro justo præhabitum est: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus. Et insurgentibus in me (injuste videlicet) malignantibus, audiet auris mea, id est, cum quadam derisione et sine pavore audiam minas eorum. Vel, Insurgentibus in me malignantibus, id est ad confusionem eorum, audiet auris mea sententiam judicis justi, qui eos damnabit, meque salvabit.
paras.en: [[91:12|My eye also hath looked down|Et despexerit oculus meus]], my intellectual eye, [[91:12|upon my enemies|inimicos meos]], demons and perverse men: because, through the hope that I have in the Lord my God, I do not fear to be overcome by them; as is said further on: [[Ps 117:6|The Lord is my helper: I will not fear what man can do unto me.|Dominus mihi adjutor; non timebo quid faciat mihi homo.]] And again it is written: [[1 Pet 3:14|be not afraid of their fear: and be not troubled|Timorem eorum ne timueritis, nec conturbemini]]. Our visible enemies, namely wicked men, are to be loved inasmuch as they are men capable of grace and glory, according to that word: [[Matt 5:44|Love your enemies|Diligite inimicos vestros]]. But inasmuch as they are wicked and adversaries of the truth, they are to be despised, hated and held cheap. Hence it was said above of the just man: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus]]. [[91:12|and my ear shall hear of the downfall of the malignant that rise up against me|Et insurgentibus in me (injuste videlicet) malignantibus, audiet auris mea]] (unjustly, that is): that is, I shall hear their threats with a certain derision and without fear [in this first reading Denis takes the verse as *my ear shall hear the malignant*, without the Douay-Rheims's *downfall*]. Or, as to [[91:12|the malignant that rise up against me|Insurgentibus in me malignantibus]], that is, to their confusion, [[91:12|my ear shall hear|audiet auris mea]] the sentence of the just Judge, who will condemn them and save me.

paras.t: Justus, id est divina mandata observans, ut palma, quæ est arbor fructifera, florebit flore caritatis, virore virtutum ac bonis operibus. Non enim florebit ut fenum, quod statim siccatur et discoloratur, sed ut palma, quæ diu virescit atque fructificat. Sicut cedrus Libani multiplicabitur, procreatione spiritualium filiorum et numero meritorum. Quemadmodum namque cedrus crescens in monte Libano, est arbor decora, imputribilis, præ ceteris arboribus in sublime exsurgens: sic justus per gratiam splendet, per justitiam intus non veterascit, et proficiendo de bono in melius, super alios volat, neque quiescit donec ad thronum gloriæ perducatur.
paras.en: [[91:13|The just|Justus]], that is, he who keeps the divine commandments, [[91:13|like the palm tree|ut palma]], which is a fruit-bearing tree, [[91:13|shall flourish|florebit]] with the flower of charity, with the green of the virtues and with good works. For he shall not flourish like grass, which is soon dried up and loses its colour, but like the palm, which stays green a long time and bears fruit. The just man [[91:13|shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus|Sicut cedrus Libani multiplicabitur]] [*multiplicabitur*, "shall be multiplied"] by the begetting of spiritual children and by the number of his merits. For as the cedar growing on Mount Libanus is a comely tree, not subject to decay, rising on high above the other trees, so the just man shines through grace, does not grow old within, through justice, and, advancing from good to better, soars above others, and does not rest until he is brought to the throne of glory.

paras.t: Plantati, id est fideles per fidem et obedientiam radicati, in domo Domini, id est in Ecclesia Christi, in atriis domus Dei nostri, id est in propriis cordibus, quæ sunt atria mansionis divinæ, quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Christum per fidem habitare in cordibus nostris, florebunt, proficiendo in gratia Dei: implentes illud Apostoli, Exhibete vos sanctos et immaculatos et irreprehensibiles coram Deo; et alibi, Renovamini spiritu mentis vestræ. Porro huic concordat comparationi, quod Dominus per Osee prophetam dicit: Ero quasi ros, et Israel germinabit quasi lilium. Erumpet radix ejus ut Libani: ibunt rami ejus, et erit quasi oliva gloria ejus, et odor ejus ut Libani. Simile quoque est in Ecclesiastico: Obaudite me, divini fructus, et quasi rosa plantata super rivos aquarum fructificate; florete flores quasi lilium, et date odorem, et frondete in gratiam.
paras.en: [[91:14|They that are planted|Plantati]], that is, the faithful, rooted through faith and obedience, [[91:14|in the house of the Lord|in domo Domini]], that is, in the Church of Christ, [[91:14|in the courts of the house of our God|in atriis domus Dei nostri]], that is, in their own hearts, which are the courts of the divine dwelling, as the Apostle says, [[Eph 3:17|That Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts|Christum per fidem habitare in cordibus nostris]], [[91:14|shall flourish|florebunt]], advancing in the grace of God: fulfilling that word of the Apostle, Present yourselves [[Col 1:22|holy and unspotted and blameless|sanctos et immaculatos et irreprehensibiles]] before God [no margin note; Denis's words are nearest to Col 1:22, where they say what Christ will make of us]; and elsewhere, [[Eph 4:23|be renewed in spirit of your mind|Renovamini spiritu mentis vestræ]]. With this comparison, moreover, agrees what the Lord says by Osee the prophet: [[Osee 14:6|I will be as the dew, Israel shall spring as the lily, and his root shall shoot forth as that of Libanus|Ero quasi ros, et Israel germinabit quasi lilium. Erumpet radix ejus ut Libani]]: [[Osee 14:7|His branches shall spread, and his glory shall be as the olive tree: and his smell as that of Libanus.|ibunt rami ejus, et erit quasi oliva gloria ejus, et odor ejus ut Libani]] There is something like it also in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 39:17|Hear me, ye divine offspring, and bud forth as the rose planted by the brooks of waters|Obaudite me, divini fructus, et quasi rosa plantata super rivos aquarum fructificate]]; [[Ecclus 39:19|Send forth flowers, as the lily, and yield a smell, and bring forth leaves in grace|florete flores quasi lilium, et date odorem, et frondete in gratiam]].

paras.t: Adhuc multiplicabuntur, id est, juxta perseverabunt in bono, et cumulabuntur multiplici dono Spiritus Sancti ac merito, in senectute alacri, id est in senectute fecunda, matura ac gravi, bonis operibus plena. De qua scribitur in libro Sapientiæ: Senectus venerabilis est, non diuturna, neque annorum numero computata; ætas senectutis, vita immaculata. Et bene patientes erunt, id est, hilariter atque feliciter patientur infusionem illustrationis divinæ. Unde secundum Philosophum, beneficiatus dicitur bene passus. Hæc namque est passio perfectiva, non destructiva.
paras.en: [[91:15|They shall still increase|Adhuc multiplicabuntur]], that is, they shall persevere in good [the text has *juxta*, probably for *jugiter*, "continually"], and shall be heaped with the manifold gift of the Holy Ghost and with merit, [[91:15|in a fruitful old age|in senectute alacri]] [Denis reads *alacri*, "lively", where the Vulgate has *uberi*, "fruitful"], that is, in an old age fruitful, ripe and grave, full of good works. Of which it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 4:8|venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years|Senectus venerabilis est, non diuturna, neque annorum numero computata]]; [[Wis 4:9|a spotless life is old age|ætas senectutis, vita immaculata]]. [[91:15|and shall be well treated|Et bene patientes erunt]] [*bene patientes*, literally "well suffering", that is, well acted upon], that is, they shall joyfully and happily undergo the infusion of divine enlightenment. Hence, according to the Philosopher, one who has received a benefit is said to have *suffered well* [*bene passus*]. For this is a passion that perfects, not one that destroys.

paras.t: Ut annuntiet laudem Dei quæ sequitur: Quoniam rectus, id est justus, Dominus Deus noster, et non est iniquitas in eo: quemadmodum et alibi dictum est: Non est apud Dominum iniquitas, nec acceptio personarum, nec cupido munerum. Et in libro Job: Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas. Opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet eis. Deus etenim sublimis et benedictus, est omnis sanctitatis, veritatis et æquitatis causa fontana, judex non errans, conservator immobilis. Propter quod a Sapiente dicitur ei: Virtus tua, justitiæ initium est.
paras.en: [[91:16|That they may shew|Ut annuntiet]] the praise of God that follows: [[91:16|That the Lord our God is righteous|Quoniam rectus]] (*righteous*, that is, just), [[91:16|and there is no iniquity in him|et non est iniquitas in eo]]: as it is also said elsewhere: [[2 Par 19:7|there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons, nor desire of gifts|Non est apud Dominum iniquitas, nec acceptio personarum, nec cupido munerum]] [the margin gives Psal. xiv, 7; the words are 2 Par 19:7]. And in the book of Job: [[Job 34:10|far from God be wickedness, and iniquity from the Almighty|Absit a Deo impietas, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas]]. [[Job 34:11|For he will render to a man his work, and according to the ways of every one he will reward them.|Opus enim hominis reddet ei, et juxta vias singulorum restituet eis]] For God, sublime and blessed, is the fountain and cause of all holiness, truth and equity, a judge who does not err, a preserver who does not change. Wherefore the Wise Man says to him: [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|Virtus tua, justitiæ initium est]].

paras.t: Ecce psalmum cœlesti melodia sonorum atque admiranda dulcedine plenum audivimus: in quo Dei laudatio commendatur, Creatoris beneficia recoluntur, Deus in suis effectibus glorificatur, inter electos reprobosque discernitur, Deus postremo benedicitur. Si ergo Dominum Deum nostrum diligimus, si ejus beneficiis grati existimus, si eum in suis operibus contemplari enitimur, si impiorum tormenta evadere, electorumque præmia adipisci conamur, studeamus hunc psalmum corde jucundo, devoto, custodito ac timorato depromere.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a psalm full of the heavenly melody of its sounds and of wonderful sweetness, in which the praise of God is commended, the benefits of the Creator are recalled, God is glorified in his effects, the elect and the reprobate are distinguished, and lastly God is blessed. If, then, we love the Lord our God, if we are grateful for his benefits, if we strive to contemplate him in his works, if we seek to escape the torments of the wicked and to obtain the rewards of the elect, let us be zealous to bring forth this psalm with a joyful, devout, watchful and God-fearing heart.

paras.t: Precatio. Virtutibus planta nos in domo tua, Domine, et ut bonum semen fac nos in omni speciosa religione fructificare: in quo ut palma flore justitiæ surgentes, in eo per te consummati, perenniter ante te floreamus exsultantes.
paras.en: Prayer. Plant us with virtues in thy house, O Lord, and make us bear fruit like good seed in every comely observance of religion: so that, rising up in it like the palm with the flower of justice, and in it made perfect by thee, we may flourish for ever before thee, rejoicing.

92.title: EXPLANATIO PSALMI NONAGESIMI SECUNDI : DOMINUS REGNAVIT, DECOREM INDUTUS EST.
92.title_en: Explanation of the ninety-second psalm: The Lord hath reigned, he is clothed with beauty.

paras.t: Assignatur autem psalmo præsenti hic titulus : Laus cantici, ipsi David, in die ante sabbatum, quando fundata est terra. Dicit vero quidam hunc titulum non haberi in Hebræo, sed ab aliquo expositore appositum secundum suam voluntatem et imaginationem : et idem dicit frequenter in aliis psalmis. Sed dato quod ab aliquo expositore additus esset, non tamen bene sonat, quod ille titulum istum apposuit secundum suam voluntatem seu imaginationem : imo firmiter est credendum, titulos psalmorum secundum Spiritus Sancti inspirationem formatos esse, atque psalmis præpositos : quoniam omnes sancti catholicique doctores communiter approbant et exponunt hos titulos. — Est igitur sensus tituli hujus : Psalmus præsens est laus cantici, convenientis ac decantandi ipsi David, id est Christo, de quo psalmus iste ad litteram scriptus est. Laus, inquam, Christo decantanda in die ante sabbatum, id est propter ea quæ fecit ac passus est sexta feria, puta in die Parasceves, quando fundata est terra, id est, formata Ecclesia per sanguinem de ejus latere emanantem. Secundum omnes expositores catholicos, psalmus iste ad litteram tractat de Christo et regno ipsius. Describit namque inchoationem, impugnationem et confirmationem regni Christi, quod est Ecclesia.
paras.en: This title is assigned to the present psalm: *Praise of a canticle, for David himself, on the day before the sabbath, when the earth was founded*[[92:1||]] [the title, which the Vulgate counts as part of verse 1, is not in the Douay-Rheims text used in this app]. Now a certain writer says that this title is not found in the Hebrew, but was set there by some expositor according to his own will and fancy; and he says the same often of other psalms. But granted that it had been added by some expositor, it still does not sound well to say that he set this title there according to his own will or fancy: rather it is to be firmly believed that the titles of the psalms were framed by the inspiration of the Holy Ghost and set before the psalms, since all the holy and catholic doctors commonly approve and expound these titles. — This, then, is the sense of this title: the present psalm is *the praise of a canticle*, fitting and to be sung *for David himself*, that is, for Christ, of whom this psalm was written literally. A praise, I say, to be sung to Christ *on the day before the sabbath*, that is, for what he did and suffered on the sixth day of the week, namely on the day of the Parasceve [that is, the day of preparation before the sabbath: Good Friday], *when the earth was founded*, that is, when the Church was formed through the blood flowing from his side[[John 19:34||]]. According to all catholic expositors, this psalm treats literally of Christ and of his kingdom. For it describes the beginning, the assault and the strengthening of the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church.

paras.t: Unde de inchoatione regni hujus ita orditur : Dominus, scilicet Christus : de quo Petrus ait, Hic est omnium Dominus ; et qui de se ipso asserit in Evangelio, Vos vocatis me, Magister et Domine, et bene dicitis, sum etenim ; regnavit, per fidem in corde credentium, seu in Ecclesia militanti. Christus namque ut Deus, a principio mundi in cordibus electorum regnavit, subjiciendo eos per gratiam voluntati divinæ per humilem servitutem ; ut homo autem, habuit potestatem regnandi in toto mundo a suæ conceptionis principio. In eodem namque instanti, quo unita est ejus humanitas Verbo, data est ei virtus atque dominium super omnem creaturam. Propter quod ante passionem de Christo assertum est : Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus. Dum vero cœpit prædicare, miracula facere, discipulosque colligere, tunc cœpit regnare in domo Jacob, et sedere super solium David. Post passionem autem, misso Spiritu Sancto, et Apostolis publice prædicantibus ac multa millia convertentibus, regnavit Christus aperte et late, donec per universum mundum diffusa est fides, Ecclesiaque constructa, et ipse Christus ab omni gente, tribu et lingua cognitus est ac honoratus. Tuncque impletum est illud Isaiæ : Redemptor tuus Sanctus Israel, Deus omnis terræ vocabitur.
paras.en: And so he begins with the beginning of this kingdom, thus: [[92:1|The Lord|Dominus]], namely Christ, of whom Peter says, [[Acts 10:36|He is Lord of all|Hic est omnium Dominus]]; and who asserts of himself in the Gospel, [[John 13:13|You call me Master and Lord. And you say well: for so I am|Vos vocatis me, Magister et Domine, et bene dicitis, sum etenim]]; [[92:1|hath reigned|regnavit]], through faith in the heart of believers, or in the Church militant. For Christ as God reigned from the beginning of the world in the hearts of the elect, subjecting them by grace to the divine will in humble service; but as man he had the power of reigning over the whole world from the first moment of his conception. For in the same instant in which his humanity was united to the Word, power and dominion over every creature were given to him. For this reason it was said of Christ before the passion: [[John 3:35|The Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus]]. But when he began to preach[[Matt 4:17||]], to work miracles and to gather disciples, then he began to [[Luke 1:32|reign in the house of Jacob|regnare in domo Jacob]], and to sit [[Is 9:7|upon the throne of David|super solium David]]. After the passion, however, when the Holy Ghost had been sent, and the Apostles were preaching openly and converting many thousands, Christ reigned openly and far and wide, until the faith was spread through the whole world and the Church built up, and Christ himself was known and honoured by every nation, tribe and tongue. And then was fulfilled that saying of Isaias: [[Is 54:5|thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of all the earth|Redemptor tuus Sanctus Israel, Deus omnis terræ vocabitur]].

paras.t: Decorem indutus est, indutus est Dominus fortitudinem. Cur non potius dicitur Dominus Christus Unigenitus Dei, tam speciosus et potens ut Pater, indutus deformitatem et infirmitatem seu fragilitatem, quia assumpsit carnem mortalem, naturam creatam, formam servilem, quæ respectu divinitatis Christi, non sunt decor et fortitudo, sed deformitas atque infirmitas ? Sed ad hoc duplex responsio est : Prima, quod Christus Deus humanam naturam assumendo, dicitur indutus decorem et fortitudinem, quoniam licet ejus humanitas secundum se considerata, et divinitati comparata, possit dici deformis ac fragilis, tamen in quantum est divinæ naturæ personali unione conjuncta, ejusque instrumentum effecta, vere appellatur decor ac fortitudo. Sic enim plena fuit a suæ creationis initio plenitudine omnium gratiarum, beatifica fruitione divinitatis, omnibusque donis Spiritus Sancti. Sic quoque per eam sunt facta miracula, debellatæ potestates aeriæ, reparatum genus humanum. Secunda responsio est, quod Christus dicitur indutus decorem, non in incarnatione, quando Verbum caro factum est; nec in passione, quando non fuit in eo species neque decor, sed erat quasi leprosus et a Deo percussus: sed in resurrectione, quoniam tunc resumpsit corpus suum, non tale quale antea fuit, sed gloriosum, splendidum, agile, subtile, immortale. Idcirco tunc indutus est fortitudinem, id est corpus impassibile. Vel, Indutus est fortitudinem, quoniam tunc cœpit potestatem suam ostendere, dicendo illud, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra: quam tamen (ut dixi) ante passionem habebat, quoniam passione instante dixit, de se ipso loquens ad Patrem, Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis, ut omne quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam æternam. Quod etiam factis ostendit, quando solo verbo hostes suos prostravit. Quum namque dixisset Judæis, Ego sum, abierunt retrorsum, et ceciderunt in terram. Tunc etiam eduxit Sanctos de limbo inferni, misitque Apostolis Spiritum Sanctum. Istud itaque divinitatis Christi indumentum decorum ac forte, est natura humana. De quo indumento scriptum est: Quare ergo rubrum est indumentum tuum?
paras.en: [[92:1|he is clothed with beauty|Decorem indutus est]]: [[92:1|the Lord is clothed with strength|indutus est Dominus fortitudinem]]. Why is it not rather said that the Lord Christ, the Only-begotten of God, as beautiful and mighty as the Father, was clothed with unsightliness and weakness or frailty, since he took mortal flesh, a created nature, the form of a servant, which in respect of the divinity of Christ are not beauty and strength but unsightliness and weakness? To this there is a twofold answer. The first is that Christ, God, in taking human nature is said to have been clothed with beauty and strength, because, although his humanity, considered in itself and compared with the divinity, may be called unsightly and frail, yet inasmuch as it is joined to the divine nature in personal union [that is, the hypostatic union, by which the two natures are one Person] and made its instrument, it is truly called beauty and strength. For in this way it was full, from the beginning of its creation, of the fullness of all graces, of the beatific enjoyment of the Godhead, and of all the gifts of the Holy Ghost. In this way too miracles were done through it, the powers of the air overthrown, and mankind restored. The second answer is that Christ is said to have been clothed with beauty not in the incarnation, when [[John 1:14|the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]]; nor in the passion, when [[Is 53:2|there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness|non fuit in eo species neque decor]], but he was [[Is 53:4|as it were a leper, and as one struck by God|quasi leprosus et a Deo percussus]]; but in the resurrection, since he then took up his body again, not such as it was before, but glorious, resplendent, agile, subtle, immortal [the gifts of the glorified body: clarity, agility, subtlety and impassibility]. Therefore he was then [[92:1|clothed with strength|indutus est fortitudinem]], that is, with an impassible body. Or, [[92:1|clothed with strength|Indutus est fortitudinem]], because he then began to show his power, saying: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]; which (as I said) he nevertheless had before the passion, since when the passion was at hand he said, speaking of himself to the Father: [[John 17:2|thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom thou hast given him|Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis, ut omne quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam æternam]]. This he showed also in deeds, when by a word alone he cast down his enemies. For when he had said to the Jews, [[John 18:6|I am he|Ego sum]], [[John 18:6|they went backward and fell to the ground|abierunt retrorsum, et ceciderunt in terram]] [the margin gives John xviii; the words are at 18:6]. Then too he led the saints out of the limbo of hell, and sent the Holy Ghost to the Apostles. This beautiful and strong garment of the divinity of Christ, then, is human nature [*indumentum*, "garment", is from the same root as *indutus*, "clothed"]; of which garment it is written: [[Is 63:2|Why then is thy apparel red|Quare ergo rubrum est indumentum tuum]]?

paras.t: Et præparavit se Christus: id est, ad redimendum genus humanum, debellandumque dæmonum turbas paravit se, dicens ad Patrem: Si non potest hic calix transire, nisi bibam illum, fiat voluntas tua. Factus est enim obediens usque ad mortem, secundum Apostolum. Et exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam: quod S. Ambrosius in hymno elegantèr et supra humanum intellectum expressit, dicendo: Procedens e thalamo suo, Pudoris aula regia, Geminæ gigas substantiæ, Alacris ut currat viam. Unde superius de Christo inductum est: Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum, potentissime.
paras.en: [[92:1|and hath girded himself|Et præparavit se]] [Denis reads *præparavit se*, "hath prepared himself", where the Vulgate has *præcinxit se*, "hath girded himself"], Christ: that is, he prepared himself to redeem mankind and to overthrow the hosts of demons, saying to the Father: [[Matt 26:42|if this chalice may not pass away, but I must drink it, thy will be done|Si non potest hic calix transire, nisi bibam illum, fiat voluntas tua]] [the margin gives Matt. xxvi, 39; these words are those of the second prayer, at 26:42]. For he became [[Phil 2:8|obedient unto death|obediens usque ad mortem]], according to the Apostle. And he [[Ps 18:6|Hath rejoiced as a giant to run the way|exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam]]: which St Ambrose expressed in a hymn elegantly and beyond human understanding, saying: *Proceeding from his bridal chamber, the royal hall of chastity, a giant of twofold substance* [that is, of two natures, divine and human], *eager to run his way.* Hence it was put above concerning Christ: [[Ps 44:4|Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O thou most mighty|Accingere gladio tuo super femur tuum, potentissime]].

paras.t: Etenim firmavit orbem terræ, qui non commovebitur. Quamvis hoc accipi posset de creatione ac firma locatione terræ in medio mundi, quam Christus Deus condidit et firmavit, juxta illud, Ego sum Dominus faciens omnia, extendens cœlos, stabiliens terram (quæ etiam terra non commovetur, quoad se totam, quum sit centrum mundi immobile: propter quod ait Scriptura, Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit, terra vero in æternum stat); convenientius tamen exponitur iste versiculus de confirmatione Ecclesiæ; eritque sensus: Etenim Dominus Christus firmavit per adjutorium seu gratiam Spiritus Sancti, orbem terræ, id est militantem Ecclesiam, per quatuor partes terræ diffusam. Christus Ecclesiam suam primitivam præcipue confirmavit in die Pentecostes, mittens ei Paracletum. Tunc enim implevit quod ante passionem promisit: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. Alibi quoque dixit ad Petrum: Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam. In tantum namque confirmavit Christus Ecclesiam, ut dicat Apostolus: Ecclesia Dei vivi est columna et firmamentum veritatis. Unde in Actibus Apostolorum Lucas testatur: Ecclesia per totam Judæam et Samariam habebat pacem; et ædificabatur ambulans in timore Domini, et consolatione Spiritus Sancti replebatur. Idcirco nunc subditur, qui non commovebitur. Ecclesia namque usque in finem mundi stabilis permanebit in fide servituteque Christi, qui regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, et regni ejus non erit finis, juxta testimonium Gabrielis.
paras.en: [[92:1|For he hath established the world which shall not be moved|Etenim firmavit orbem terræ, qui non commovebitur]]. Although this could be taken of the creation and the firm setting of the earth in the middle of the world, which Christ as God made and established, according to that saying, [[Is 44:24|I am the Lord, that make all things, that alone stretch out the heavens, that established the earth|Ego sum Dominus faciens omnia, extendens cœlos, stabiliens terram]] (and this earth is indeed not moved, as a whole, since it is the immovable centre of the world; for which reason Scripture says, [[Eccles 1:4|One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth standeth for ever|Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit, terra vero in æternum stat]]), yet this verse is more fittingly expounded of the strengthening of the Church; and the sense will be: [[92:1|For|Etenim]] the Lord Christ [[92:1|hath established|firmavit]], by the help or grace of the Holy Ghost, [[92:1|the world|orbem terræ]], that is, the Church militant, spread through the four quarters of the earth. Christ strengthened his early Church above all on the day of Pentecost, sending it the Paraclete. For then he fulfilled what he had promised before the passion: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. Elsewhere too he said to Peter: [[Matt 16:18|thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it|Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eam]]. For so far did Christ strengthen the Church that the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 3:15|the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth|Ecclesia Dei vivi est columna et firmamentum veritatis]]. Hence Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 9:31|the church had peace throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria: and was edified, walking in the fear of the Lord: and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Ghost|Ecclesia per totam Judæam et Samariam habebat pacem; et ædificabatur ambulans in timore Domini, et consolatione Spiritus Sancti replebatur]]. Therefore it now goes on: [[92:1|which shall not be moved|qui non commovebitur]]. For the Church will remain steadfast until the end of the world in the faith and service of Christ, who [[Luke 1:32|shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever|regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum]], [[Luke 1:33|And of his kingdom there shall be no end|et regni ejus non erit finis]], according to the testimony of Gabriel.

paras.t: Parata sedes tua, o Christe, id est throno quo sedes ad dexteram Patris, de quo dicis : Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus ; ex tunc, id est a principio mundi. Si enim omnibus sanctis hominibus paratum est regnum cœlorum ab origine mundi, juxta illud, Venite, benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum a constitutione mundi : quanto magis sedes tua cœlestis tibi parata est ab exordio sæculi? Vel, Parata est sedes tua, id est cœlum empyreum : quod est sedes tua, juxta illud, Cœlum mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum ; quod etiam dicitur thronus tuus et omnium electorum, de quo contestaris : Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, id est in cœlo empyreo, in quo omnes Beati feliciter resident. Vel, Parata est sedes tua, id est Ecclesia seu anima justi, quæ est sedes sapientiæ, ex tunc, id est a tempore prædicto, quo eam firmasti per gratiam Spiritus Sancti. Ex tunc enim parata est ad tuam inhabitationem, obedientiam atque adventum, adimplens quod ei dixisti : Vigilate itaque omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini stare ante Filium hominis.
paras.en: Thy [[92:2|throne is prepared|Parata sedes tua]], O Christ, that is, the throne on which thou sittest at the right hand of the Father, of which thou sayest: [[Apoc 3:21|I also have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne|Ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]]; [[92:2|from of old|ex tunc]], that is, from the beginning of the world. For if the kingdom of heaven has been prepared for all holy men from the origin of the world, according to that saying, [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess you the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world|Venite, benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum a constitutione mundi]], how much more has thy heavenly throne been prepared for thee from the beginning of the ages? Or, thy [[92:2|throne is prepared|Parata est sedes tua]], that is, the empyrean heaven [the highest heaven, the dwelling of God and of the blessed], which is thy throne, according to that saying, [[Acts 7:49|Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool|Cœlum mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum]] [the words are those of Is 66:1; Denis's form is that in which Stephen quotes them in Acts 7:49]; which is also called thy throne and the throne of all the elect, of which thou testifiest: [[Apoc 3:21|To him that shall overcome, I will give to sit with me in my throne|Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo]], that is, in the empyrean heaven, in which all the Blessed happily abide. Or, thy [[92:2|throne is prepared|Parata est sedes tua]], that is, the Church or the soul of the just man, which is the seat of wisdom [*sedes*, "seat" or "throne": the same word as in the verse], [[92:2|from of old|ex tunc]], that is, from the time spoken of before, when thou didst establish it by the grace of the Holy Ghost. For from then it has been prepared for thy indwelling, for obedience to thee and for thy coming, fulfilling what thou saidst to it: [[Luke 21:36|Watch ye, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be accounted worthy|Vigilate itaque omni tempore orantes, ut digni habeamini]] [[Luke 21:36|to stand before the Son of man|stare ante Filium hominis]].

paras.t: A sæculo, id est ab æterno, tu es invariabiliter, secundum quod Deus. Unde dicit Apostolus : Jesus Christus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula. Et congrue ait, A sæculo tu es ; et non, Fuisti : quoniam Christus ut Deus, incommutabiliter per modum æternæ præsentiæ est, in qua non est prius aut posterius. Propter quod ait : Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum. Esse quippe, Deo verissime, plenissime, atque propriissime convenit, quoniam in eo est infinita plenitudo, immensa nobilitas, incircumscripta perfectio, simplicitasque perfecta essendi. Omnis autem creatura, per comparationem ad esse divinum, est potius nihil seu non esse, quam aliquid. Propterea Dominus ait ad Moysen : Ego sum qui sum. Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos. Hinc quoque septimo de Trinitate Hilarius asserit : Esse non est accidens Deo, sed subsistens veritas, manens causa, et naturalis proprietas.
paras.en: [[92:2|from everlasting|A sæculo]], that is, from eternity, [[92:2|thou art|tu es]] unchangeably, as God. Hence the Apostle says: [[Heb 13:8|Jesus Christ, yesterday, and today: and the same for ever.|Jesus Christus heri et hodie, ipse et in sæcula]] And fittingly he says, [[92:2|thou art from everlasting|A sæculo tu es]], and not *Thou wast*: since Christ as God is unchangeably, after the manner of an eternal present, in which there is no before or after. For this reason he says: [[John 8:58|before Abraham was made, I AM|Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum]]. For *to be* belongs to God most truly, most fully and most properly, since in him is the infinite fullness, the immense nobility, the uncircumscribed perfection and the perfect simplicity of being. But every creature, compared with the divine being, is rather nothing, or not-being, than something. Therefore the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. [[Ex 3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. Hence too Hilary asserts in the seventh book On the Trinity: *Being* is not an accident in God, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and natural property.

paras.t: Elevaverunt flumina, Domine, elevaverunt flumina vocem suam. Elevaverunt flumina fluctus suos. Per flumina quæ elevaverunt vocem suam, quidam intelligunt primos ac principales christianæ fidei prædicatores : qui flumina appellantur, quoniam aquam sapientiæ salutaris cordibus hominum infuderunt : et hi, tanquam fideles, elevaverunt vocem suam, rationabiliter loquendo et fidem Christi publice prædicando. Per flumina vero quæ elevaverunt fluctus suos, intelligunt persecutores Ecclesiæ, scilicet principes sacerdotum, imperatores Romanos, cæterosque tyrannos, christianam doctrinam reprobantes et exstirpare conantes. Hi namque, sicut perversi ac reprobi, elevaverunt non vocem rationabilem, sed fluctus suos, id est graves comminationes, verba blasphemiæ, impetus passionum, persecutionesque duras contra Ecclesiam Christi et flumina Dei. Quidam vero utraque flumina cum suis elevationibus, exponunt de adversariis Christi et persecutoribus sacrosanctæ Ecclesiæ. Flumina autem, id est tyranni, elevaverunt fluctus suos a vocibus multarum multitudinum, id est per sermones seu verba multorum populorum, qui edicta tyrannorum perduxerunt ad actum. Erant namque ministri et exsecutores sententiæ, quam contra Ecclesiam dictabant tyranni.
paras.en: [[92:3|The floods have lifted up, O Lord: the floods have lifted up their voice|Elevaverunt flumina, Domine, elevaverunt flumina vocem suam]]. [[92:3|The floods have lifted up their waves|Elevaverunt flumina fluctus suos]]. By the floods that lifted up their voice some understand the first and chief preachers of the Christian faith, who are called floods because they poured [[Ecclus 15:3|the water of wholesome wisdom|aquam sapientiæ salutaris]] into the hearts of men; and these, as faithful men, lifted up their voice, speaking reasonably and preaching the faith of Christ publicly. But by the floods that lifted up their waves they understand the persecutors of the Church, namely the chief priests, the Roman emperors and the other tyrants, who rejected Christian doctrine and strove to root it out. For these, as perverse and reprobate men, lifted up not a reasonable voice but their waves, that is, grave threats, words of blasphemy, assaults of passion, and harsh persecutions against the Church of Christ and the floods of God. Others, however, expound both floods, with their liftings up, of the adversaries of Christ and the persecutors of the holy Church. And the floods, that is, the tyrants, lifted up their waves [[92:4|With the noise|a vocibus]] of many multitudes [Denis reads *a vocibus multarum multitudinum*, "with the voices of many multitudes", where the Vulgate has *aquarum multarum*, "of many waters"], that is, through the speeches or words of many peoples, who carried the edicts of the tyrants into deed.
