paras.en: [[98:7|In the pillar of the cloud|In columna nubis]], that is, in a cloud appearing in the form of a pillar, the Lord [[98:7|spoke to them|loquebatur ad eos]], not in his own person but through a ministering angel; of whom the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 23:20|Behold I will send my angel, who shall go before thee|Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, qui præcedat te]]. That the Lord spoke in this way to Moses and Aaron in the pillar of the cloud, we read in Exodus; but of Samuel this is not read plainly in canonical Scripture, except in the present psalm, on account of which it is certain that it was so. Yet in the first book of Kings it is plainly described how, at Samuel's prayer, the Lord gave thunders and rains[[1 Kings 12:17||]][[1 Kings 12:18||]] [the Latin *voces*, "thunders", means literally "voices"], which were not without a cloud. And perhaps the Lord was then speaking to Samuel in the pillar of the cloud, though the others did not hear that speech: just as the rest did not hear (as some assert) the voice of the Father saying of Christ: [[Matt 3:17|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]; which John the Baptist nevertheless heard, when Christ had been baptized and was praying, as Luke says[[Luke 3:21||]][[Luke 3:22||]].

paras.t: Domine Deus noster, Trinitas adoranda et superbenedicta, tu exaudiebas eos in justis eorum petitionibus. Deus, tu propitius fuisti eis, id est, pie ipsis indulsisti tam propria quam aliorum peccata: quod maxime patet in Aaron, qui graviter nimis peccavit in formatione vituli aurei et murmuratione contra Moysen; et ulciscens, id est paterne in præsenti vita castigans, in omnes adinventiones eorum, id est in omnia peccata ipsorum: quæ non processerunt ex inspiratione divina, sed ex adinventione humana. Hæc namque eorum peccata Deus in hoc mundo clementer ac temporaliter ultus est, ne in futuro sæculo gravius punirentur. Unde propter incredulitatem, qua ad aquas Contradictionis Moyses et Aaron Deo increduli erant, prohibiti sunt ingredi terram promissionis. Constat ergo quod Dominus nonnunquam permittat sanctos suos ex humana infirmitate cadere: tuncque clementer adhibet temporalis pœnæ remedium, quatenus tam ex propria culpa, quam ex divina vindicta suam fragilitatem advertant, et humiliores cautioresque resurgant. Quem vero Deus odit, hujus adinventiones non ulciscitur complete vel semper in sæculo isto, sed futuro: interdum tamen ulciscitur eas in præsenti per inchoationem, ut patet in reprobis quorum pœna nunc incipit, et in inferno sine fine perdurat.
paras.en: [[98:8|O Lord our God|Domine Deus noster]], Trinity to be adored and blessed above all, [[98:8|Thou didst hear them|tu exaudiebas eos]] in their just petitions. [[98:8|thou wast a merciful God to them|Deus, tu propitius fuisti eis]], that is, thou didst lovingly forgive them their sins, both their own and others': which is most plain in Aaron, who sinned very grievously in the making of the golden calf[[Ex 32:4||]] and in murmuring against Moses[[Num 12:1||]]; [[98:8|and taking vengeance|et ulciscens]], that is, chastising them as a father in the present life, [[98:8|on all their inventions|in omnes adinventiones eorum]], that is, on all their sins: which did not proceed from divine inspiration but from human invention. For God avenged these sins of theirs in this world, mercifully and in time, lest they should be punished more heavily in the world to come. Hence, because of the unbelief with which Moses and Aaron did not believe God at the waters of Contradiction, they were forbidden to enter the land of promise[[Num 20:12||]]. It is clear, then, that the Lord sometimes permits his saints to fall through human weakness, and then mercifully applies the remedy of temporal punishment, so that from their own fault as well as from God's chastisement they may take note of their frailty, and rise again humbler and more wary. But him whom God hates, he does not avenge his inventions fully, or always, in this world, but in the world to come; though sometimes he avenges them in the present by way of a beginning, as is plain in the reprobate, whose punishment begins now and lasts without end in hell.

paras.t: Exaltate cum reverentia mentis, cum præconio oris, cum obsequio operis, Dominum Deum nostrum, Christum Dei Filium, qui est verus Deus ac vita æterna; et adorate eum in monte sancto ejus, id est in Ecclesia militanti, in Christo monte summo fundata; et non solum in monte Sion, qui erat in Jerusalem, aut in monte sito juxta Sichar, de quibus ait Salvator mulieri Samaritanæ: Crede mihi, quia veniet hora, quando neque in monte hoc, neque in Jerusalem adorabitis Patrem. Quoniam sanctus Dominus Deus noster. Ipse enim est substantialiter sanctus, et sanctitas pura, separata et infinita. Ipse quoque est prima origo, mensura et causa omnis sanctitatis, virtutis atque munditiæ. Propter quod Pater noster cœlestis, volens nos esse sibi consimiles, quatenus vere ac digne ejus adoptivi filii nominemur, ait: Nolite contaminare animas vestras. Sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum. Maculatos autem, immundos, seu vitiosos abominatur, odit et damnat, quemadmodum Josue dicit: Deus sanctus et fortis æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris. Sed et Christus Deum Patrem, sanctum appellat, suosque fideles ab eo sanctificari precatur, dicens in Evangelio: Pater sancte, sanctifica eos in veritate. Agamus ergo propter quod Christus venit ad nos. Juravit namque daturum se nobis, ut serviamus illi in sanctitate et justitia omnibus diebus nostris.
paras.en: [[98:9|Exalt ye|Exaltate]], with reverence of mind, with proclaiming of the mouth, with the service of deeds, [[98:9|the Lord our God|Dominum Deum nostrum]], Christ the Son of God, who is the true God and life everlasting; [[98:9|and adore|et adorate]] him [[98:9|at his holy mountain|in monte sancto ejus]], that is, in the Church militant, founded on Christ the highest mountain; and not only on mount Sion, which was in Jerusalem, or on the mountain that lies near Sichar, of which the Saviour said to the Samaritan woman: [[John 4:21|believe me that the hour cometh, when you shall neither on this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, adore the Father|Crede mihi, quia veniet hora, quando neque in monte hoc, neque in Jerusalem adorabitis Patrem]]. [[98:9|for the Lord our God is holy|Quoniam sanctus Dominus Deus noster]]. For he is holy in his substance, and holiness pure, separate and infinite. He is also the first origin, measure and cause of all holiness, virtue and cleanness. Wherefore our heavenly Father, wishing us to be like himself, so that we may truly and worthily be called his adopted sons, says: [[Lev 11:43|Do not defile your souls|Nolite contaminare animas vestras]]. [[Lev 11:44|Be holy because I am holy|Sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum]]. But the stained, the unclean and the vicious he abhors, hates and condemns, as Josue says: [[Jos 24:19|he is a holy God, and mighty and jealous, and will not forgive your wickedness|Deus sanctus et fortis æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris]]. And Christ too calls God the Father holy, and prays that his faithful may be sanctified by him, saying in the Gospel: [[John 17:11|Holy Father|Pater sancte]], [[John 17:17|Sanctify them in truth|sanctifica eos in veritate]]. Let us therefore do that for which Christ came to us. For [[Luke 1:73|he swore|Juravit]] [[Luke 1:73|that he would grant to us|daturum se nobis]], that [[Luke 1:74|we may serve him|serviamus illi]] [[Luke 1:75|in holiness and justice|in sanctitate et justitia]] [[Luke 1:75|all our days|omnibus diebus nostris]].

paras.t: Ecce psalmum præsentem laudibus Dei suavem, beneficia Christi recolentem, nosque ad Dei venerationem repetitis vicibus exhortantem, decet nos non sine jucunditate interna, devotioneque præcipua decantare, et Deum non solum verbis, sed humili quoque ac diligenti obsequio exaltare.
paras.en: Behold the present psalm, sweet with the praises of God, recalling the benefits of Christ, and exhorting us again and again to the veneration of God: it befits us to sing it through not without inward joy and special devotion, and to exalt God not only with words but also with humble and diligent service.

paras.t: Precatio. Excelsus super omnes populos Deus, famulis tuis esto propitius; da nobis, quæsumus, custodire testimonia et sancta quæ dedisti nobis præcepta: ut ea in finem usque observantes devote, mercedem a te in beata sortiamur æternitate.
paras.en: Prayer. O God, high above all peoples, be merciful to thy servants; grant us, we beseech thee, to keep the testimonies and the holy commandments which thou hast given us: that, devoutly observing them even to the end, we may obtain our reward from thee in blessed eternity.

99.title: ELUCIDATIO PSALMI NONAGESIMI NONI : JUBILATE DOMINO, OMNIS TERRA.
99.title_en: Explanation of the ninety-ninth psalm: Sing joyfully to the Lord, all the earth.

paras.t: Psalmi nunc declarandi titulus est: Psalmus in confessione: id est, psalmus iste agit de confessione divinæ laudationis, de confessione quoque propriæ accusationis. Principaliter tamen tractat de confessione laudis divinæ, quia intendit nos inflammare atque inducere ad laudandum, regratiandum, ac benedicendum Deo creatori nostro.
paras.en: The title of the psalm now to be explained is: *A psalm in confession*[[99:1||]] [the Douay-Rheims has "A psalm of praise"; the Latin *confessio* means both the confession of praise and the confession of sins]: that is, this psalm treats of the confession of God's praise, and also of the confession by which one accuses oneself. Yet it treats chiefly of the confession of God's praise, for it means to kindle us and lead us on to praise, thank and bless God our Creator.

paras.t: Dicit ergo: Jubilate Domino: id est, tam exuberanter ineffabiliter gaudete, ac hymnum dicite Deo, ut sanctæ devotionis lætitia contineri compescique nequeat, quin foras per sensibilia signa erumpat, nec tamen integre exprimi possit. Sic Jubilate Domino, omnis terra, id est, o universi incolæ terræ. Tam copiose decet nos Domino jubilare, quoniam sicut ejus majestas nostram parvitatem infinite excedit, sic nostra jucunditas de Deo concepta, propriam infirmitatem et elocutionem transcendere debet. Debemus autem Domino jubilare: Primo et summe, propter propriam bonitatem ac beatitudinem ejus, cui decet nos ineffabiliter congaudere, si tamen diligimus eum, sicut et Christus ait Apostolis: Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique, quia ad Patrem vado, id est, meæ exsultationi et glorificationi congratularemini. Secundo, propter multiplicia beneficia Dei nobis exhibita, scilicet propter dona naturæ ac munera gratiæ. Dedit enim nobis esse, vivere, sentire, intelligere, corpus et animam, vires ac membra, multiformia quoque dona gratiæ atque misericordiæ suæ immensæ. Tertio, propter maxima bona nobis promissa, in cœlestibusque parata.
paras.en: He says, then: [[99:2|Sing joyfully to God|Jubilate Domino]] [Denis reads *Domino*, "to the Lord"; the margin notes the other reading *Deo*, "to God"]: that is, rejoice so overflowingly and unspeakably, and sing a hymn to God, that the gladness of holy devotion cannot be held in or restrained from breaking out through outward signs, and yet cannot be fully expressed. So: [[99:2|Sing joyfully to God, all the earth|Jubilate Domino, omnis terra]], that is, O all ye dwellers on the earth. It is fitting that we sing joyfully to the Lord so abundantly because, as his majesty exceeds our littleness infinitely, so our joy conceived of God ought to go beyond our own weakness and our power of speech. And we ought to sing joyfully to the Lord: first and above all, for his own goodness and blessedness, in which it is fitting that we rejoice with him unspeakably, if indeed we love him, as Christ also says to the Apostles: [[John 14:28|If you loved me you would indeed be glad, because I go to the Father|Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique, quia ad Patrem vado]], that is, you would share in the joy of my exultation and glorification. Secondly, for the manifold benefits of God shewn to us, namely for the gifts of nature and the gifts of grace. For he has given us being, life, sense and understanding, body and soul, strength and limbs, and also the manifold gifts of his grace and of his immense mercy. Thirdly, for the very great goods promised us and prepared in heaven.

paras.t: Hinc ergo, o homines cuncti, servite Domino in lætitia, id est prompte atque hilariter, non tamen dissolute ac irreverenter, sed in lætitia timori conjuncta, sicut superius dictum est, Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore. Quid autem est, Domino in lætitia deservire, nisi divinis præceptis ex vera et fervida caritate parere? Nulla quippe forma tam facile, prompte et delectabiliter operatur, ut caritas; habetque caritas fervida in omni sua operatione annexam cordialem lætitiam. Non enim gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet autem veritati, secundum Apostolum. Debemus itaque Domino in lætitia ministrare, quia non complacet ei famulatus coactus. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis. Ad Colossenses quoque: Quodcumque, inquit, facitis, ex animo operamini. Quanto autem Deo ex promptiori ac hilariori affectu servimus, tanto pleniorem ab eodem mercedem sortiemur, videlicet ampliorem gratiam in præsenti, gloriamque majorem in cœlo.
paras.en: Hence, then, O all ye men, [[99:2|serve ye the Lord with gladness|servite Domino in lætitia]], that is, readily and cheerfully, yet not loosely and irreverently, but with a gladness joined to fear, as was said above: [[Ps 2:11|Serve ye the Lord with fear: and rejoice unto him with trembling|Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore]]. And what is it to serve the Lord with gladness, but to obey the divine commandments out of true and fervent charity? For no form [that is, no principle of action, in the scholastic sense] works so easily, readily and delightfully as charity; and fervent charity has heartfelt gladness joined to all its working. For it [[1 Cor 13:6|Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth with the truth|Non enim gaudet super iniquitate, congaudet autem veritati]], according to the Apostle. We ought therefore to minister to the Lord with gladness, since forced service does not please him. For this reason the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 1:7|God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power and of love and of sobriety|Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis]]. And to the Colossians: [[Col 3:23|Whatsoever|Quodcumque]], he says, [[Col 3:23|you do, do it from the heart|facitis, ex animo operamini]]. And the more ready and cheerful the affection with which we serve God, the fuller the reward we shall receive from him: greater grace, that is, in the present, and greater glory in heaven.

paras.t: Introite in templum Domini in conspectu ejus: quia supra templum Domini aperti sunt oculi misericordiæ ejus, quemadmodum Salomon oravit: Audi, Domine, hymnum et orationem servi tui, ut sint oculi tui aperti super domum istam die ac nocte. Quamvis autem hoc de templo materiali accipi possit, quod est domus orationis, in quam adspicit Deus; in qua etiam domo homines adspiciuntur a Deo, id est, per approbationem cognoscuntur ab eo et misericorditer attenduntur: aptius tamen accipitur de templo immateriali, quod est anima rationalis, quæ est cubiculum, thalamus, thronus, sedes, domus ac templum sui Creatoris ac Salvatoris. Debemus ergo introire in animam nostram, id est redire ad cor, et considerare divina, atque discutere nostra interiora, in conspectu ejus, id est coram Deo, cogitando præsentiam Dei, et coram eo statuendo nos ipsos, dicentes illud Genesis: Testis est Deus, qui præsens respicit. Sic autem introite in exsultatione: id est, introeundo confiteamini Deo ejus præconia et vestra facinora, quatenus in contemplatione divinæ bonitatis lætemini, in consideratione autem vestræ pravitatis tristemini, ut contristando consolari mereamini consolatione æterna.
paras.en: [[99:2|Come in|Introite]] into the temple of the Lord [[99:2|before his presence|in conspectu ejus]] [Denis's text adds "into the temple of the Lord", which the Douay-Rheims does not have]: for the eyes of his mercy are open upon the temple of the Lord, as Solomon prayed: [[3 Kings 8:28|hear|Audi]], O Lord, [[3 Kings 8:28|the hymn and the prayer|hymnum et orationem]] of thy servant, [[3 Kings 8:29|That thy eyes may be open upon this house, night and day|ut sint oculi tui aperti super domum istam die ac nocte]]. Now although this may be taken of the material temple, which is the house of prayer[[Is 56:7||]], upon which God looks, and in which house men are looked upon by God, that is, are known by him with approval and regarded with mercy: yet it is more fittingly taken of the immaterial temple, which is the rational soul, the chamber, bridal room, throne, seat, house and temple of its Creator and Saviour. We ought, then, to enter into our soul, that is, to return to the heart[[Is 46:8||]], and to consider divine things and search out our inward parts, [[99:2|before his presence|in conspectu ejus]], that is, before God, thinking on God's presence and setting ourselves before him, saying that word of Genesis: The witness is [[Gen 31:50|God, who is present and beholdeth|Deus, qui præsens respicit]]. And so come in [[99:2|with exceeding great joy|in exsultatione]]: that is, as you come in, confess to God his praises and your own misdeeds, so that you may rejoice in contemplating the divine goodness and grieve in considering your own wickedness, that by grieving you may deserve to be consoled with everlasting consolation.

paras.t: Scitote, non solum per fidem, sed etiam per naturalem rationem et gustum seu experientiam, quoniam, id est quod, Dominus universorum ipse est Deus, creator, gubernatorque vester; ipse fecit nos per creationem, refecit etiam nos per suam incarnationem ac gratiæ infusionem, et non ipsi nos. Quod autem Deus creando omnia fecit, omnia protestantur et clamant, ordo rerum ostendit, ratio dictat, Scriptura affirmat, philosophi cognoverunt, theologi prædicant. Videmus namque ordinem decentissimum esse in speciebus universi, quoniam una natura est posterior, compositior, vilior, ac dependentior alia. Oportet ergo venire ad unam naturam simpliciter primam, maxime simplicem, summe dignissimam, penitusque independentem, seu nullius egentem: et ista est Deus. Primum autem atque dignissimum in omni genere rerum, est causa posteriorum in genere suo: quemadmodum primum calidum est causa caloris in aliis; et primum lucidum, scilicet sol, est causa claritatis in omnibus aliis. Deus ergo, qui est primum ens, summe perfectum, simplex ac independens, est causa omnis entitatis, veritatis ac perfectionis in ceteris omnibus. Quod etiam Aristoteles secundo Primæ philosophiæ demonstrat. Propter quod alibi dicit: Ab hoc ente, omnibus communicatum est esse et vivere, his quidem clarius, his autem obscurius.
paras.en: [[99:3|Know ye|Scitote]], not only by faith but also by natural reason and by taste or experience, [[99:3|that|quoniam]] the Lord of all, [[99:3|he is God|ipse est Deus]], your Creator and Governor; [[99:3|he made us|ipse fecit nos]] by creation, and made us anew by his incarnation and the infusion of grace, [[99:3|and not we ourselves|et non ipsi nos]]. And that God made all things by creating them, all things bear witness and cry out: the order of things shews it, reason dictates it, Scripture affirms it[[Gen 1:1||]], the philosophers have known it, the theologians preach it. For we see that there is a most fitting order among the kinds of things in the universe, since one nature is later, more composite, baser and more dependent than another. We must therefore come to one nature that is first without qualification, supremely simple, most worthy of all, and wholly independent, that is, needing nothing: and this is God. Now what is first and most worthy in every kind of things is the cause of what comes after it in that kind: as the first hot thing is the cause of heat in the others, and the first bright thing, namely the sun, is the cause of brightness in all the others. God, then, who is the first being, supremely perfect, simple and independent, is the cause of all being, truth and perfection in everything else. This Aristotle also demonstrates in the second book of the First Philosophy [that is, the *Metaphysics*]. Hence he says elsewhere: From this being, being and life are imparted to all things, to some more clearly, to others more obscurely [Aristotle, *On the Heavens* I, 9].

paras.t: Quemadmodum itaque omne quod habemus et sumus, a Deo recepimus, ita nos ipsos et omnia interiora exterioraque nostra Deo offerre, et in Dei laudem ac servitutem expendere obligamur. Ideo subditur: Populus ejus et oves pascuæ ejus, id est, o universi fideles, quos possidet Deus per fidem et gratiam, qui estis oves pascuæ ejus, id est, qui sacramentis ejus reficimini, et mente et corpore donis Dei sustentamini atque alimini; introite, non tam corporis gressu, quam mentis profectu, portas ejus, id est virtutes seu opera virtuosa, quibus ad regnum cœleste pertingitur, in confessione peccatorum vestrorum. Oportet enim confessionem propriæ culpæ præcedere cetera opera virtuosa. Per confessionem namque culpa deletur, gratia datur, et homo idoneus laudator efficitur. Unde de non confitentibus Dominus per Isaiam ait: Quum extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos: manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt.
paras.en: As, then, we have received from God all that we have and are, so we are bound to offer ourselves and all that is ours, within and without, to God, and to spend it in God's praise and service. Therefore it is added: [[99:3|his people and the sheep of his pasture|Populus ejus et oves pascuæ ejus]], that is, O all ye faithful, whom God possesses by faith and grace, who are the sheep of his pasture, that is, who are refreshed by his sacraments and sustained and fed in mind and body by the gifts of God: [[99:4|Go ye into|introite]], not so much by the step of the body as by the progress of the mind, [[99:4|his gates|portas ejus]], that is, the virtues or virtuous works by which the heavenly kingdom is reached, [[99:4|with praise|in confessione]] [Latin *in confessione*, "in confession", which Denis here takes of the confession of sins] of your sins. For the confession of one's own guilt must go before the other virtuous works. For by confession guilt is blotted out, grace is given, and a man is made a fit praiser of God. Hence the Lord says through Isaias of those who do not confess: [[Is 1:15|when you stretch forth your hands, I will turn away my eyes|Quum extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos]]: [[Is 1:15|for your hands are full of blood|manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt]].

paras.t: Introite quoque atria ejus, id est latitudinem caritatis, implentes illud beatissimi principis Apostolorum: Ante omnia mutuam in vobismetipsis caritatem continuam habentes, quoniam caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum. Unde et Paulus: Ambulate, inquit, in dilectione, sicut et Christus dilexit nos. Nam plenitudo legis est dilectio; et qui diligit proximum, legem implevit. Vel: Introite atria ejus, id est, per contemplationem et spem intrate amplitudinem cœlestis palatii, et oculis fidei circumspicite plateas regni cœlorum, ac ordines Beatorum, habentes conversationem in cœlo. Denique potest hic versus intelligi de materialibus portis atriisque ecclesiæ ex lapidibus fabricatæ: ita quod admonemur visitare ac ingredi ecclesiam Dei, ubi divina aguntur, Missæ celebrantur, prædicatio verbi cœlestis auditur. In hymnis, id est spiritualibus laudibus, confitemini illi, id est, Deum laudate: sicut in Apocalypsi admonetur: Laudem dicite Deo, omnes servi ejus, et qui timetis eum pusilli et magni.
paras.en: Go in also [[99:4|into his courts|atria ejus]], that is, into the breadth of charity, fulfilling that word of the most blessed prince of the Apostles: [[1 Pet 4:8|before all things have a constant mutual charity among yourselves: for charity covereth a multitude of sins|Ante omnia mutuam in vobismetipsis caritatem continuam habentes, quoniam caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum]]. Hence Paul too: [[Eph 5:2|walk|Ambulate]], he says, [[Eph 5:2|in love, as Christ also hath loved us|in dilectione, sicut et Christus dilexit nos]]. For: [[Rom 13:10|Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law|plenitudo legis est dilectio]]; and [[Rom 13:8|he that loveth his neighbour hath fulfilled the law|qui diligit proximum, legem implevit]]. Or: go [[99:4|into his courts|atria ejus]], that is, by contemplation and hope enter the breadth of the heavenly palace, and with the eyes of faith look about the streets of the kingdom of heaven and the orders of the Blessed, having your conversation in heaven[[Phil 3:20||]]. Lastly, this verse can be understood of the material gates and courts of a church built of stones: so that we are admonished to visit and enter the church of God, where divine things are performed, Masses are celebrated, and the preaching of the heavenly word is heard. [[99:4|with hymns|In hymnis]], that is, with spiritual praises, [[99:4|and give glory to him|confitemini illi]], that is, praise God: as we are admonished in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:5|Give praise to our God, all ye his servants: and you that fear him, little and great|Laudem dicite Deo, omnes servi ejus, et qui timetis eum pusilli et magni]].

paras.t: Laudate nomen ejus, mente devota, collecta, et amorosa, quoniam suavis est Dominus. Est enim Deus benedictus et sanctus, essentialiter dulcis; et ejus infinita essentia aliud nihil est, nisi dulcedo prorsus immensa, a cujus odore, suavitate ac amœnitate in infinitum occumbit omnis dulcedo creata. Hanc tamen dulcedinem Dei aliqualiter gustare meretur, qui in continuis laudibus ejus diligenter persistit, dicens ac implens quod dictum est supra: Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore; semper laus ejus in ore meo. Et Ecclesiasticus: Confitebor (inquit) tibi, Domine Rex, et collaudabo te Deum salvatorem meum. Laudabo nomen tuum assidue. In æternum misericordia ejus. Misericordia enim Dei est ipsemet Deus misericors: et ita æterna est, sicut et Deus. Vel, In æternum misericordia ejus, id est, effectus pietatis divinæ æternaliter permanebit in electis, qui sunt vasa misericordiæ. Et usque in generationem et generationem, id est per omnes generationes et sine fine, permanet veritas ejus, id est veritas sacræ Scripturæ: quemadmodum Christus testatur, Cœlum et terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt. Propter quod etiam in Isaia habetur: Verbum Dei nostri stabit in æternum. Vel veritas Dei, intelligi potest ipsemet Deus verax, seu vera impletio promissionum ipsius: quæ nunquam cessabit, quoniam ibunt reprobi in ignem æternum, electi vero in vitam æternam.
paras.en: [[99:4|Praise ye his name|Laudate nomen ejus]] with a devout, recollected and loving mind, [[99:5|For the Lord is sweet|quoniam suavis est Dominus]]. For God, blessed and holy, is sweet in his very essence; and his infinite essence is nothing else but a sweetness wholly immeasurable, before whose fragrance, sweetness and delightfulness all created sweetness sinks away infinitely. Yet this sweetness of God he deserves in some measure to taste who perseveres diligently in his unceasing praises, saying and fulfilling what was said above: [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore; semper laus ejus in ore meo]]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 51:1|I will give glory|Confitebor]] (he says) [[Ecclus 51:1|to thee, O Lord, O King, and I will praise thee, O God my Saviour|tibi, Domine Rex, et collaudabo te Deum salvatorem meum]]. [[Ecclus 51:15|I will praise thy name continually|Laudabo nomen tuum assidue]]. [[99:5|his mercy endureth for ever|In æternum misericordia ejus]]. For the mercy of God is God himself, the merciful: and so it is eternal, as God is. Or: [[99:5|his mercy endureth for ever|In æternum misericordia ejus]], that is, the effect of the divine loving-kindness will abide eternally in the elect, who are vessels of mercy. [[99:5|to generation and generation|Et usque in generationem et generationem]], that is, through all generations and without end, abides [[99:5|his truth|veritas ejus]], that is, the truth of Holy Scripture: as Christ bears witness, [[Matt 24:35|Heaven and earth shall pass: but my words shall not pass|Cœlum et terra transibunt, verba autem mea non transibunt]] [no margin reference; Denis's wording is that of Mark 13:31]. For this reason it is also said in Isaias: [[Is 40:8|the word of our Lord endureth for ever|Verbum Dei nostri stabit in æternum]] [no margin reference; Denis's *stabit*, "shall stand", for the Vulgate's *manet*]. Or the truth of God may be understood as God himself, who is true, or as the true fulfilment of his promises: which will never cease, since the reprobate shall go into everlasting fire, and the elect [[Matt 25:46|into life everlasting|in vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Ecce psalmum dulcifluum, angelica jucunditate repletum, Dei præconiis redolentem audivimus: quem debemus in persona Ecclesiæ cum ingenti attentione proferre, ejusque exhortationibus efficaciter obedire, Domino jubilando, ei hilariter serviendo, ejusque præsentiam jugiter cogitando, ipsumque esse Deum nostrum fide ac opere profitendo, nec unquam ab ejus præconio segniter discedendo. Quod facere nullo modo poterimus, nisi quotidie gravia vitia integerrimo corde abhorreamus, venialia quoque diligenter pro posse vitemus, corrigamus, ac deploremus, confitendo frequenter et emendando ferventer, pensantes illud Salomonis: Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur. Hæc requiruntur ad actus ad quos invitamur in psalmo præsenti, quoniam actus isti omnino deiformes sunt, cœlestes atque angelici, saluberrimi et incomparabilis meriti.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a psalm flowing with sweetness, filled with angelic joy, fragrant with the praises of God: which we ought to recite in the person of the Church with great attention, and to obey its exhortations effectually, singing joyfully to the Lord, serving him cheerfully, thinking continually on his presence, professing by faith and deed that he is our God, and never slothfully leaving off his praise. This we shall in no way be able to do unless every day we abhor grave sins with a wholly sincere heart, and also diligently avoid, correct and bewail venial ones as far as we can, confessing often and amending fervently, weighing that saying of Solomon: [[Prov 28:13|He that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy|Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur]]. These things are required for the acts to which we are invited in the present psalm, since those acts are altogether godlike, heavenly and angelic, most wholesome, and of incomparable merit.

paras.t: Precatio. Æterna cœli gloria, Deus, fac nos portas tuas in confessione, et atria tua in hymnis introire: ut confitentes majestati tuæ, coronam vitæ quam repromisisti te diligentibus, te donante, accipiamus.
paras.en: Prayer. O God, eternal glory of heaven, make us go into thy gates with praise and into thy courts with hymns: that, confessing thy majesty, we may by thy gift receive the crown of life which thou hast promised to them that love thee.

100.title: EXPOSITIO PSALMI CENTESIMI : MISERICORDIAM ET JUDICIUM CANTABO TIBI, DOMINE.
100.title_en: Exposition of the hundredth psalm: Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord.

paras.t: Titulus psalmi novissimi hujus quinquagenæ secundæ, talis est: Psalmus David. Est enim hic psalmus David prophetæ tanquam auctoris, sed Christo cantatur tanquam largitori omnium perfectionum, virtutum seu gratiarum, de quibus tractat hic psalmus. Convenit vero cuilibet homini virtuoso, cujus vita aliis in exemplum proponi potest. Fatetur enim in hoc psalmo vir perfectus suas virtutes, non præsumptuose aut ad gloriam propriam, sed ad Dei honorem et proximorum ædificationem: quemadmodum Job, Tobias, Jeremias, et alii multi Sanctorum diligenter describunt bona propria. Quod etiam Paulus in suis epistolis sæpius agit, in tantum ut dicat aliquoties: Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis, id est, caritas qua vestram salutem desidero, compulit me laudare me ipsum: quod insipientiæ simile est, et divinæ Scripturæ videtur contrarium, quoniam Salomon dicit: Laudet te alienus, et non os tuum; extraneus, et non labia tua. Sed hoc ideo dictum est, ne quis laudet se ipsum sine ratione legitima, aut ex gloria vana. Non autem prohibemur per hoc, ad gloriam Creatoris, ædificationemque auditoris, et maxime subditorum, propria enarrare virtutes, præcipue quoniam Christus in Evangelio: Sic luceat, inquit, lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est. Unde et Petrus ait: Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis, tanquam de malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum in die visitationis. Et Paulus dilecto discipulo ait: Profectus tuus manifestus sit omnibus.
paras.en: The title of this psalm, the last of the second fifty, is as follows: A psalm of David[[100:1||]] [the Vulgate reads *Psalmus ipsi David*, "a psalm for David himself"; Denis gives it in short]. For this psalm is David the prophet's as its author, but it is sung to Christ as the giver of all the perfections, virtues or graces of which this psalm treats. It suits, moreover, any virtuous man whose life can be set before others as an example. For in this psalm the perfect man confesses his virtues, not presumptuously or for his own glory, but for the honour of God and the edification of his neighbours: just as Job, Tobias, Jeremias and many other Saints carefully describe their own good deeds. Paul too does this often in his epistles, so far that he says more than once: [[2 Cor 12:11|I am become foolish. You have compelled me|Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis]] [the margin gives II Cor. xi, 11; the words are at 2 Cor 12:11], that is, the charity with which I desire your salvation has driven me to praise myself: which is like folly, and seems contrary to divine Scripture, since Solomon says: [[Prov 27:2|Let another praise thee, and not thy own mouth: a stranger, and not thy own lips.|Laudet te alienus, et non os tuum; extraneus, et non labia tua]] But this was said so that no one should praise himself without lawful reason, or out of vainglory. We are not, however, forbidden by it to recount our own virtues for the glory of the Creator and the edification of the hearer, and above all of those under us; especially since Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 5:16|So let your light shine before men|Sic luceat]], [[Matt 5:16|that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est]]. Hence Peter too says: [[1 Pet 2:12|Having your conversation good among the Gentiles: that whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may, by the good works which they shall behold in you, glorify God in the day of visitation|Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis, tanquam de malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum in die visitationis]]. And Paul says to his beloved disciple: [[1 Tim 4:15|thy profiting may be manifest to all|Profectus tuus manifestus sit omnibus]].

paras.t: Loquens ergo David in persona Ecclesiæ, seu cujuslibet viri perfecti, sic orsus est: Misericordiam et judicium cantabo tibi, Domine: id est, pietatem et æquitatem tibi, o Deus, cum laude jucunda adscribam, id est, non solum laudabo te tanquam misericordem, misericorditer indulgentem, miserationesque maximas peccatoribus facientem, sed etiam tanquam justum, justa judicia diligentem ac facientem, terribiliter ulciscentem, et nil mali impunitum, imo nil penitus indiscussum, injudicatum, impræmiatumque derelinquentem. Nunc enim frequenter prædictum est, quomodo universæ viæ Domini sint misericordia et veritas, intelligendo per veritatem justitiam seu judicium. Cantamus autem Domino judicium multiplex: videlicet particulare, quod singulis, dum moriuntur, facit seorsum; et universale, quod in fine mundi facturus est. Cantamus ejus judicium discretionis, quod agit in nobis quotidie, electos a reprobis in vita hac dividens gratia, voto et merito; judicium quoque retributionis finalis, quod erit in fine sæculi, quando separabuntur boni a malis loco et præmio. — Vel sic: Misericordiam in prosperis, et judicium in adversis, cantabo tibi, id est ad laudem tuam, o Domine, ita quod quidquid boni seu consolationis tuæ mihi acciderit, et quidquid meriti in me fuerit, totum tibi attribuam, et tuæ misericordissimæ bonitati adscribam. Porro quidquid adversitatis, imperfectionis aut culpæ contigerit, hoc meis peccatis et tuo justo judicio deputabo, cantans tibi illud Danielis: Justus es, Domine, in omnibus quæ fecisti nobis, et universa opera tua vera; et omnia quæ fecisti nobis, in vero judicio fecisti, quia peccavimus tibi, et mandatis tuis non obedivimus.
paras.en: Speaking, then, in the person of the Church, or of any perfect man, David began thus: [[100:1|Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord|Misericordiam et judicium cantabo tibi, Domine]]: that is, with joyful praise I will ascribe to thee, O God, kindness and equity; that is, I will praise thee not only as merciful, mercifully forgiving and showing the greatest mercies to sinners, but also as just, loving and doing just judgments, punishing terribly, and leaving nothing evil unpunished[[Prov 19:5||]], nay nothing at all undiscussed, unjudged and unrewarded. For it has often been said already how [[Ps 24:10|All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth|universæ viæ Domini sint misericordia et veritas]], understanding by truth justice or judgment. Now we sing to the Lord a manifold judgment: namely the particular, which he makes for each one apart when he dies; and the universal, which he will make at the end of the world. We sing his judgment of discernment, which he works in us daily, dividing the elect from the reprobate in this life by grace, desire and merit; and also the judgment of final retribution, which will be at the end of the world, when the good shall be separated from the wicked in place and reward[[Matt 13:49||]] [the margin gives Matth. xviii, 19, which does not fit; probably Matt 13:49 is meant]. — Or thus: [[100:1|Mercy|Misericordiam]] in prosperity, [[100:1|and judgment|et judicium]] in adversity, [[100:1|I will sing to thee|cantabo tibi]], that is, to thy praise, O Lord; so that whatever good or consolation of thine befalls me, and whatever merit there is in me, I will attribute it all to thee and ascribe it to thy most merciful goodness. But whatever adversity, imperfection or fault befalls, this I will put down to my sins and to thy just judgment, singing to thee that word of Daniel: [[Dan 3:27|thou art just in all that thou hast done to us, and all thy works are true|Justus es, Domine, in omnibus quæ fecisti nobis, et universa opera tua vera]]; [[Dan 3:31|every thing that thou hast done to us, thou hast done in true judgment|et omnia quæ fecisti nobis, in vero judicio fecisti]], [[Dan 3:29|For we have sinned|quia peccavimus tibi]], [[Dan 3:30|And we have not hearkened to thy commandments|et mandatis tuis non obedivimus]].

paras.t: Sicut ergo Deus singulariter præcipit nobis misericordiam, quantum ad proximos, et judicium, quantum ad nos ipsos (secundum illud Zachariæ: Judicium verum judicate, et misericordiam et miserationes facite, unusquisque cum fratre suo; et Michææ: Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam); sic Deus in omni opere suo misericordiam judiciumque committet. Propter quod hæc duo sibi specialiter decantantur, ne vel judicium Dei nos desperare compellat, vel misericordia intimoratos efficiat; sed utrumque horum pensando, timendo speremus, et sperando timeamus, atque sollicite ambulemus cum Deo nostro, cum metu et timore ac tremore nostram operantes salutem, juxta admonitionem divini Apostoli.
paras.en: As, then, God especially commands us mercy as regards our neighbours, and judgment as regards ourselves (according to that word of Zacharias: [[Zach 7:9|Judge ye true judgment, and shew ye mercy and compassion every man to his brother|Judicium verum judicate, et misericordiam et miserationes facite, unusquisque cum fratre suo]]; and of Micheas: [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment, and to love mercy|Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam]]), so God in every work of his joins mercy and judgment. For this reason these two are especially sung to him, so that neither the judgment of God should drive us to despair, nor his mercy make us fearless; but weighing both of them, we may hope in fearing and fear in hoping, and [[Mich 6:8|walk solicitous with thy God|sollicite ambulemus cum Deo nostro]] [Denis has "walk solicitously with our God"], working out our salvation with fear and dread and trembling[[Phil 2:12||]], according to the admonition of the divine Apostle.

paras.t: Psallam, spiritualia cantica proferendo, et intelligam, id est, intus legam, seu intente advertam quæ psallo, ne sim vagus et mente inanis, sed impleam illud Apostoli: Psallam spiritu, psallam et mente. Unde supra dictum est, Psallite sapienter. Sic autem psallam et intelligam in via immaculata, id est cum intentione sincera, in desiderio puro, in observatione legis divinæ, quatenus vita voci concordet. Hæ namque sunt viæ immaculatæ, quibus ad Deum anima tendit: de quibus legitur in Proverbiis, Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ. In via vero sancti desiderii, quo sitivit anima mea ad te, dixi, tuam præsentiam vehementer optando: Quando venies ad me? id est, utinam cito venias, quotidie quidem per gratiæ accumulationem, et in brevi tollendo me de isto exsilio ad patriam: cupio enim dissolvi et esse tecum, quia hoc multo melius.
paras.en: [[100:1|I will sing|Psallam]], bringing forth spiritual songs, [[100:2|And I will understand|et intelligam]] [*intelligere*, read as *intus legere*, "to read within"], that is, I will read within, or attentively mark what I sing, so as not to be wandering and empty in mind, but to fulfil that word of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 14:15|I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the understanding|Psallam spiritu, psallam et mente]]. Hence it was said above: [[Ps 46:8|sing ye wisely|Psallite sapienter]]. And so I will sing and understand [[100:2|in the unspotted way|in via immaculata]], that is, with a sincere intention, in pure desire, in the keeping of the divine law, so that the life may agree with the voice. For these are the unspotted ways by which the soul tends to God: of which we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable.|Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ]] And in the way of holy desire, with which my soul has thirsted for thee, I said, vehemently longing for thy presence: [[100:2|when thou shalt come to me|Quando venies ad me]]? that is, would that thou wouldst come soon: daily indeed by the heaping up of grace, and shortly by taking me from this exile to the fatherland: for I desire [[Phil 1:23|to be dissolved|dissolvi]] and to be with thee, for this is far better.

paras.t: Consequenter prosequitur in speciali, qualiter in via immaculata psallebat, dicendo: Perambulabam, id est, in hac valle lacrimarum conversabar in innocentia cordis mei, ita quod non feci alteri quod mihi nollem fieri, sed in simplicitate ac puritate conscientiæ vixi: quemadmodum dum ait Apostolus, Neminem læsimus, neminem corrupimus, neque aliquando in sermone adulationis fuimus; in medio domus meæ, id est in medio Ecclesiæ seu fratrum meorum, nullum malo exemplo intoxicando.
paras.en: Next he goes on to say in particular how he sang in the unspotted way, saying: [[100:2|I walked|Perambulabam]], that is, in this vale of tears I lived [[100:2|in the innocence of my heart|in innocentia cordis mei]], so that I did not do to another what I would not have done to me[[Tob 4:16||]], but lived in simplicity and purity of conscience: as when the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 7:2|We have injured no man: we have corrupted no man|Neminem læsimus, neminem corrupimus]], [[1 Thess 2:5|neither have we used at any time the speech of flattery|neque aliquando in sermone adulationis fuimus]]; [[100:2|in the midst of my house|in medio domus meæ]], that is, in the midst of the Church or of my brethren, poisoning none by bad example.

paras.t: Non proponebam ante oculos meos corporales seu interiores rem injustam, id est quidquam illicitum, ut appeterem: sicut in Job habetur, Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis, ne cogitarem quidem de virgine. Unde iterum scriptum est: Unusquisque offensiones oculorum suorum abjiciat, dicit Dominus. Maxime enim nocet oculus incustoditus, sicut in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Oculo quid nequius creatum est? Semper ergo oculum cordis et corporis refrenemus, si corde puro Domino complacere optamus. Si hoc modo David oculos suos custodisset, in adulterium homicidiumque lapsus non fuisset. Facientes prævaricationes, id est divina mandata transgredientes, odivi, in quantum hujusmodi sunt: dilexi tamen eos secundum quod homines sunt et gratiæ atque salutis capaces, quia eorum conversionem desidero, quoniam pro inimicis et impiis orare præcipior. Et in hoc ostendit se divinæ voluntati conformem, quoniam, sicut Sapiens dicit, Odio sunt Deo impii et impietas ejus. Et de impiis apud Jeremiam Dominus ait: Non est anima mea ad populum istum.
paras.en: [[100:3|I will not set before my eyes|Non proponebam ante oculos meos]], bodily or inward, [[100:3|any unjust thing|rem injustam]], that is, anything unlawful, so as to desire it: as we have in Job: [[Job 31:1|I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin|Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis, ne cogitarem quidem de virgine]]. Hence it is written again: [[Ezech 20:7|Let every man cast away the scandals of his eyes|Unusquisque offensiones oculorum suorum abjiciat]], saith the Lord. For the unguarded eye does the greatest harm, as is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:15|What is created more wicked than an eye?|Oculo quid nequius creatum est?]] Let us then always curb the eye of the heart and of the body, if we wish to please the Lord with a pure heart. Had David guarded his eyes in this way, he would not have fallen into adultery and murder[[2 Kings 11:1||]]. [[100:3|the workers of iniquities|Facientes prævaricationes]] [Latin *facientes prævaricationes*, "those that commit transgressions"], that is, those who transgress the divine commandments, [[100:3|I hated|odivi]], in so far as they are such: yet I loved them in so far as they are men and capable of grace and salvation, since I desire their conversion, because I am commanded to pray for enemies and the wicked[[Matt 5:44||]]. And in this he shows himself conformed to the divine will, since, as the Wise Man says: [[Wis 14:9|to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful alike|Odio sunt Deo impii et impietas ejus]] [Denis: "the wicked and their wickedness"]. And of the wicked the Lord says in Jeremias: [[Jer 15:1|my soul is not towards this people|Non est anima mea ad populum istum]].

paras.t: Non adhæsit mihi cor pravum, id est, affectio cordis mala mihi non placuit. Multum quippe pœnales sunt homini justo affectus et actus hominis pravi, quemadmodum Petrus testatur de Lot: Adspectu et auditu justus erat, habitans inter eos qui de die in diem animam justam iniquis operibus cruciabant. Verumtamen in tali eventu seu casu servanda est patientia, et immoderata ac impetuosa displicentia removenda, atque pia compassio impendenda, prout docet Apostolus: Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis. Et rursus: Alter, inquit, alterius onera portate. Declinantem a me malignum, id est igne vitiorum accensum, a mea recta voluntate aversum, et mihi in vita dissimilem, non cognoscebam per approbationem, quoniam mihi non placuerunt opera ejus. Et in hoc Deo se ipsum conformat, qui impiis dicet in die judicii: Nescio vos. De quibus etiam alibi ait: Non est mihi voluntas in vobis.
paras.en: [[100:4|The perverse heart did not cleave to me|Non adhæsit mihi cor pravum]], that is, an evil affection of the heart did not please me. For the affections and acts of a wicked man are very painful to a just man, as Peter testifies of Lot: [[2 Pet 2:8|in sight and hearing he was just, dwelling among them who from day to day vexed the just soul with unjust works|Adspectu et auditu justus erat, habitans inter eos qui de die in diem animam justam iniquis operibus cruciabant]]. Yet in such an event or case patience must be kept, immoderate and impetuous displeasure put away, and loving compassion shown, as the Apostle teaches: [[Gal 6:1|Brethren, and if a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness|Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis]]. And again: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens|Alter, inquit, alterius onera portate]]. [[100:4|and the malignant, that turned aside from me|Declinantem a me malignum]] [*malignum* is taken as from *ignis*, "fire"], that is, inflamed with the fire of vices, turned away from my right will and unlike me in life, [[100:4|I would not know|non cognoscebam]] by approving him, since his works did not please me. And in this he conforms himself to God, who will say to the wicked on the day of judgment: [[Luke 13:25|I know you not|Nescio vos]]. Of whom he also says elsewhere: [[Mal 1:10|I have no pleasure in you|Non est mihi voluntas in vobis]].

paras.t: Detrahentem secreto proximo suo, ejus famam denigrando coram me, seu me sciente, hunc persequebar affligendo, increpando seu fugiendo. Est enim detractionis vitium grave nimis, et gravius furto, quod tamen ex suo genere est mortale. Unde scriptum est: Si mordeat serpens in occulto, nihil eo minus habet qui occulte detrahit. Detractorem igitur persequi debet verus diligensque prælatus, et quilibet nostrum eum arguere debet, si est spes de emendatione ipsius; si vero correctionem verborum non recipit, debet ei ostendere vultum tristem, vel omnino faciem ab eo avertere, seu aliquid boni proponere, quatenus sic erubescat et emendetur. Hinc enim Salomon dicit: Per tristitiam vultus, corrigitur animus delinquentis. Et alibi habetur: Sepi aures tuas spinis, et noli audire linguam nequam. Hic itaque persecutor detractoris, bonus ac pius est, non crudelis; et quicumque cupit vere proficere, debet in primis vitium detractionis penitus abhorrere et funditus exstirpare, nec omni spiritui credere, seu de facili assensum præbere omni narrationi aliorum, præcipue imperfectorum. Maxime namque animam inquietat, mentisque stabilitatem ac gravitatem tollit ac impedit, quam cito omnia credere, obloquentiumque sermonibus leviter adhærere cœperit. Hinc etenim frequentes discordiæ et injusta odia generantur, ita ut interdum de amicissimis fiant inimici, dum unanimes quidem, sed nimium credulas animas maliloqua lingua disjungit. Magna vero quies est animæ, et ingens gravitas morum, non temere neque facile de aliquo quidquam sinistrum velle recipere aut audire. Et ista valde pensanda sunt innocentibus atque simplicibus, quia facilius totum credunt, putantes alios tales, quales sunt ipsi. Propter quod Salomon: Innocens, inquit, credit omni verbo.
paras.en: [[100:5|The man that in private detracted his neighbour|Detrahentem secreto proximo suo]], blackening his good name before me or with my knowledge, [[100:5|him did I persecute|hunc persequebar]] by afflicting, rebuking or shunning him. For the vice of detraction is very grievous, and more grievous than theft, which yet is mortal of its kind. Hence it is written: [[Eccles 10:11|If a serpent bite in silence, he is nothing better that backbiteth secretly.|Si mordeat serpens in occulto, nihil eo minus habet qui occulte detrahit]] [Denis reads *in occulto*, "in secret", for the Vulgate's *in silentio*]. A true and diligent prelate, therefore, ought to persecute the detractor, and any one of us ought to rebuke him, if there is hope of his amendment; but if he does not accept correction in words, one ought to show him a sad countenance, or turn one's face from him altogether, or put forward something good, so that he may thus blush and amend. For hence Solomon says: [[Eccles 7:4|by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected|Per tristitiam vultus, corrigitur animus delinquentis]]. And elsewhere we have: [[Ecclus 28:28|Hedge in thy ears with thorns, hear not a wicked tongue|Sepi aures tuas spinis: linguam nequam]]. This persecutor of the detractor, then, is good and kind, not cruel; and whoever desires truly to make progress must first of all utterly abhor the vice of detraction and root it out entirely, and [[1 John 4:1|believe not every spirit|nec omni spiritui credere]], nor readily give assent to every tale of others, especially of the imperfect. For it greatly disquiets the soul, and takes away and hinders the steadiness and gravity of the mind, once it begins to believe everything quickly and to cleave lightly to the words of slanderers. For hence arise frequent discords and unjust hatreds, so that at times the dearest friends become enemies, when an evil-speaking tongue parts souls that were of one mind indeed, but too credulous. But it is a great quiet of soul, and a great gravity of manners, to be unwilling to receive or hear anything ill of anyone rashly or easily. And these things must be well weighed by the innocent and simple, because they more easily believe everything, thinking others to be such as they are themselves. Wherefore Solomon says: [[Prov 14:15|The innocent|Innocens]], [[Prov 14:15|believeth every word|credit omni verbo]].

paras.t: Superbo oculo et insatiabili corde, id est avaro qui non impletur pecunia, cum hoc non edebam cum interiori consensu. Et ad litteram, si fieri potest sine dispendio, vitandi sunt in mensa superbi atque avari, juxta illud: Viri justi sint tibi convivæ. Et Apostolus dicit: Si quis non obedierit verbo per epistolam, hunc notate, et ne commisceamini cum illo, ut confundatur. Alibi quoque: Cum hujusmodi, inquit, nec cibum sumere. Propter correctionem tamen et informationem seu aliam rationabilem causam, possumus cum talibus manducare, præsertim quum Christus cum publicanis et peccatoribus comedisse legatur, quatenus eos converteret.
paras.en: [[100:5|With him that had a proud eye, and an unsatiable heart|Superbo oculo et insatiabili corde]], that is, a covetous man, who is not filled with money, [[100:5|I would not eat|cum hoc non edebam]] with inward consent. And literally, if it can be done without loss, the proud and covetous are to be avoided at table, according to that word: [[Ecclus 9:22|Let just men be thy guests|Viri justi sint tibi convivæ]]. And the Apostle says: [[2 Thess 3:14|if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man and do not keep company with him, that he may be ashamed|Si quis non obedierit verbo per epistolam, hunc notate, et ne commisceamini cum illo, ut confundatur]]. And elsewhere: [[1 Cor 5:11|with such a one|Cum hujusmodi]], he says, [[1 Cor 5:11|not so much as to eat|nec cibum sumere]]. Yet for the sake of correction and instruction, or another reasonable cause, we may eat with such men, especially since we read that Christ ate with publicans and sinners, so as to convert them.

paras.t: Oculi mei interiores et etiam exteriores, ad fideles terræ, id est ad homines Deo fideliter servientes, ut sedeant mecum in consiliis, mensis atque judiciis, quia ad tales affectuose respicio, eisque communicare desidero. Ambulans in via immaculata, id est sine labe peccati conversans, et Deo in puritate cordis deserviens, hic mihi ministrabat. Tales namque esse decet ministros prælatorum ac principum; præcipue autem decet religiosos habere devotos servos, non sæculares, leves, vanos, in vestitu curiosos, et opere inconstantes.
paras.en: [[100:6|My eyes|Oculi mei]], inward and outward too, [[100:6|were upon the faithful of the earth|ad fideles terræ]], that is, upon men who serve God faithfully, [[100:6|to sit with me|ut sedeant mecum]] in counsels, at table and in judgments; for I look with affection upon such, and desire to share with them. [[100:6|the man that walked in the perfect way|Ambulans in via immaculata]], that is, living without stain of sin and serving God in purity of heart, [[100:6|he served me|hic mihi ministrabat]]. For such ought the ministers of prelates and princes to be; and above all it becomes religious to have devout servants, not worldly, light, vain, fussy about their dress and inconstant in their work.

paras.t: Non habitabit in medio domus meæ qui facit superbiam: id est, superbis non cohabitabo, ne cum perverso pervertar; et si corpore ei cohabito, mente tamen longe distabo ab eo, quoniam scriptum est: Qui tetigerit picem, inquinabitur ab ea; et qui communicaverit superbo, induet superbiam. Unde Sapientia asserit: Arrogantiam et superbiam et viam pravam et os bilingue detestor. Qui loquitur iniqua, non direxit in conspectu oculorum meorum: id est, meo judicio non fecit bene, nec ambulavit ad Deum directe; imo reprobo eum.
paras.en: [[100:7|He that worketh pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house|Non habitabit in medio domus meæ qui facit superbiam]]: that is, I will not live with the proud, lest with the perverse I be perverted[[Ps 17:27||]]; and if I live with him in body, yet in mind I will stand far from him, since it is written: [[Ecclus 13:1|He that toucheth pitch, shall be defiled with it: and he that hath fellowship with the proud, shall put on pride.|Qui tetigerit picem, inquinabitur ab ea; et qui communicaverit superbo, induet superbiam]] Hence Wisdom declares: [[Prov 8:13|I hate arrogance, and pride, and every wicked way, and a mouth with a double tongue|Arrogantiam et superbiam et viam pravam et os bilingue detestor]]. [[100:7|he that speaketh unjust things did not prosper before my eyes|Qui loquitur iniqua, non direxit in conspectu oculorum meorum]] [Latin *non direxit*, "did not go straight"]: that is, in my judgment he did not do well, nor walk straight towards God; nay, I reject him.

paras.t: In matutino, id est tam cito ut commode justeque potui, interficiebam gladio materiali vel spirituali omnes peccatores terræ, hoc est omnes graviter criminosos, causas morte dignas habentes, ut disperderem de civitate Domini, id est de Ecclesia seu congregatione justorum, omnes operantes iniquitatem tam gravem, ut dictum est. Debent namque principes sæculares gladio materiali, prælati autem gladio spirituali, iniquos occidere, seu intus mortuos declarare, ut mundent Ecclesiam a commixtione pravorum, secundum Decreta. — Vel: In matutino, id est in exordio tentationis, interficiebam, id est, cadere atque deficere feci, per orationem devotam et adjutorium gratiæ Christi, omnes peccatores terræ, id est diabolos me tentantes, et terrenas concupiscentias mihi suggerentes; ut disperderem de civitate Domini, id est de consensu animæ meæ, quæ est civitas Dei, omnes operantes iniquitatem, id est omnia diabolica tentamenta, me ad opera mala inducere quærentia.
paras.en: [[100:8|In the morning|In matutino]], that is, as soon as I fitly and justly could, [[100:8|I put to death|interficiebam]] with the material or the spiritual sword [[100:8|all the wicked of the land|omnes peccatores terræ]], that is, all grievous criminals, guilty of crimes worthy of death, [[100:8|that I might cut off all the workers of iniquity from the city of the Lord|ut disperderem de civitate Domini]], that is, from the Church or congregation of the just, [[100:8|all the workers of iniquity|omnes operantes iniquitatem]] so grievous, as has been said. For secular princes ought to slay the wicked with the material sword, and prelates with the spiritual sword, or declare them dead within, so as to cleanse the Church of mingling with the wicked, according to the Decrees [the margin gives "24, q. 1, Augustinus", that is, Gratian's Decretum, causa 24, question 1, citing Augustine]. — Or: [[100:8|In the morning|In matutino]], that is, at the beginning of temptation, [[100:8|I put to death|interficiebam]], that is, I made fall and fail, by devout prayer and the help of the grace of Christ, [[100:8|all the wicked of the land|omnes peccatores terræ]], that is, the devils tempting me and suggesting earthly lusts to me; [[100:8|that I might cut off all the workers of iniquity from the city of the Lord|ut disperderem de civitate Domini]], that is, from the consent of my soul, which is the city of God, [[100:8|all the workers of iniquity|omnes operantes iniquitatem]], that is, all the temptations of the devil, seeking to lead me to evil works.

paras.t: Quomodo autem hic psalmus Christo conveniat, certum ac facile est. Ipse enim ut perfectissimus cantavit Deo Patri ac toti Trinitati misericordiam et judicium, quia in toto Evangelio docet Deum pium esse ac justum. Psallebat quoque et intelligebat in via immaculata, id est in tota sua conversatione sanctissima: Quando venies ad me? id est, quando, o Deus Pater, veniam ad te? Optabat namque redire ad Patrem, quemadmodum testatur: O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? Non adhæsit etiam Christo cor pravum, ut patet de Juda proditore. Cetera omnia plana sunt.
paras.en: How this psalm suits Christ is certain and easy. For he, as the most perfect, sang to God the Father and to the whole Trinity mercy and judgment, since throughout the Gospel he teaches that God is kind and just. He also sang and understood in the unspotted way, that is, in his whole most holy life: [[100:2|when thou shalt come to me|Quando venies ad me]]? that is, when, O God the Father, shall I come to thee? For he longed to return to the Father, as he testifies: [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero?]] Nor did a perverse heart cleave to Christ, as is plain in the case of Judas the traitor[[John 15:3||]] [the margin gives Joann. xv, 3–8: "Now you are clean", said after Judas had gone out, and the branches that are cut off]. All the rest is plain.

paras.t: Porro, secundum doctores, tres sunt status christianæ religionis. Primus est incipientium, quorum est in luctu et actibus pœnitentiæ occupari: et huic appropriatur prima quinquagena Psalterii, quæ terminatur in psalmo pœnitentiali, videlicet, Miserere mei, Deus. Secundus est status proficientium, qui in spiritu ambulant, quorum est in actu justitiæ exerceri, eundo de virtute in virtutem: et huic appropriatur hæc secunda quinquagena, quæ terminatur in psalmo præsenti, de rigore justitiæ pertractante. Tertius vero est status perfectorum, a vita activa ad contemplativam ascendentium, quorum est laudibus Dei jugiter inhærere: et huic appropriatur tertia quinquagena, quæ terminatur in laude divina.
paras.en: Further, according to the doctors, there are three states of the Christian religion. The first is that of beginners, whose part is to be busied in mourning and in works of penance: and to this is assigned the first fifty of the Psalter, which ends in a penitential psalm, namely [[Ps 50:3|Have mercy on me, O God|Miserere mei, Deus]] [the margin gives Ps. l]. The second is the state of the proficient, who walk in the spirit[[Gal 5:16||]], whose part is to be exercised in the practice of justice, going [[Ps 83:8|from virtue to virtue|de virtute in virtutem]]: and to this is assigned this second fifty, which ends in the present psalm, treating of the rigour of justice. The third is the state of the perfect, who rise from the active life to the contemplative, whose part is to cleave continually to the praises of God: and to this is assigned the third fifty, which ends in divine praise.

paras.t: Docetur denique unusquisque superior ex psalmo præsenti, ut habeat se devote ad Deum, juste ad proximum, immaculate ac sancte ad se ipsum. Imo singulis nobis conandum est, ut taliter conversemur in hoc mundo fallaci, ac fragili corpore, quod vita nostra aliis exemplaris reddatur, atque in propria persona, verba psalmi hujus a nobis cantentur ad gloriam Salvatoris, qui est super omnia Deus sublimis et benedictus. Amen.
paras.en: Lastly, every superior is taught by the present psalm to bear himself devoutly towards God, justly towards his neighbour, and spotlessly and holily towards himself. Nay, each of us must strive so to live in this deceitful world and frail body that our life may be made an example to others, and that the words of this psalm may be sung by us in our own person to the glory of the Saviour, who is God, exalted and blessed above all. Amen.

paras.t: Precatio. Misericordia tua, Domine, interveniente, præsta nobis, quæsumus, cordi pravo non adhærere; sed fac nos domus tuæ innocenter semper perambulare atria, quo tibi placentes, æternæ gloriæ tuæ nos digneris associare.
paras.en: Prayer. By the intercession of thy mercy, O Lord, grant us, we beseech thee, not to cleave to a perverse heart; but make us ever walk in innocence through the courts of thy house, that, pleasing thee, thou mayest vouchsafe to join us to thy eternal glory.

101.title: EXPOSITIO IN PERSONA POENITENTIS, PSALMI CENTESIMI PRIMI : DOMINE, EXAUDI ORATIONEM MEAM.
101.title_en: Exposition of the hundred and first psalm in the person of a penitent: Hear, O Lord, my prayer.

paras.t: Psalmi nunc declarandi titulus est : Oratio pauperis, quum anxius fuerit, et in conspectu Domini effuderit precem suam : id est, psalmus præsens est oratio hominis pœnitentis, quum anxiatur timore futuri judicii ac suppliciorum inferni ex recordatione peccatorum suorum, et in conspectu Domini effuderit precem suam, quatenus misericordiam consequatur, videlicet a præsentibus tribulationibus relevamen, peccatorum indulgentiam, innocentiæ restitutionem, et gloriam in futuro.
paras.en: The title of the psalm now to be explained is: [[101:1|The prayer of the poor man, when he was anxious, and poured out his supplication before the Lord|Oratio pauperis, quum anxius fuerit, et in conspectu Domini effuderit precem suam]]: that is, the present psalm is the prayer of a penitent man, when he is in anguish with fear of the judgment to come and of the torments of hell from the remembrance of his sins, and [[101:1|poured out his supplication before the Lord|in conspectu Domini effuderit precem suam]], so that he may obtain mercy: namely, relief from present tribulations, pardon of his sins, restoration of innocence, and glory in the life to come.

paras.t: Loquens igitur sanctus Propheta in persona hominis, propriam infirmitatem, iniquitatem atque miseriam recognoscentis, ac spiritualem inopiam deplorantis, ait : Domine, Deus omnipotens, simplex ac trinus, totaliter naturaliterque misericors, exaudi, id est, cognoscendo adimple, orationem meam, id est petitionem decentium peti a te ; et clamor meus mentalis, videlicet ardens affectio, desideriumque cœleste, seu clamor vocalis, qui est magni ac sancti desiderii nuntius, ad te veniat, id est, tibi acceptus sit, tibi complaceat, et attendatur ac impleatur a te, quemadmodum de quibusdam ait Scriptura : Clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit. Et tu ipse dicis : Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me. Venit autem clamor noster ad Dominum, non loco, sed acceptatione.
paras.en: The holy Prophet, then, speaking in the person of a man who acknowledges his own weakness, iniquity and misery and bewails his spiritual want, says: [[101:2|O Lord|Domine]], almighty God, simple and three, wholly and by nature merciful, [[101:2|Hear|exaudi]], that is, take knowledge of and fulfil, [[101:2|my prayer|orationem meam]], that is, my petition for things fitting to be asked of thee; [[101:2|and let my cry|et clamor meus]], the cry of the mind, namely burning affection and heavenly desire, or the cry of the voice, which is the messenger of a great and holy desire, [[101:2|come to thee|ad te veniat]], that is, be acceptable to thee, be pleasing to thee, and be heeded and fulfilled by thee; as Scripture says of certain men: [[Jas 5:4|the cry of them hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth|Clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit]]. And thou thyself sayest: [[Ex 3:9|the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me|Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me]]. Now our cry comes to the Lord not by place, but by acceptance.

paras.t: Non avertas faciem tuam, id est pietatis tuæ adspectum, a me, vili ac paupere peccatore, sed pœnitente. Loquitur autem Propheta de Deo modo humano, quasi in Deo essent auris et facies, aversio ac conversio novæ sive recentes, secundum novitatem meritorum ac demeritorum nostrorum; sed omnia hæc in Deo spiritualiter immutabiliterque consistunt. Facies enim Dei, est divini intellectus respectus ; auris Dei, est misericordia ejus subveniens ; aversio Dei, est detestatio mali ; conversio autem, approbatio boni. In quacumque die tribulor, id est corde affligor propter peccata commissa, vel tentamenta seu aspera mundi ac dæmonum, inclina ad me aurem tuam, id est, misericordiam tuam applica mihi, pietatis tuæ effectum declarando in me, id est, consolando animam tristem, roborando corpus infirmum, mitigando seu auferendo tribulationes quas patior, prout expedire noveris animæ meæ. In quacumque die, imo quacumque hora aut momento diei seu noctis, invocavero te, ex intimo mentis affectu tuam bonitatem precando, velociter, id est sine mora, sicut indigeo, exaudi me, ostendendo mihi lucem atque præsentiam miserationum tuarum, quemadmodum dicit Scriptura homini justo : Invocabis, et Dominus exaudiet ; clamabis, et dicet, Ecce adsum.
paras.en: [[101:3|Turn not away thy face|Non avertas faciem tuam]], that is, the regard of thy loving-kindness, [[101:3|from me|a me]], a vile and poor sinner, but a penitent one. Now the Prophet speaks of God in a human way, as though there were in God an ear and a face, and a turning away and a turning towards that were new or recent, according to the newness of our merits and demerits; but all these things are in God spiritually and unchangeably. For the face of God is the regard of the divine intellect; the ear of God is his mercy coming to our aid; God's turning away is his detestation of evil, and his turning towards, his approval of good. [[101:3|In the day when I am in trouble|In quacumque die tribulor]], that is, am afflicted in heart for the sins I have committed, or by the temptations or harsh assaults of the world and of the demons, [[101:3|incline thy ear to me|inclina ad me aurem tuam]], that is, apply thy mercy to me, showing forth in me the effect of thy loving-kindness: that is, by consoling my sad soul, strengthening my weak body, lessening or taking away the tribulations I suffer, as thou knowest to be expedient for my soul. [[101:3|In what day soever|In quacumque die]], nay, in whatever hour or moment of the day or night, [[101:3|I shall call upon thee|invocavero te]], beseeching thy goodness from the inmost affection of my mind, [[101:3|hear me|exaudi me]] [[101:3|speedily|velociter]], that is, without delay, as I need, by showing me the light and presence of thy mercies; as Scripture says to the just man: [[Is 58:9|Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall hear: thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am|Invocabis, et Dominus exaudiet ; clamabis, et dicet, Ecce adsum]].

paras.t: Ecce quam sæpe repetit sensum eumdem sub aliis verbis. Est enim consuetudo Scripturæ (præsertim in his quæ pertinent ad affectum), frequenter eamdem sententiam alio sermone resumere. Quod valde salubre est. Quoties namque verba affectuosa reiterantur, toties interna affectio renovatur, augetur, perficitur : quoniam una bona affectio, ad aliam similem præparat mentem. Et in repetitione affectus accenditur appetitus : sicque oratio exaudibilior redditur, quia tanto amplius grata est Deo, quanto ex calidiore manat affectu. Propter quod expedit eidem sancto desiderio immorari in prece, ipsum multoties revolvendo, nec pigre aut frigide ab ipso cessando. Omnino enim cavere debemus, ne ab oratione segniter desistamus ; sed ferventer inchoandum ac consummandum est omne opus divinum, præcipue laudatio Dei atque oratio.
paras.en: See how often he repeats the same sense in other words. For it is the custom of Scripture (especially in things that belong to the affections) often to take up the same thought again in other words. And this is very wholesome. For as often as words full of affection are repeated, so often is the inward affection renewed, increased and perfected, since one good affection prepares the mind for another like it. And in the repeating of an affection desire is kindled; and so prayer is made more fit to be heard, because it is the more pleasing to God the warmer the affection from which it flows. For this reason it is expedient to dwell in prayer on the same holy desire, turning it over many times, and not to leave off from it sluggishly or coldly. For we must take every care not to give up prayer listlessly; rather, every divine work, and above all the praise of God and prayer, is to be begun and finished with fervour.

paras.t: Demum ad exauditionem orationis tria requiruntur, secundum Augustinum : Primo, ut salubria petantur. Hoc enim est petere in nomine Jesu seu Salvatoris, ea rogare quæ spectant ad veram salutem. Propter quod Paulus exauditus non est, petens sibi auferri stimulum carnis. Stimulus etenim ille ei, tanquam viro exercitato ac strenuo militi, cooperabatur ad bonum, quoniam erat occasio meriti amplioris. Secundo, ut perseveranter oremus, quemadmodum ait Salvator : Oportet semper orare, et non deficere ; et Apostolus, Orantes omni tempore in spiritu, et in ipso vigilantes in omni instantia et obsecratione. Tertio, ut pro nobis ipsis precemur. Non enim semper exauditur pro aliis, propter incapacitatem eorum. Et sicut B. Thomas testatur, ad hoc ut homo exaudiatur pro alio, necessaria quodammodo est quædam plenitudo et exuberantia bonitatis, gratiæ, virtutis seu meriti in orante, quatenus scilicet de plenitudine ejus accipiat alter. Non tamen ob id cessare debemus, nos imperfecti, ab auxilio mutuæ orationis, quum scriptum sit : Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini. Sed qui pro alio orationem assumit, talem se coram Deo recte vivendo exhibeat, ut pro alio recipi fiat idoneus.
paras.en: Finally, according to Augustine, three things are required for a prayer to be heard. First, that wholesome things be asked; for to ask in the name of Jesus, that is, of the Saviour[[John 15:16||]], is to ask for the things that look to true salvation. For this reason Paul was not heard when he asked that the sting of the flesh be taken from him[[2 Cor 12:7||]] [the margin gives II Cor. vii, 7–9; the passage is 2 Cor. xii, 7–9]. For that sting, to him as a well-trained man and a valiant soldier, worked together unto good[[Rom 8:28||]], since it was the occasion of greater merit. Second, that we pray perseveringly, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 18:1|we ought always to pray and not to faint|Oportet semper orare, et non deficere]]; and the Apostle: [[Eph 6:18|praying at all times in the spirit: and in the same watching with all instance and supplication|Orantes omni tempore in spiritu, et in ipso vigilantes in omni instantia et obsecratione]]. Third, that we pray for ourselves. For one is not always heard for others, because of their incapacity. And, as Blessed Thomas testifies, for a man to be heard on behalf of another there is needed in some way a certain fullness and overflowing of goodness, grace, virtue or merit in him who prays, so that the other may receive of his fullness. Yet we who are imperfect must not on that account cease from the help of praying for one another, since it is written: [[Jas 5:16|pray one for another, that you may be saved|Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini]]. But let him who takes upon himself to pray for another so show himself before God by living rightly that he may become fit to be received on another's behalf.

paras.t: Merito autem, o Domine, ista precatus sum, Quia defecerunt, id est, velociter defluxerunt, sicut fumus dies mei, id est tempora quibus vixi. Quemadmodum enim fumus ascendit, ascendendoque deficit ; sic dies nostri crescendo ascendunt, et ascendendo fini propinquant. Unde in Job habetur : Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore ; transierunt quasi naves poma portantes. Et Jacobus ait : Quæ enim est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens ; deinceps exterminabitur. Vel, Defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei, id est, sine fructu et bonis operibus sunt consumpti, et quidquid vanitatis, voluptatis et impietatis in eis feci ac habui, cito pertransiit : juxta illud : Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut quid divitiarum jactantia contulit nobis? Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra et quasi nuntius præcurrens. Hinc quoque Apostolus peccatoribus conversis dicit : Quem fructum habuistis tunc in illis, in quibus nunc erubescitis? Nam finis illorum mors est. Vere enim inanes et vacui sunt dies pravorum ; plenitudinem vero sortiuntur dies justorum, secundum Ambrosium.
paras.en: Rightly, O Lord, have I prayed for these things, [[101:4|For my days are vanished|Quia defecerunt]], that is, have swiftly flowed away, [[101:4|like smoke|sicut fumus]]: [[101:4|my days|dies mei]], that is, the times in which I have lived. For as smoke rises, and in rising fails, so our days rise as they grow, and in rising draw near to their end. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 9:25|My days have been swifter than a post|Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore]]; [[Job 9:26|They have passed by as ships carrying fruits|transierunt quasi naves poma portantes]]. And James says: [[Jas 4:15|For what is your life? It is a vapour which appeareth for a little while and afterwards shall vanish away|Quæ enim est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens ; deinceps exterminabitur]]. Or: [[101:4|my days are vanished like smoke|Defecerunt sicut fumus dies mei]], that is, they have been spent without fruit and good works, and whatever vanity, pleasure and impiety I did and had in them has quickly passed away, according to the words: [[Wis 5:8|What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?|Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut quid divitiarum jactantia contulit nobis?]] [[Wis 5:9|All those things are passed away like a shadow, and like a post that runneth on|Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra et quasi nuntius præcurrens]]. Hence also the Apostle says to converted sinners: [[Rom 6:21|What fruit therefore had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of them is death.|Quem fructum habuistis tunc in illis, in quibus nunc erubescitis? Nam finis illorum mors est.]] For truly the days of the wicked are empty and void, while the days of the just are given fullness, according to Ambrose.

paras.t: Et ossa mea sicut cremium aruerunt. Cremium appellatur caro cremata seu frixa quæ remanet, pinguedine per ignem extracta. Cremium namque a cremando nomen accepit.
