Oceanus terram circumdans, est magnum quantitate, quoniam terram in mole vehementer nimis excedit, et spatiosum manibus, id est latum ad mensurandum; illic, id est in eo, sunt reptilia, id est pisces natando repentes, quorum non est numerus nobis cognitus, quamvis non sit nec esse possit in creaturis aliquid simpliciter infinitum. Animalia pusilla cum magnis, id est, pisces parvi et magni reperiuntur in mari.
paras.en: Next, and lastly, the holy Prophet brings in a ground for the praise of God from the ordering and beauty of the sea, the Ocean. [[103:25|So is this great sea|Hoc mare]]: the Ocean, which encircles the earth, is [[103:25|great|magnum]] in quantity, since it exceeds the earth in bulk very greatly indeed, [[103:25|which stretcheth wide its arms|et spatiosum manibus]], that is, broad to measure [*spatiosum manibus*, literally "spacious in hands", as if measured out by the hands]; [[103:25|there|illic]], that is, in it, [[103:25|are creeping things|sunt reptilia]], that is, fishes that creep along by swimming, [[103:25|without number|quorum non est numerus]] known to us; although there is not, nor can there be, anything among creatures that is simply infinite. [[103:25|Creatures little and great|Animalia pusilla cum magnis]]: that is, fishes small and great are found in the sea.

paras.t: Spiritualiter hoc mare magnum et spatiosum manibus, est præsens sæculum nequam, tribulationibus et amaritudinibus ac vitiis plenum. Illic reptilia quorum non est numerus, id est peccatores innumeri, terræ cordialiter adhærentes, vitiis involuti, et more pecorum in vanis sensibilibusque repentes: quorum nonnulli sunt magni in hoc mundo, alii vero parvi et ministri eorum.
paras.en: Spiritually, [[103:25|this great sea, which stretcheth wide its arms|hoc mare magnum et spatiosum manibus]] is this present wicked world, full of tribulations, bitternesses and vices. And [[103:25|there are creeping things without number|Illic reptilia quorum non est numerus]]: that is, sinners without number, cleaving to the earth with all their heart, wrapped up in vices, and creeping like cattle among vain things of sense; some of whom are great in this world, and others small, and their servants.

paras.t: Illic, id est in mari, naves pertransibunt cum nautis, diversa onera de loco et regno ad locum et regnum ferentes. Spiritualiter navis appellatur Ecclesia, quæ filios suos defert ad patriam regni cœlestis. Naves vero sunt particulares Ecclesiæ seu digni prælati, qui sibi commissos portant ad Christum. Hæ naves, Christo duce ac nauta, secure pertranseunt fluctuantem hunc mundum, tandemque perveniunt ad portum salutis æternæ.
paras.en: [[103:26|There|Illic]], that is, in the sea, [[103:26|the ships shall go|naves pertransibunt]] across with their sailors, carrying various cargoes from place to place and from kingdom to kingdom. Spiritually, the Church is called a ship, which carries her sons to the fatherland of the heavenly kingdom. And the ships are the particular Churches, or worthy prelates, who carry those entrusted to them to Christ. These ships, with Christ for their captain and pilot, pass safely across this tossing world, and at last come to the haven of eternal salvation.

paras.t: Deinde specialiter nominat unum animal magnum in mari exsistens. Draco iste, id est cetus, qui est piscis maximus: cujus (secundum Plinium) magnitudo est quatuor jugerum terræ. Unde Moyses ait: Creavit Deus cete grandia. Quem formasti, id est creasti primo per te, et produxisti exinde per causas secundas, ad illudendum ei, id est, ut huic draconi illudatur. Et tenetur hæc dictio, ut, consecutive, non causaliter. Non enim finaliter factus est ut ei illudatur; imo ad ostendendum potentiam Dei, et complendum ordinem universi formatus est. Sed ista illusio ejus formationem consequitur. Nam quamvis sit corpore et fortitudine maximus, multipliciter tamen, itemque facile ei (ut fertur) illuditur, scilicet per symphoniam quam audit libenter, et ob hoc ad ripam accedit; per gallinam quoque assatam, quæ sibi in pertica seu veru ostenditur, eamque insequitur, donec sibi aquæ deficiant et capiatur. Insuper, quum sit corpore magnus, multo indiget cibo, et pisces plurimos devorat: propter quod pisces eo viso ex naturali instinctu ad ripas confugiunt, ubi quum cetus insequendo pervenit, impingit in terram; et quoniam propter aquæ parvitatem non valet natare, ergo a piscatoribus occiditur, quia se movere non potest: sicque spe sua frustratus, illuditur.
paras.en: Then he names in particular one great animal that lives in the sea. [[103:26|This sea dragon|Draco iste]] [the Latin has only "this dragon"], that is, the whale, which is the greatest of fishes, whose size (according to Pliny) is four acres of land [*jugera*, the Roman measure of land]. Hence Moses says: [[Gen 1:21|God created the great whales|Creavit Deus cete grandia]]. [[103:26|which thou hast formed|Quem formasti]]: that is, didst create at first by thyself, and didst bring forth thereafter through secondary causes, [[103:26|to play therein|ad illudendum ei]]: that is, so that this dragon is made sport of [*ad illudendum ei* can mean "to play in it", as the Douay-Rheims takes it, or "for making sport of him", as Denis takes it]. And this word *so that* is taken consecutively, not causally [that is, as stating what follows from his making, not the end for which he was made]. For he was not made for the end that he might be made sport of; rather, he was formed to show the power of God and to complete the order of the universe. But this making sport of him follows upon his formation. For although he is the greatest in body and strength, yet he is made sport of in many ways, and easily too (so it is said): namely, by music, which he gladly listens to, and for this reason comes to the shore; by a roasted hen also, which is shown to him on a pole or spit, and he follows it until the water fails him and he is caught. Moreover, since he is great in body, he needs much food and devours very many fishes: for which reason the fishes, on seeing him, flee by natural instinct to the shores; and when the whale, pursuing them, gets there, he runs aground; and since for the shallowness of the water he cannot swim, he is killed by the fishermen, because he cannot move: and so, cheated of his hope, he is made sport of.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, draco iste est angelus apostata, serpens antiquus, diabolus et Satanas: quem Isaias Luciferum, Ezechiel Cherub, Job autem Leviathan nuncupat. Iste in cœlo per naturam factus est bonus, sed propria voluntate factus est malus et de cœlo prolapsus; et consecutive factus est et in hunc mundum retrusus, ut illudatur ei, quia a Christo, ab angelis sanctis, a fortibus Christi militibus, scilicet bonis hominibus, ei illuditur. Dum enim Christum devorare tentavit, victus et captus est, perdiditque quos in inferno tenebat. Sed et regno hujus mundi spoliatus est, cunctis ad Christum conversis. Angeli etiam sancti dum eum ab intento seu cœpto malo prohibent, homines quoque dum ejus tentationi resistunt, ei illudunt.
paras.en: Spiritually, [[103:26|This sea dragon|draco iste]] is the apostate angel, [[Apoc 12:9|that old serpent|serpens antiquus]], [[Apoc 12:9|the devil and Satan|diabolus et Satanas]]: whom Isaias calls Lucifer[[Is 14:12||]], Ezechiel a Cherub[[Ezech 28:14||]], and Job Leviathan[[Job 3:8||]]. He was made good by nature in heaven, but by his own will became evil and fell from heaven; and in consequence he was made, and thrust down into this world, so that he is made sport of: for he is made sport of by Christ, by the holy angels, and by the strong soldiers of Christ, that is, good men. For when he tried to devour Christ, he was overcome and caught[[Matt 4:1||]][[Luke 4:1||]] [the margin gives Matt. iv, 1–11 and Luke iv, 1–13, the temptation in the desert], and lost those whom he held in hell. And he was also stripped of the kingdom of this world, when all were converted to Christ. The holy angels too make sport of him when they keep him from the evil he intends or has begun, and men also when they resist his temptation.

paras.t: Omnia animantia et reptilia jam prædicta, a te expectant ut des illis escam in tempore, id est, expectare coguntur cibum a te, quoniam aliunde non habent, nisi a te, qui omnium bonorum causale principium es. Dante te illis quod exspectant, colligent necessaria sibi pro conservatione individui et speciei; aperiente te manum tuam, id est, potestate tua illis necessaria largiente, omnia implebuntur bonitate, id est bono sibi conveniente. (Spiritualiter, draco iste, id est diabolus, præstolatur sibi cibum dari a Deo, id est animas peccatrices, quas colligit, Domino eas damnante.)
paras.en: [[103:27|All|Omnia]] the living things and creeping things already mentioned [[103:27|expect of thee that thou give them food in season|a te expectant ut des illis escam in tempore]]: that is, they are bound to look for their food from thee, since they have it from nowhere else but from thee, who art the causal principle of all good things. [[103:28|What thou givest to them|Dante te illis]], what they look for, [[103:28|they shall gather up|colligent]], the things they need for the preservation of the individual and of the species; [[103:28|when thou openest thy hand|aperiente te manum tuam]], that is, when thy power bestows on them what they need, [[103:28|they shall all be filled with good|omnia implebuntur bonitate]], that is, with the good that suits them. (Spiritually, this dragon, that is, the devil, waits for food to be given him by God, that is, sinful souls, which he gathers up when the Lord condemns them.)

paras.t: Avertente autem te ab illis faciem tuam, id est providentiæ tuæ benignam ac largam præsentiam, turbabuntur, id est, inordinationem magnam famis, sitis, atque clamoris incurrent; auferes spiritum eorum, id est, animas irrationales ipsorum tolles a vita per alimentorum defectum, et deficient animalia ista a vita naturali, et in pulverem suum revertentur, id est, in præjacentem resolventur materiam: quæ pro majori parte terra censetur. Unumquodque enim in ea resolvitur, ex quibus componitur.
paras.en: [[103:29|But if thou turnest away|Avertente autem te]] from them [[103:29|thy face|faciem tuam]], that is, the kindly and bountiful presence of thy providence, [[103:29|they shall be troubled|turbabuntur]]: that is, they will fall into the great disorder of hunger, thirst and crying out; [[103:29|thou shalt take away their breath|auferes spiritum eorum]] [*spiritus*, "breath" or "spirit"], that is, thou wilt take their irrational souls from life by the failing of their food, [[103:29|and they shall fail|et deficient]], these animals, from natural life, [[103:29|and shall return to their dust|et in pulverem suum revertentur]], that is, they will be resolved into the underlying matter, which for the greater part is reckoned to be earth. For each thing is resolved into the things of which it is composed.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, dante Domino nobis sua divina charismata, congregamus spiritualia ejus dona; quumque manum suam aperuerit nobis, omnia viscera animarum nostrarum, divinorum participatione bonorum, videlicet caritate, sapientia, gratiaque replentur. Dum vero faciem suam avertit, id est, gratiam suam dispensative suspendit vel juste aufert, turbamur, id est, interius deordinamur, anxiamur, tristamur, seu in vitia multa illabimur, propriamque debilitatem experimur. Dum enim aufert spiritum nostrum, id est Spiritum Sanctum nobis divinitus datum, subtrahendo nobis consolationem ac munera ejus, deficimus et in pulverem nostrum revertimur, id est, rebus terrenis miserabiliter inhæremus, involvimur, implicamur.
paras.en: Spiritually, when the Lord gives us his divine gifts of grace, we gather up his spiritual gifts; and when he has opened his hand to us, all the inmost parts of our souls are filled with a share in divine goods, namely charity, wisdom and grace. But when he turns away his face, that is, suspends his grace by way of dispensation [that is, for a time and for a wise purpose of his own], or justly takes it away, we are troubled: that is, we are thrown into disorder within, we are anxious, we are sad, or we slip into many vices, and we feel our own weakness. For when he takes away our spirit, that is, the Holy Ghost given us from God, by withdrawing from us his consolation and his gifts, we fail and return to our dust: that is, we wretchedly cleave to earthly things, and are wrapped up and entangled in them.

paras.t: Emittes spiritum tuum, id est, potentiam tuam exercebis, et creabuntur, id est, reformabuntur quæ erant per mortem destructa: quia per potentiam Dei eadem specie revertuntur, non autem eadem numero, sicut opinabantur Platonici; interdum tamen miraculose redeunt eadem numero; et renovabis faciem, id est superficiem, terræ, producendo in ea nova jumenta, volatilia atque reptilia. Sumitur autem hoc verbum, Creabuntur, communiter pro productione seu generatione. Non enim proprie creantur hæc bruta, quum formæ eorum de potentia materiæ educantur, secundum philosophos atque theologos.
paras.en: [[103:30|Thou shalt send forth thy spirit|Emittes spiritum tuum]]: that is, thou wilt exercise thy power, [[103:30|and they shall be created|et creabuntur]], that is, the things destroyed by death will be formed again: for by the power of God they come back the same in species, but not the same in number [that is, not the very same individuals], as the Platonists supposed; though sometimes, by miracle, they do come back the same in number; [[103:30|and thou shalt renew the face|et renovabis faciem]], that is, the surface, [[103:30|of the earth|terræ]], by bringing forth on it new beasts, birds and creeping things. And this word *they shall be created* is taken loosely for production or generation. For these brute beasts are not created in the proper sense, since their forms are drawn out of the potency of matter, according to the philosophers and theologians.

paras.t: Possunt quoque hæc explanari de consummatione sæculi, et resurrectione hominum, innovationeque mundi, ut sit sensus: Avertente te faciem tuam, id est, quando eam averteris, scilicet circa tempus judicii, turbabuntur irrationalia animalia; auferes tunc spiritum eorum per ignem conflagrationis, vel ante, et deficient omnino, quia nunquam redibunt ad pristinum statum, nec secundum speciem quidem. Emittes spiritum tuum, et creabuntur: non utique animalia ista, sed homines creabuntur, id est, de novo resurgent; et renovabis faciem terræ, id est, terram in meliorem dignioremque qualitatem mutabis. Propter quod scriptum est: Novum cœlum et novam terram et promissa ipsius exspectamus.
paras.en: These words can also be explained of the end of the world, the resurrection of men and the renewal of the world, so that the sense is: [[103:29|But if thou turnest away thy face|Avertente te faciem tuam]], that is, when thou shalt turn it away, namely about the time of the judgment, [[103:29|they shall be troubled|turbabuntur]], the irrational animals; [[103:29|thou shalt take away|auferes]] then [[103:29|their breath|spiritum eorum]] by the fire of the great burning, or before it, [[103:29|and they shall fail|et deficient]] altogether, since they will never return to their former state, not even in species. [[103:30|Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created|Emittes spiritum tuum, et creabuntur]]: not, indeed, these animals, but men shall be created, that is, shall rise anew; [[103:30|and thou shalt renew the face of the earth|et renovabis faciem terræ]], that is, thou wilt change the earth into a better and worthier condition. For which reason it is written: [[2 Pet 3:13|we look for new heavens and a new earth according to his promises|Novum cœlum et novam terram et promissa ipsius exspectamus]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, o Domine, emittes spiritum tuum, id est, dona Spiritus Sancti nobis, ut speramus, infundes; et creabuntur, id est, corda munda in nobis consurgent; et renovabis faciem terræ, id est corpus nostrum, faciendo illud spiritui obedire, et honeste ac sobrie agere.
paras.en: Spiritually: O Lord, [[103:30|thou shalt send forth thy spirit|emittes spiritum tuum]], that is, thou wilt pour the gifts of the Holy Ghost into us, as we hope; [[103:30|and they shall be created|et creabuntur]], that is, clean hearts will arise in us; [[103:30|and thou shalt renew the face of the earth|et renovabis faciem terræ]], that is, our body, by making it obey the spirit and act uprightly and soberly.

paras.t: Patet ex isto, quod non semper in sacra Scriptura nomine spiritus Dei, designatur Spiritus Sanctus, qui est tertia in supersanctæ Trinitate Persona; sed interdum per spiritum Dei intelligitur ejus voluntas, imperium seu potestas.
paras.en: It is plain from this that the name *spirit of God* in holy Scripture does not always signify the Holy Ghost, who is the third Person in the most holy Trinity; but sometimes by the spirit of God is understood his will, command or power.

paras.t: Quoniam autem omnia præinducta idcirco commemorata sunt, quatenus ex contemplatione operum divinorum excitemur ad laudandum, honorandum et diligendum omnium Creatorem, ideo jam Propheta in laudem Dei affectuose ac pulchre prorumpit: Sit gloria Domini, id est excellentia, fama, honor et laus Creatoris, in sæculum, id est perpetuo, ita quod semper ab omnibus superexaltetur, laudetur, et honoretur. Lætabitur Dominus in operibus suis naturalibus et supernaturalibus, eo quod omnia sint optime facta. Non tamen est hoc ita intelligendum, quasi aliud a Deo sit ei causa lætandi aut ratio exsultandi, præsertim quum lætitia mentis divinæ sit æterna, incausata et independens. Sed dicitur Dominus in operibus suis lætari, in quantum in propria potestate lætatur, per quam omnia tam gloriose produxit, quemadmodum voluit.
paras.en: Now since all the things brought in above have been recalled so that, from contemplating the divine works, we may be roused to praise, honour and love the Creator of all, the Prophet now breaks out, with feeling and beautifully, into the praise of God: [[103:31|May the glory of the Lord|Sit gloria Domini]], that is, the excellence, fame, honour and praise of the Creator, [[103:31|endure for ever|in sæculum]], that is, perpetually, so that he may always be exalted above all, praised and honoured by all. [[103:31|the Lord shall rejoice in his works|Lætabitur Dominus in operibus suis]], natural and supernatural, because all things are made very well. Yet this is not to be understood as though anything other than God were a cause of his rejoicing or a reason for his exulting, especially since the joy of the divine mind is eternal, uncaused and independent. But the Lord is said to rejoice in his works inasmuch as he rejoices in his own power, by which he brought forth all things so gloriously, just as he willed.

paras.t: Qui respicit terram oculo sui imperii, et facit eam tremere: sicut videmus in terræ motu; qui tangit montes per fulgura, et fumigant, id est, fumum emittunt: ignis enim sulfureus potius fumigat quam accendit. Unde Job dicit: Qui commovet terram de loco suo, et columnæ ejus concutiuntur. Et Ecclesiasticus: Montes, inquit, simul et colles et fundamenta terræ, quum perspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur.
paras.en: [[103:32|He looketh upon the earth|Qui respicit terram]] with the eye of his command, [[103:32|and maketh it tremble|et facit eam tremere]], as we see in an earthquake; [[103:32|he troubleth the mountains|qui tangit montes]] [Latin *tangit*, "toucheth"] with lightnings, [[103:32|and they smoke|et fumigant]], that is, give out smoke: for sulphurous fire smokes rather than burns. Hence Job says: [[Job 9:6|Who shaketh the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble|Qui commovet terram de loco suo, et columnæ ejus concutiuntur]]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 16:19|The mountains also, and the hills|Montes]], he says, [[Ecclus 16:19|and the foundations of the earth: when God shall look upon them, they shall be shaken with trembling|simul et colles et fundamenta terræ, quum perspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur]].

paras.t: Nec obstat, quod dictum est supra, terram non inclinari in sæculum sæculi. Tremit namque et inclinatur, quoad aliquam sui partem; sed quantum ad se totam, manet semper in loco eodem. Similiter enim quod dictum est supra, Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam, non obviat quod alibi inducitur, Appendit terram super nihili. Dicitur namque appensa super nihili, quia quod infra eam est, non magis eam sustentat, quam si nihil exsisteret. Causa vero naturalis cur terra non inclinatur, sed manet in medio universi immobiliter stans, est, quia omnes partes ejus naturaliter tendunt ad centrum ipsius, secundum Philosophum.
paras.en: Nor does it stand in the way that it was said above that the earth [[103:5|shall not be moved for ever and ever|non inclinari in sæculum sæculi]]. For it trembles and is moved in some part of itself; but as regards its whole self it remains always in the same place. So likewise what was said above, [[103:5|Who hast founded the earth upon its own bases|Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam]], is not against what is brought in elsewhere: He [[Job 26:7|hangeth the earth upon nothing|Appendit terram super nihili]]. For it is said to be hung upon nothing because what is beneath it holds it up no more than if nothing were there. And the natural cause why the earth is not moved, but stays immovably in the middle of the universe, is that all its parts tend by nature to its centre, according to the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle].

paras.t: Mystice, respicit Deus oculo pietatis terram, id est corda humana, et facit eam tremere, ex consideratione districti judicii Dei atque pœnarum inferni, prout Job inquit: Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum, et pondus ejus ferre non potui. Tangit etiam montes, id est, gratiose illuminat magnos atque perfectos, et fumigant, id est, lacrimis fluunt desiderio exsistendi cum Christo. Vel, Tangit montes, id est superbos, et fumigant, id est, lacrimas fundunt pro remissione peccati. — Ad litteram, respexit Deus terram, in qua erat primitiva Ecclesia, fecitque eam tremere motu locali. Tetigit montes, id est Apostolos, aliosque cum eis collectos; et fumigaverunt, id est, ex plenitudine Spiritus Sancti fumum verborum ignitorum effuderunt, quando accidit illud in Actis: Quum orassent, motus est locus in quo erant; et repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto, et loquebantur verbum Dei cum fiducia. Similiter recitatur in Actis de Paulo et Sila, qui quum vincti et incarcerati fuissent, in ipsa nocte lumen cœleste refulsit in carcere, et fundamenta carceris mota sunt, ostiaque ipsius aperta. Paulus vero et Silas Dominum laudabant.
paras.en: Mystically, God [[103:32|looketh upon|respicit]] with the eye of loving-kindness [[103:32|the earth|terram]], that is, human hearts, [[103:32|and maketh it tremble|et facit eam tremere]], through the thought of God's strict judgment and of the pains of hell; as Job says: [[Job 31:23|For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and his weight I was unable to bear|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum, et pondus ejus ferre non potui]]. [[103:32|he troubleth the mountains|Tangit etiam montes]] too, that is, he graciously enlightens the great and perfect, [[103:32|and they smoke|et fumigant]], that is, they flow with tears in their longing to be with Christ. Or: [[103:32|he troubleth the mountains|Tangit montes]], that is, the proud, [[103:32|and they smoke|et fumigant]], that is, they shed tears for the forgiveness of their sin. — Literally: God looked upon the earth in which the primitive Church was, and made it tremble with a movement of the place. He touched the mountains, that is, the Apostles and the others gathered with them; and they smoked, that is, out of the fullness of the Holy Ghost they poured forth the smoke of fiery words, when there happened what is told in the Acts: [[Acts 4:31|And when they had prayed, the place was moved wherein they were assembled: and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost: and they spoke the word of God with confidence|Quum orassent, motus est locus in quo erant; et repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto, et loquebantur verbum Dei cum fiducia]]. In the same way it is told in the Acts of Paul and Silas, that when they had been bound and put in prison, in that very night a heavenly light shone in the prison [the light is not in Acts 16; compare Acts 12:7, of Peter in prison], and the foundations of the prison were shaken, and its doors opened[[Acts 16:26||]]. And Paul and Silas were praising the Lord[[Acts 16:25||]].

paras.t: Cantabo Domino, id est, sacrificium laudis offeram Deo, in vita mea: quia non mortui laudabunt Dominum. Propter quod scriptum est: A mortuo quasi nihil perit confessio; confiteberis vivens et sanus. Psallam Deo meo, omnium quidem Deo, sed specialiter Deo meo, propter singularem misericordiam ejus circa me, quamdiu sum, id est indesinenter: quia qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Non ergo cantabo et psallam Creatori meo solum in vita præsenti, sed etiam in vita futura. Psallam enim ei in vita naturæ, in vita gratiæ, in vita gloriæ, animo prompto atque ardenti, quemadmodum Ecclesiasticus monet: Et nunc in omni corde et ore collaudate et benedicite nomen Domini.
paras.en: [[103:33|I will sing to the Lord|Cantabo Domino]], that is, I will offer the sacrifice of praise to God, [[103:33|as long as I live|in vita mea]]: because [[Ps 113:25|The dead shall not praise|non mortui laudabunt]] the Lord [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 17 (Hebr.), that is, Ps 115:17 in the Hebrew count; in the Vulgate it is Ps 113:25]. For which reason it is written: [[Ecclus 17:26|Praise perisheth from the dead as nothing|A mortuo quasi nihil perit confessio]]; [[Ecclus 17:27|whilst thou art alive and in health thou shalt give thanks|confiteberis vivens et sanus]]. [[103:33|I will sing praise to my God|Psallam Deo meo]]: the God of all, indeed, but especially my God, because of his singular mercy towards me; [[103:33|while I have my being|quamdiu sum]], that is, without ceasing: because [[Matt 10:22|he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved|qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]][[Matt 24:13||]]. So I will sing and sing praise to my Creator not only in the present life, but also in the life to come. For I will sing praise to him in the life of nature, in the life of grace, in the life of glory, with a ready and ardent mind, as Ecclesiasticus urges: [[Ecclus 39:41|Now therefore with the whole heart and mouth praise ye him, and bless the name of the Lord|Et nunc in omni corde et ore collaudate et benedicite nomen Domini]].

paras.t: Jucundum sit ei eloquium meum, id est, Deo complaceat, et ex vera caritate ac sancta devotione procedat. Jucundum est Deo eorum eloquium, de quibus per Salomonem testatur: Deliciæ meæ esse cum filiis hominum: non utique cum omnibus filiis hominum, quoniam virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus; sed cum humilibus et simplicibus, de quibus in Proverbiis dicitur, Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Jucunda est Deo laudatio ejus qui cum jucunditate spirituali cantat et psallit. Ego vero delectabor in Domino, ex contemplatione et dilectione bonitatis ac beneficiorum ipsius. Hæc est delectatio sancta ac nobilis, quam qui gustaverit, immundas delectationes facile vilipendit.
paras.en: [[103:34|Let my speech be acceptable to him|Jucundum sit ei eloquium meum]]: that is, may it please God, and proceed from true charity and holy devotion. Acceptable to God is the speech of those of whom he bears witness through Solomon: [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|Deliciæ meæ esse cum filiis hominum]]: not indeed with all the children of men, since [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]; but with the humble and simple, of whom it is said in the Proverbs: [[Prov 3:32|his communication is with the simple|Cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. Acceptable [*jucunda*, "pleasant", as *jucundum* in the verse] to God is the praise of him who sings and sings praise with spiritual gladness. [[103:34|but I will take delight in the Lord|Ego vero delectabor in Domino]], from contemplating and loving his goodness and his benefits. This is a holy and noble delight; whoever has tasted it easily despises unclean delights.

paras.t: Deficiant peccatores a terra, etc. Versiculus iste primo exponi potest in malo, ut sit vox hominis pro Deo zelantis, atque divinæ justitiæ se conformantis, vel quid futurum sit prænuntiantis; eritque sensus: Deficiant peccatores obstinati in vitiis a terra præsenti, ita quod moriantur, ne noceant justis, et a terra viventium, ne felicitentur: quemadmodum scriptum est, Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei; et iniqui, ita ut non sint in vita gratiæ aut gloriæ, sed solum in vita naturæ et pœnæ. Et hoc modo scriptum est, Sic pereant inimici tui, Domine; et alibi, Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus. Secundo exponitur in bono: Deficiant peccatores a terra (id est, a conversatione et affectione terrena desistant), et iniqui, ita ut non sint quales fuerunt, nec sint quod erant per culpam et propriam voluntatem, sed maneant quod erant per essentiam et gratiam. Unde in Proverbiis dicitur: Vertite impios, et non erunt.
paras.en: [[103:35|Let sinners be consumed out of the earth|Deficiant peccatores a terra]], etc. This little verse can first be expounded in the bad sense, so that it is the voice of a man zealous for God and conforming himself to the divine justice, or foretelling what is to come; and the sense will be: [[103:35|Let sinners be consumed|Deficiant peccatores]] who are obstinate in vices, [[103:35|out of the earth|a terra]] of the present, so that they die, lest they harm the just, and out of the land of the living, lest they be made happy: as it is written, Let the wicked be taken away, so that [[Is 26:10|he shall not see the glory of the Lord|ne videat gloriam Dei]] [Denis quotes the older reading *Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei*; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "he shall not see the glory of the Lord"]; [[103:35|and the unjust, so that they be no more|et iniqui, ita ut non sint]] in the life of grace or of glory, but only in the life of nature and of punishment. And in this way it is written: [[Judg 5:31|So let all thy enemies perish, O Lord|Sic pereant inimici tui, Domine]]; and elsewhere: [[Eccles 8:13|let it not be well with the wicked, neither let his days be prolonged|Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus]]. Secondly, it is expounded in the good sense: [[103:35|Let sinners be consumed out of the earth|Deficiant peccatores a terra]] (that is, let them leave off earthly ways and earthly affection), [[103:35|and the unjust, so that they be no more|et iniqui, ita ut non sint]] such as they were, nor be what they were through sin and their own will, but remain what they were through their being and through grace. Hence it is said in the Proverbs: [[Prov 12:7|Turn the wicked, and they shall not be|Vertite impios, et non erunt]].

paras.t: Benedic anima mea Domino, Deum laudando de omnibus magnificentiis suis jam enarratis.
paras.en: [[103:35|O my soul, bless thou the Lord|Benedic anima mea Domino]], praising God for all his magnificent works now recounted.

paras.t: Ecce psalmum spirituali lætitia plenum audivimus: in quo ostenditur, sanctum David non solum fuisse magnum theologum, sed etiam excellentem philosophum: quorum utrumque sibi ex divina inspiratione concessum est. Debemus ergo hunc psalmum cum omni gratiarum actione et hilaritate mentali Domino decantare, commemorando beneficia ejus non segni torpentique corde. Præcipue vero in principio atque in fine, delectabilis valdeque dulcis est psalmus hic nobilis. Et conandum est nobis, ut impleamus quæ dicimus in fine psalmi præsentis: Cantabo Domino in vita mea, psallam Deo meo quamdiu sum. Debet etiam anima nostra in divino timore proficere, ex consideratione potestatis divinæ, quæ respicit terram, et facit eam tremere. Ideo namque ait Scriptura: Magnus es tu, Domine, et magnum nomen tuum in fortitudine: quis non timebit te, o Rex gentium?
paras.en: See, we have heard a psalm full of spiritual joy, in which it is shown that holy David was not only a great theologian but also an excellent philosopher; both of which were granted him by divine inspiration. We ought therefore to sing this psalm to the Lord with all thanksgiving and gladness of mind, recalling his benefits with no slow and sluggish heart. Especially at the beginning and at the end this noble psalm is delightful and very sweet. And we must strive to fulfil what we say at the end of this psalm: [[103:33|I will sing to the Lord as long as I live: I will sing praise to my God while I have my being|Cantabo Domino in vita mea, psallam Deo meo quamdiu sum]]. Our soul ought also to advance in the fear of God, from considering the divine power which [[103:32|looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble|respicit terram, et facit eam tremere]]. For this is why the Scripture says: [[Jer 10:6|thou art great, and great is thy name in might|Magnus es tu, Domine, et magnum nomen tuum in fortitudine]]: [[Jer 10:7|Who shall not fear thee, O king of nations?|quis non timebit te, o Rex gentium?]]

paras.t: Precatio. Deus, qui respicis terram et facis eam tremere, timorem tuum salutarem cordibus nostris immitte: ut relictis malis quibus te graviter offendimus, per spiritum tuum renovata in nobis facie peccati, sancta tibi devotione adhæreamus, et in jucunditate perceptæ salutis semper tibi psallamus.
paras.en: Prayer. O God, who lookest upon the earth and makest it tremble, send thy saving fear into our hearts: that, forsaking the evils by which we have grievously offended thee, and the face of sin being renewed in us by thy spirit, we may cleave to thee with holy devotion, and in the joy of the salvation we have received may ever sing praise to thee.

104.title: ELUCIDATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI QUARTI : CONFITEMINI DOMINO, ET INVOCATE NOMEN EJUS.
104.title_en: Explanation of the hundred and fourth psalm: Give glory to the Lord, and call upon his name.

paras.t: Hujus psalmi titulus talis est : Alleluia, quod significat, Laudate Dominum : et sunt duæ dictiones, quoniam in Hebræo HALELU significat, Laudate ; YAH autem, Deum. Sunt autem viginti psalmi hoc titulo prænotati, quorum iste est primus : nec invenitur aliquis Sanctorum hoc divinum nomen scripsisse ante auctorem psalmi præsentis. Est autem hoc nomen, Alleluia, spirituale, virtuosum ac mysticum, ineffabilem Beatorum lætitiam designans magis quam exprimens. Propter quod nulla lingua mutare præsumpsit hoc nomen. Psalmus itaque præsens ita intitulatur, quia ad laudem Dei invitat. Recolit namque beneficia Dei populo Israelitico præstita temporibus Abrahæ, Isaac, Jacob, Moysis, et Josue. Et non est difficultas ad intelligendum sensum litteralem hujus psalmi : multa tamen in eo spiritualiter atque subtiliter intelligi possunt.
paras.en: The title of this psalm is as follows: *Alleluia*, which means, Praise ye the Lord; and it is two words, since in Hebrew HALELU means "Praise ye", and YAH "God". Now there are twenty psalms headed with this title, of which this is the first; nor is any of the Saints found to have written this divine name before the author of the present psalm. This name, *Alleluia*, is spiritual, full of power and mystical, signifying rather than expressing the unspeakable joy of the Blessed. For this reason no language has presumed to change this name. The present psalm, then, is so entitled because it invites to the praise of God. For it recalls the benefits of God bestowed on the people of Israel in the times of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses and Josue. And there is no difficulty in understanding the literal sense of this psalm; yet many things in it can be understood spiritually and subtly.

paras.t: Ait ergo : Confitemini Domino, confessione laudis, id est, Deum laudate, et invocate nomen ejus, id est, ex intimo cordis affectu et mente collecta eum orate. Et hic est ordo pulcherrimus in homine justo. Justus enim (quia in eo speciosa est laus Creatoris) dum Deum vult invocare, debet ipsum primo laudare, et exaudietur. Unde superius dictum est : Laudans invocabo Dominum, et ab inimicis meis salvus ero. Injustus vero primo oret, ut dignus fiat Deum laudare. Annuntiate inter gentes opera ejus, id est, aliis magnalia Dei narrate, consulendo proximorum saluti secundum exigentiam caritatis fraternæ. Propter quod in Tobia legitur : Coram omnibus viventibus confitemini ei.
paras.en: He says, then: [[104:1|Give glory to the Lord|Confitemini Domino]] with the confession of praise [that is, *confitemini* taken as confessing God's praise, not one's sins], that is, praise God, [[104:1|and call upon his name|et invocate nomen ejus]], that is, pray to him from the inmost affection of the heart and with a recollected mind. And this is the most beautiful order in a just man. For the just man (since in him the praise of the Creator is seemly[[Ecclus 15:9||]]), when he wishes to call upon God, ought first to praise him, and he will be heard. Hence it was said above: [[Ps 17:4|Praising, I will call upon the Lord: and I shall be saved from my enemies|Laudans invocabo Dominum, et ab inimicis meis salvus ero]]. But the unjust man should first pray, that he may become worthy to praise God. [[104:1|declare his deeds among the Gentiles|Annuntiate inter gentes opera ejus]], that is, tell others of the great works of God, looking to the salvation of your neighbours as fraternal charity requires. For this reason we read in Tobias: [[Tob 12:6|give glory to him in the sight of all that live|Coram omnibus viventibus confitemini ei]].

paras.t: Cantate ei laude vocali, et psallite ei operatione fideli ; narrate coram aliis prædicando, cum aliis psallendo, vel seorsum coram Deo, omnia mirabilia ejus quæ scripta sunt, vel omnia in generali, seu quædam ex omnibus. Sic enim omnia valent narrari, juxta illud Ecclesiastici : Nonne Dominus enarrare fecit sanctos suos omnia mirabilia sua ? Sic quoque in Actibus Paulus ait : Non subterfugi, quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei. Non autem enarrare valemus omnia mirabilia Dei in speciali, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Quis sufficiet enarrare opera ejus ?
paras.en: [[104:2|Sing to him|Cantate ei]] with vocal praise, [[104:2|yea sing praises to him|et psallite ei]] [*psallite*, properly to sing to the psaltery, which the Fathers take of good works] with faithful working; [[104:2|relate|narrate]] before others by preaching, with others by singing psalms, or apart before God, [[104:2|all his wondrous works|omnia mirabilia ejus]] that are written, or all of them in general, or some out of all. For in this way all of them can be related, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 42:17|Hath not the Lord made the saints to declare all his wonderful works|Nonne Dominus enarrare fecit sanctos suos omnia mirabilia sua]]? [the margin gives Eccli. xvii, 17; the words are Ecclus 42:17] So too Paul says in the Acts: [[Acts 20:27|For I have not spread to declare unto you all, the counsel of God|Non subterfugi, quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei]]. But we are not able to relate all the wonders of God one by one, as is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:2|Who is able to declare his works?|Quis sufficiet enarrare opera ejus ?]]

paras.t: Laudamini in nomine sancto ejus, id est, non in vobis, sed in Domino laudari optate, videlicet ut bona de quibus laudamini, non vobis, sed Domino adscribantur. Sic etiam vivite, ut mereamini in Deo laudari. Quidam vero in se ipsis laudantur, et fallaciter commendantur, atque interdum laudibus talibus delectantur : de quibus scriptum est, Popule meus, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt. Non ergo delectemur inaniter dum laudamur, recolentes illud Ecclesiastici : In die honoris tui non extollaris. Denique licitum est, interdum se ipsum laudare et laudem recipere, propter Dei honorem augendum et proximorum ædificationem. Sic enim sancti Apostoli et Prophetæ, virtutes et gratias suas copiose describunt. Hoc autem perfectis atque prælatis præcipue licet, qui in hoc, divino instinctu reguntur ; ceteris vero non expedit, eo quod scriptum sit, Non te justifices ante Deum.
paras.en: [[104:3|Glory ye in his holy name|Laudamini in nomine sancto ejus]] [*laudamini*, literally "be ye praised", which Denis goes on to explain], that is, desire to be praised not in yourselves but in the Lord, namely so that the good things for which you are praised may be ascribed not to you but to the Lord. Live also in such a way that you may deserve to be praised in God. But some are praised in themselves, and commended falsely, and at times take delight in such praises: of whom it is written, [[Is 3:12|O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee|Popule meus, qui te beatum dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt]]. Let us not, then, take an idle delight when we are praised, recalling that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:4|be not exalted in the day of thy honour|In die honoris tui non extollaris]] [the margin gives Eccli. xi, 1; the words are in v. 4]. Lastly, it is lawful at times to praise oneself and to receive praise, for the increase of God's honour and the edification of one's neighbours. For so the holy Apostles and Prophets describe their virtues and graces at length. But this is allowed chiefly to the perfect and to prelates, who in this are guided by a divine prompting; for the rest it is not expedient, since it is written: [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God|Non te justifices ante Deum]].

paras.t: Sed quæri potest, quomodo liceat hominem in hac vita laudare, quum ab Ecclesiastico dictum sit : Ante mortem non laudes hominem quemquam. Et respondendum, quod nullus in se ipso laudandus est, sed solum in Domino ; nec expedit de lege communi quemquam laudare, nisi ut provocetur ad meliora, vel ob similem rationabilem et quasi necessariam causam : præsertim tamen periculosum videtur imperfectos laudare, ne extollantur. Videmus tamen quam ubertim Apostolus in suis epistolis discipulos suos commendet. Auctoritas autem libri Ecclesiastici non cogit simpliciter, quoniam liber iste non est in canone : non autem compellimur absolute consentire, nisi libris canonicis, sicut in epistola ad Hieronymum asserit Augustinus : et istud Thomas dicit. Verumtamen non est auctoritas libri illius parvipendenda, aut cito neganda.
paras.en: But it may be asked how it is lawful to praise a man in this life, since it is said by Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:30|Praise not any man before death|Ante mortem non laudes hominem quemquam]] [the margin gives Ibid. vi, 30; the words are Ecclus 11:30]. And the answer must be that no one is to be praised in himself, but only in the Lord; nor by the common rule is it expedient to praise anyone, except that he may be spurred on to better things, or for some like reasonable and as it were necessary cause: yet it seems especially dangerous to praise the imperfect, lest they be lifted up. Still, we see how abundantly the Apostle commends his disciples in his epistles. Moreover, the authority of the book of Ecclesiasticus does not bind absolutely, since that book is not in the canon [Denis follows the opinion, common in his day after Jerome, that Ecclesiasticus stood outside the Hebrew canon; the Council of Trent later defined it canonical]: for we are not compelled to assent absolutely save to the canonical books, as Augustine affirms in his letter to Jerome; and Thomas says the same. Nevertheless the authority of that book is not to be thought little of, or quickly denied.

paras.t: Lætetur spirituali lætitia de bona atque salubri sua occupatione, cor quærentium Dominum fide et opere, quatenus eum clarius contemplentur, ferventius diligant, perfectiusque honorent. Omne equidem opus bonum lætanter agendum est.
paras.en: [[104:3|let the heart of them rejoice|Lætetur]] with spiritual joy in their good and wholesome occupation, [[104:3|that seek the Lord|cor quærentium Dominum]] by faith and works, so that they may contemplate him more clearly, love him more fervently and honour him more perfectly. Indeed every good work is to be done joyfully.

paras.t: Quærite Dominum modo prædicto, et confirmamini, id est, quærendo nolite deficere, fatigari, pusillanimes fieri. Quamvis enim Deum perfecte nequeatis attingere, neque per speciem in hac vita conspicere, tamen quo perseverantius quæritur, eo copiosius invenitur, gratia major infunditur, fides illuminatur, spes roboratur, amor succenditur. Hinc enim Christus in Evangelio : Quærite, inquit, et invenietis. Omnis enim qui quærit, invenit. Et secundo Paralipomenon ait Scriptura : Vos autem confortamini, et non dissolvantur manus vestræ : erit enim merces operi vestro. Quid vero est, quærere Deum et confortari, nisi quod Dominus jubet, Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro ? Quærite faciem ejus semper : id est, Dei notitiam incessanter appetite, ne vobis contingat quod apud Isaiam ait Altissimus : Captivus ductus est populus meus, quia non habuit scientiam : propterea dilatavit infernus animam suam. Vel, Quærite faciem ejus semper, id est, in omni opere Dei præsentiam finaliter adipisci optate, nec propter aliud præmium juste vivatis. Oportet namque, ut intentio cordis feratur semper in ultimum finem. Propter quod dicit Salvator : Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex, id est intentio recta, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit ; si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit.
paras.en: [[104:4|Seek ye the Lord|Quærite Dominum]] in the way just described, [[104:4|and be strengthened|et confirmamini]], that is, in seeking do not fail, grow weary or become faint-hearted. For although you cannot reach God perfectly, nor behold him by sight in this life, yet the more perseveringly he is sought, the more abundantly he is found: greater grace is poured in, faith is enlightened, hope strengthened, love kindled. Hence Christ says in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:9|seek, and you shall find|Quærite, inquit, et invenietis]]. For every one [[Luke 11:10|that seeketh findeth|qui quærit, invenit]]. And in the second book of Paralipomenon the Scripture says: [[2 Par 15:7|Do you therefore take courage, and let not your hands be weakened: for there shall be a reward for your work|Vos autem confortamini, et non dissolvantur manus vestræ : erit enim merces operi vestro]]. And what is it to seek God and to be strengthened, but what the Lord commands: [[Joel 2:12|Be converted to me with all your heart|Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro]]? [[104:4|seek his face evermore|Quærite faciem ejus semper]]: that is, desire without ceasing the knowledge of God, lest there befall you what the Most High says in Isaias: [[Is 5:13|Therefore is my people led away captive, because they had not knowledge|Captivus ductus est populus meus, quia non habuit scientiam]]: [[Is 5:14|Therefore hath hell enlarged her soul|propterea dilatavit infernus animam suam]]. Or, [[104:4|seek his face evermore|Quærite faciem ejus semper]], that is, in every work desire finally to attain to the presence of God, and do not live justly for the sake of any other reward. For the intention of the heart must always be borne towards the last end. For this reason the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:22|If thy eye be single|Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex]], that is, a right intention, [[Matt 6:22|thy whole body shall be lightsome|totum corpus tuum lucidum erit]]; [[Matt 6:23|But if thy eye be evil thy whole body shall be darksome|si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit]].

paras.t: Mementote mirabilium ejus quæ fecit cum Patriarchis veteris Testamenti : mementote, inquam, horum mirabilium, quæ sunt prodigia ejus, id est opera mira procul a digito facta, quia causa eorum est voluntas divina nobis incognita, et judicia oris ejus, id est effectus divinæ justitiæ, a Deo ad Moysen annuntiati. Judicia Dei dicuntur, vel opera divinæ justitiæ, vel divina præcepta atque consilia, quæ Deus judicat esse justa ; vel censuræ seu conceptiones, quas mens divina intra se de rebus pronuntiat.
paras.en: [[104:5|Remember his marvellous works which he hath done|Mementote mirabilium ejus quæ fecit]] with the Patriarchs of the Old Testament: remember, I say, these marvellous works, which are [[104:5|his wonders|prodigia ejus]], that is, wonderful works done far from the finger [that is, beyond the reach of any created hand; the phrase seems to play on *prodigia*, as if from *procul a digito*], because their cause is the divine will, unknown to us, [[104:5|and the judgments of his mouth|et judicia oris ejus]], that is, the effects of divine justice, announced by God to Moses. The judgments of God are the name given either to the works of divine justice, or to the divine precepts and counsels, which God judges to be just; or to the sentences or conceptions which the divine mind pronounces within itself concerning things.

paras.t: Horum mementote, semen Abraham, id est filii Abrahæ patriarchæ, servi ejus : quia Abraham servus Dei fuit ; et vos, o filii Jacob patriarchæ, electi ejus, id est, qui fuit electus a Deo : quemadmodum Dominus ait, Jacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui. Hoc quoque quod dicitur, Servi, et, Electi, referri potest ad semen et filios, quia et ipsi fuerunt servi electique Dei. Propter quod in Deuteronomio Moyses dicit filiis Israel : En Domini Dei tui cœlum est et cœli cœlorum ; et tamen patribus vestris conglutinatus est Dominus, et elegit eos, amavitque semen eorum post eos.
paras.en: Remember these things, [[104:6|O ye seed of Abraham|semen Abraham]], that is, the sons of the patriarch Abraham, [[104:6|his servant|servi ejus]]: for Abraham was the servant of God; and you, [[104:6|ye sons of Jacob|filii Jacob]] the patriarch, [[104:6|his chosen|electi ejus]], that is, who was chosen by God, as the Lord says: [[Mal 1:2|I have loved Jacob|Jacob dilexi]], [[Mal 1:3|But have hated Esau|Esau autem odio habui]]. This also, that is said, "servant" and "chosen", can be referred to the seed and the sons, since they too were servants and chosen ones of God [in the Latin *servi* and *electi* can be either singular genitive or plural nominative]. For this reason Moses says to the sons of Israel in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 10:14|Behold heaven is the Lord's thy God, and the heaven of heaven|En Domini Dei tui cœlum est et cœli cœlorum]]; [[Deut 10:15|And yet the Lord hath been closely joined to thy fathers, and loved them and chose their seed after them|et tamen patribus vestris conglutinatus est Dominus, et elegit eos, amavitque semen eorum post eos]].

paras.t: Ipse Dominus Deus noster. Aliis enim nationibus ad idololatriam se vertentibus, permansit fides et cultus Dei in populo Judæorum. Unde scriptum est : Qui fecit stellas, hic est Deus noster. In universa terra judicia ejus, id est, effectus divinæ justitiæ ad omnes habitatores terræ extenduntur, ita quod omnes judicantur a Deo, recipiendo quod meruerunt, quemadmodum in Ezechiele protestatur : Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo. Vel dicuntur judicia Dei in universa terra, quia judicia ista quæ exercuit circa Pharaonem, et Ægyptios atque Chananæos, per totum mundum sunt divulgata. Propterea namque Dominus ait ad Pharaonem : Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, et narretur nomen meum in omni terra.
paras.en: [[104:7|He is the Lord our God|Ipse Dominus Deus noster]]. For while the other nations turned to idolatry, the faith and worship of God remained in the people of the Jews. Hence it is written: He that made the stars[[Bar 3:35||]], [[Bar 3:36|This is our God|hic est Deus noster]]. [[104:7|his judgments are in all the earth|In universa terra judicia ejus]], that is, the effects of divine justice extend to all the inhabitants of the earth, so that all are judged by God, receiving what they have deserved, as he declares in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:30|Therefore will I judge every man according to his ways|Unumquemque juxta vias suas judicabo]]. Or the judgments of God are said to be in all the earth because those judgments which he executed upon Pharao, the Egyptians and the Chanaanites were spread abroad through the whole world. For this is why the Lord says to Pharao: [[Ex 9:16|therefore have I raised thee, that I may shew my power in thee, and my name may be spoken of throughout all the earth|Idcirco posui te, ut ostendam in te fortitudinem meam, et narretur nomen meum in omni terra]].

paras.t: Memor fuit Deus in sæculum testamenti sui, id est promissionis seu pacti vel legis, et verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes, id est omnes generationes. Istud est vetus testamentum Abrahæ datum, et omnibus posteris ejus præceptum. Dicitur autem Deus memor fuisse hujus testamenti, quia frequenter approbavit, reiteravitque illud. Primo enim mandavit id Abrahæ, sicut subjungitur : Quod disposuit ad Abraham, et confirmavit hoc filio ejus cum juramento, affirmans se impleturum quod Abrahæ repromisit : ideo additur, et juramenti sui ad Isaac facti, subaudi, memor fuit. Et statuit illud testamentum seu verbum Jacob filio Isaac in præceptum, præcipiendo ut firmiter crederet illud implendum ; et Israel, id est Jacob prædicto, qui dictus est Israel, id est videns Deum, quia angelum Dei vidit : propter quod ait, Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem ; in testamentum æternum, id est semper mansurum, quantum ad fructum, seu quantum ad præcepta moralia.
paras.en: [[104:8|He hath remembered his covenant for ever|Memor fuit Deus in sæculum testamenti sui]], that is, his promise, or pact, or law, [[104:8|the word which he commanded to a thousand generations|et verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes]], that is, all generations. This is the old covenant given to Abraham[[Gen 17:2||]] and enjoined on all his posterity. God is said to have remembered this covenant because he often ratified it and renewed it. For first he enjoined it on Abraham, as is added: [[104:9|Which he made to Abraham|Quod disposuit ad Abraham]]; and he confirmed it to his son with an oath, affirming that he would fulfil what he had promised to Abraham[[Gen 26:3||]]: therefore it is added, [[104:9|and his oath to Isaac|et juramenti sui ad Isaac]] made to him, understand: he hath remembered. [[104:10|And he appointed the same|Et statuit illud]] covenant or word to Jacob the son of Isaac [[104:10|for a law|in præceptum]][[Gen 28:13||]] [the margin gives Gen. xxvi, 13-15, which does not fit; God's promise to Jacob is Gen 28:13-15], commanding him to believe firmly that it would be fulfilled; [[104:10|and to Israel|et Israel]], that is, to the aforesaid Jacob, who was called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]], that is, "seeing God", because he saw the angel of God: for which reason he says, [[Gen 32:30|I have seen God face to face|Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem]]; [[104:10|for an everlasting testament|in testamentum æternum]], that is, one that would always abide, as to its fruit, or as to the moral precepts.

paras.t: De hoc testamento ad Abraham disposito, scribitur in Genesi : Benedicam tibi, et multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas cœli ; et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes tribus terræ. Et alibi ait ad Abraham : In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen. Promisit quoque (sicut in Genesi scribitur) Isaac, quod terram Chanaan daret semini suo.
paras.en: Of this covenant made to Abraham it is written in Genesis: [[Gen 22:17|I will bless thee, and I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven|Benedicam tibi, et multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas cœli]]; and [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|in semine tuo omnes tribus terræ]] [Denis has *tribus*, "tribes", where Gen 22:18 has *gentes*, "nations"; *tribus* is the word of Gen 28:14]. And elsewhere he says to Abraham: [[Gen 21:12|in Isaac shall thy seed be called|In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen]]. He also promised Isaac (as is written in Genesis) that he would give the land of Chanaan to his seed[[Gen 26:3||]].

paras.t: Dicens, ipse Dominus Jacob patriarchæ : Tibi, id est semini tuo, dabo terram Chanaan : in qua habitaverunt Chananæi, orti ex Cham filio juniore Noë ; funiculum, id est partem seu sortem, hereditatis vestræ, ita quod inter ceteras terræ partes, istam vobis dabo hereditarie possidendam, tanquam vobis proprie deputatam. Hinc enim ait ad Jacob : Ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham patris tui, et Deus Isaac ; terram in qua dormis, tibi dabo et semini tuo.
paras.en: [[104:11|Saying|Dicens]], the Lord himself to the patriarch Jacob: [[104:11|To thee|Tibi]], that is, to thy seed, [[104:11|will I give the land of Chanaan|dabo terram Chanaan]], in which dwelt the Chanaanites, sprung from Cham the younger son of Noe[[Gen 10:6||]]; [[104:11|the lot|funiculum]] [literally "the little cord", the measuring line by which land was allotted], that is, the portion or share, [[104:11|of your inheritance|hereditatis vestræ]], so that among the other parts of the earth I will give you this one to be possessed by inheritance, as allotted properly to you. For hence he says to Jacob: [[Gen 28:13|I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: The land, wherein thou sleepest, I will give to thee and to thy seed|Ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham patris tui, et Deus Isaac ; terram in qua dormis, tibi dabo et semini tuo]].

paras.t: Quum esset prædicti Patriarchæ numero brevi, id est modici numero : quando videlicet Abraham non habuit nisi Saram uxorem suam, et Lot nepotem suum, parvamque familiam ; similiter quando Isaac paucos secum habebat ; quando etiam Jacob nondum aliquem genuit, et quando omnes filios suos generavit, qui in comparatione aliorum modici erant. Unde subjungitur, paucissimi et incolæ ejus, id est, quum ipsi inhabitantes terram tanquam peregrini et hospites, essent paucissimi respectu aliarum nationum.
paras.en: [[104:12|When they were but a small number|Quum esset prædicti Patriarchæ numero brevi]] (the aforesaid Patriarchs), that is, few in number: namely when Abraham had none but Sara his wife and Lot his nephew, and a small household; likewise when Isaac had few with him; when also Jacob had not yet begotten anyone, and when he had begotten all his sons, who were few in comparison with others. Hence it is added: [[104:12|yea very few, and sojourners therein|paucissimi et incolæ ejus]], that is, since they, dwelling in the land as pilgrims and strangers, were very few compared with the other nations.

paras.t: Et pertransierunt de gente in gentem, et de regno ad populum alterum. Hoc ex libro Geneseos clarius elucescit. Exivit enim Abraham cum Sara et Lot de Mesopotamia Syriæ, intrans terram Chanaan, prout in Geneseos libro habetur. Deinde ingressus est Geraram et Philistiim, atque Ægyptum. Similiter Isaac aliquas harum terrarum intravit. Jacob quoque primo fugit de regno Chananæorum in Syriam ; postea cum omni domo sua introivit regnum Ægypti.
paras.en: [[104:13|And they passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people.|Et pertransierunt de gente in gentem, et de regno ad populum alterum]] This shines out quite clearly from the book of Genesis. For Abraham went out with Sara and Lot from Mesopotamia of Syria, entering the land of Chanaan, as is found in the book of Genesis. Then he entered Gerara and the land of the Philistines, and Egypt. Isaac likewise entered some of these lands. Jacob too first fled from the kingdom of the Chanaanites into Syria; afterwards, with all his house, he entered the kingdom of Egypt.

paras.t: Non reliquit Deus hominem aliquem nocere eis nocumento letali. Frequenter tamen molestabant Philistæi seu pastores Geraræ Isaac et ejus pastores, obstruendo puteos eorum : similiter Laban quandoque persecutus est Jacob. Et corripuit pro eis reges, scilicet regem Ægypti atque Abimelech regem Geraræ, quorum uterque sibi afferri fecit Saram conjugem Abrahæ. Propter quod Deus conclusit omnem parientem in domo eorum, donec reddita fuerat Sara viro suo.
paras.en: [[104:14|He suffered no man to hurt them|Non reliquit Deus hominem aliquem nocere eis]] with a deadly hurt. Yet the Philistines, or the herdsmen of Gerara, often troubled Isaac and his herdsmen by stopping up their wells; likewise Laban at one time pursued Jacob. [[104:14|and he reproved kings for their sakes|Et corripuit pro eis reges]], namely the king of Egypt and Abimelech king of Gerara, each of whom had Sara the wife of Abraham brought to him. For this reason God closed up every woman that bore in their house, until Sara had been given back to her husband.

paras.t: Increpavit autem homines et reges prædictos, dicens per angelum seu inspirationem in somno : Nolite tangere, per violentiam, christos meos, id est prædictos sanctos a me spiritualiter unctos oleo et affluentia Spiritus Sancti. Non enim dicuntur christi, quasi corporaliter uncti : quoniam unctio corporalis et exterior regum atque pontificum primo ordinata est a Deo per Moysen. Et in prophetis meis nolite malignari, id est maligne operari. Hi enim Patriarchæ prophetæ fuerunt. Unde de Abraham scriptum est in Geneseos libro : Orabit pro te, quia propheta est. Isaac etiam plurima vaticinabatur filiis suis Jacob et Esau, posterisque eorum, ut patet ex Genesi. Sed et Jacob moriens excellentissimas prophetias contexuit, prout in Geneseos libro describitur.
paras.en: And he rebuked the aforesaid men and kings, saying through an angel or by an inspiration in sleep: [[104:15|Touch ye not|Nolite tangere]] by violence [[104:15|my anointed|christos meos]], that is, the aforesaid saints, anointed by me spiritually with the oil and abundance of the Holy Ghost. For they are not called anointed [*christi*] as if anointed bodily: for the bodily and outward anointing of kings and priests was first ordained by God through Moses[[Ex 30:25||]][[Lev 8:2||]][[Lev 8:12||]] [the margin gives Ibid. xxx, 25-33, that is, after the notes on Genesis, but the anointing oil is ordained in Exodus 30:25-33]. [[104:15|and do no evil to my prophets|Et in prophetis meis nolite malignari]], that is, do not work evil against them. For these Patriarchs were prophets. Hence it is written of Abraham in the book of Genesis: [[Gen 20:7|he shall pray for thee|Orabit pro te]], [[Gen 20:7|for he is a prophet|quia propheta est]] [the margin gives Gen. xv, 7; the words are Gen 20:7]. Isaac also prophesied a great many things to his sons Jacob and Esau and to their posterity, as is plain from Genesis[[Gen 27:28||]][[Gen 27:39||]]. And Jacob too, when dying, wove together most excellent prophecies, as is described in the book of Genesis[[Gen 49:1||]].

paras.t: Et vocavit Deus famem super terram, id est, præcepit et dixit, ut esset fames in terra, et omne firmamentum panis contrivit, id est, omnem panem, cor manducantis confirmantem, deficere fecit quantum ad vulgus. Quamvis autem illud specialiter referri possit ad famem septem annorum factam in Ægypto tempore Pharaonis et in terra Chanaan, quia has duas terras maxime oppresserat fames, sicut in Genesi legitur ; potest tamen referri ad famem factam in terra Chanaan tempore Abrahæ, propter quam descendit in Ægyptum, ut dicitur in Genesi. Melius tamen refertur ad famem factam in Ægypto et Chanaan, quia subjungitur :
paras.en: [[104:16|And he called a famine upon the land|Et vocavit Deus famem super terram]], that is, he commanded and said that there should be famine in the land, [[104:16|and he broke in pieces all the support of bread|et omne firmamentum panis contrivit]], that is, he made all bread, which strengthens the heart of him who eats it, to fail as far as the common people were concerned. Now although this can be referred especially to the famine of seven years that came in Egypt in the time of Pharao and in the land of Chanaan, since the famine had weighed most heavily on these two lands, as we read in Genesis[[Gen 41:54||]][[Gen 42:5||]]; yet it can be referred to the famine that came in the land of Chanaan in the time of Abraham, on account of which he went down into Egypt, as is said in Genesis[[Gen 12:10||]]. It is better, however, referred to the famine that came in Egypt and Chanaan, because there follows:

paras.t: Misit Deus ante eos, scilicet Jacob et filios suos, virum, id est Joseph virtuosum viriliter in cunctis agentem. Hunc Deus dicitur in Ægyptum misisse, quia permisit eum a fratribus vendi, et in Ægyptum deduci, illicque venundari. Convertit namque malum, quod fratres Joseph ei inferre intendebant, in bonum, tam ipsi Joseph, quam patri ac fratribus ejus. Propter quod Joseph dixit fratribus suis : Pro salute vestra misit me Deus ante vos in Ægyptum, ut reservemini super terram. Non vestro consilio, sed Dei voluntate huc adductus sum. In servum venundatus est Joseph ab Ismaelitis, Putiphar principi militiæ regis Ægypti, ut dicitur in Genesi.
paras.en: God [[104:17|sent|Misit]] [[104:17|before them|ante eos]], namely Jacob and his sons, [[104:17|a man|virum]], that is, Joseph, a man of virtue, acting manfully in all things [Denis plays on *vir*, "man", and *viriliter*, "manfully"]. God is said to have sent him into Egypt because he permitted him to be sold by his brethren and led down into Egypt[[Gen 37:28||]], and there to be sold again[[Gen 37:36||]]. For he turned the evil which Joseph's brethren meant to do him into good, both for Joseph himself and for his father and brethren. Wherefore Joseph said to his brethren: [[Gen 45:5|God sent me before you into Egypt for your preservation|Pro salute vestra misit me Deus ante vos in Ægyptum]], [[Gen 45:7|that you may be preserved upon the earth|ut reservemini super terram]]. [[Gen 45:8|Not by your counsel was I sent hither, but by the will of God|Non vestro consilio, sed Dei voluntate huc adductus sum]] [Denis has *adductus*, "brought", for the Vulgate's *missus*, "sent"]. [[104:17|Joseph, who was sold for a slave|In servum venundatus est Joseph]] by the Ismaelites to Putiphar, captain of the soldiery of the king of Egypt, as is said in Genesis[[Gen 39:1||]].

paras.t: Humiliaverunt in compedibus pedes ejus : id est, Ægyptii ex mandato principis militiæ vinculis ligaverunt, incarceraveruntque Joseph, propter querelam uxoris principis jam præfati, quæ false accusavit castissimum Joseph, dicens marito suo : Ingressus est ad me servus Hebræus, quem adduxisti, ut illuderet mihi. Qui iratus, tradidit Joseph in carcerem, ubi vincti regis custodiebantur. Ferrum, id est tribulatio dura, pertransiit animam ejus, id est, vehementer afflixit spiritum Joseph : non tamen impatiens exstitit, sed dolor ex compedibus pedum in anima ortus est ; donec veniret verbum ejus, id est interpretatio divinitus inspirata, qua non solum exposuit somnium principis pincernarum, principisque pistorum, sed etiam Pharaonis. Hac etiam interpretatione peracta, cœpit recreari, et se in brevi liberandum cognoscere. De hoc vero ait Joseph : Numquid non Dei est interpretatio?
paras.en: [[104:18|They humbled his feet in fetters|Humiliaverunt in compedibus pedes ejus]]: that is, the Egyptians, at the command of the captain of the soldiers, bound Joseph with chains and imprisoned him, because of the complaint of the wife of the captain already named, who falsely accused the most chaste Joseph, saying to her husband: [[Gen 39:17|The Hebrew servant, whom thou hast brought, came to me to abuse me|Ingressus est ad me servus Hebræus, quem adduxisti, ut illuderet mihi]]. And he, being angry,[[Gen 39:19||]] [[Gen 39:20|cast Joseph into the prison, where the king's prisoners were kept|tradidit Joseph in carcerem, ubi vincti regis custodiebantur]]. [[104:18|The iron|Ferrum]], that is, hard tribulation, [[104:18|pierced his soul|pertransiit animam ejus]], that is, sorely afflicted the spirit of Joseph: yet he did not become impatient, but the pain from the fetters of his feet rose up into his soul; [[104:19|until his word came|donec veniret verbum ejus]], that is, the interpretation inspired by God, by which he expounded not only the dream of the chief butler and of the chief baker, but also that of Pharao[[Gen 40:1||]][[Gen 41:1||]]. And once this interpretation was given, he began to be refreshed, and to know that he would soon be set free. Of this Joseph says: [[Gen 40:8|Doth not interpretation belong to God?|Numquid non Dei est interpretatio?]]

paras.t: Eloquium Domini inflammavit eum, id est, prædicta inspiratio et interpretatio accendit et docuit Joseph : ideo misit servos suos rex Ægypti Pharao, et solvit eum, id est, sanctum Joseph educi de carcere jussit, audito a principe pincernarum quantam industriam Joseph haberet somnia exponendo. Princeps populorum, id est prædictus rex Ægyptiorum, misit, et dimisit eum de carcere. Unde in Genesi habetur : Protinus ad imperium regis eductum de carcere totonderunt Joseph, ac veste mutata obtulerunt regi.
paras.en: [[104:19|The word of the Lord inflamed him|Eloquium Domini inflammavit eum]], that is, the inspiration and interpretation just spoken of kindled and taught Joseph. Therefore Pharao the king of Egypt [[104:20|sent|misit]] his servants, [[104:20|and he released him|et solvit eum]], that is, he ordered holy Joseph to be brought out of prison, having heard from the chief butler how great a skill Joseph had in expounding dreams[[Gen 41:9||]]. [[104:20|The ruler of the people|Princeps populorum]], that is, the aforesaid king of the Egyptians, sent, [[104:20|and he set him at liberty|et dimisit eum]] from the prison. Hence we have in Genesis: [[Gen 41:14|Forthwith at the king's command Joseph was brought out of the prison, and they shaved him: and changing his apparel brought him in to him|Protinus ad imperium regis eductum de carcere totonderunt Joseph, ac veste mutata obtulerunt regi]].

paras.t: Constituit rex Ægypti eum, scilicet Joseph, dominum domus suæ, id est familiæ et populi sui, et principem omnis possessionis suæ, id est totius terræ Ægypti, omniumque horreorum ac frumentorum suorum. Unde ipse Pharao ait ad Joseph : Tu eris super domum meam, et ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet ; uno tantum regni solio te præcedam. Et rursum : Ego sum Pharao. Absque tuo imperio non movebit quisquam manum aut pedem in omni terra Ægypti.
paras.en: The king of Egypt [[104:21|made him|Constituit rex Ægypti eum]], namely Joseph, [[104:21|master of his house|dominum domus suæ]], that is, of his household and his people, [[104:21|and ruler of all his possession|et principem omnis possessionis suæ]], that is, of the whole land of Egypt, and of all his granaries and corn. Hence Pharao himself said to Joseph: [[Gen 41:40|Thou shalt be over my house, and at the commandment of thy mouth all the people shall obey: only in the kingly throne will I be above thee|Tu eris super domum meam, et ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet ; uno tantum regni solio te præcedam]]. And again: [[Gen 41:44|I am Pharao: without thy commandment no man shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|Ego sum Pharao. Absque tuo imperio non movebit quisquam manum aut pedem in omni terra Ægypti]].

paras.t: Ut erudiret ipse Joseph principes ejus, videlicet Pharaonis, sicut semetipsum, id est, sua instructione faceret eos sibi in sapientia similes, docendo eos non solum de rebus corporalibus, negotiisque humanis, sed etiam de moribus in agendis. Et secundum Cassiodorum, Pharao æstimavit quod Joseph docere posset Ægyptios artem interpretandi occultissima somnia, sicut et ipse Deo revelante exposuit. Et sensus ejus prudentiam docebat, instruendo eos in scientia œconomica, ethica, atque politica. Œconomica quippe docet regere domum, ethica semetipsum, politica communitatem seu civitatem. Credi etiam pie potest, quod tam sanctus Patriarcha, Propheta et cultor Dei, docebat nonnullos Ægyptiorum de cultu et fide unius veri summique Dei.
paras.en: [[104:22|That he might instruct|Ut erudiret]], Joseph himself, [[104:22|his princes|principes ejus]], that is, Pharao's, [[104:22|as himself|sicut semetipsum]]: that is, that by his teaching he might make them like himself in wisdom, teaching them not only about bodily things and human affairs, but also about morals, in the things to be done. And according to Cassiodorus, Pharao thought that Joseph could teach the Egyptians the art of interpreting the most hidden dreams, as he himself had expounded them by God's revelation. [[104:22|And teach his ancients wisdom|Et sensus ejus prudentiam docebat]] [Denis's text reads *sensus ejus*, "his understanding", for the Vulgate's *senes ejus*, "his ancients": so in his reading, "and his understanding taught prudence"], instructing them in the science of economics, ethics and politics. For economics teaches how to rule a household, ethics how to rule oneself, politics how to rule a community or city. It may also piously be believed that so holy a Patriarch, Prophet and worshipper of God taught some of the Egyptians about the worship of the one true and highest God, and faith in him.

paras.t: Et intravit Israel, scilicet pater Joseph cum filiis suis et filiis filiorum in animabus septuaginta, in Ægyptum; et Jacob, qui et Israel dictus est, accola, id est peregrinus et colonus, fuit cum semine suo in terra Cham, id est in Ægypto: quæ fuit terra atque possessio filiorum Cham filii Noe. Unde Joseph ait fratribus suis: Nuntiate patri meo universam gloriam meam, et adducite eum ad me. Et de Jacob scriptum est: Habitavit Israel in Ægypto, id est in terra Gessen; et vixit in ea decem et septem annis.
paras.en: [[104:23|And Israel went|Et intravit Israel]], namely Joseph's father, with his sons and his sons' sons, seventy souls[[Gen 46:27||]], [[104:23|into Egypt|in Ægyptum]]; [[104:23|and Jacob|et Jacob]], who was also called Israel[[Gen 32:28||]] [the margin gives Gen. xxxvii, 28, which does not fit; Jacob is named Israel at Gen 32:28], [[104:23|was a sojourner|accola]], that is, a stranger and settler, with his seed [[104:23|in the land of Cham|in terra Cham]], that is, in Egypt, which was the land and possession of the sons of Cham, the son of Noe. Hence Joseph said to his brethren: [[Gen 45:13|You shall tell my father of all my glory|Nuntiate patri meo universam gloriam meam]], and [[Gen 45:13|bring him to me|adducite eum ad me]]. And of Jacob it is written: [[Gen 47:27|Israel dwelt in Egypt, that is, in the land of Gessen|Habitavit Israel in Ægypto, id est in terra Gessen]]; and [[Gen 47:28|he lived in it seventeen years|vixit in ea decem et septem annis]].

paras.t: Et auxit Jacob in terra Ægypti populum suum vehementer: non quod ipse aliquem in Ægypto generavit; sed ipse fecisse asseritur, quod ejus posteritas fecit. Et hoc modo Dominus ait ad eum: In gentem magnam faciam te in Ægypto. Ego descendam tecum illuc, et ego inde adducam revertentem: non quod Jacob redierit, quia in Ægypto decessit. Et firmavit Jacob eum, scilicet populum ex se natum, super inimicos ejus, id est super Ægyptios. Sicut enim populum suum auxit, sic eum firmavit. Vel sic: Et auxit Deus populum suum, id est Israelitas. Propter quod in Exodo dicitur: Filii Israel creverunt, et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt, ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram. Et iterum: Rex Ægypti ait ad populum suum, Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus et fortior nobis est.
paras.en: And Jacob [[104:24|increased|auxit]] in the land of Egypt [[104:24|his people exceedingly|populum suum vehementer]]: not that he himself begot anyone in Egypt, but he is said to have done what his posterity did. And in this way the Lord said to him: [[Gen 46:3|I will make a great nation of thee|In gentem magnam faciam te]] in Egypt. [[Gen 46:4|I will go down with thee thither, and will bring thee back again from thence|Ego descendam tecum illuc, et ego inde adducam revertentem]]: not that Jacob came back, for he died in Egypt. And Jacob [[104:24|strengthened them|firmavit Jacob eum]], namely the people born of him, [[104:24|over their enemies|super inimicos ejus]], that is, over the Egyptians. For as he increased his people, so he strengthened them. Or thus: God [[104:24|increased his people|Et auxit Deus populum suum]], that is, the Israelites. Wherefore it is said in Exodus: [[Ex 1:7|The children of Israel increased, and sprung up into multitudes, and growing exceedingly strong they filled the land.|Filii Israel creverunt, et quasi germinantes multiplicati sunt, ac roborati nimis, impleverunt terram]] And again: the king of Egypt said to his people: [[Ex 1:9|Behold the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we|Ecce populus filiorum Israel multus et fortior nobis est]].

paras.t: Convertit Deus, non effective sed permissive, quomodo etiam induravit Pharaonem, cor eorum, id est Ægyptiorum, de malo in pejus, ut odirent populum ejus, id est Israeliticam plebem, et dolum facerent in servos ejus, id est in populum istum qui veri Dei fidem et cultum habebat. Hinc enim in Exodo dicitur: Oderant filios Israel Ægyptii et affligebant, illudentes eis, atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam illorum operibus luti et lateris. Rursusque: Surrexit rex novus super Ægyptum, qui ignorabat Joseph, et ait ad populum suum: Venite, sapienter opprimamus populum Israel, ne forte multiplicetur.
paras.en: God [[104:25|turned|Convertit]], not effectively but permissively [that is, not by causing it but by allowing it], in the same way as he hardened Pharao, [[104:25|their heart|cor eorum]], that is, the Egyptians', from bad to worse, [[104:25|to hate his people|ut odirent populum ejus]], that is, the Israelite folk, [[104:25|and to deal deceitfully with his servants|et dolum facerent in servos ejus]], that is, against this people which had the faith and worship of the true God. For hence it is said in Exodus: [[Ex 1:13|the Egyptians hated the children of Israel, and afflicted them and mocked them|Oderant filios Israel Ægyptii et affligebant, illudentes eis]], [[Ex 1:14|they made their life bitter with hard works in clay and brick|atque ad amaritudinem perducebant vitam illorum operibus luti et lateris]]. And again: [[Ex 1:8|there arose a new king over Egypt, that knew not Joseph|Surrexit rex novus super Ægyptum, qui ignorabat Joseph]], and said to his people: [[Ex 1:10|Come let us wisely oppress them, lest they multiply|Venite, sapienter opprimamus populum Israel, ne forte multiplicetur]] [the margin gives Exod. i, 10 only; the first words are from Ex 1:8].

paras.t: Misit Deus Moysen servum suum ad Pharaonem, ut dimitteret filios Israel, prout in Exodo scribitur. Misit et Aaron fratrem Moysis quem elegit ipsum. Elegit enim Aaron fratrem Moysis ad hoc, quod adjutor esset Moysi in tanto negotio. Misit autem Deus Moysen de deserto Sinai, Aaron vero exsistentem in Ægypto fecit occurrere Moysi. Sicque ambos simul misit ad Pharaonem: Moysen, ut faceret signa; Aaron, ut loqueretur ad regem, quoniam eloquens erat.
paras.en: God [[104:26|sent Moses his servant|Misit Deus Moysen servum suum]] to Pharao, that he might let the children of Israel go, as is written in Exodus[[Ex 3:10||]]. He sent also [[104:26|Aaron|Misit et Aaron]], the brother of Moses, [[104:26|whom he had chosen|quem elegit ipsum]]. For he chose Aaron, the brother of Moses, for this, that he should be a helper to Moses in so great a business[[Ex 4:14||]]. Now God sent Moses from the desert of Sinai[[Ex 3:1||]], and made Aaron, who was living in Egypt, come to meet Moses[[Ex 4:27||]]. And so he sent both of them together to Pharao: Moses, to work signs; Aaron, to speak to the king, since he was eloquent.

paras.t: Posuit Deus in eis, id est in Moyse et Aaron, verba signorum suorum, id est minorum mirabilium, et prodigiorum, id est majorum miraculorum, in terra Cham, id est in Ægypto. Per hos enim Deus prædixit Pharaoni, quæ signa atque prodigia die sequenti essent futura, ut sæpe in Exodo recitatur.
