paras.en: [[118:168|I have kept thy commandments|Servavi mandata tua]] by obedience, [[118:168|and thy testimonies|et testimonia tua]] by formed faith, that is, faith united to charity, [[118:168|because all my ways are in thy sight|quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]], that is, everything that I think, desire, speak and do is seen and judged by thee. For hence holy Job says: Doth not God know my way, [[Job 31:4|and number all my steps?|et cunctos gressus meos dinumerat?]] [Denis's text reads *Nonne Deus scit viam meam*, "Doth not God know my way"; the Vulgate has "Doth not he consider my ways"] And again: [[Job 14:17|Thou hast sealed up my offences as it were in a bag|Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea]]; and likewise: Thou [[Job 13:27|hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]. O how great cause we have to walk solicitously and fearfully before God our judge[[Mich 6:8||]]! For he does the greatest wrong to a judge who does evil while the judge is present and forbids it. So we, who know that God beholds all our works, dishonour him most grievously in that we go about before him without diligent watch over the heart. Therefore Boethius said excellently: A great necessity of uprightness is laid upon you, if you will not dissemble, since you do all things before the eyes of a Judge who sees all things. Let us then always think of the presence of the divine majesty, saying with Elias: [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth|Vivit Dominus]], [[3 Kings 17:1|in whose sight I stand|in cujus conspectu sto]] this day[[3 Kings 18:15||]]; and let us live as men soon to be judged by him. And surely, if we weigh these things, we shall begin to fear God greatly, so much that we shall be able to say with blessed Job: [[Job 23:15|when I consider him|Considerans Deum]], [[Job 23:15|I am made pensive with fear|timore sollicitor]]; and again: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and his weight I was unable to bear|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum, et pondus ejus ferre non potui]]. And this noble fear makes us shun sins and keep the commandments, as Solomon declares: [[Prov 14:27|The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to decline from the ruin of death|Timor Domini fons vitæ, ut declinet a ruina mortis]].

paras.t: Precatio. Diligentibus nobis, Domine, legem tuam, pacem largire perpetuam ; diligat anima nostra testimonia tua : unde nullum sit nobis scandalum, quod in te speramus, sed gloria et perpetua salus.
paras.en: Prayer. Grant everlasting peace, O Lord, to us who love thy law; may our soul love thy testimonies, so that our hoping in thee may be to us no stumbling block, but glory and everlasting salvation.

paras.t: Thau. Appropinquet deprecatio mea in conspectu tuo, Domine, id est, tibi complaceat, non repellatur a te, sed effectum salutarem obtineat, prout scriptum est : Oratio humiliantis se, nubes penetrabit. Juxta eloquium tuum, id est, sicut dixisti et promisisti in sacra Scriptura, te daturum intellectum orantibus te, da mihi intellectum, id est illuminationem intellectivam. Scriptum enim est : Si quis vestrum indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo ; et dabitur ei. Et Apostolus : Dabit tibi Dominus in omnibus intellectum. Supra quoque dixisti : Intellectum tibi dabo, et instruam te. Vel, Juxta eloquium tuum, id est secundum conditionem et altitudinem sacræ Scripturæ, da mihi intellectum eam intelligendi veraciter : quatenus sicut illa supernaturalis atque altissima est, sic conferas mihi sublimem mentis elevationem, supernaturalemque intellectus mei illustrationem.
paras.en: Thau. [[118:169|Let my supplication, O Lord, come near in thy sight|Appropinquet deprecatio mea in conspectu tuo, Domine]], that is, let it be pleasing to thee, let it not be repelled by thee, but let it obtain a saving effect, as it is written: [[Ecclus 35:21|The prayer of him that humbleth himself, shall pierce the clouds|Oratio humiliantis se, nubes penetrabit]]. [[118:169|According to thy word|Juxta eloquium tuum]], that is, as thou hast said and promised in holy Scripture that thou wouldst give understanding to those who pray to thee[[Luke 11:13||]], [[118:169|give me understanding|da mihi intellectum]], that is, the illumination of the intellect. For it is written: [[Jas 1:5|if any of you want wisdom, let him ask of God|Si quis vestrum indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo]]; [[Jas 1:5|And it shall be given him|et dabitur ei]]. And the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:7|the Lord will give thee in all things understanding|Dabit tibi Dominus in omnibus intellectum]]. Above, too [that is, earlier in the Psalter], thou hast said: [[Ps 31:8|I will give thee understanding, and I will instruct thee|Intellectum tibi dabo, et instruam te]]. Or: [[118:169|According to thy word|Juxta eloquium tuum]], that is, according to the nature and loftiness of holy Scripture, [[118:169|give me understanding|da mihi intellectum]] to understand it truly: so that, as it is supernatural and most high, thou mayest bestow on me a sublime elevation of mind and a supernatural illumination of my intellect.

paras.t: Intret postulatio mea in conspectu tuo, ut omnino admittatur ac impleatur a te. Moris est sacræ Scripturæ, in his quæ affectum concernunt, eumdem sensum sub aliis verbis frequenter repetere, ut accendatur et reaccendatur, atque in se ipsa æstuanter fervescat voluntas in divino amore et sancto affectu. Secundum eloquium tuum, quo misericorditer prædixisti te auxiliaturum egenis ad te clamantibus, eripe me ab omni periculo.
paras.en: [[118:170|Let my request come in before thee|Intret postulatio mea in conspectu tuo]], that it may be wholly admitted and fulfilled by thee. It is the custom of holy Scripture, in things that concern the affections, often to repeat the same sense in other words, so that the will may be kindled and rekindled and may glow fervently within itself in divine love and holy affection. [[118:170|According to thy word|Secundum eloquium tuum]], by which thou hast mercifully foretold that thou wouldst help the needy who cry to thee, [[118:170|deliver thou me|eripe me]] from every danger.

paras.t: Eructabunt labia mea hymnum, id est, ex interiori lætitia proferent labia oris mei laudem et gratiarum actionem, quum docueris me actualiter justificationes tuas, id est mandata, ut ea luculenter et operative cognoscam. Tunc quoque pronuntiabit lingua mea eloquium tuum, cantando laudes divinas, quia omnia mandata tua æquitas, id est, adeo justa et sancta sunt, ut melius nuncupentur æquitas, quam æqua.
paras.en: [[118:171|My lips shall utter a hymn|Eructabunt labia mea hymnum]], that is, out of inward gladness the lips of my mouth shall bring forth praise and thanksgiving, [[118:171|when thou shalt teach me|quum docueris me]] in act [[118:171|thy justifications|justificationes tuas]], that is, thy commandments, so that I may know them clearly and in practice. Then too [[118:172|my tongue shall pronounce thy word|pronuntiabit lingua mea eloquium tuum]], by singing the divine praises, [[118:172|because all thy commandments are justice|quia omnia mandata tua æquitas]], that is, they are so just and holy that they are better called *equity* than *equitable* [the psalm calls the commandments *æquitas*, "equity" (the Douay-Rheims "justice"), not merely *æqua*, "equitable"].

paras.t: Fiat manus tua, id est, potestas tua, o Deus omnipotens, ita se habeat circa me, ut salvet me, liberando animam meam a malis, corroborandoque eam in bonis, quoniam mandata tua elegi implere magis quam hominibus complacere, aut mundo servire.
paras.en: [[118:173|Let thy hand be with me|Fiat manus tua]], that is, let thy power, O almighty God, so bear itself toward me as [[118:173|to save me|ut salvet me]], by delivering my soul from evils and strengthening it in good things, [[118:173|for I have chosen thy precepts|quoniam mandata tua elegi]], to fulfil them rather than to please men or to serve the world.

paras.t: Concupivi salutare tuum, Domine, id est, Christum et ejus adventum ac fruitionem optavi. De quo utique salutari seu Christo scriptum est : Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus. Vel, Concupivi salutare tuum, id est salutem seu gratiam salutarem, vitam æternam, et gloriam consummatam. Et lex tua meditatio mea est objectaliter, quia de ea est, et circa eam indesinenter versatur cogitatio mea.
paras.en: [[118:174|I have longed for thy salvation, O Lord|Concupivi salutare tuum, Domine]], that is, I have desired Christ, and his coming, and the enjoyment of him. Of which *salvation*, that is, of Christ, it is written: [[Agg 2:8|the desired of all nations shall come|Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus]]. Or: [[118:174|I have longed for thy salvation|Concupivi salutare tuum]], that is, salvation or saving grace, eternal life and consummated glory. [[118:174|And thy law is my meditation|Et lex tua meditatio mea est]] as its object, because my thought is about it and ceaselessly busies itself with it.

paras.t: Vivet, ut spero in tua bonitate, o Domine, anima mea per gratiam in via, per gloriam quoque in patria, et laudabit te, hic inchoative et imperfecte, illic vero consummative, plene ac sempiterne, sicut prædictum est : Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine ; in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te. Et judicia tua, id est considerationes judiciorum tuorum, et mandata ac verba divina quæ tu justa judicas, seu flagella quibus in præsenti tuos electos castigas, adjuvabunt me : quia eorum auxilio gratiam adipiscar, per quam ad vitam æternam perducar.
paras.en: [[118:175|My soul|anima mea]], as I hope in thy goodness, O Lord, [[118:175|shall live|Vivet]], by grace in the way and by glory too in the fatherland, [[118:175|and shall praise thee|et laudabit te]], here in a beginning and imperfect manner, but there consummately, fully and everlastingly, as was foretold: [[Ps 83:5|Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord: they shall praise thee for ever and ever|Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine ; in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te]]. [[118:175|And thy judgments|Et judicia tua]], that is, the considering of thy judgments, and the commandments and divine words which thou judgest just, or the scourges with which thou chastisest thy elect in this present life, [[118:175|shall help me|adjuvabunt me]]: because by their help I shall obtain grace, by which I shall be brought to eternal life.

paras.t: Erravi sicut ovis quæ periit. Nicolaus de Lyra, et quidam post eum, opinantur hoc non esse intelligendum de errore in moribus, vel de errore peccati et ignorantiæ, quia subjungitur, Mandata tua non sum oblitus ; sed de errore quo viri contemplativi ad loca solitaria confugientes, æstimantur ab hominibus mundanis errare, insipienterque agere. Sed quia post verba hæc immediate subjungitur, Quære servum tuum, ad quod refertur quod subditur, Quia mandata tua non sum oblitus ; idcirco aptius arbitror, ut intelligatur de errore culpæ et ignorantiæ. In multis enim (ut Jacobus protestatur) offendimus omnes. Et secundum Apostolum, Conclusit Deus omnia sub peccato, ut omnium misereatur. Loquens ergo Propheta in persona populi fidelis, seu hominis justi, qui interdum a via veritatis recessit : Erravi, inquit, a te Domino Deo meo et tuis præceptis, sequendo malignum, sicut ovis quæ periit, eo quod pastorem reliquit, propter quod lupi morsibus patuit. Unde scriptum est : Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus ; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit. Idcirco, o Domine, quære servum tuum, id est, de manibus lupi seu dæmonis erue me, per gratiam visita me, et reduc me ad ovile ovium electarum, pro quibus animam tuam posuisti, quia mandata tua non sum oblitus finaliter, quamvis ad tempus ea neglexi.
paras.en: [[118:176|I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost|Erravi sicut ovis quæ periit]]. Nicholas of Lyra, and some after him, think that this is not to be understood of straying in conduct, or of the straying of sin and ignorance, because there follows: [[118:176|I have not forgotten thy commandments|Mandata tua non sum oblitus]]; but of the straying by which contemplative men, fleeing to solitary places, are reckoned by worldly men to stray and to act foolishly. But since immediately after these words there follows, [[118:176|seek thy servant|Quære servum tuum]], to which refers what is added, [[118:176|because I have not forgotten thy commandments|Quia mandata tua non sum oblitus]], I therefore judge it more fitting that it be understood of the straying of fault and ignorance. [[Jas 3:2|For in many things|In multis enim]] (as James declares) [[Jas 3:2|we all offend|offendimus omnes]]. And according to the Apostle, [[Rom 11:32|God hath concluded all|Conclusit Deus omnia]] [[Gal 3:22|under sin|sub peccato]], [[Rom 11:32|that he may have mercy on all|ut omnium misereatur]] [Denis joins Rom 11:32 with "under sin" from Gal 3:22]. The Prophet, then, speaking in the person of the faithful people, or of a just man who has at times departed from the way of truth, says: [[118:176|I have gone astray|Erravi]] from thee, the Lord my God, and from thy precepts, by following the evil one, [[118:176|like a sheep that is lost|sicut ovis quæ periit]], because it has left its shepherd, and so lies open to the bites of the wolf. Whence it is written: [[Is 53:6|All we like sheep have gone astray, every one hath turned aside into his own way|Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus ; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit]]. Therefore, O Lord, [[118:176|seek thy servant|quære servum tuum]], that is, snatch me out of the hands of the wolf, or the devil, visit me by grace, and bring me back to the fold of the elect sheep, for whom thou hast laid down thy life, [[118:176|because I have not forgotten thy commandments|quia mandata tua non sum oblitus]] for good, although for a time I neglected them.

paras.t: Ecce psalmum quantitate verborum magnum, sed sensuum excellentia multo majorem, audivimus. In quo quasi per singulos versus anima fidelis Deum amorose fiducialiterque affatur; in quo saluberrima documenta refulgent velut stellæ in firmamento; in quo affectuosissimæ preces conscriptæ sunt; in quo docemur quid ad virum perfectum pertineat, quatenus si eas virtutes et opera sancta quæ cantamus, in nobis viderimus, Deo gratissimi simus, et tanto humiliores quanto ex donis receptis obligamur Deum amplius amare et honorare. Porro si bona ista nondum recepimus, sed vitiis et imperfectionibus variis implicamur, gemamus atque ploremus, et ad perfectionem (sicut Apostolus monet) feramur, nec segnes efficiamur.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a psalm great in the number of its words, but far greater in the excellence of its meanings: one in which, almost verse by verse, the faithful soul speaks to God lovingly and trustfully; in which the most wholesome teachings shine like stars in the firmament; in which the most affectionate prayers are set down; in which we are taught what belongs to the perfect man, so that, if we see in ourselves the virtues and holy works that we sing, we may be most grateful to God, and the more humble the more we are bound by the gifts received to love and honour God. But if we have not yet received these goods, and are entangled in vices and various imperfections, let us groan and weep, and let us [[Heb 6:1|go on|feramur]] (as the Apostle admonishes) [[Heb 6:1|to things more perfect|ad perfectionem]], and [[Heb 6:12|become not slothful|nec segnes efficiamur]].

paras.t: Precatio. Domine Jesu Christe, Pastor bone, qui pro humani generis redemptione ignominiam crucis voluisti sustinere, nos servos tuos, qui sicut oves pereuntes erravimus, require ; fiat manus tua ut salvet nos, et in gloria regni redde beatos.
paras.en: Prayer. Lord Jesus Christ, good Shepherd, who for the redemption of mankind didst will to bear the shame of the cross, seek us thy servants, who have gone astray like perishing sheep; let thy hand be with us to save us, and make us blessed in the glory of thy kingdom.

119.title: EXPLANATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI NONIDECIMI : AD DOMINUM, QUUM TRIBULARER, ETC.
119.title_en: Explanation of the hundred and nineteenth psalm: In my trouble I cried to the Lord, etc.

paras.t: Titulus psalmi nunc exponendi est : Canticum graduum. Dicuntur autem psalmus iste et quatuordecim immediate sequentes, psalmi seu cantica graduum, quoniam a sacerdotibus atque Levitis cantabantur in ascensu templi, qui erat per quindecim gradus. Per hos autem corporales ascensus, secundum doctores catholicos, designantur ascensus virtutum in gradibus spiritualis ædificii seu profectus, sicut de virtuosis prædictum est : Ibunt de virtute in virtutem. Gradatim enim et ordinate proficit homo. Hi ergo spirituales gradus virtutum tanguntur in psalmis istis. Quorum graduum primus est, a vitiis hujus sæculi recedere, et futurum sæculum desiderare. Sensus autem tituli est : Psalmus iste est canticum graduum, quia in ascensu graduum templi cantabatur ad litteram ; spiritualiter vero dicitur canticum graduum, id est exsultatio mentis de spirituali processu virtutum.
paras.en: The title of the psalm now to be expounded is: A gradual canticle [Latin *canticum graduum*, literally "song of the steps"]. Now this psalm and the fourteen immediately following are called psalms or canticles of the steps, because they were sung by the priests and Levites in going up to the temple, which was by fifteen steps. And by these bodily ascents, according to the Catholic doctors, are signified the ascents of the virtues in the steps of the spiritual building, or of spiritual progress, as was foretold above of the virtuous: [[Ps 83:8|they shall go from virtue to virtue|Ibunt de virtute in virtutem]]. For a man makes progress step by step and in order. These spiritual steps of the virtues, then, are touched on in these psalms. And the first of these steps is to withdraw from the vices of this world and to desire the world to come. The sense of the title, then, is: This psalm is a canticle of the steps, because literally it was sung in going up the steps of the temple; but spiritually it is called a canticle of the steps, that is, the exultation of the mind at its spiritual advance in the virtues.

paras.t: Loquens ergo Propheta in persona hominis spiritualiter proficere cupientis, suumque profectum a prædicto fundamento seu primo gradu jam dicto inchoantis, ait : Ad Dominum, quum tribularer, clamavi : id est, quum mente aut corpore infirmarer, quum a mundo, diabolo et carne tentarer, aut aliquo modo dire affligerer, Deum pro adjutore et salvatore invocavi, ad eum confugi, ad eum clamavi, id est, affectuose locutus sum : sicut et ipse supra consuluit, Invoca me in die tribulationis. Unde et scriptum est : Domine, Deus Israel, anima in angustiis, et spiritus anxius clamat ad te. Istud quippe est unicum optimumque in omni tribulatione solatium, ad Deum clamare, juxta illud : In nobis quidem non est tanta fortitudo, ut possimus huic multitudini resistere, quæ irruit super nos ; sed quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te. Unde venerabilis illa Sara vehementer afflicta, ait : Ad te, Domine, faciem meam converto, ad te oculos meos erigo. Et sanctissima illa Esther ita precata est : Domine mi rex, adjuva me solitariam, cujus præter te nullus alius auxiliator est.
paras.en: Speaking, then, in the person of a man who longs to make spiritual progress and who begins his progress from the foundation spoken of, that is, the first step already named, the Prophet says: [[119:1|In my trouble I cried to the Lord|Ad Dominum, quum tribularer, clamavi]]: that is, when I was weak in mind or body, when I was tempted by the world, the devil and the flesh, or was in any way grievously afflicted, I called upon God as my helper and saviour, I fled to him, I cried to him, that is, I spoke to him with deep feeling; as he himself counselled above: [[Ps 49:15|call upon me in the day of trouble|Invoca me in die tribulationis]]. Hence it is also written: O Lord, [[Bar 3:1|the God of Israel, the soul in anguish, and the troubled spirit crieth to thee|Deus Israel, anima in angustiis, et spiritus anxius clamat ad te]]. For this is the one and the best comfort in every trouble, to cry to God, according to that: [[2 Par 20:12|as for us we have not strength enough, to be able to resist this multitude, which cometh violently upon us. But as we know not what to do, we can only turn our eyes to thee|In nobis quidem non est tanta fortitudo, ut possimus huic multitudini resistere, quæ irruit super nos ; sed quum ignoremus quid agere debeamus, hoc solum habemus residui, ut oculos nostros dirigamus ad te]]. Hence that venerable Sara, sorely afflicted, says: [[Tob 3:14|To thee, O Lord, I turn my face, to thee I direct my eyes.|Ad te, Domine, faciem meam converto, ad te oculos meos erigo]] And that most holy Esther prayed thus: [[Esth 14:3|O my Lord, who alone art our king, help me a desolate woman, and who have no other helper but thee|Domine mi rex, adjuva me solitariam, cujus præter te nullus alius auxiliator est]].

paras.t: Sic ergo tribulatus, clamavi ad Dominum : nec frustra. Nam et exaudivit me : quemadmodum scriptum est : Salus populi ego sum, dicit Dominus ; de quacumque tribulatione clamaverint ad me, exaudiam eos. Et supra dixit : Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum. Istum versiculum Jonas propheta taliter cecinit : Clamavi ad Dominum de tribulatione, et exaudivit me. Maxime enim adest misericors Deus famulis suis tempore tribulationis, eosque indubitanter exaudit tempore congruo, dummodo ipsi perseveranter clamaverint, et in nomine Jesu petierint, id est, ea rogaverint quæ ad veram salutem proficua sunt. Unde Sara illa filia Raguelis ait : Pro certo habet is qui colit te, Domine, quia vita ejus si in probatione fuerit, coronabitur ; si autem in tribulatione fuerit, liberabitur ; et si in correptione fuerit, ad misericordiam pervenire licebit.
paras.en: So then, being troubled, I cried to the Lord; and not in vain. For [[119:1|and he heard me|et exaudivit me]]: as it is written: I am the salvation of the people, saith the Lord; from whatever tribulation they shall cry to me, I will hear them[[Is 43:1||]] [the margin gives only "cf. Is. xliii": these words are not found word for word in Scripture; they are the Introit of the Mass of the nineteenth Sunday after Pentecost, which echoes Isaias 43:2–3, "I will be with thee … thy Saviour"]. And he said above: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him, and I will glorify him|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum]]. The prophet Jonas sang this little verse thus: [[Jon 2:3|I cried out of my affliction to the Lord, and he heard me|Clamavi ad Dominum de tribulatione, et exaudivit me]]. For the merciful God is most of all at hand to his servants in the time of trouble, and without doubt hears them at the fitting time, provided they cry perseveringly and ask in the name of Jesus, that is, ask for those things that profit for true salvation. Hence Sara, the daughter of Raguel, says: [[Tob 3:21|this every one is sure of that worshippeth thee, that his life, if it be under trial, shall be crowned and if it be under tribulation, it shall be delivered: and if it be under correction, it shall be allowed to come to thy mercy|Pro certo habet is qui colit te, Domine, quia vita ejus si in probatione fuerit, coronabitur ; si autem in tribulatione fuerit, liberabitur ; et si in correptione fuerit, ad misericordiam pervenire licebit]].

paras.t: Domine, libera animam meam a labiis iniquis, id est ab his qui verba evidenter maligna, pungitiva, derisiva, detractoria contra me proferunt, et a lingua dolosa, id est ab eo qui blandiendo, et mala sub specie boni proponendo, conatur animam meam a Deo avertere, a spirituali profectu retrahere, aut aliquo modo decipere. Ab his petit homo fidelis liberari : vel ut omnino ista non patiatur, quatenus Deo liberius atque quietius vacet : nam et Apostolus, Orate, inquit, ut liberemur a malis et importunis hominibus ; vel ne per ista turbetur, et in bonis operibus impediatur, impatiensque reddatur, sicut Apostolus ait : Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum.
paras.en: [[119:2|O Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips|Domine, libera animam meam a labiis iniquis]], that is, from those who utter against me words plainly malicious, stinging, mocking and slanderous, [[119:2|and a deceitful tongue|et a lingua dolosa]], that is, from him who by flattering, and by putting forward evil under the appearance of good, tries to turn my soul away from God, to draw it back from spiritual progress, or in some way to deceive it. From these the faithful man asks to be delivered: either so that he may not suffer them at all, and may be free for God more freely and more quietly (for the Apostle too says: [[2 Thess 3:1|pray|Orate]], he says, [[2 Thess 3:2|that we may be delivered from importunate and evil men|ut liberemur a malis et importunis hominibus]]); or so that he may not be troubled by them, nor hindered in good works, nor made impatient, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good.|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]

paras.t: Quæ autem sequuntur, dupliciter exponuntur. Primo, ut sint verba Prophetæ ad iniquum et dolosum ; eritque sensus : Quid detur tibi, aut quid apponatur tibi ad linguam dolosam ? id est, quid tibi, o impie, prodest, et quis fructus te consequetur, quod verba tam mala atque fallacia contra famulum Dei pronuntias ? Vel sic : Quid detur tibi, etc. ? id est, quæ, qualis, et quanta tibi pœna infligetur pro peccatis locutionis tuæ ? Et respondetur : Sagittæ potentis acutæ, id est, pœnæ omnipotentis Dei, quæ sunt valde acutæ et afflictivæ, tibi reddentur pro tuis peccatis, cum carbonibus desolatoriis, id est cum igne inferni inexstinguibili desolatorio, in quo nulla est consolatio de liberatione futura, sed desperatio sempiterna. Per sagittas acutas, intelliguntur pœnæ præsentis vitæ quæ impiis inferuntur, vel pœnæ futuræ, aliæ a pœna ignis tartarei. Per carbones vero desolatorios, significatur pœna infernalis incendii, quæ omnium pœnarum gravissima est.
paras.en: What follows is expounded in two ways. First, as words of the Prophet to the wicked and deceitful man; and the sense will be: [[119:3|What shall be given to thee, or what shall be added to thee, to a deceitful tongue?|Quid detur tibi, aut quid apponatur tibi ad linguam dolosam ?]] that is, what does it profit thee, O wicked man, and what fruit will come to thee, that thou utterest words so evil and false against the servant of God? Or thus: [[119:3|What shall be given to thee|Quid detur tibi]], etc.? that is, what punishment, of what kind and how great, shall be inflicted on thee for the sins of thy speech? And the answer is: [[119:4|The sharp arrows of the mighty|Sagittæ potentis acutæ]], that is, the punishments of almighty God, which are very sharp and painful, shall be paid back to thee for thy sins, [[119:4|with coals that lay waste|cum carbonibus desolatoriis]], that is, with the unquenchable, desolating fire of hell, in which there is no comfort of future deliverance, but everlasting despair. By the sharp arrows are understood the punishments of this present life that are brought upon the wicked, or the punishments to come other than the punishment of the fire of hell. But by the coals that lay waste [Latin *desolatorii*, "desolating"] is signified the punishment of the burning of hell, which is the heaviest of all punishments.

paras.t: Secundo exponuntur, ut sint verba Dei seu Prophetæ ad hominem virtuosum. Eritque sensus : O homo fidelis, Quid detur tibi auxilii, aut quid apponatur tibi remedii ad linguam dolosam vincendam ? tanquam dicat : Quid poterit tibi consilii atque subsidii dari, quo contra linguam iniquam armeris et superes ? Et respondet : Sagittæ potentis acutæ, id est verba Dei omnipotentis ignita et penetrativa, cum carbonibus desolatoriis, id est cum exemplis eorum qui post vitam facinorosam ad conversationem religiosam conversi sunt, dabuntur tibi pro armis contra linguam dolosam.
paras.en: Second, they are expounded as words of God, or of the Prophet, to the virtuous man. And the sense will be: O faithful man, [[119:3|What shall be given to thee|Quid detur tibi]] by way of help, [[119:3|or what shall be added to thee|aut quid apponatur tibi]] by way of remedy, [[119:3|to a deceitful tongue|ad linguam dolosam]], to overcome it? As if he said: What counsel and aid can be given thee, with which thou mayest be armed against the wicked tongue and overcome it? And he answers: [[119:4|The sharp arrows of the mighty|Sagittæ potentis acutæ]], that is, the fiery and piercing words of almighty God, [[119:4|with coals that lay waste|cum carbonibus desolatoriis]], that is, with the examples of those who after a life of crime have turned to the religious life, shall be given thee as arms against the deceitful tongue.

paras.t: Scientia enim Scripturarum, seu verba Spiritus Sancti, maxime valent contra linguam dolosam, ita ut nec ipsi efficiamur in loquendo dolosi, nec a lingua dolosa fallamur, neque per impatientiam superemur. Omnia enim ista implemus, si perpendamus quantum divina Scriptura reprobat linguam dolosam. Scriptum est enim : Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt ; et iterum, Maledictus dolosus ; denique, Virum sanguinem et dolosum abominabitur Dominus. In Ecclesiastico quoque : Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est ; in omni re fraudabitur. Non est illi data gratia a Deo, omni enim sapientia defraudatus est. Dicuntur autem verba sacræ Scripturæ sagittæ acutæ, quoniam animam vulnere caritatis transfigunt, peccata mortificant, interiora animæ penetrant. Unde scriptum est : Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum, et posuit me quasi sagittam electam. Et Apostolus ait : Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, et pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ ac spiritus. De his Christi sagittis dictum est ante : Sagittæ tuæ acutæ, populi sub te cadent, etc. Porro exempla Sanctorum dicuntur carbones desolatorii, id est vastatorii, quia ad amorem et imitationem nos invitant, et quidquid dæmon in nobis construxit, videlicet vitia et peccata, devastant, destruunt et expellunt.
paras.en: For the knowledge of the Scriptures, that is, the words of the Holy Ghost, avail most of all against the deceitful tongue, so that we ourselves do not become deceitful in speaking, nor are deceived by a deceitful tongue, nor are overcome through impatience. For we fulfil all these things if we weigh how greatly divine Scripture condemns the deceitful tongue. For it is written: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked|Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt]]; and again: [[Mal 1:14|Cursed is the deceitful man|Maledictus dolosus]]; and lastly: [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|Virum sanguinem et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]. In Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 37:23|He that speaketh sophistically, is hateful: he shall be destitute of every thing.|Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est ; in omni re fraudabitur.]] [[Ecclus 37:24|Grace is not given him from the Lord: for he is deprived of all wisdom.|Non est illi data gratia a Deo, omni enim sapientia defraudatus est.]] Now the words of holy Scripture are called sharp arrows because they pierce the soul through with the wound of charity, put sins to death, and penetrate the inmost parts of the soul. Hence it is written: [[Is 49:2|he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword|Posuit Dominus os meum quasi gladium acutum]], [[Is 49:2|and hath made me as a chosen arrow|et posuit me quasi sagittam electam]]. And the Apostle says: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living and effectual and more piercing than any two edged sword; and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit|Vivus est sermo Dei et efficax et penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, et pertingens usque ad divisionem animæ ac spiritus]]. Of these arrows of Christ it was said before: [[Ps 44:6|Thy arrows are sharp: under thee shall people fall|Sagittæ tuæ acutæ, populi sub te cadent]], etc. Further, the examples of the saints are called coals that lay waste, that is, that devastate, because they invite us to love and imitation, and whatever the devil has built up in us, namely vices and sins, they lay waste, destroy and drive out.

paras.t: Heu mihi misero et peregrino, quia incolatus meus, id est habitatio mea in præsenti exsilio, prolongatus est, id est, nimis longus mihi ad patriam adspiranti videtur. Hoc convenit his, qui fessi de vita præsenti, toto desiderio patriam appetunt : qui cum Apostolo dicere possunt, Nostra conversatio in cœlis est ; et, Cupio dissolvi et esse cum Christo ; et, Non habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus. Hi tales dicere possunt illud Tobiæ : Nunc, Domine, secundum voluntatem tuam fac mecum, et præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum ; expedit enim mihi mori magis quam vivere. Tales fuerunt antiqui Sancti, de quibus a Paulo dicitur : Defuncti sunt omnes isti, non acceptis repromissionibus, sed a longe eas adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram. Habitavi in isto exsilio cum habitantibus Cedar, id est cum peccatoribus tenebrosis et excæcatis. Cedar enim interpretatur tenebræ. Eratque Cedar filius Ismaelis.
paras.en: [[119:5|Woe is me|Heu mihi]], wretched man and stranger that I am, [[119:5|that my sojourning|quia incolatus meus]], that is, my dwelling in this present exile, [[119:5|is prolonged|prolongatus est]], that is, seems to me far too long as I yearn for my fatherland. This befits those who, weary of the present life, seek their fatherland with all their desire; who can say with the Apostle: [[Phil 3:20|our conversation is in heaven|Nostra conversatio in cœlis est]]; and: I desire [[Phil 1:23|to be dissolved and to be with Christ|dissolvi et esse cum Christo]]; and: [[Heb 13:14|we have not here a lasting city: but we seek one that is to come|Non habemus hic manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus]]. Such as these can say that word of Tobias: [[Tob 3:6|now, O Lord, do with me according to thy will, and command my spirit to be received in peace: for it is better for me to die, than to live|Nunc, Domine, secundum voluntatem tuam fac mecum, et præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum ; expedit enim mihi mori magis quam vivere]]. Such were the holy men of old, of whom Paul says: [[Heb 11:13|All these died|Defuncti sunt omnes isti]], [[Heb 11:13|not having received the promises but beholding them afar off and saluting them and confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth|non acceptis repromissionibus, sed a longe eas adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram]]. [[119:5|I have dwelt|Habitavi]] in this exile [[119:5|with the inhabitants of Cedar|cum habitantibus Cedar]], that is, with sinners darkened and blinded. For Cedar is interpreted "darkness". And Cedar was the son of Ismael[[Gen 25:13||]].

paras.t: Multum incola, id est exsul et peregrina, fuit anima mea in sæculo isto. Hic enim degit in regione dissimilitudinis, in carcere mortis, in gravi exsilio, ad patriam properans : a multis, in quibus quotidie evagatur, ad unum illud altissimum, in quo perpetue stabiliatur, gemens atque festinans.
paras.en: [[119:6|long a sojourner|Multum incola]], that is, an exile and a pilgrim, [[119:6|My soul hath been|fuit anima mea]] in this world. For here it lives in the region of unlikeness [the phrase of Augustine and St Bernard for the soul's estrangement from God, in whose likeness it was made], in the prison of death, in grievous exile, hastening towards its fatherland: from the many things among which it daily wanders, towards that one most high Good in which it may be established for ever, groaning and making haste.

paras.t: Cum his qui oderunt pacem, id est cum turbulentis et murmuratoribus, et sanctæ unitatis divisoribus, eram pacificus, non litigando, sed omnia patienter ferendo ; quum loquebar illis caritative, increpatorie, rationabiliter et modeste, impugnabant me gratis, id est sine causa condigna reddentes malum pro bono : prout apud Amos inducitur, Odio habuerunt corripientem, et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt.
paras.en: [[119:7|With them that hated peace|Cum his qui oderunt pacem]], that is, with the turbulent and the murmurers and the dividers of holy unity, [[119:7|I was peaceable|eram pacificus]], not by quarrelling, but by bearing all things patiently; [[119:7|when I spoke to them|quum loquebar illis]] in charity, in reproof, reasonably and modestly, [[119:7|they fought against me without cause|impugnabant me gratis]], that is, rendering evil for good without a just cause: as is set down in Amos: [[Amos 5:10|They have hated him that rebuketh|Odio habuerunt corripientem]], [[Amos 5:10|and have abhorred him that speaketh perfectly|et loquentem perfecte abominati sunt]].

119.title: EXPLANATIO ALLEGORICA PSALMI EJUSDEM CENTESIMI NONIDECIMI DE CHRISTO.
119.title_en: Allegorical explanation of the same hundred and nineteenth psalm, concerning Christ.

paras.t: Aliqui autem exponunt hunc psalmum ad litteram de populo Judæorum, in captivitate Babylonica exsistenti. Et quamvis littera ad hoc valeat applicari, parum tamen devotionis continet expositio talis. Melius ergo est, ut de Christo exponatur :
paras.en: Some, however, expound this psalm literally of the Jewish people in the Babylonian captivity. And although the letter can be applied to this, such an exposition holds little devotion. It is better, therefore, that it be expounded of Christ,

paras.t: in cujus persona loquens Propheta, ait : Ad Dominum, id est ad Deum Patrem, quum tribularer, id est passione instante seu præsente, quando cœpi tristari et pavere, quando factus est sudor meus sicut guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram, clamavi, dicendo : Pater, si fieri potest, transeat a me calix iste. Imo factus in agonia, prolixius oravi. Et exaudivit me Pater in eo quod dixi, Verumtamen non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua : quod intelligendum est de appetitu naturali, quo Christus homo horruit mortem. Hoc est quod dicit Apostolus : Christus in diebus carnis suæ, preces supplicationesque ad eum, qui possit illum salvum facere a morte, cum clamore valido et lacrimis offerens, exauditus est pro sua reverentia.
paras.en: in whose person the Prophet speaks, saying: [[119:1|to the Lord|Ad Dominum]], that is, to God the Father, [[119:1|In my trouble|quum tribularer]], that is, when my passion was at hand or present, when I began to be sorrowful and to fear[[Mark 14:33||]], when my sweat became [[Luke 22:44|as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground|sicut guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram]], [[119:1|I cried|clamavi]], saying: Father, if it be possible, [[Matt 26:39|let this chalice pass from me|transeat a me calix iste]]. Nay more, [[Luke 22:43|being in an agony|factus in agonia]], I prayed the longer. [[119:1|and he heard me|Et exaudivit me]], the Father, in that I said: [[Luke 22:42|but yet not my will, but thine be done|Verumtamen non mea voluntas fiat, sed tua]]: which is to be understood of the natural appetite by which Christ as man shrank from death. This is what the Apostle says: Christ, [[Heb 5:7|in the days of his flesh, with a strong cry and tears, offering up prayers and supplications to him that was able to save him from death, was heard for his reverence|in diebus carnis suæ, preces supplicationesque ad eum, qui possit illum salvum facere a morte, cum clamore valido et lacrimis offerens, exauditus est pro sua reverentia]].

paras.t: Domine Pater, libera animam meam, id est me ipsum, seu vitam meam corporalem, a labiis iniquis Judæorum clamantium, Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum, et a lingua dolosa Judæ proditoris, qui dixit : Quemcumque osculatus fuero, ipse est, tenete eum, et ducite eum caute. Postulat autem Christus liberari ab iis, non ut non occidatur, sed ne in morte detineatur.
paras.en: [[119:2|O Lord|Domine]] Father, [[119:2|deliver my soul|libera animam meam]], that is, myself, or my bodily life, [[119:2|from wicked lips|a labiis iniquis]] of the Jews crying out: [[John 19:15|Away with him: Away with him: Crucify him|Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum]], [[119:2|and a deceitful tongue|et a lingua dolosa]] of Judas the traitor, who said: [[Mark 14:44|Whomsoever I shall kiss, that is he. Lay hold on him: and lead him away carefully|Quemcumque osculatus fuero, ipse est, tenete eum, et ducite eum caute]]. Now Christ asks to be delivered from these, not so that he may not be slain, but so that he may not be held fast in death.

paras.t: Quod vero subjungitur, Quid detur tibi, aut quid apponatur tibi, etc. ? potest esse verbum Prophetæ ad adversarios Christi Judæos, secundum sensum in præcedenti articulo positum. Et respondetur : Sagittæ potentis acutæ, etc. Ubi per sagittas potentis acutas, intelliguntur pœnæ Judæis inflictæ a potente exercitu Romanorum, in ultionem sanguinis Christi. Per carbones quoque desolatorios intelliguntur combustiones, quibus Romani incenderunt et combusserunt templum et civitatem Jerusalem, et ceteras urbes Juda cum magna parte populi. De qua pœna Judæorum Isaias evidenter vaticinans, inter cetera ait : Laqueus juvenum omnes, et in domibus carceris absconditi : facti sunt in ruinam, nec est qui eruat ; in direptionem, nec est qui dicat, Redde. Quis dedit Jacob in direptionem, et Israel vastantibus eum ? Nonne Dominus ? Ipse est cui peccaverunt ; et noluerunt in viis ejus ambulare. Ipse combussit eum in circuitu, et non cognovit ; et succendit eum, et non intellexit. Hæc verba beatissimi Isaiæ de nulla alia oppressione Judæorum intelligi possunt, nisi de ea quam a Romanis perpessi sunt, in qua nunc usque premuntur et permanent ; nec tamen cognoscunt suum peccatum : idcirco veniam nullam merentur.
paras.en: But what follows, [[119:3|What shall be given to thee, or what shall be added to thee|Quid detur tibi, aut quid apponatur tibi]], etc.? can be the word of the Prophet to the Jews, the adversaries of Christ, in the sense set out in the preceding article. And the answer is: [[119:4|The sharp arrows of the mighty|Sagittæ potentis acutæ]], etc. Here by the sharp arrows of the mighty are understood the punishments inflicted on the Jews by the mighty army of the Romans in vengeance for the blood of Christ. And by the coals that lay waste are understood the burnings with which the Romans set on fire and burned down the temple and the city of Jerusalem and the other cities of Juda, with a great part of the people. Isaias, plainly prophesying of this punishment of the Jews, says among other things: [[Is 42:22|they are all the snare of young men, and they are hid in the houses of prisons: they are made a prey, and there is none to deliver them: a spoil, and there is none that saith: Restore|Laqueus juvenum omnes, et in domibus carceris absconditi : facti sunt in ruinam, nec est qui eruat ; in direptionem, nec est qui dicat, Redde]]. [[Is 42:24|Who hath given Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to robbers? hath not the Lord himself, against whom we have sinned? And they would not walk in his ways|Quis dedit Jacob in direptionem, et Israel vastantibus eum ? Nonne Dominus ? Ipse est cui peccaverunt ; et noluerunt in viis ejus ambulare]]. He [[Is 42:25|hath burnt him round about, and he knew not: and set him on fire, and he understood not|combussit eum in circuitu, et non cognovit ; et succendit eum, et non intellexit]]. These words of the most blessed Isaias can be understood of no other oppression of the Jews than that which they suffered from the Romans, under which they are weighed down and remain to this day; and yet they do not acknowledge their sin: therefore they merit no pardon.

paras.t: Deinde Christus ut viator aliquo modo exsistens atque passibilis, glorificandus, nondum glorificatus, ait : Heu mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Desideravit enim Christus ab isto exsilio liberari, ad patriamque reverti. Propter quod locutus est : O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero ? quamdiu patiar vos ? Et iterum : Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique, quia vado ad Patrem, id est, mihi de meo reditu ad Patrem gratulanti, congratularemini. Habitavi cum habitantibus Cedar, id est cum excæcatis et obtenebratis Judæis, inter quos multo conversatus sum tempore : prout alibi dicitur, Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est.
paras.en: Then Christ, being in some manner a wayfarer [Latin *viator*, one still on the way to the heavenly fatherland, as opposed to *comprehensor*, one who has reached it] and able to suffer, to be glorified but not yet glorified, says: [[119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] For Christ desired to be freed from this exile and to return to his fatherland. Because of this he said: [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I suffer you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero ? quamdiu patiar vos ?]] And again: [[John 14:28|If you loved me you would indeed be glad, because I go to the Father|Si diligeretis me, gauderetis utique, quia vado ad Patrem]] [the margin gives John xv, 28; the words are John 14:28]: that is, you would rejoice with me as I rejoice at my return to the Father. [[119:5|I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar|Habitavi cum habitantibus Cedar]], that is, with the blinded and darkened Jews, among whom I lived for a long time: as is said elsewhere: [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men.|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est.]]

paras.t: Multum incola, id est peregrina in hoc mundo, fuit anima mea. Incola enim vocatur, qui alienam terram immoratur vel colit, et a patria sua longe sejunctus est. Sic autem Christus peregrinus et incola erat in vita præsenti, quemadmodum Jeremias dixit ad eum : Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum ? Unde et Christus testatus est : Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo. Quamvis enim terra ista non sit aliena Christo conditione, quia creavit eam, et venit in propria ; dicitur tamen aliena, quoniam non erat ei pro patria.
paras.en: [[119:6|long a sojourner|Multum incola]], that is, a pilgrim in this world, [[119:6|My soul hath been|fuit anima mea]]. For he is called a sojourner [Latin *incola*, from *colere*, "to dwell in" or "to till"] who dwells in or tills a land not his own and is far separated from his fatherland. And so Christ was a pilgrim and a sojourner in this present life, as Jeremias said to him: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum ?]] Hence Christ too bore witness: [[John 18:36|My kingdom is not of this world|Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo]]. For although this earth is not foreign to Christ by its condition, since he created it, and [[John 1:11|He came unto his own|venit in propria]], yet it is called foreign, because it was not his fatherland.

paras.t: Cum his qui oderunt pacem, id est cum Judæis qui fraternæ caritatis concordiam, evangelicæ prædicationis pacem, veramque mentis in Deo tranquillitatem abjecerunt, adversantes mihi et meis discipulis, eram pacificus, nihil eis molestiæ inferens, imo bona pro malis restituens ; quum loquebar illis, redarguendo pessimam vitam eorum, prædicando eis contemptum divitiarum, et regnum cœlorum, dicendoque eis me esse Christum in lege promissum, impugnabant me verbis et ictibus gratis, dicentes, Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum ; et nunc tentantes me præcipitare, nunc lapidare, tandem vero me crucifigentes.
paras.en: [[119:7|With them that hated peace|Cum his qui oderunt pacem]], that is, with the Jews, who cast away the concord of brotherly charity, the peace of the gospel preaching, and the true tranquillity of the mind in God, opposing me and my disciples, [[119:7|I was peaceable|eram pacificus]], doing them no harm, nay, rendering good for evil; [[119:7|when I spoke to them|quum loquebar illis]], reproving their most wicked life, preaching to them contempt of riches and the kingdom of heaven, and telling them that I am the Christ promised in the law, [[119:7|they fought against me|impugnabant me]] with words and with blows [[119:7|without cause|gratis]], saying: [[John 8:13|Thou givest testimony of thyself. Thy testimony is not true|Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum]]; and now trying to cast me down headlong[[Luke 4:29||]], now to stone me[[John 10:31||]], and at last crucifying me[[Mark 15:25||]].

paras.t: Ecce in psalmo hoc brevi ac sententioso docemur, profectum nostrum spiritualem gradatim incipere per recessum a pristinis vitiis, sicut Scriptura hortatur : Fili, peccasti ? Ne adjicias iterum ; sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur ; et quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata. Docemur insuper, in omni tribulatione ad Deum clamare, eumque præcipue exorare, ut modis prædictis liberemur a labiis iniquis et lingua dolosa, tam aliorum quam propria. Corrumpunt enim mores bonos colloquia mala, secundum Apostolum. Edocet quoque nos psalmus iste, præsentem vitam cum omni sua voluptate et gloria aspernari, cœlestisque patriæ felicitatem præcordialissimo appetitu desiderare, et cum turbulentis hominibus pacifice conversari, quoniam Christo testante, Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.
paras.en: See, in this short and pithy psalm we are taught to begin our spiritual progress step by step by withdrawing from our former vices, as Scripture exhorts: [[Ecclus 21:1|My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more: but for thy former sins also pray that they may be forgiven thee|Fili, peccasti ? Ne adjicias iterum ; sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur]]; and [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata]]. We are taught besides to cry to God in every trouble, and above all to entreat him that, in the ways described, we may be delivered from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue, others' as well as our own. For [[1 Cor 15:33|Evil communications corrupt good manners|Corrumpunt enim mores bonos colloquia mala]], according to the Apostle. This psalm also teaches us to despise the present life with all its pleasure and glory, to desire the happiness of the heavenly fatherland with a longing from the depths of the heart, and to live peaceably with turbulent men, since, as Christ testifies: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.|Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.]]

paras.t: Precatio. Tribulationum nostrarum clamorem exaudi, Domine, et da nos in pace tua jugiter exsultare : ut contra pacem odientes, nosque impugnare quærentes, fortiter stemus, et tuæ potentiæ auxilio de his triumphemus.
paras.en: Prayer. Hear, O Lord, the cry of our troubles, and grant us to rejoice continually in thy peace: that we may stand firm against those who hate peace and seek to fight against us, and by the help of thy power may triumph over them.

120.title: DECLARATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI VICESIMI : LEVAVI OCULOS MEOS IN MONTES.
120.title_en: Explanation of the hundred and twentieth psalm: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains.

paras.t: Titulus psalmi est: Canticum graduum: cujus intellectus in præcedentis psalmi expositione apertus est. Hic autem est secundus psalmus gradualis: in quo agitur de secundo gradu spiritualis profectus, videlicet de imploratione divini auxilii, quod relinquentibus pristina vitia maxime necessarium est.
paras.en: The title of the psalm is: A Gradual Canticle; its meaning was made plain in the exposition of the preceding psalm. This is the second gradual psalm, in which the second step of spiritual progress is treated, namely the imploring of divine help, which is most necessary for those who are leaving their former vices behind.

paras.t: Ait ergo Propheta in persona hominis spiritualiter ascendentis, et priora peccata derelinquentis: Levavi, contemplando, orando, psallendo, amando, oculos meos præsertim intellectuales et etiam corporales, quatenus per exterioris visus elevationem, visus interior erigatur, in montes, id est ad cœlos, ad angelos sanctos, ad cives cœlestes. Unde ad sanctum Job dicitur: Ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere. Unde, id est de quibus montibus, veniet, ut confido, auxilium mihi: quia per angelos sanctos mittit nobis Creator omnipotens gratiam cœlestis auxilii. Omnes namque (secundum Apostolum) sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi, propter eos qui hereditatem capiunt salutis. Quoniam tamen auxilium istud est ab angelis instrumentaliter et ministerialiter, a Deo autem principaliter, ideo subditur: Auxilium meum a Domino, qui fecit cœlum et terram.
paras.en: The Prophet therefore says, in the person of a man who is ascending spiritually and leaving his former sins behind: [[120:1|I have lifted up|Levavi]], by contemplating, praying, singing psalms, loving, [[120:1|my eyes|oculos meos]], above all the eyes of the mind, and also those of the body, so that by the raising of the outward sight the inward sight may be lifted up, [[120:1|to the mountains|in montes]], that is, to the heavens, to the holy angels, to the citizens of heaven. Hence it is said to holy Job: [[Job 5:1|turn to some of the saints|Ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere]]. [[120:1|from whence|Unde]], that is, from which mountains, [[120:1|help shall come to me|veniet, ut confido, auxilium mihi]], as I trust: for through the holy angels the almighty Creator sends us the grace of heavenly help. For (according to the Apostle) they are all [[Heb 1:14|ministering spirits, sent to minister for them who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?|administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi, propter eos qui hereditatem capiunt salutis]] Yet since this help comes from the angels as instruments and ministers, but from God as its principal cause, it is added: [[120:2|My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.|Auxilium meum a Domino, qui fecit cælum et terram.]]

paras.t: Possunt quoque ista aliter explanari, hoc modo: Levavi oculos meos interiores in montes, id est ad altas considerationes, ad contemplationes sublimes. Ideo quæro: Unde veniet auxilium mihi? Et Spiritu Sancto instructus, respondeo: Auxilium meum a Domino, qui ait: Perditio tua, Israel, ex te; in me tantummodo auxilium tuum. Et alibi: Non in exercitu nec in robore, sed in spiritu meo, dicit Dominus. Itaque auxilium meum a Domino, non particulari, sed universali, omnibus dominante, qui fecit cœlum et terram, quemadmodum in Genesi scribitur: In principio creavit Deus cœlum et terram. Per cœlum vero et terram, hoc loco intelligenda sunt omnia intermedia atque universa in eis contenta. Præsertim autem per cœlum intelligitur cœlum empyreum, quod (secundum Damascenum) est continentia visibilium et invisibilium.
paras.en: These words can also be explained otherwise, in this way: [[120:1|I have lifted up my eyes|Levavi oculos meos]], the inward ones, [[120:1|to the mountains|in montes]], that is, to lofty considerations, to sublime contemplations. Therefore I ask: [[120:1|from whence help shall come to me|Unde veniet auxilium mihi]]? And, taught by the Holy Ghost, I answer: [[120:2|My help is from the Lord|Auxilium meum a Domino]], who says: [[Osee 13:9|Destruction is thy own, O Israel: thy help is only in me|Perditio tua, Israel, ex te; in me tantummodo auxilium tuum]] [the margin gives Osee xii, 9; the words are at Osee 13:9]. And elsewhere: [[Zach 4:6|Not with an army, nor by might, but by my spirit, saith the Lord|Non in exercitu nec in robore, sed in spiritu meo, dicit Dominus]]. So [[120:2|My help is from the Lord|auxilium meum a Domino]], not from a particular lord but from the universal Lord, ruling over all, [[120:2|who made heaven and earth|qui fecit cœlum et terram]], as is written in Genesis: [[Gen 1:1|In the beginning God created heaven, and earth|In principio creavit Deus cælum et terram.]]. By heaven and earth are to be understood here all that lies between them and everything contained in them. But by heaven is meant above all the empyrean heaven, which (according to Damascene) is the container of things visible and invisible.

paras.t: Hac igitur divini auxilii fultus fiducia, vir fidelis se ipsum affatur, dicendo: Non det in commotionem pedem tuum, id est, spiritualem tuum profectum, cordis tui affectum, animæ tuæ stabilitatem non permittat Deus deficere, cadere, disperire; neque dormitet, id est, per modum fatigati seu dormientis se non habeat, qui custodit te, id est Deus omnipotens, qui est omnium electorum præcipuus custos. Et ecce vir sanctus ex interiori Spiritus Sancti instinctu se exauditum advertens, adjecit:
paras.en: Upheld, then, by this trust in God's help, the faithful man speaks to himself, saying: [[120:3|May he not suffer thy foot to be moved|Non det in commotionem pedem tuum]], that is, may God not allow thy spiritual progress, the affection of thy heart, the stability of thy soul, to fail, to fall, to perish; [[120:3|neither let him slumber|neque dormitet]], that is, let him not behave as one weary or asleep, [[120:3|that keepeth thee|qui custodit te]], that is, almighty God, who is the chief keeper of all the elect. And behold, the holy man, perceiving by the inward prompting of the Holy Ghost that he has been heard, added:

paras.t: Ecce non dormitabit, tanquam lassus, neque dormiet, tanquam ab exteriori exercitio cessans, qui custodit per gratiam et angelorum subministrationem Israel, id est plebem fidelium, seu unumquemque fidelem: quoniam Deus electos suos incessanter custodit, gubernat et protegit, juxta illud, Ego Deus tuus docens te utilia, gubernans te in via qua ambulas. Dicuntur autem Deus et angeli sancti dormire seu dormitare, sicut dicuntur irasci et pœnitere, videlicet secundum similitudinem, non secundum veritatem. Dicitur ergo Deus dormire, dum cessat gratiose succurrere.
paras.en: [[120:4|Behold he shall neither slumber|Ecce non dormitabit]], as one tired, [[120:4|nor sleep|neque dormiet]], as one ceasing from outward activity, [[120:4|that keepeth|qui custodit]], by grace and by the ministry of the angels, [[120:4|Israel|Israel]], that is, the people of the faithful, or each one of the faithful: for God unceasingly keeps, governs and protects his elect, according to the words: [[Is 48:17|I am the Lord thy God that teach thee profitable things, that govern thee in the way that thou walkest|Ego Deus tuus docens te utilia, gubernans te in via qua ambulas]]. Now God and the holy angels are said to sleep or to slumber in the way they are said to be angry and to repent, that is, by a likeness, not in truth. God, then, is said to sleep when he ceases to come to our aid with his grace.

paras.t: Dominus custodit te, in bono conservans, et a malo præservans te in via præsentis exsilii. Unde a viro sancto dicitur: Sit Dominus in itinere vestro, et angelus ejus comitetur vobiscum. Dominus protectio tua, id est causa protectionis tuæ seu protector tuus, super manum dexteram tuam, id est, magis ac fortius quam dextera tua, quæ fortius defendere solet, te protegere posset. Propter quod ait: Ego protector tuus sum.
paras.en: [[120:5|The Lord is thy keeper|Dominus custodit te]], keeping thee in good and guarding thee from evil on the way of this present exile. Hence a holy man says: [[Tob 5:21|God be with you in your way, and his angel accompany you|Sit Dominus in itinere vestro, et angelus ejus comitetur vobiscum]]. [[120:5|the Lord is thy protection|Dominus protectio tua]], that is, the cause of thy protection, or thy protector, [[120:5|upon thy right hand|super manum dexteram tuam]], that is, he could protect thee more, and more strongly, than thy right hand, which is the stronger hand in defence. Therefore he says: [[Gen 15:1|I am thy protector|Ego protector tuus sum]].

paras.t: Per diem sol non uret te, neque luna per noctem. Quemadmodum tempus seu dies et nox dicuntur facere quæ in ipsis fiunt, prout in libro Machabæorum habetur, Vidit Jonathas quia tempus eum juvat; sic sol qui præest diei, eamque causat, et luna præsidens nocti, asseruntur ea efficere quæ in die fiunt aut nocte. Et hoc modo dixit quidam anachoreta ad alium: Infra quadraginta annos non vidit me sol manducantem. Cui alter: Nec me, inquit, irascentem. Et in libro Judicum: Stellæ manentes in cursu et ordine suo, adversum Sisaram dimicaverunt. Est itaque sensus: Per diem sol non uret te, id est, in die non ureris, non destrueris, neque peribis; neque luna per noctem, id est, tempore nocturno non ureris sicut nec in die. Quem enim Deus custodit et protegit, nunquam uritur, id est, nunquam spiritualiter consumitur flamma libidinis, igne impietatis, ardore peccati. Sicque scriptum est: Quum ambulaveris in igne, non combureris, et flamma non ardebit in te. Hoc cantat Ecclesia de sanctis quibusdam martyribus, qui utique corporaliter combusti sunt igne, non autem secundum sensum prædictum.
paras.en: [[120:6|The sun shall not burn thee by day: nor the moon by night.|Per diem sol non uret te, neque luna per noctem.]] Just as time, or day and night, are said to do what is done in them, as we read in the book of the Machabees, [[1 Mach 12:1|Jonathan saw that the time served him|Vidit Jonathas quia tempus eum juvat]], so the sun, which rules the day and causes it, and the moon, which presides over the night, are said to do what is done by day or by night. In this way a certain anchorite said to another: In forty years the sun has not seen me eating. And the other answered: Nor me angry. And in the book of Judges: [[Judg 5:20|the stars, remaining in their order and courses, fought against Sisara|Stellæ manentes in cursu et ordine suo, adversum Sisaram dimicaverunt]]. So the sense is: [[120:6|The sun shall not burn thee by day|Per diem sol non uret te]], that is, by day thou shalt not be burned, not be destroyed, nor perish; [[120:6|nor the moon by night|neque luna per noctem]], that is, in the night-time thou shalt not be burned, any more than by day. For he whom God keeps and protects is never burned, that is, is never spiritually consumed by the flame of lust, the fire of impiety, the heat of sin. And so it is written: [[Is 43:2|when thou shalt walk in the fire, thou shalt not be burnt, and the flames shall not burn in thee|Quum ambulaveris in igne, non combureris, et flamma non ardebit in te]]. The Church sings this of certain holy martyrs, who were indeed burned with fire in the body, but not in the sense just given.

paras.t: Dominus custodit te ab omni malo culpæ mortalis, et etiam a malo pœnæ: non ut non patiaris, quum per multas tribulationes oporteat nos salvari; sed ne pœna animæ tuæ noceat; imo Deo ordinante, ineffabiliter proficit ei, quia per eam servando patientiam, meretur vitam æternam. Itaque Dominus custodit te, o homo electe, ab omni malo: vel simpliciter ab omni malo, si nullum incidis malum; vel, ab omni malo, a quo custodiris seu præservaris, ut scias donum Dei esse, si aliquod malum evadis. Custodiat animam tuam Dominus, ne gratiam perdas, ne caro ei prævaleat, ne finaliter pereat.
paras.en: [[120:7|The Lord keepeth thee from all evil|Dominus custodit te ab omni malo]] of mortal guilt, and also from the evil of punishment: not so that thou shouldst not suffer, since [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must|per multas tribulationes oporteat nos]] be saved [Denis has "be saved" where the Acts has "enter into the kingdom of God"], but so that the punishment may not harm thy soul; rather, by God's ordering, it profits the soul beyond words, since by keeping patience through it the soul merits eternal life. So [[120:7|The Lord keepeth thee|Dominus custodit te]], O elect man, [[120:7|from all evil|ab omni malo]]: either simply from all evil, if thou fallest into no evil at all; or, from all evil from which thou art kept or preserved, so that thou mayest know that it is the gift of God if thou escapest any evil. [[120:7|may the Lord keep thy soul|Custodiat animam tuam Dominus]], that thou lose not grace, that the flesh prevail not against it, that it perish not in the end.

paras.t: Dominus custodiat introitum tuum et exitum tuum, ex hoc nunc et usque in sæculum, id est omnia opera tua interiora et exteriora. Vel: Introitum tuum, id est inchoationem, dum opus bonum aggrediris; et exitum tuum, id est operis consummationem, quatenus cuncta operatio tua a Deo semper incipiat, et per eum cœpta finiatur. Vel: Introitum tuum, id est conversationem tuam in hoc mundo, per quam hunc locum peregrinationis præsentis ingrederis; et exitum tuum, quo a corpore separaberis, mundum exibis. De isto introitu et exitu ait Salvator: Ego sum ostium; per me si quis introierit, salvabitur; et ingredietur et egredietur, et pascua inveniet.
paras.en: [[120:8|May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; from henceforth now and for ever|Dominus custodiat introitum tuum et exitum tuum, ex hoc nunc et usque in sæculum]]: that is, all thy works, inward and outward. Or: [[120:8|thy coming in|introitum tuum]], that is, the beginning, when thou undertakest a good work; [[120:8|and thy going out|et exitum tuum]], that is, the completion of the work, so that all thy working may always begin from God and, once begun, be finished through him. Or: [[120:8|thy coming in|introitum tuum]], that is, thy life in this world, by which thou enterest this place of present pilgrimage; [[120:8|and thy going out|et exitum tuum]], by which thou shalt be separated from the body and go out of the world. Of this coming in and going out the Saviour says: [[John 10:9|I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved: and he shall go in and go out, and shall find pastures|Ego sum ostium; per me si quis introierit, salvabitur; et ingredietur et egredietur, et pascua inveniet]].

paras.t: Ecce psalmum jucundum et doctrinalem audivimus: in quo nobis divina providentia hilariter commendatur. Levemus igitur oculos nostros ad angelos sanctos, devotissime invocantes singuli eos, quibus specialiter sumus commissi, ut nunquam desinant nos propitie intueri, custodire, defendere; totumque nostrum auxilium constituamus in Deo, dicentes illud Job: Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a delightful and instructive psalm, in which divine providence is joyfully commended to us. Let us therefore lift up our eyes to the holy angels, each of us most devoutly calling upon those to whom we have been especially committed, that they may never cease to look upon us with favour, to keep us, to defend us; and let us place all our help in God, saying those words of Job: [[Job 6:13|Behold there is no help for me in myself|Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me]].

paras.t: Precatio. Custos Israel indefessus, qui non dormitas neque dormis, Deus, sis (quæsumus), Domine, nobis assidua protectio, custodiens nos ab omni malo, fidei nostræ introitum et vitæ exitum usque in sæculum disponens.
paras.en: Prayer. O God, unwearied Keeper of Israel, who dost neither slumber nor sleep, be thou (we beseech thee), O Lord, our unfailing protection, keeping us from all evil, and ordering the coming in of our faith and the going out of our life for ever.

121.title_en: Explanation of the hundred and twenty-first psalm: I rejoiced at the things that were said to me.

paras.t: Porro titulus psalmi præsentis, est in sensu et verbis idem cum titulo psalmi præcedentis, videlicet, Canticum graduum. Videturque ad litteram psalmus iste loqui de ædificatione templi a Salomone constructi: quod David sciens futurum, ita exorsus est:
paras.en: Now the title of the present psalm is the same in sense and in words as the title of the preceding psalm, namely, [[121:1|A gradual canticle|Canticum graduum]]. And according to the letter this psalm seems to speak of the building of the temple built by Solomon[[3 Kings 5:1||]]; knowing that this was to come, David began thus:

paras.t: Lætatus […] sunt mihi, per revelationem divinam et Nathan prophetam. Et quæ sint hæc, pandit: In domum Domini, id est in templum a filio meo Salomone ædificandum, ibimus. Quamvis autem domum istam David ingressus non sit, quoniam ante ejus constructionem defunctus est, connumerat tamen se aliis qui introierunt, eo modo loquendi quo aliquid dicitur fieri a communitate, quoniam fit ab aliquibus ad communitatem pertinentibus. Legitur autem, qualiter David proposuit ædificare templum Deo Israel, qui misit ad eum Nathan prophetam, dicens per eum, quod ipse non ædificaret sibi templum, sed filius ejus.
paras.en: [[121:1|I rejoiced|Lætatus]] […] [[121:1|to me|sunt mihi]], through divine revelation and through Nathan the prophet[[2 Kings 7:12||]][[2 Kings 7:13||]]. And what these things are, he discloses: [[121:1|into the house of the Lord|In domum Domini]], that is, into the temple to be built by my son Solomon, [[121:1|We shall go|ibimus]]. Now although David did not enter this house, since he died before it was built, he nevertheless counts himself among the others who entered it, in the manner of speaking by which something is said to be done by a community because it is done by some who belong to that community. For we read how David purposed to build a temple to the God of Israel, who sent Nathan the prophet to him, saying through him that he himself should not build him a temple, but his son[[2 Kings 7:1||]].

paras.t: Stantes erant pedes nostri, id est, nos ipsi populus Dei, seu filii Israel, stetimus corporaliter in atriis tuis, o Jerusalem, id est in atriis templi et civitatis. Habuit namque templum Salomonis plura atria. Unum, in quo stabant et offerebant sacerdotes; aliud, in quo stabant et exorabant homines mundi; tertium erat atrium immundorum. Similiter civitatem Jerusalem clausit Salomon triplici muro: sicque plura atria habuit civitas. De qua subditur:
paras.en: [[121:2|Our feet were standing|Stantes erant pedes nostri]], that is, we ourselves, the people of God, or the children of Israel, stood bodily [[121:2|in thy courts, O Jerusalem|in atriis tuis, o Jerusalem]], that is, in the courts of the temple and of the city. For Solomon's temple had several courts[[3 Kings 6:36||]]: one, in which the priests stood and offered; another, in which the clean [homines mundi, that is, those free of legal uncleanness] stood and prayed; the third was the court of the unclean. In the same way Solomon enclosed the city of Jerusalem with a triple wall[[3 Kings 9:15||]], and so the city had several courts. Of it there follows:

paras.t: Jerusalem est quæ ædificatur ut civitas, id est, a Salomone ædificatur, vel potius in ædificiis melioratur, tam excellenter atque regaliter, sicut decet regiam civitatem seu regni metropolim ædificari; cujus participatio ejus in id ipsum, id est, civitas ista associata est templo: nam in Hebraeo habetur, Quæ associatur ei simul. Vel dicitur, Participatio ejus in id ipsum, propter civium communionem et pacificam conversationem, vel propter ædificiorum mutuam confortationem ac decorationem.
paras.en: [[121:3|Jerusalem, which is built as a city|Jerusalem est quæ ædificatur ut civitas]], that is, is built by Solomon, or rather is bettered in its buildings, as excellently and royally as befits the building of a royal city, the capital of a kingdom; [[121:3|which is compact together|cujus participatio ejus in id ipsum]] [literally "whose sharing is in the selfsame": hence Denis's several readings], that is, this city is joined to the temple: for in the Hebrew we have: Which is joined to it together. Or it is said to be [[121:3|compact together|participatio ejus in id ipsum]] because of the fellowship and peaceful life of the citizens, or because the buildings strengthen and adorn one another.

paras.t: Illuc enim, id est ad hanc civitatem et templum in ea constructum, ascenderunt tribus, videlicet tribus Domini, id est duodecim tribus Israel: quæ dicuntur tribus Domini, quia ceteris gentibus ad idololatriam devolutis, ipsi unum verum Deum coluerunt; testimonium Israel, id est, sicut Jacob, alio nomine Israel dictus, testatus est, et sicut ei Deus prædixit. Nam de ædificatione templi Jacob prophetavit: Quam terribilis, inquiens, est locus iste! Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei. Ascenderunt itaque ad confitendum nomini Domini, id est, ut Deum laudarent, ejusque beneficia recognoscerent in templo diebus solennibus, sicut in lege Moysis continetur. Non enim poterant offerre sacrificium, nisi in uno loco, id est templo ædificato.
paras.en: [[121:4|For thither|Illuc enim]], that is, to this city and to the temple built in it, [[121:4|did the tribes go up|ascenderunt tribus]], namely [[121:4|the tribes of the Lord|tribus Domini]], that is, the twelve tribes of Israel, which are called the tribes of the Lord because, while the other nations had sunk into idolatry, they worshipped the one true God; [[121:4|the testimony of Israel|testimonium Israel]], that is, as Jacob, called by another name Israel[[Gen 32:28||]][[Gen 35:10||]], testified, and as God foretold to him. For Jacob prophesied of the building of the temple, saying: [[Gen 28:17|How terrible|Quam terribilis]], he said, [[Gen 28:17|is this place? this is no other but the house of God|est locus iste! Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei]]. They went up, then, [[121:4|to praise the name of the Lord|ad confitendum nomini Domini]], that is, to praise God and to acknowledge his benefits in the temple on the solemn days, as is laid down in the law of Moses[[Deut 16:16||]]. For they could not offer sacrifice except in one place, that is, in the temple once it was built.

paras.t: Quia illic, videlicet in civitate et templo Jerusalem, sederunt sedes: ponitur continens pro contento, ut sit sensus, Sedes, id est sedentes in sedibus judicialibus; in judicio, id est, ut judicarent populum. Ad reges namque et summos sacerdotes in Jerusalem habitantes, pertinebat determinare causas dubiosas et magnas emergentes, sicut in Deuteronomio scriptum est. Sedes super domum David, id est, sedentes seu præsidentes isti sederunt super domum David, quatenus populum seu familiam David regis juste judicarent.
paras.en: [[121:5|Because|Quia illic]] there, namely in the city and temple of Jerusalem, [[121:5|their seats have sat|sederunt sedes]]: the container is put for what it contains, so that the sense is: the seats, that is, those sitting on the seats of judgment; [[121:5|in judgment|in judicio]], that is, to judge the people. For it belonged to the kings and high priests dwelling in Jerusalem to decide the doubtful and great cases that arose, as is written in Deuteronomy[[Deut 17:8||]]. [[121:5|seats upon the house of David|Sedes super domum David]], that is, these who sat or presided sat over the house of David, so as to judge justly the people or household of King David.

paras.t: Deinde invitat Propheta alios ad orandum pro bono statu Jerusalem. Rogate, o filii Israel, Deum ea quæ ad pacem sunt Jerusalem, id est populo habitanti in ea; et abundantia spiritualium et temporalium bonorum detur divinitus diligentibus te, o Jerusalem, civitas Dei summi.
paras.en: Then the Prophet invites others to pray for the good estate of Jerusalem. [[121:6|Pray ye|Rogate]], O children of Israel, to God [[121:6|for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem|ea quæ ad pacem sunt Jerusalem]], that is, of the people dwelling in it; [[121:6|and abundance|et abundantia]] of spiritual and temporal goods be given by God [[121:6|for them that love thee|diligentibus te]], O Jerusalem, city of the most high God.

paras.t: Fiat pax in virtute tua, id est in forti tua structura, ne adversarius te expugnet; et abundantia victualium fiat, o Jerusalem, in turribus tuis: in quibus custodes civitatis vigilare et arma reponere solent.
paras.en: [[121:7|Let peace be in thy strength|Fiat pax in virtute tua]], that is, in thy strong building, lest an enemy take thee by storm; [[121:7|and abundance|et abundantia]] of victuals be, O Jerusalem, [[121:7|in thy towers|in turribus tuis]], in which the watchmen of the city are wont to keep watch and to store their arms.

paras.t: Propter fratres meos, id est Judæos cognatos, et proximos meos, id est ceteros fideles, loquebar pacem de te, id est, Deum in oratione affatus sum, deprecans eum pro pace tua. Ordinatur enim locus seu civitas ad populum, non populus ad civitatem. Idcirco orandum est pro pace civitatis propter populum, non econtra.
paras.en: [[121:8|For the sake of my brethren|Propter fratres meos]], that is, the Jews, my kinsmen, [[121:8|and of my neighbours|et proximos meos]], that is, the rest of the faithful, [[121:8|I spoke peace of thee|loquebar pacem de te]], that is, I addressed God in prayer, beseeching him for thy peace. For a place or city is ordered to the people, not the people to the city. Therefore one must pray for the peace of the city for the sake of the people, not the other way round.

paras.t: Maxime vero orandum est pro pace loci, quatenus cultus Dei augeatur. Ideo additur: Propter domum Domini Dei nostri, id est propter templum et cultum divinum in eo perficiendum, quæsivi orando bona, id est statum pacificum abundantiamque bonorum, tibi, o Jerusalem.
paras.en: But above all one must pray for the peace of the place, so that the worship of God may be increased. Therefore it is added: [[121:9|Because of the house of the Lord our God|Propter domum Domini Dei nostri]], that is, for the sake of the temple and of the divine worship to be carried out in it, [[121:9|I have sought|quæsivi]] in prayer [[121:9|good things|bona]], that is, a peaceful state and an abundance of goods, [[121:9|for thee|tibi]], O Jerusalem.

121.note: The heading of this article (its number and Latin title) is missing from the transcription; the English title is supplied. A few words at the start of v. 1 are also lost, marked […].

121.title: EXPOSITIO EJUSDEM PSALMI CENTESIMI VICESIMI PRIMI ANAGOGICA, ET QUOMODO ALLEGORICE POSSIT EXPONI.
121.title_en: Anagogical exposition of the same hundred and twenty-first psalm, and how it can be expounded allegorically.

paras.t: Anagogicum denique intellectum sequendo, loquitur Propheta de cœlesti Jerusalem, de qua ait Apostolus: Illa quæ sursum est Jerusalem, libera est: quæ est mater nostra. Congrue autem ponitur hic tertius psalmus gradualis post duos præcedentes: quoniam primus gradus ascensionis internæ, est exire de malis et vitiis sæculi; secundus, implorare auxilium Dei; tertius, confidere de perventione ad ultimum finem seu vitam æternam: de quo utique gradu hic psalmus pertractat.
paras.en: Finally, following the anagogical sense [that is, the sense that leads the mind up to the things of heaven], the Prophet speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says: [[Gal 4:26|that Jerusalem which is above is free: which is our mother|Illa quæ sursum est Jerusalem, libera est: quæ est mater nostra]]. And this third gradual psalm is fittingly set after the two before it: for the first step of the inward ascent is to go out from the evils and vices of the world; the second, to implore the help of God; the third, to be confident of reaching the last end, that is, eternal life: and it is of this step that this psalm treats.

paras.t: Loquens ergo Propheta in persona hominis præsentia cuncta parvi pendentis, mansionemque cœlestem præcordialiter cupientis, ait: Lætatus sum in Domino, spirituali lætitia, in his, id est ex consideratione horum, quæ dicta sunt mihi a Prophetis atque Apostolis successoribusque ipsorum, vel per revelationem angelicam, seu inspirationem internam. Quæ autem dicta sint, subdit: In domum Domini, id est in Ecclesiam triumphantem, in patriam Beatorum, in regnum cœlorum, ibimus, post hujus vitæ incolatum, quum ab omni reatu fuerimus expurgati.
