Consuetudo namque Scripturæ est, præsertim in his quæ pertinent ad affectum, idem sub aliis verbis frequenter repetere : quod fit propter rationabilissimam ac utilissimam causam, videlicet ut affectus in se ipso incalescat et recalescat, dum proprium desiderium replicatur et renovatur. Una quippe bona affectio aliam nutrit : imo una affectio ardens, aliam sibi in specie similem multum inflammat. Ideo adhuc subditur : in veritate tua exaudi me, id est, sicuti promisisti quod orantem exaudires, ita exaudi me. Scriptum est enim : Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum; et iterum, Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit; et rursus, Quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum ? Itaque, In veritate tua exaudi me in tua justitia, id est, sicut hoc justum est coram te, ut facias sicut dixisti. Vel, In tua justitia, id est, merito conversationis seu operationis meæ justæ : quæ dicitur tua justitia, quoniam a te mihi collata est, propter quod non mihi, sed tibi, eam adscribo. Hoc modo exaudiri in justitia Dei oravit Ezechias, dicens : Obsecro, Domine, memento, quæso, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et in corde perfecto.
paras.en: Now although a distinction can be drawn between prayer and supplication, since supplication is properly so called when we ask something of God by some holy thing, as when we say, "By thy nativity deliver us, O Lord" [from the Litany of the Saints], or, "For thy mercy's or thy goodness' sake hear me, O Lord", yet in this place they can be taken for the same thing. For it is the custom of Scripture, especially in what belongs to the affections, often to repeat the same thing in other words: and this is done for a most reasonable and most profitable cause, namely that the affection may grow warm and warm again within itself, while its own desire is turned over and renewed. For one good affection feeds another; nay, one burning affection greatly kindles another like it in kind. Therefore he adds further: [[142:1|in thy truth: hear me|in veritate tua exaudi me]]; that is, as thou hast promised that thou wouldst hear one who prays, so hear me. For it is written: [[Deut 4:29|when thou shalt seek there the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him|Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum]]; and again, [[Joel 2:32|every one that shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved|Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit]]; and once more, [[Ecclus 2:12|who hath called upon him, and he despised him?|Quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum]] So then, [[142:1|in thy truth: hear me|In veritate tua exaudi me]] [[142:1|in thy justice|in tua justitia]], that is, as this is just before thee, that thou do as thou hast said. Or, [[142:1|in thy justice|In tua justitia]], that is, by the merit of my just conduct or working, which is called thy justice because it was bestowed on me by thee, and for that reason I ascribe it not to myself but to thee. In this way Ezechias prayed to be heard in the justice of God, saying: [[Is 38:3|I beseech thee, O Lord, remember how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart|Obsecro, Domine, memento, quæso, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et in corde perfecto]].

paras.t: Et non intres in judicium cum servo tuo. Superius sæpe dixit Psalmista, Judica me, Domine, seu aliquid simile. Nunc vero precatur ut Deus non intret secum in judicium. Illic ergo locutus est de judicio discretionis, quo in præsenti vita boni discernuntur a malis voto et merito. Sicque orare debemus ut Deus judicet nos, id est, a malis discernat ac dividat. Nunc vero loquitur de judicio districtæ discussionis, seu justæ ultionis. Est igitur sensus : Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, id est, noli me servum tuum secundum rigorem tuæ justitiæ judicare et condemnare. Noli mihi reddere secundum exigentiam iniquitatis meæ ; sed secundum misericordiam tuam indulge mihi et salva me. — Ad litteram dixit hoc David pro se ipso. Persecutionem enim filii sui patiebatur propter adulterium suum cum Bethsabee, homicidiumque Uriæ, sicut Nathan propheta sibi prædixit. Secundum rigorem vero divinæ justitiæ, meruit mortem propter utrumque. Lex namque tam adulterium, quam homicidium ulciscitur morte. Idcirco David oravit ne sicut justitia exigebat, reciperet. Adducit autem et persuasionem ad hoc :
paras.en: [[142:2|And enter not into judgment with thy servant|Et non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]]. Above, the Psalmist often said, [[Ps 7:9|Judge me, O Lord|Judica me, Domine]][[Ps 25:1||]][[Ps 34:24||]][[Ps 42:1||]], or something like it. But now he prays that God enter not into judgment with him. There, then, he spoke of the judgment of discernment, by which in the present life the good are distinguished from the wicked in will and in merit; and so we ought to pray that God judge us, that is, distinguish and separate us from the wicked. But here he speaks of the judgment of strict examination, or of just vengeance. The sense, then, is: [[142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]]; that is, do not judge and condemn me thy servant according to the rigour of thy justice. Do not repay me as my iniquity demands; but according to thy mercy pardon me and save me. Literally, David said this for himself. For he suffered persecution from his son on account of his adultery with Bethsabee and the murder of Urias[[2 Kings 12:9||]], as Nathan the prophet had foretold to him[[2 Kings 12:11||]]. And according to the rigour of divine justice he deserved death for each of them; for the Law punishes with death both adultery[[Deut 22:22||]] and murder[[Lev 24:17||]]. Therefore David prayed that he might not receive as justice demanded. And he brings forward an argument for this:

paras.t: Quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens : id est, nullus homo vivens in sæculo isto, justus est coram te perfecta justitia, quasi nihil habeat de injustitia seu peccato ; sed omnis homo viator aliquid habet de injustitia, propter quam petere debet ne intres secum in judicium. Hinc enim Joannes : Si dixerimus, inquit, quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus. Paulus quoque : Omnes peccaverunt et egent gloria (id est gloriosa misericordia) Dei. Denique, Salomone testante, septies in die cadit justus. Et : Quis potest dicere, Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato ? Hinc in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Non te justifices ante Deum. Sed si hæc ita se habent, quid est quod Ezechias, Jeremias, Esther, Judith, et alii multi leguntur suas coram Deo justitias atque perfectiones præcipuas allegasse, sicut nunc sæpe commemoratum recordor ? Et respondendum, quod non simpliciter, sed humano modo se justos dixerunt, scientes utique quod omnes eorum justitiæ essent coram Deo sicut pannus menstruatæ. Unde quod dictum est, Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens, non est ita intelligendum, quod nullus homo vivens, coram Deo aliquo modo justificabitur : imo in die judicii non solum in conspectu Dei, sed etiam a Deo justificabuntur, seu justi dicentur, omnes qui audient, Venite, benedicti Patris mei. Sic ergo convenienter accipitur : Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo, id est in comparatione tuæ justitiæ, omnis vivens. Propter quod scriptum est : Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo. Et iterum : Ecce luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus : quanto magis homo putredo, et filius hominis vermis ! Hinc rursus apertissime scriptum est : Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur? Bene ergo et vere ait sanctus Apostolus : Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis. Alia enim sunt judicia Dei, et alia judicia hominum. Indesinenter igitur cum omni humilitate dicamus Deo : Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, Domine, quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens.
paras.en: [[142:2|for in thy sight no man living shall be justified|Quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]]: that is, no man living in this world is just before thee with a perfect justice, as though he had nothing of injustice or sin; but every man on the way [that is, still a pilgrim in this life, not yet in the homeland] has something of injustice, on account of which he ought to ask that thou enter not into judgment with him. Hence John: [[1 John 1:8|If we say|Si dixerimus]], he says, [[1 John 1:8|that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves|quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus]]. Paul also: [[Rom 3:23|all have sinned and do need the glory|Omnes peccaverunt et egent gloria]] (that is, the glorious mercy) [[Rom 3:23|of God|Dei]]. Lastly, as Solomon testifies, [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times|septies in die cadit justus]] [Denis reads "falls seven times in a day"]. And: [[Prov 20:9|Who can say: My heart is clean, I am pure from sin?|Quis potest dicere, Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato]] Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God|Non te justifices ante Deum]]. But if these things are so, how is it that Ezechias[[Is 38:3||]], Jeremias[[Jer 15:15||]], Esther[[Esth 14:15||]], Judith[[Jdt 16:8||]] [the margin gives Judith xvi, 8–12], and many others are read to have pleaded before God their justice and their outstanding perfections, as I remember having now often mentioned? The answer is that they called themselves just not simply, but in a human way, knowing well that all their justices were before God [[Is 64:6|as the rag of a menstruous woman|sicut pannus menstruatæ]]. Hence what is said, [[142:2|in thy sight no man living shall be justified|Non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]], is not to be understood as though no man living will in any way be justified before God: nay, on the day of judgment all shall be justified, or called just, not only in the sight of God but also by God, who shall hear, [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father|Venite, benedicti Patris mei]]. So, then, it is fittingly taken thus: [[142:2|in thy sight|in conspectu tuo]], that is, in comparison with thy justice, [[142:2|no man living shall be justified|omnis vivens]]. For which reason it is written: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo]]. And again: [[Job 25:5|Behold even the moon doth not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight|Ecce luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus]]: [[Job 25:6|How much more is man than rottenness and the son of man than a worm?|quanto magis homo putredo, et filius hominis vermis]] Hence once more it is written most plainly: [[Job 25:4|Can man be justified compared with God|Numquid homo Dei comparatione justificabitur?]]? Well and truly, then, does the holy Apostle say: [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.|Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis.]] For the judgments of God are one thing, and the judgments of men another. Let us, then, say to God unceasingly with all humility: [[142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], O Lord, [[142:2|for in thy sight no man living shall be justified|quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]].

paras.t: Idcirco quoque, o Domine, exaudiri precor et ego : Quia persecutus est inimicus, videlicet dæmon, caro et mundus, animam meam, ipsam tentando, affligendo, contristando. Omnes enim qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, hujusmodi persecutiones patientur. Nam et carnalia desideria militant contra animam. Et caro quæ corrumpitur, aggravat animam. Humiliavit, id est, dejecit, et suo dominio subjugavit, in terra vitam meam, id est conversationem meam, pertrahendo eam ad infima atque illicita. Propter quod facta est vilis, carnalis, et detestanda. Dum enim caro dominatur spiritui, et dum mundus et dæmon prævalent homini, tunc humiliatur, id est, vilis efficitur in terra vita ejus. Collocavit me inimicus jam dictus in obscuris, id est in tenebris vitiorum, in caligine tentationum, in adversitatibus tribulationum, sicut collocavit mortuos sæculi, id est homines sæculares spiritualiter mortuos, in vitiis obstinatos. Et anxiatus est super me spiritus meus, id est, anima mea in se ipsa perterrita est, propter tot mala atque pericula quæ incidit et incidere potest ; in me turbatum est cor meum, ex consideratione et dolore malorum pœnalium et peccatorum quibus subjectus sum.
paras.en: For this reason too, O Lord, I also pray to be heard: [[142:3|For the enemy hath persecuted|Quia persecutus est inimicus]], namely the devil, the flesh and the world, [[142:3|my soul|animam meam]], tempting it, afflicting it, saddening it. For [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|Omnes enim qui volunt pie vivere in Christo]] shall suffer persecutions of this kind. For [[1 Pet 2:11|carnal desires which war against the soul|carnalia desideria militant contra animam]]. And [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul|caro quæ corrumpitur, aggravat animam]] [Denis reads *caro*, "the flesh", for *corpus*, "the body"]. [[142:3|He hath brought down|Humiliavit]], that is, cast down and subdued to his dominion, [[142:3|my life to the earth|in terra vitam meam]], that is, my manner of life, dragging it down to the lowest and unlawful things; on account of which it has become vile, carnal and detestable. For when the flesh rules the spirit, and when the world and the devil prevail over a man, then his life is brought down, that is, made vile, on the earth. [[142:3|He hath made me to dwell|Collocavit me]], the enemy just mentioned, [[142:3|in darkness|in obscuris]], that is, in the darkness of vices, in the gloom of temptations, in the adversities of tribulations, [[142:3|as|sicut]] he has made to dwell [[142:3|those that have been dead of old|mortuos sæculi]], that is, worldly men, spiritually dead, obstinate in vices [*mortuos sæculi* can also be read "the dead of the world", which Denis takes of worldly men]. [[142:4|And my spirit is in anguish within me|Et anxiatus est super me spiritus meus]], that is, my soul is terrified within itself, because of so many evils and dangers into which it has fallen and can fall; [[142:4|my heart within me is troubled|in me turbatum est cor meum]], from the consideration of, and grief over, the evils of punishment and the sins to which I am subject.

paras.t: Ad litteram vero David ait : Persecutus est inimicus, scilicet Absalon, animam meam, id est me ipsum ; humiliavit in terra vitam meam, quoniam fecit me fugere, et stratum meum fœdavit, meque gravissime diffamavit. Collocavit me in obscuris, id est in locis desertis, tetris et cavernosis, in quibus ejus timore me abscondi, donec Chusai mihi intimavit quid facerem ; sicut mortuos sæculi, id est, sicut ponuntur defuncti in monumentis sub terra. — Hæc quoque conveniunt Christo : quem inimicus, id est Judas proditor seu populus Judæorum, persecutus est ; et vitam ejus humiliavit, quia turpissima morte eam exstinxit. Collocavit etiam eum in obscuris sicut mortuos sæculi, eo modo quo dixit superius : Posuerunt me in lacu inferiori, in tenebrosis et in umbra mortis. Nam et corpus ejus in sepulcro locatum est, et anima ejus fuit in limbo ; et secundum reputationem Judæorum, fuit blasphemus et perditus, sicut et ceteri desperati. Et anxiatus est super eum spiritus ejus, quoniam dixit : Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem. In eo quoque fuit turbatum cor ejus, sicut fatebatur : Nunc anima mea turbata est : non quod fuerit aliquo modo inordinata, sed vehementer affecta.
paras.en: Literally, however, David says: [[142:3|the enemy hath persecuted|Persecutus est inimicus]], namely Absalom, [[142:3|my soul|animam meam]], that is, myself; [[142:3|he hath brought down my life to the earth|humiliavit in terra vitam meam]], since he made me flee[[2 Kings 15:14||]][[2 Kings 15:16||]], and defiled my bed[[2 Kings 16:21||]][[2 Kings 16:22||]], and defamed me most grievously. [[142:3|He hath made me to dwell in darkness|Collocavit me in obscuris]], that is, in deserted, gloomy and cavernous places, in which I hid myself for fear of him[[2 Kings 15:28||]], until Chusai let me know what I should do[[2 Kings 17:15||]][[2 Kings 17:16||]]; [[142:3|as those that have been dead of old|sicut mortuos sæculi]], that is, as the departed are laid in tombs under the earth. These things also fit Christ, whom the enemy, that is, Judas the traitor or the people of the Jews, persecuted; and brought down his life, since they put it out by a most shameful death. He also made him dwell [[142:3|in darkness|in obscuris]] [[142:3|as those that have been dead of old|sicut mortuos sæculi]], in the way he said above: [[Ps 87:7|They have laid me in the lower pit: in the dark places, and in the shadow of death.|Posuerunt me in lacu inferiori, in tenebrosis et in umbra mortis]] For his body was laid in the sepulchre[[Matt 27:60||]], and his soul was in limbo [that is, the abode of the just who died before Christ]; and in the reckoning of the Jews he was a blasphemer and a lost man, like the other desperate men. And his spirit was in anguish upon him, since he said: [[Matt 26:38|My soul is sorrowful even unto death|Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem]]. In him too his heart was troubled, as he confessed: [[John 12:27|Now is my soul troubled|Nunc anima mea turbata est]]: not that it was in any way disordered, but vehemently moved.

paras.t: Præterea loquens Propheta in persona pœnitentis, adjecit : Memor fui dierum antiquorum, id est diu præteritorum ab initio mundi : videlicet dierum Adæ, quem pro uno peccato, cum omni sua posteritate, paradiso atque originali justitia destituisti; dierumque Noe, quibus propter peccata carnis universum mundum mersisti. Meditatus sum in omnibus operibus tuis, saltem in genere, considerando qualiter a principio mundi te circa homines habuisti, quosdam ad pœnitentiam misericorditer assumendo, alios juste deserendo et condemnando. Hisque diligenter pensatis, vehementer formido ne ego cum reprobis peream, quibus peccando similis factus sum. Vel, Meditatus sum in omnibus operibus tuis, id est in operibus creationis, recreationis et glorificationis. In factis manuum tuarum prædictis meditabar.
paras.en: Moreover, the Prophet, speaking in the person of a penitent, added: [[142:5|I remembered the days of old|Memor fui dierum antiquorum]], that is, long past, from the beginning of the world: namely the days of Adam, whom for one sin, with all his posterity, thou didst strip of paradise and of original justice[[Gen 3:1||]]; and the days of Noe, in which for the sins of the flesh thou didst drown the whole world[[Gen 7:1||]]. [[142:5|I meditated on all thy works|Meditatus sum in omnibus operibus tuis]], at least in general, considering how from the beginning of the world thou hast dealt with men, mercifully taking up some to repentance, justly forsaking and condemning others. And having weighed these things carefully, I greatly fear lest I perish with the reprobate, whom I have become like by sinning. Or, [[142:5|I meditated on all thy works|Meditatus sum in omnibus operibus tuis]], that is, on the works of creation, of re-creation and of glorification. [[142:5|upon the works of thy hands|In factis manuum tuarum]] just mentioned [[142:5|I meditated|meditabar]].

paras.t: Expandi manus meas corporales ad te, id est ad cœlum, ex interiori et magno desiderio consequendi misericordiam tuam. Vel : Expandi, id est dilatavi, manus meas, id est desideria sancta et opera bona, ad te, id est, ad hoc ut ad te merear pervenire, tanquam ad fontem beatitudinis meæ et ultimum finem omnium exercitiorum meorum. Unde Jeremias : Leva, inquit, ad eum manus tuas, et miserebitur tui ; et Apostolus, Volo viros orare levantes puras manus. Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi : id est, sicut terra sicca imbrem seu pluviam sitit, sic anima mea tibi inhiat, quærens rorem gratiæ, pluviam fecunditatis internæ, aquam sapientiæ. Quemadmodum enim terra sine aqua, infecunda est, sicca, et in pulverem decidens ; sic anima mea sine gratia tua, o Domine, infructuosa et arida est, atque in spiritualem dissipationem annihilationemque cadens.
paras.en: [[142:6|I stretched forth my hands|Expandi manus meas]], my bodily hands, [[142:6|to thee|ad te]], that is, to heaven, out of an inward and great desire of obtaining thy mercy. Or: [[142:6|I stretched forth|Expandi]], that is, I opened wide, [[142:6|my hands|manus meas]], that is, holy desires and good works, [[142:6|to thee|ad te]], that is, so that I may deserve to come to thee, as to the fountain of my beatitude and the last end of all my exercises. Hence Jeremias: [[Lam 2:19|lift up|Leva]], he says, [[Lam 2:19|thy hands to him|ad eum manus tuas]], and he will have mercy on thee [these last words are not in the verse]; and the Apostle: [[1 Tim 2:8|I will therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands|Volo viros orare levantes puras manus]]. [[142:6|my soul is as earth without water unto thee|Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi]]: that is, as dry earth thirsts for the shower or the rain, so my soul gapes after thee, seeking the dew of grace, the rain of inward fruitfulness, the water of wisdom. For as earth without water is barren, dry, and crumbling into dust, so my soul without thy grace, O Lord, is fruitless and arid, and falling into spiritual dissolution and annihilation.

paras.t: Velociter exaudi me, Domine, quoniam omni momento misericordia tua indigeo. Cujus ratio subditur : defecit spiritus meus, id est, anima mea propter adversa infirmata est, et nec bona agere, nec mala cavere potest sine subsidio gratiæ tuæ. Non avertas faciem tuam, id est misericordiæ tuæ adspectum, a me : id est, noli mihi gratiosam tuam præsentiam denegare, noli irasci aut indignari, ne gravius cadam, atque instabilis fiam : quod utique mihi continget, si averteris a me faciem tuam, prout alibi protestaris : Abscondi, inquiens, faciem meam, et abiit vagus in via cordis sui. Rursusque Isaias : Ecce, ait, tu iratus es, et peccavimus. Imo si eam a me averteris, et similis ero descendentibus in lacum gehennæ. In hac siquidem vita assimilabor eis per culpam, in futuro autem per pœnam.
paras.en: [[142:7|Hear me speedily, O Lord|Velociter exaudi me, Domine]], since at every moment I need thy mercy. The reason for which is added: [[142:7|my spirit hath fainted away|defecit spiritus meus]], that is, my soul has been weakened by adversities, and can neither do good nor guard against evil without the help of thy grace. [[142:7|Turn not away thy face|Non avertas faciem tuam]], that is, the regard of thy mercy, [[142:7|from me|a me]]: that is, do not deny me thy gracious presence, do not be angry or indignant, lest I fall more grievously and become unstable; which will surely befall me if thou turn away thy face from me, as thou declarest elsewhere: [[Is 57:17|I hid|Abscondi]], thou sayest, [[Is 57:17|my face|faciem meam]], and [[Is 57:17|he went away wandering in his own heart|abiit vagus in via cordis sui]]. And again Isaias: [[Is 64:5|behold|Ecce]], he says, [[Is 64:5|thou art angry, and we have sinned|tu iratus es, et peccavimus]]. Nay, if thou turn it away from me, [[142:7|lest I be like unto them that go down into the pit|et similis ero descendentibus in lacum]] of hell [the Latin runs "and I shall be like"]. For in this life I shall be made like them by guilt, and in the life to come by punishment.

paras.t: Auditam fac mihi mane misericordiam tuam, id est, cito fac me experiri pietatis tuæ effectum, videlicet gratiæ collationem, omniumque eorum quæ postulo, misericordem exauditionem, quia in te speravi, non in rebus creatis et vanis. Verificetur ergo in me quod dictum est supra : Sperantem autem in Domino misericordia circumdabit. Quod tu ipse alibi affirmas : Eruens liberabo te, et erit tibi anima tua in salutem, quia in me habuisti fiduciam. Notam fac mihi per illuminationem Spiritus Sancti, per ministerium angeli, per prædicationem Ecclesiæ, viam in qua ambulem, id est rectum iter perveniendi ad te, seu bonam conversationem qua tibi complaceam ; quia ad te tanquam ad creatorem, salvatorem, et ultimum finem, levavi animam meam penna contemplationis, volatu fervidæ dilectionis, longanimiter quoque sperando, et laudabiliter conversando.
paras.en: [[142:8|Cause me to hear thy mercy in the morning|Auditam fac mihi mane misericordiam tuam]], that is, make me soon feel the effect of thy loving-kindness, namely the bestowal of grace, and the merciful granting of all that I ask; [[142:8|for in thee have I hoped|quia in te speravi]], not in created and vain things. Let there be fulfilled in me, then, what was said above: [[Ps 31:10|mercy shall encompass him that hopeth in the Lord|Sperantem autem in Domino misericordia circumdabit]]. Which thou thyself affirmest elsewhere: [[Jer 39:18|delivering, I will deliver thee|Eruens liberabo te]], and [[Jer 39:18|thy life shall be saved for thee, because thou hast put thy trust in me|erit tibi anima tua in salutem, quia in me habuisti fiduciam]]. [[142:8|Make the way known to me|Notam fac mihi]], by the enlightening of the Holy Ghost, by the ministry of an angel, by the preaching of the Church, [[142:8|wherein I should walk|viam in qua ambulem]], that is, the right road for coming to thee, or the good manner of life by which I may please thee; for [[142:8|to thee|quia ad te]], as to my creator, my saviour and my last end, [[142:8|I have lifted up my soul|levavi animam meam]] on the wing of contemplation, in the flight of fervent love, by hoping also with long patience, and by living in a praiseworthy way.

paras.t: Eripe me de inimicis meis visibilibus et invisibilibus, ne mihi eorum impugnatio, detractio, perversitas noceat, sed omnia cooperentur mihi in bonum. Domine, ad te confugi, sicut ad Patrem misericordiarum et Deum totius consolationis, qui solus me defendere, confortare, salvareque potes. Doce me facere voluntatem tuam, id est præceptum tuum, et omne quod complacet tibi ; quia Deus meus es tu : idcirco me totum tibi debeo, et tibi in omnibus deservire, adhærere, atque subesse obligatus sum. Non ergo quæramus dumtaxat scire, sed insuper facere voluntatem Dei. Scienti enim, et non facienti, peccatum est illi. Sic etiam studeamus Deo uniri et inhærere, ut ei digne veraciterque dicamus : Deus meus es tu. Deus enim omnipotens, qui omnium Deus est, illorum specialiter Deus est, qui se totos offerunt Deo, et ejus obsequio se totaliter mancipant, extra Deum nihil desiderant, et qualiter Deum semper honorent, indesinenter solliciti sunt.
paras.en: [[142:9|Deliver me from my enemies|Eripe me de inimicis meis]], visible and invisible, lest their assault, detraction and perversity harm me, but rather that all things may work together unto my good. [[142:9|O Lord, to thee have I fled|Domine, ad te confugi]], as to the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who alone canst defend, strengthen and save me. [[142:10|Teach me to do thy will|Doce me facere voluntatem tuam]], that is, thy commandment, and all that is pleasing to thee; [[142:10|for thou art my God|quia Deus meus es tu]]: therefore I owe my whole self to thee, and am bound to serve thee in all things, to cleave to thee and to be subject to thee. Let us not, then, seek only to know the will of God, but also to do it. For [[Jas 4:17|To him therefore who knoweth to do good and doth it not, to him it is sin.|Scienti enim, et non facienti, peccatum est illi]] [Denis shortens the verse: “to him who knows, and does not, it is sin”] Let us strive also so to be united to God and to cleave to him, that we may say to him worthily and truly: [[142:10|thou art my God|Deus meus es tu]]. For almighty God, who is the God of all, is in a special way the God of those who offer themselves wholly to God and give themselves over entirely to his service, who desire nothing outside God, and are unceasingly careful how they may always honour God.

paras.t: Spiritus tuus bonus, videlicet Spiritus Sanctus, deducet me in terram rectam, id est in regionem cœlestem, in terram viventium, in qua omnia justa et recta sunt, prout scriptum est : Populus tuus, omnes justi. In hanc terram deducet nos Spiritus Sanctus per opera bona et desideria sancta. Propter nomen tuum, id est propter te ipsum, non propter merita mea, Domine, vivificabis me, nunc vita gratiæ, et postmodum vita gloriæ, in æquitate tua, id est, sicut justum est coram te ut illum vivifices, qui totam spem suam ponit in te; vel, In æquitate tua, id est in justitia mihi a te concessa. Non enim a Deo vivificatur, nisi qui bona et justa operatur.
paras.en: [[142:10|Thy good spirit|Spiritus tuus bonus]], namely the Holy Ghost, [[142:10|shall lead me into the right land|deducet me in terram rectam]], that is, into the heavenly country, into the land of the living, in which all things are just and right, as it is written: [[Is 60:21|thy people shall be all just|Populus tuus, omnes justi]]. Into this land the Holy Ghost will lead us by good works and holy desires. [[142:11|for thy name's sake|Propter nomen tuum]], that is, for thine own sake, not for my merits, [[142:11|O Lord, thou wilt quicken me|Domine, vivificabis me]], now with the life of grace and afterwards with the life of glory, [[142:11|in thy justice|in æquitate tua]] [*æquitas*, "equity"; the Douay-Rheims has "justice"], that is, as it is just before thee that thou quicken him who places all his hope in thee; or, [[142:11|in thy justice|In æquitate tua]], that is, in the justice granted me by thee. For none is quickened by God but he who does good and just works.

paras.t: Educes de tribulatione animam meam, in præsenti vita tribulationes ejus minuendo, et in futuro eas totaliter auferendo. Unde habetur : Novit Dominus pios de tentatione eripere; et alibi, Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum, et auferet lacrimam et opprobrium populi sui.
paras.en: [[142:11|Thou wilt bring my soul out of trouble|Educes de tribulatione animam meam]], lessening its troubles in the present life, and in the life to come taking them away entirely. Hence we have: [[2 Pet 2:9|The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation|Novit Dominus pios de tentatione eripere]]; and elsewhere: [[Is 25:8|He shall cast death down headlong for ever|Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum]], and he shall take away the tears and [[Is 25:8|the reproach of his people|opprobrium populi sui]].

paras.t: Et in misericordia tua, id est misericorditer quantum ad me, disperdes, id est, dissipabis ac perdes, inimicos meos, in tua justitia, eos juste damnando, nisi pœniteant. Vel : In misericordia tua disperdes inimicos meos, citra condignum eos puniendo, aut certe misericorditer ipsos convertendo, destruens in eis non naturam, sed culpam. Et perdes in futuro judicio omnes qui tribulant animam meam invide atque injuste; quoniam ego servus tuus sum : idcirco decet te ut me famulum tuum eripias.
paras.en: [[142:12|And in thy mercy|Et in misericordia tua]], that is, mercifully as regards me, [[142:12|thou wilt destroy|disperdes]], that is, thou wilt scatter and ruin, [[142:12|my enemies|inimicos meos]], in thy justice, condemning them justly, unless they repent. Or: [[142:12|in thy mercy thou wilt destroy my enemies|In misericordia tua disperdes inimicos meos]], punishing them less than they deserve, or rather mercifully converting them, destroying in them not their nature but their guilt. [[142:12|And thou wilt cut off|Et perdes]] at the judgment to come [[142:12|all them that afflict my soul|omnes qui tribulant animam meam]] out of envy and injustice; [[142:12|for I am thy servant|quoniam ego servus tuus sum]]: therefore it befits thee to rescue me, thy servant.

paras.t: Ecce psalmum virtuosum et affectuosum, pœnitentialiumque psalmorum novissimum, clare audivimus : in quo pœnitens Deum ardentissime deprecatur. Et in fine psalmi fiducialiter loquitur, dicendo : Spiritus tuus bonus deducet me, etc., usque ad finem : quæ omnia sunt verba bonæ spei, ex singulari caritate conceptæ. Virtualiter quoque talia verba oratio sunt. Cum præcordiali igitur contritione et vera devotione conemur hunc psalmum cantare, omnesque preces in eo contentas desideranter exprimere.
paras.en: Behold, we have clearly heard a psalm full of virtue and of feeling, the last of the penitential psalms, in which the penitent entreats God most ardently. And at the end of the psalm he speaks with confidence, saying: [[142:10|Thy good spirit shall lead me|Spiritus tuus bonus deducet me]], etc., to the end: all of which are words of good hope, conceived from a singular charity. Such words are also virtually a prayer [that is, they have the force of a prayer, though not worded as a petition]. Let us strive, then, with heartfelt contrition and true devotion to sing this psalm, and to utter with longing all the prayers contained in it.

paras.t: Precatio. Spiritu nostro deficiente, velociter exaudi nos, Domine; conforta nos, et notam fac nobis viam in qua placentes tibi ambulemus : ut spiritu tuo bono nos deducente, animam nostram de omni educas tribulatione, ac in tua vivifices nos æquitate.
paras.en: Prayer. As our spirit faints, hear us speedily, O Lord; strengthen us, and make known to us the way in which we may walk pleasing to thee: that, with thy good spirit leading us, thou mayest bring our soul out of all tribulation, and quicken us in thy justice.

143.title: […] PSALMI CENTESIMI QUADRAGESIMI TERTII : BENEDICTUS DOMINUS DEUS MEUS.
143.title_en: On the hundred and forty-third psalm: Blessed be the Lord my God.
143.note: The first word of the Latin title (Expositio, Elucidatio or the like) is lost in the transcription.

paras.t: Præsentis psalmi titulus talis est: Psalmus David, adversus Goliath. Ad litteram enim, secundum Hieronymum, David fecit hunc psalmum, processurus ad pugnam contra Philistæum, seu Goliath Gethæum: quam pugnam iniit David ex revelatione divina, ex qua etiam certificatus fuit de victoria, secundum Augustinum. Litteralis igitur expositio psalmi hujus, est de ipso David contra Goliath præliante. Hanc autem expositionem breviter tangam, ubi aliquid obscuritatis includit. Moraliter vero, exponitur de homine virtuoso contra diabolum atque peccata pugnante.
paras.en: The title of the present psalm is this: A psalm of David, against Goliath[[143:1||]]. For according to the letter, as Jerome says, David made this psalm when he was about to go forth to battle against the Philistine, that is, Goliath of Geth[[1 Kings 17:40||]]; and David entered upon this battle by divine revelation, by which, as Augustine says, he was also made certain of the victory. The literal exposition of this psalm, then, is of David himself fighting against Goliath. This exposition I shall touch on briefly, where it holds some obscurity. Morally, however, the psalm is expounded of the virtuous man fighting against the devil and against sins.

paras.t: In talis igitur viri persona loquens Psalmista, ait: Benedictus exsistat, imo in se ipso æternaliter sanctus, et omni benedictione seu laude dignus est, Dominus Deus meus, qui est omnium Dominus per gubernationem, Deus per creationem, Deus meus per specialem cultum, devotionem et gratiam; qui docet manus meas, id est potentias operativas, videlicet intellectum practicum et voluntatem, ad prælium contra occasiones seu causas peccandi. Non enim vitari potest peccatum, nec spiritualis victoria adipisci, nisi occasiones peccati vitentur. Qui docet et digitos meos, id est habitus virtuosos seu discretionem, ad bellum spirituale contra aerias potestates et ipsa peccata. Non enim est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed contra principes et potestates, contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus. Prælium autem proprie dicitur, quod de longinquo imminet atque committitur, sicut dum sagittando bellatur: idcirco per prælium intelligitur pugna animæ contra occasiones peccandi. Bellum vero vocatur, quod fit de propinquo, ut quum pugnatur manu ad manum: sicque per bellum exprimitur pugna quæ est directe contra ipsum peccatum.
paras.en: Speaking, then, in the person of such a man, the Psalmist says: [[143:1|Blessed|Benedictus]] be, nay, in himself eternally holy and worthy of all blessing or praise, is [[143:1|the Lord my God|Dominus Deus meus]], who is Lord of all by governing them, God by creating them, and my God by a special worship, devotion and grace; [[143:1|who teacheth my hands|qui docet manus meas]], that is, my operative powers, namely the practical intellect and the will, [[143:1|to fight|ad prælium]] against the occasions or causes of sinning. For sin cannot be avoided, nor a spiritual victory won, unless the occasions of sin are avoided. He teacheth [[143:1|and my fingers|et digitos meos]], that is, virtuous habits, or discretion, [[143:1|to war|ad bellum]], a spiritual war, against the powers of the air and against sins themselves. For [[Eph 6:12|our wrestling is not against flesh and blood|Non enim est nobis colluctatio adversus carnem et sanguinem]]; [[Eph 6:12|but against principalities and powers|sed contra principes et potestates]], [[Eph 6:12|against the spirits of wickedness in the high places|contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus]]. Now a "fight" [prælium] is properly so called when it threatens and is joined from afar, as when war is waged by shooting arrows: and so by "fight" is understood the soul's struggle against the occasions of sinning. But "war" [bellum] is so called when it is waged at close quarters, as when men fight hand to hand: and so by "war" is expressed the struggle that is directly against sin itself.

paras.t: Tunc insuper docet Deus manus nostras ad bellum, dum confert nobis discretionem spirituum, ita ut cum Apostolo dicere valeamus: Non ignoramus cogitationes Satanæ. Qui sic docentur a Deo, agnoscunt qualiter sit singulis vitiis resistendum. Quædam enim peccata aptius superantur per hoc, quod cogitationem nostram ab eis omnino avertimus, ut sunt gula, luxuria, atque similia. Cujus ratio est: nam quanto cogitatio illis diutius immoratur, tanto affectus magis illicitur, propter delectationem materiæ circa quam versantur, videlicet quoniam actus in quibus fundantur talia vitia, in se ipsis delectabiles sunt. Omnino ergo vitare debemus memoriam, adspectum et materiam eorum ex quibus talia oriuntur peccata. Cetera vero vitia superantur per hoc, quod contra ea bellum assumitur, scilicet discutiendo, et considerando diligenter naturam et qualitatem eorum, ut sunt ira, impatientia, amaritudo, invidia, etc. Talia enim in se amara atque pœnalia sunt: ideo quanto diligentius considerantur, tanto plus displicent, sicque facilius exstirpantur. Docet etiam Deus habitus virtutum quæ in nobis sunt, quomodo unaquæque obviet vitio sibi opposito; prudentiam vero docet, ad repugnandum vitiis universis. Hæc autem docet, infundendo nobis dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ virtutes perficiunt, movent atque expediunt, sicut virtutes perficiunt et movent potentias in quibus subjective consistunt. Per donum namque scientiæ, anima edocetur quis sit compendiosior modus proficiendi in omni virtute: quod sciri non potest, nisi sciatur modus resistendi impedimentis spiritualis profectus. Quoniam vero contra invisibiles, expertissimos ac subtilissimos hostes luctamur, indigemus incessabiliter Dominum invocare: ut doceat manus nostras ad prælium, ut occasiones peccandi abscindamus; et digitos nostros ad bellum, ut sit rationabile obsequium nostrum, ut neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram declinemus, ut in omnibus debitas virtutis circumstantias observemus.
paras.en: Moreover, God teaches our hands to war when he confers on us the discernment of spirits, so that we can say with the Apostle: [[2 Cor 2:11|we are not ignorant of his devices|Non ignoramus cogitationes Satanæ]] [Denis has "the thoughts of Satan"]. Those who are thus taught by God know how each vice is to be resisted. For some sins are more fitly overcome by turning our thought away from them altogether, such as gluttony, lust and the like. The reason is this: the longer the thought dwells on them, the more the affection is enticed, because of the delight of the matter they are concerned with; that is, because the acts on which such vices are founded are delightful in themselves. We must therefore wholly avoid the memory, the sight and the matter of the things from which such sins arise. Other vices, however, are overcome by taking up war against them, that is, by examining them and carefully considering their nature and quality, such as anger, impatience, bitterness, envy, etc. For such things are bitter and painful in themselves: and so the more carefully they are considered, the more they displease, and thus they are the more easily rooted out. God also teaches the habits of the virtues that are in us how each one is to meet the vice opposed to it; and he teaches prudence to fight against all vices together. And he teaches these things by pouring into us the gifts of the Holy Ghost, which perfect, move and make ready the virtues, as the virtues perfect and move the powers in which they reside as in their subject [that is, the faculties of the soul in which the virtues inhere]. For by the gift of knowledge the soul is taught which is the shortest way of advancing in every virtue: and this cannot be known unless one knows the way of resisting the hindrances to spiritual progress. And since we wrestle against invisible, most skilful and most subtle enemies, we need to call upon the Lord unceasingly: that he may teach our hands to fight, so that we may cut off the occasions of sinning; and our fingers to war, so that ours may be a [[Rom 12:1|reasonable service|rationabile obsequium]], that we may not [[Deut 5:32|go aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram declinemus]], that in all things we may observe the due circumstances of virtue.

paras.t: Ad litteram vero dixit David hunc versum, Domino gratias referendo quod sibi modum pugnandi contra Philistæum ostendit seu inspiravit.
paras.en: According to the letter, David said this verse giving thanks to the Lord for having shown or inspired him the way to fight against the Philistine.

paras.t: Misericordia mea et refugium meum. Ponit abstractum pro concreto, ad designandum ineffabilem magnitudinem divinæ pietatis circa se, seu miserationis divinæ sibi exhibitæ. Ait ergo: Misericordia mea, id est, Deus est miserator meus, mihi adeo clemens, ut melius eum appellem misericordiam meam, quam miseratorem meum. Ipse est etiam refugium meum, id est terminus fugæ meæ, videlicet is ad quem in omni necessitate confidenter confugio, in quo solo tota salus mea consistit. Susceptor meus, id est precum mearum pius auditor et animæ meæ misericors amplexator: qui venientem ad se corde contrito ac humili nunquam repellit nec despicit, sed ulnis clementiæ recipit. Unde per Osee dicit: Ego quasi nutricius portavi eos in brachiis meis. Et Moyses loquitur: Portavit te Dominus Deus tuus, sicut portare solet homo parvulum filium suum. Et liberator meus ab hostibus atque periculis. Protector meus in adversis, et in ipso speravi, tanquam in summo bono, in quo solo finaliter est sperandum.
paras.en: [[143:2|My mercy, and my refuge|Misericordia mea et refugium meum]]. He puts the abstract for the concrete, to signify the unspeakable greatness of God's loving kindness towards him, or of the divine compassion shown him. He says therefore: [[143:2|My mercy|Misericordia mea]], that is, God is the one who has mercy on me, so merciful to me that I had better call him my mercy than the one who has mercy on me. He is also [[143:2|my refuge|refugium meum]], that is, the end of my flight, namely the one to whom I flee with confidence in every need, in whom alone my whole salvation lies. [[143:2|my support|Susceptor meus]] [susceptor, "one who takes up"], that is, the kindly hearer of my prayers and the merciful embracer of my soul: who never repels nor despises one who comes to him with [[Ps 50:19|a contrite and humbled heart|corde contrito ac humili]], but receives him in the arms of his clemency. Hence he says through Osee: [[Osee 11:3|I was like a foster father|Ego quasi nutricius]], [[Osee 11:3|I carried them in my arms|portavi eos in brachiis meis]]. And Moses says: [[Deut 1:31|the Lord thy God hath carried thee, as a man is wont to carry his little son|Portavit te Dominus Deus tuus, sicut portare solet homo parvulum filium suum]]. [[143:2|and my deliverer|Et liberator meus]] from enemies and dangers. [[143:2|My protector|Protector meus]] in adversity, [[143:2|and I have hoped in him|et in ipso speravi]], as in the highest good, in which alone our hope is finally to be placed.

paras.t: Qui subdit populum meum sub me. Hoc ad litteram dixit David de populo quorum vel erat vel paulo post futurus fuit princeps. Postquam Philistæum dejecit, constituit eum Saul super viros bellatores: eratque educens et reducens Israel, atque in omnibus se prudenter gerebat, ut scribitur primo et secundo Regum. Prælati quoque et principes Christianorum, qui populum sibi subjectum pacifice regunt, istud verissime dicere possunt, imo et debent, quia non suæ industriæ, sed gratiæ Dei adscribere obligantur quod eorum subjecti eis virtuose et prompte obediant: quoniam superiorum prudens gubernatio, et inferiorum bona subjectio, dona sunt Dei. De quo in libro Job habetur: Potestas et terror apud ipsum est, qui facit concordiam in sublimibus suis. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Deus solatii det vobis id ipsum sapere in alterutrum secundum Jesum Christum. Aliqui vero subduntur suis prælatis etiam in rebus illicitis, sed istam subjectionem Deus non facit. Potius vero fit a timore humano aut propria cupiditate, aut dæmone, seu simili malo principio. Verumtamen, sicut Petrus in sua Canonica docet, servi subditi esse debent dominis suis, et inferiores superioribus, non solum modestis et bonis, sed etiam dyscolis: non autem in omnibus, sed in licitis et honestis.
paras.en: [[143:2|who subdueth my people under me|Qui subdit populum meum sub me]]. According to the letter, David said this of the people whose prince he either was or was soon to be. After he had struck down the Philistine, Saul set him over the men of war[[1 Kings 18:5||]]; and he led out and brought in Israel[[1 Kings 18:13||]][[2 Kings 5:2||]], and behaved himself prudently in all things[[1 Kings 18:14||]], as is written in the first and second books of Kings. Prelates also, and Christian princes, who rule in peace the people subject to them, can say this most truly, nay, they ought to say it, because they are bound to ascribe it not to their own diligence but to the grace of God that their subjects obey them virtuously and promptly: for the prudent government of superiors and the good subjection of inferiors are gifts of God. Of which it is said in the book of Job: [[Job 25:2|Power and terror are with him, who maketh peace in his high places|Potestas et terror apud ipsum est, qui facit concordiam in sublimibus suis]]. For which reason the Apostle says: [[Rom 15:5|the God of patience and of comfort grant you to be of one mind, one towards another, according to Jesus Christ|Deus solatii det vobis id ipsum sapere in alterutrum secundum Jesum Christum]]. Some, however, are subject to their prelates even in unlawful things, but this subjection God does not bring about. Rather it comes from human fear, or from their own greed, or from the devil, or from some like evil principle. Yet, as Peter teaches in his canonical Epistle, servants ought to be subject to their masters, and inferiors to their superiors, [[1 Pet 2:18|not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward|non solum modestis et bonis, sed etiam dyscolis]]: not, however, in all things, but in what is lawful and honest.

paras.t: Spiritualiter quoque quilibet virtuosus dicere potest: Qui subdit populum meum, id est cogitationes, affectiones, et actus animæ meæ, sub me, id est sub rationis meæ imperio, ne inordinati motus et cogitatus mihi dominentur, sed per rationem refrenentur et exstirpentur. Sicque similis reddar fidelissimo illi centurioni, qui dixit huic, Vade, et ivit; et huic, Veni, et venit; et servo suo, Fac hoc, et fecit. Simili modo ego populo animæ meæ sic dominer, ut dicam huic cogitationi affectionive malæ, Vade, id est, recede a me, et vadat, nec diutius me pulset; et huic cogitationi et affectioni laudabili, Veni, id est, mane et esto in me, et veniat; et servo meo, id est appetitui meo sensitivo seu corpori, Fac hoc, scilicet jejunando, continendo, vigilando, et faciat.
paras.en: Spiritually, too, any virtuous man can say: [[143:2|who subdueth my people|Qui subdit populum meum]], that is, the thoughts, affections and acts of my soul, [[143:2|under me|sub me]], that is, under the command of my reason, so that disordered motions and thoughts may not lord it over me, but may be curbed and rooted out by reason. And so I shall be made like that most faithful centurion who said [[Matt 8:9|to this, Go, and he goeth, and to another Come, and he cometh, and to my servant, Do this, and he doeth it|huic, Vade, et ivit; et huic, Veni, et venit; et servo suo, Fac hoc, et fecit]] [Denis has the past tense: "and he went … and he came … and he did it"]. In like manner may I so rule the people of my soul that I say to this evil thought or affection, Go, that is, depart from me, and it goes, and troubles me no longer; and to this praiseworthy thought and affection, Come, that is, stay and abide in me, and it comes; and to my servant, that is, to my sensitive appetite or my body, Do this, namely by fasting, by continence, by watching, and it does it.

paras.t: Consequenter Propheta admirans inæstimabilia viscera misericordiæ Dei circa totum genus humanum, adjungit: Domine, quid est homo, id est, cujus nobilitatis et perfectionis exsistit, quia innotuisti ei per fidem, per supernaturalem cognitionem, per tui ipsius incarnationem, gratiamque multiplicem? aut quid est filius hominis, id est Adæ seu primi parentis, quia reputas eum, id est, quod dignum ducis tantam gratiam ei conferre, quod tanta pro ejus redemptione fecisti? Quasi dicat: Tantæ dignitatis es tu, et tantæ vilitatis est homo, quod vehementer mirandum est quia sic ei innotuisti, et taliter eum reputasti. Hinc quoque sanctus Job ait: Quid est homo quia magnificas eum? aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum?
paras.en: Next the Prophet, marvelling at the inestimable bowels of God's mercy towards the whole human race, adds: [[143:3|Lord, what is man|Domine, quid est homo]], that is, of what nobility and perfection is he, [[143:3|that thou art made known to him|quia innotuisti ei]] by faith, by supernatural knowledge, by thine own incarnation and by manifold grace? or what is [[143:3|the son of man|filius hominis]], that is, of Adam, the first parent, [[143:3|that thou makest account of him|quia reputas eum]], that is, that thou deemest it worthy to confer so great a grace on him, that thou hast done such great things for his redemption? As if to say: Thou art of such dignity, and man of such vileness, that it is greatly to be wondered at that thou hast so made thyself known to him and made such account of him. Hence holy Job too says: [[Job 7:17|What is a man, that thou shouldst magnify him or why dost thou set thy heart upon him?|Quid est homo quia magnificas eum? aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum?]]

paras.t: Homo vanitati similis factus est peccando. Peccatum enim est nihil et vanitas. Unde dum peccat homo, non solum vanus, sed etiam vanitas, id est vehementer vanus ac nihil efficitur. Deus autem fecit hominem ab initio rectum; ipse vero per culpam fecit se ipsum vanitati consimilem. Itaque propter multiplicem fragilitatem, instabilitatem et culpam, dicitur homo vanitati similis factus. Unde supra dictum est: Verumtamen universa vanitas, omnis homo vivens. Dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt, id est, cito et indesinenter defluunt atque deficiunt. Propter quod in primo libro Paralipomenon habetur: Peregrini sumus coram te, Domine; dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. In libro quoque Job ait quidam: Hesterni sumus, et ignoramus quoniam sicut umbra dies nostri super terram. Et sanctus Job orat: Parce mihi, Domine, nihil enim sunt dies mei.
paras.en: [[143:4|Man is like to vanity|Homo vanitati similis factus est]] [literally, "is made like to vanity"] by sinning. For sin is nothing, and vanity. Hence when man sins he becomes not only vain but vanity itself, that is, exceedingly vain and nothing. Now [[Eccles 7:30|God made man right|Deus autem fecit hominem ab initio rectum]] from the beginning; but he, by his fault, made himself like to vanity. Therefore, because of his manifold frailty, instability and guilt, man is said to have been made like to vanity. Hence it was said above: [[Ps 38:6|And indeed all things are vanity: every man living|Verumtamen universa vanitas, omnis homo vivens]]. [[143:4|his days pass away like a shadow|Dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt]], that is, they flow away and fail swiftly and unceasingly. For which reason it is said in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|we are sojourners before thee|Peregrini sumus coram te]], O Lord; [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. In the book of Job also a certain man says: [[Job 8:9|we are but of yesterday, and are ignorant that our days upon earth are but a shadow|Hesterni sumus, et ignoramus quoniam sicut umbra dies nostri super terram]]. And holy Job prays: [[Job 7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]], O Lord, [[Job 7:16|for my days are nothing|nihil enim sunt dies mei]].

paras.t: Deinde Propheta de Christi veri Dei incarnatione vaticinatus, subdit: Domine, Fili Dei, inclina cœlos tuos, id est, altitudinem tuam in cœlis habitantem exinanire seu humiliare digneris, et descende, non locum mutando, sed per incarnationem humanam naturam assumendo, inter homines conversando, te ipsum hominibus ostendendo. Hunc Dei descensum concupivit Isaias, dicens: Utinam dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes. Unde per cœlos intelligi possunt cœli materiales, præsertim cœlum empyreum: quos dicitur Deus inclinare sive dirumpere, non localiter neque realiter, sed per similitudinem quamdam. Loquitur enim Scriptura de Deo modo humano. Homo autem, in loco sublimi nullam aperturam habens exsistens, non valet descendere, nisi locus inclinetur aut dirumpatur. Idcirco rogatur Deus cœlos inclinare atque dirumpere. Vel sic: Domine, inclina cœlos tuos, id est, angelos sanctos, civesque cœlestes, depone et mitte ad nos, et descende, id est, gratiam et misericordiam infundendo veni ad me. Utroque modo Christus descendit. Carnem enim assumpsit, et misericordiæ suæ effectum nobis impendit.
paras.en: Then the Prophet, foretelling the incarnation of Christ, true God, goes on: [[143:5|Lord|Domine]], Son of God, [[143:5|bow down thy heavens|inclina cœlos tuos]], that is, deign to empty and humble thy loftiness that dwells in the heavens, [[143:5|and descend|et descende]], not by changing place, but by taking human nature through the incarnation, by living among men, by showing thyself to men. This descent of God Isaias longed for, saying: [[Is 64:1|O that thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down|Utinam dirumperes cœlos, et descenderes]]. Hence by the heavens may be understood the material heavens, especially the empyrean heaven [that is, the highest heaven, the dwelling of the blessed]: which God is said to bow down or rend, not locally nor really, but by a kind of likeness. For Scripture speaks of God in a human way. Now a man who is in a high place with no opening cannot come down unless the place is bowed down or rent. Therefore God is asked to bow down and rend the heavens. Or thus: [[143:5|Lord, bow down thy heavens|Domine, inclina cœlos tuos]], that is, put down and send to us the holy angels and the citizens of heaven, [[143:5|and descend|et descende]], that is, come to me by pouring in grace and mercy. In both ways Christ came down. For he took flesh, and bestowed on us the effect of his mercy.

paras.t: Tange montes, id est superbos, se ipsos inaniter erigentes per vindictam; et fumigabunt, id est dissolventur et corrumpentur, quemadmodum candela dum extincta fuerit, fumigat. Vel, Tange montes istos per misericordissimam gratiæ infusionem, et fumigabunt, id est, lacrimas pro suis excessibus fundent, gement, et ad cœlestia suspirabunt. Fulgura coruscationes, id est, terribiles exerce ultiones; et dissipabis eos, id est, superbos confringes et condemnabis. Vel: Fulgura, id est, evidenter emitte, coruscationes, id est miracula et verba sanctæ prædicationis ignita ac splendida; et dissipabis eos, id est, superbos a sua elatione disperge, convertes et immutabis, faciendo humiles de elatis, parvos de magnis. Emitte sagittas tuas, id est comminationes horribiles, commemorando per sanctos prædicatores districtionem futuri judicii ac pœnas inferni; vel, Sagittas, id est pœnas castigatorias; et conturbabis, id est terrebis, eos ad pœnitentiam salutarem. Talia namque audiendo impii convertuntur.
paras.en: [[143:5|touch the mountains|Tange montes]], that is, the proud, who vainly lift themselves up, by thy vengeance; [[143:5|and they shall smoke|et fumigabunt]], that is, they shall be dissolved and corrupted, as a candle smokes when it has been put out. Or, [[143:5|touch the mountains|Tange montes]], these mountains, by the most merciful infusion of grace, [[143:5|and they shall smoke|et fumigabunt]], that is, they shall shed tears for their excesses, they shall groan, and sigh after heavenly things. [[143:6|Send forth lightning|Fulgura coruscationes]] [Denis reads coruscationes, "lightnings"], that is, carry out terrible vengeance; [[143:6|and thou shalt scatter them|et dissipabis eos]], that is, thou shalt break and condemn the proud. Or: [[143:6|Send forth|Fulgura]], that is, send forth openly, [[143:6|lightning|coruscationes]], that is, miracles and the fiery and shining words of holy preaching; [[143:6|and thou shalt scatter them|et dissipabis eos]], that is, scatter the proud from their pride: thou shalt convert and change them, making the lifted-up humble, and the great small. [[143:6|shoot out thy arrows|Emitte sagittas tuas]], that is, terrible threats, by recalling through holy preachers the strictness of the judgement to come and the pains of hell; or, [[143:6|arrows|Sagittas]], that is, chastising punishments; [[143:6|and thou shalt trouble them|et conturbabis]], that is, thou shalt frighten them into saving penance. For by hearing such things the wicked are converted.

paras.t: Ad litteram, David oravit ut Deus ad ipsum descenderet, sibi adstando et victoriam præstando adversus Goliath. Tange montes, id est Philistæos superbos, per vindictam, et fumigabunt, id est deficient, prout de impiis ab Isaia dicitur: Radix eorum quasi favilla erit, et germen eorum ut pulvis ascendet. Nam et Philistæi, occiso suo gigante, fugerunt.
paras.en: According to the letter, David prayed that God would come down to him, standing by him and giving him the victory against Goliath[[1 Kings 17:45||]][[1 Kings 17:46||]][[1 Kings 17:47||]]. [[143:5|touch the mountains|Tange montes]], that is, the proud Philistines, by thy vengeance, [[143:5|and they shall smoke|et fumigabunt]], that is, they shall fail, as Isaias says of the wicked: [[Is 5:24|their root be as ashes, and their bud shall go up as dust|Radix eorum quasi favilla erit, et germen eorum ut pulvis ascendet]]. For the Philistines too fled when their giant was slain[[1 Kings 17:51||]].

paras.t: Deinde vir justus divinum auxilium postulans, subdit: Emitte manum tuam de alto, id est, de cœlo mitte mihi subsidium, tuamque potestatem extende super me; eripe me et libera me de aquis multis, id est ab hominibus malis, a tribulationibus variis, a dæmonum tentamentis. Per aquas enim interdum populi designantur, juxta illud: Aquæ quas vidisti, populi sunt. Interdum vero per aquam tribulatio importatur, sicut quum a Jeremia dicitur: Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum. Et de manu filiorum alienorum, id est hominum perversorum ac dæmonum: qui per naturam sunt filii Creatoris, tanquam ad ejus similitudinem conditi; per inobedientiam autem sunt filii iniquitatis: suntque alieni a Deo, et nesciuntur ab eo. Quorum os locutum est vanitatem, id est vana consilia, verba iniqua, et dextera, id est potestas eorum, est dextera iniquitatis, id est origo et causa peccati. Potestate enim sibi divinitus præstita abutuntur, exhibentes vires seu membra sua servire immunditiæ et iniquitati ad iniquitatem, sicut Apostolus dicit.
paras.en: Then the just man, asking for divine help, goes on: [[143:7|Put forth thy hand from on high|Emitte manum tuam de alto]], that is, send me help from heaven, and stretch out thy power over me; [[143:7|take me out, and deliver me from many waters|eripe me et libera me de aquis multis]], that is, from evil men, from various tribulations, from the temptings of the demons. For by waters peoples are sometimes signified, according to that text: [[Apoc 17:15|The waters which thou sawest|Aquæ quas vidisti]] [[Apoc 17:15|are peoples|populi sunt]]. But sometimes tribulation is meant by water, as when Jeremias says: [[Lam 3:54|Waters have flowed over my head|Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum]]. [[143:7|from the hand of strange children|Et de manu filiorum alienorum]], that is, of perverse men and of demons: who by nature are sons of the Creator, as having been made to his likeness, but by disobedience are sons of iniquity; and they are strangers to God, and are not known by him. [[143:8|Whose mouth hath spoken vanity|Quorum os locutum est vanitatem]], that is, vain counsels and wicked words, [[143:8|and their right hand|et dextera]], that is, their power, is [[143:8|the right hand of iniquity|dextera iniquitatis]], that is, the source and cause of sin. For they abuse the power given them by God, yielding their strength or their [[Rom 6:19|members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, unto iniquity|membra sua servire immunditiæ et iniquitati ad iniquitatem]], as the Apostle says.

paras.t: Quoniam vero de his malis misericorditer eripuisti me, Domine, ideo, o Deus, canticum novum, id est laudem recentem, ex recenti devotione prodeuntem, cantabo tibi, gratias referendo; in psalterio decachordo, id est decem chordas habente, videlicet in spirituali psalterio, quod est observatio præceptorum Decalogi, psallam tibi: id est, laudabo te, non solum pulchris sermonibus, sed etiam sanctis operibus, ne inter eos computer de quibus testatus es: Populus iste labiis suis glorificat me, cor autem ejus longe est a me.
paras.en: And since thou hast mercifully delivered me from these evils, O Lord, therefore, [[143:9|O God|Deus]], [[143:9|a new canticle|canticum novum]], that is, fresh praise, coming from fresh devotion, [[143:9|I will sing|cantabo tibi]] to thee, giving thanks; [[143:9|on the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings|in psalterio decachordo]] [the Latin has one instrument, "a ten-stringed psaltery"], that is, having ten strings, namely on the spiritual psaltery, which is the keeping of the commandments of the Decalogue, [[143:9|I will sing praises to thee|psallam tibi]]: that is, I will praise thee not only with fair words but also with holy works, lest I be counted among those of whom thou hast testified: This people [[Is 29:13|with their lips glorify me, but their heart is far from me|labiis suis glorificat me, cor autem ejus longe est a me]][[Matt 15:8||]].

paras.t: Qui das salutem regibus, id est victoriam principibus. Unde Salomon loquitur: Equus paratur ad prælium; Dominus autem salutem tribuit. Et iterum Sapiens protestatur: Per me reges regnant, et principes imperant. Vel: Qui das salutem, id est veram prosperitatem seu felicitatem, regibus, id est omnibus sensualitati suæ ac proprio animo dominantibus, quorum ratio regit omnes vires inferiores.
paras.en: [[143:10|Who givest salvation to kings|Qui das salutem regibus]], that is, victory to princes. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 21:31|The horse is prepared for the day of battle: but the Lord giveth safety|Equus paratur ad prælium; Dominus autem salutem tribuit]] [Denis reads ad prælium, "for battle"]. And again the Wise Man declares: [[Prov 8:15|By me kings reign|Per me reges regnant]], and [[Prov 8:16|princes rule|principes imperant]]. Or: [[143:10|Who givest salvation|Qui das salutem]], that is, true prosperity or happiness, [[143:10|to kings|regibus]], that is, to all who rule over their sensuality and their own mind, whose reason governs all the lower powers.

paras.t: Qui redemisti David servum tuum de ore leonis et ursi, quos occidit, de gladio maligno, scilicet Goliath, eripe me. Et erue me de manu filiorum alienorum, scilicet Philistæorum. Iste est sensus litteralis. Spiritualiter sic: Qui redemisti David, id est fidelem per gratiam manu fortem, et virtutibus speciosum, servum tuum, de gladio maligno, id est ab omni persecutione injusta, eripe me. Et erue me de manu filiorum alienorum, etc. Iste versiculus modo expositus est.
paras.en: [[143:10|who hast redeemed thy servant David|Qui redemisti David servum tuum]] from the mouth of the lion and the bear, which he slew[[1 Kings 17:34||]][[1 Kings 17:35||]][[1 Kings 17:36||]], [[143:10|from the malicious sword|de gladio maligno]], namely Goliath, [[143:11|Deliver me|eripe me]]. [[143:11|And rescue me out of the hand of strange children|Et erue me de manu filiorum alienorum]], namely of the Philistines. This is the literal sense. Spiritually, thus: [[143:10|who hast redeemed thy servant David|Qui redemisti David]], that is, the faithful man, strong of hand by grace and comely with virtues [the name David was taken to mean "strong of hand" and "comely to behold"], [[143:10|thy servant|servum tuum]], [[143:10|from the malicious sword|de gladio maligno]], that is, from every unjust persecution, [[143:11|Deliver me|eripe me]]. [[143:11|And rescue me out of the hand of strange children|Et erue me de manu filiorum alienorum]], etc. This little verse has just been expounded.

paras.t: Et quoniam reprobi frequenter in hoc sæculo prosperantur in propria persona, in prole, in possessionibus (juxta illud: Justus es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te: Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur? plantasti eos, et proficiunt), ideo de eis subjungitur: Quorum filii sunt sicut novellæ plantationes, id est fortes, sani, pulchri atque jucundi, in juventute sua. Filiæ eorum compositæ sunt, non moribus virtuosis, sed sæcularibus honestatibus, circumornatæ in vestibus et ceteris ornamentis, ut similitudo templi, id est tantum, quod similes sunt templo undique perornato; vel, Ut similitudo templi, id est, sicut ornatur imago seu statua in templo locata.
paras.en: And since the reprobate often prosper in this world in their own persons, in their offspring and in their possessions (according to that text: [[Jer 12:1|Thou indeed, O Lord, art just, if I plead with thee, but yet I will speak what is just to thee: Why doth the way of the wicked prosper: why is it well with all them that transgress|Justus es, Domine, si disputem tecum; verumtamen justa loquar ad te: Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur]]? [[Jer 12:2|Thou hast planted them|plantasti eos]], and [[Jer 12:2|they prosper|proficiunt]]), therefore it is added of them: [[143:12|Whose sons are as new plants|Quorum filii sunt sicut novellæ plantationes]], that is, strong, healthy, fair and pleasant, [[143:12|in their youth|in juventute sua]]. [[143:12|Their daughters decked out|Filiæ eorum compositæ sunt]], not with virtuous manners but with worldly graces, [[143:12|adorned round about|circumornatæ]] in their garments and other ornaments, [[143:12|after the similitude of a temple|ut similitudo templi]], that is, so much that they are like a temple adorned on every side; or, [[143:12|after the similitude of a temple|Ut similitudo templi]], that is, as an image or statue set in a temple is adorned.

paras.t: Promptuaria eorum plena omni genere victualium, eructantia, id est affluentia, ex hoc in illud: quia plenitudine unius aliud adimpletur. Oves eorum fœtosæ, id est, prole seu fœtibus plenæ sunt, abundantes numero fœtuum, puta agnorum, in egressibus suis ex ovili, ita quod cum magna multitudine agnorum egrediuntur ad pascua; boves eorum crassæ. Per hæc autem signatur aliorum brutorum affluentia. Non est ruina maceriæ, id est casus parietis, neque transitus adversitatis, seu inimicorum occursus, neque clamor, id est planctus seu vociferatio dolorosa, in plateis, id est in locis seu habitationibus eorum; sed in omnibus bene eis succedit, et domus eorum firmæ et fortes sunt.
paras.en: [[143:13|Their storehouses full|Promptuaria eorum plena]] of every kind of victuals, [[143:13|flowing out|eructantia]], that is, overflowing, [[143:13|of this into that|ex hoc in illud]]: because by the fulness of one the other is filled. [[143:13|Their sheep fruitful in young|Oves eorum fœtosæ]], that is, they are full of offspring or young, [[143:13|abounding|abundantes]] in the number of their young, that is, of lambs, [[143:13|in their goings forth|in egressibus suis]] from the fold, so that they go out to pasture with a great multitude of lambs; [[143:14|Their oxen fat|boves eorum crassæ]]. And by these things is signified an abundance of the other beasts. [[143:14|There is no breach of wall|Non est ruina maceriæ]], that is, no fall of a wall, [[143:14|nor passage|neque transitus]] of adversity, or onset of enemies, [[143:14|nor crying out|neque clamor]], that is, lamentation or sorrowful outcry, [[143:14|in their streets|in plateis]], that is, in their places or dwellings; but all things go well with them, and their houses are firm and strong.

paras.t: Porro hæc omnia plenissime scripta sunt, ubi sanctus Job ait: Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est, ut merito non debeam contristari? Quare ergo impii vivunt, sublevati sunt, confortatique divitiis? Semen eorum permanet coram eis, propinquorum turba et nepotum in conspectu eorum. Domus eorum securæ sunt et pacatæ, et non est virga Dei super eos. Bos eorum concepit et non abortivit; vacca peperit. Egrediuntur quasi greges parvuli eorum; tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi.
paras.en: Moreover all these things are written most fully where holy Job says: [[Job 21:4|Is my debate against man, that I should not have just reason to be troubled|Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est, ut merito non debeam contristari]]? [the margin gives Job xxi, 7–12; this first question is Job 21:4] [[Job 21:7|Why then do the wicked live, are they advanced, and strengthened with riches?|Quare ergo impii vivunt, sublevati sunt, confortatique divitiis?]] [[Job 21:8|Their seed continueth before them, a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children in their sight|Semen eorum permanet coram eis, propinquorum turba et nepotum in conspectu eorum]]. [[Job 21:9|Their houses are secure and peaceable, and the rod of God is not upon them|Domus eorum securæ sunt et pacatæ, et non est virga Dei super eos]]. [[Job 21:10|Their cattle have conceived, and failed not: their cow has calved|Bos eorum concepit et non abortivit; vacca peperit]]. [[Job 21:11|Their little ones go out like a flock|Egrediuntur quasi greges parvuli eorum]]; [[Job 21:12|They take the timbrel, and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ|tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi]].

paras.t: Beatum dixerunt homines excæcati, carnales, sola temporalia considerantes, populum cui hæc sunt, id est, qui prædictis terrenis prosperitatibus florent. Quum enim non nisi bona præsentis vitæ quærant, tanto alios magis beatificant, quanto viderint eos in talibus amplius abundare. Unde dicunt: Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes; siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem.
paras.en: [[143:15|They have called the people happy|Beatum dixerunt]], that is, blinded and carnal men, who consider temporal things alone, [[143:15|the people happy, that hath these things|populum cui hæc sunt]], that is, which flourishes in the earthly prosperity just described. For since they seek nothing but the goods of the present life, the more they see others abound in such things, the more they call them happy. Hence they say: [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up|Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes; siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem]].

paras.t: Verumtamen, sicut non omnes infelices et reprobi sunt, qui in prædictis terrenis bonis abundant et abundaverunt (certum est enim quod Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Gedeon, David et alii sancti, ditissimi erant, multosque filios habuerunt): sic non omnes perversi et reprobi prædictis bonis abundant; imo multi eorum mendici atque pauperrimi fuerunt et sunt. Non ergo universaliter, sed particulariter intelligenda sunt præinducta verba Prophetæ. Sunt enim aliqui reprobi, qui non solum in futuro, sed etiam in præsenti miseri sunt, tam in spiritualibus, quam in corporalibus. Denique, sicut electis non obest temporalium affluentia, eo quod non afficiantur ad ea inordinato affectu, sed solum eis utantur quantum necesse est aut utile ad propriæ vitæ sustentationem, seu aliam rationabilem causam, omnia ad Dei honorem finaliter referendo, Deumque super omnia diligendo; sic reprobis non prodest temporalium rerum carentia, quoniam non sponte, sed coacte seu invite talibus carent. Rebus namque caducis adhærent finaliter et bona creata plus amant quam summum bonum, quod est bonum essentialiter. Igitur inter bonos et malos hoc interest, quod boni utuntur creaturis, mali vero eis fruuntur. Boni enim utuntur eis tanquam mediis seu instrumentis perveniendi ad Deum; mali autem constituunt sibi finem in eis, adhærentes et inhærentes creaturis magis quam Creatori. Propter quod in libro Sapientiæ legitur: Creaturæ Dei factæ sunt in tentationem animæ hominum et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium. Id enim quod amabilitatis, suavitatis delectationis et pulchritudinis in creaturis invenitur, non ordinant ad Creatoris amorem atque honorem seu cultum, sed sistunt in rebus creatis.
paras.en: However, just as not all who abound and have abounded in the earthly goods described are unhappy and reprobate (for it is certain that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Gedeon, David and other saints were very rich and had many sons), so not all the perverse and reprobate abound in these goods; nay, many of them have been and are beggars and very poor. The words of the Prophet set down above are therefore to be understood not universally but particularly. For there are some reprobate who are wretched not only in the life to come but also in the present, in spiritual as well as bodily things. Lastly, as the abundance of temporal things does no harm to the elect, because they are not attached to them with a disordered affection, but use them only so far as is necessary or useful for sustaining their own life, or for some other reasonable cause, referring all things finally to the honour of God and loving God above all things; so the lack of temporal things does the reprobate no good, since they go without such things not willingly, but by force or against their will. For they cleave to perishable things as their end, and love created goods more than the highest good, which is good by its essence. This, then, is the difference between the good and the wicked: the good use creatures, but the wicked enjoy them [uti and frui, Augustine's distinction: to use a thing for the sake of another, and to rest in it for its own sake]. For the good use them as means or instruments for coming to God; but the wicked set up their end in them, cleaving and clinging to creatures more than to the Creator. For which reason we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 14:11|the creatures of God|Creaturæ Dei]] were made [[Wis 14:11|a temptation to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise|in tentationem animæ hominum et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]]. For whatever of loveliness, sweetness, delight and beauty is found in creatures they do not direct to the love and honour or worship of the Creator, but stop short in created things.

paras.t: Cur ergo Propheta hæc dixit de prosperitate malorum? nisi quoniam justo Dei judicio, sæpe permittuntur in hoc sæculo prosperari, quatenus eorum damnatio appareat justior, vel ut bonorum quæ forte fecerint, mercedem in hoc mundo recipiant; et ne homines boni turbentur, dum impios prosperari in transitoriis intuentur; imo transitoria spernant, quæ vident reprobis dari ad damnationem eorum majorem; sed neque mirentur dum cernunt justos affligi, atque in omnibus aspera pensantes quod per talia a reatu vitiorum purgantur, vel præmia copiosiora adipiscuntur.
paras.en: Why, then, did the Prophet say these things of the prosperity of the wicked? Only because by God's just judgement they are often allowed to prosper in this world, so that their damnation may appear the more just, or that they may receive in this world the reward of any good things they may have done; and so that good men may not be troubled when they see the wicked prospering in passing things, but may rather despise passing things, which they see given to the reprobate for their greater damnation; nor may they wonder when they see the just afflicted, but, in all hardships, may consider that by such things they are cleansed from the guilt of their vices, or gain more abundant rewards.

paras.t: Postremo, quasi interrogaremus sanctum Prophetam, beatissimum David, quid ipse ad opinionem horum responderet, qui beatum dixerunt populum cui hæc sunt: ipse ostendens falsam et frivolam esse talium opinionem, et veram beatitudinem non nisi in Dei fruitione seu possessione consistere, addit: Beatus populus cujus Dominus Deus ejus: id est, ego beatum esse definio omnem hominem, qui habet Dominum universorum pro Deo suo, ita quod Dominus est Deus ejus, non aurum, non venter, non Venus, nec quidquam creatum, caducum et vanum. Deus autem uniuscujusque id dicitur, quod ab eo magis amatur et colitur. Illorum ergo Dominus est Deus, qui Deum præ omnibus diligunt, venerantur seu colunt, qui ad Deum omnia referunt, qui omne bonum in eo quærunt atque inveniunt, quorum tota spes Deus est, et totum spiritum suum ad ejus dilectionem convertunt. Talis homo, talisque populus est beatus, nunc per spem et gratiam, postmodum vero beatus erit per rem, seu tentionem et gloriam.
paras.en: Lastly, as though we were asking the holy Prophet, most blessed David, what he would answer to the opinion of those who [[143:15|have called the people happy, that hath these things|beatum dixerunt populum cui hæc sunt]], he shows that their opinion is false and frivolous, and that true happiness consists only in the enjoyment or possession of God, and adds: [[143:15|but happy is that people whose God is the Lord|Beatus populus cujus Dominus Deus ejus]] [literally, "whose Lord is its God"]: that is, I define as happy every man who has the Lord of all things for his God, so that the Lord is his God, not gold, not his belly, not Venus, nor anything created, perishable and vain. For that is called each man's God which he most loves and worships. The Lord, therefore, is the God of those who love, venerate and worship God above all things, who refer all things to God, who seek and find all good in him, whose whole hope is God, and who turn their whole spirit to his love. Such a man and such a people is happy now by hope and grace, and hereafter will be happy in reality, that is, by possession [tentio, the "holding" of God, one of the endowments of the blessed] and glory.

paras.t: Ecce psalmum veraciter gloriosum atque præclarum audivimus: psalmum utique laudibus plenum, morali doctrina præfulgidum.
