For it has already been said before that [[145:4|in that day all their thoughts shall perish|in illa die peribunt omnes cogitationes eorum]]; and in the first psalm we have, [[Ps 1:6|the way of the wicked shall perish|Iter impiorum peribit]].

paras.t: Regnabit Dominus in Ecclesia militanti ac triumphanti in sæcula, qui est Deus tuus, o Sion, id est, o Ecclesia seu anima Deum per fidem aut speciem videns: est, inquam, Deus tuus in generationem et generationem, id est per omnium generationum intervalla et tempora. De hoc in præcedenti psalmo plurima dicta sunt, ubi habetur: Regnum tuum, regnum omnium sæculorum, et dominatio tua in omni generatione et generationem.
paras.en: [[145:10|The Lord shall reign|Regnabit Dominus]] in the Church militant and triumphant [[145:10|for ever|in sæcula]], he who is [[145:10|thy God, O Sion|Deus tuus, o Sion]], that is, O Church, or O soul that sees God by faith or by sight [Latin *per speciem*: face to face, as the blessed see him]: he is, I say, thy God [[145:10|unto generation and generation|in generationem et generationem]], that is, through the intervals and times of all generations. Of this much was said in the preceding psalm, where we have: [[Ps 144:13|Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages: and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations|Regnum tuum, regnum omnium sæculorum, et dominatio tua in omni generatione et generationem]].

paras.t: Ecce psalmum laudibus Dei dulciter resonantem audivimus: in quo misericordia Creatoris copiose laudatur; in quo ejus omnipotentia, veritas, justitia, liberalitas et beneficentia commemorantur; in quo docemur, in Deo summe finaliterque confidere. Indesinenter igitur laudet anima nostra Dominum, atque cum omni fiducia convertatur in ipsum, ei inhæreat, ei confidat in prosperis et adversis, imo in omni eventu, loco, causa et tempore, dicens cum sancto Job : Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Non enim mentitur Scriptura divina, quæ speranti in Deum, beatitudinem repromittit, sicut est illud Isaiæ : Deus judicii Dominus; beati omnes qui exspectant eum.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a psalm sweetly resounding with the praises of God: in which the mercy of the Creator is abundantly praised; in which his omnipotence, truth, justice, liberality and beneficence are recalled; in which we are taught to trust in God supremely and as our last end. Let our soul, then, praise the Lord unceasingly, and turn to him with all confidence, cleave to him, trust in him in prosperity and in adversity, nay, in every event, place, cause and time, saying with holy Job: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. For the divine Scripture does not lie, which promises beatitude to him who hopes in God, as in that saying of Isaias: [[Is 30:18|the Lord is the God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him|Deus judicii Dominus; beati omnes qui exspectant eum]].

paras.t: Precatio. Viam nostram in peccatis pronam dextera potentiæ tuæ, Domine, disperge : erige nos elisos, ac malis operibus compeditos solve; atque justos redditos dilige, et in dilectione tua in perpetuum fac perseverare.
paras.en: Prayer. With the right hand of thy power, O Lord, scatter our way, which is prone to sin: lift us up who are cast down, and loose us who are fettered by evil works; and love us when we have been made just, and make us persevere in thy love for ever.

146.title: DECLARATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI QUADRAGESIMI SEXTI : LAUDATE DOMINUM, QUONIAM BONUS EST PSALMUS.
146.title_en: Declaration of the hundred and forty-sixth psalm: Praise ye the Lord, because psalm is good.

paras.t: Præponitur autem psalmo nunc exponendo hic titulus : Alleluia : cujus ratio plana est. Psalmus etenim præsens totaliter pertinet ad laudem divinam ; et describuntur in psalmo hoc multa magnifica opera atque piissima beneficia Creatoris, propter quæ merito semper ac incessanter laudandus est.
paras.en: Now to the psalm which is now to be expounded this title is prefixed: [[146:1|Alleluia|Alleluia]], the reason of which is plain. For the present psalm belongs wholly to the praise of God; and in this psalm are described many magnificent works and most loving benefits of the Creator, for which he is deservedly to be praised always and without ceasing.

paras.t: Ait ergo : Laudate Dominum corde devoto ac hilari, voce strenua atque decenti, opere virtuoso seu vita laudabili, quoniam bonus est psalmus, id est, bona est laudatio Dei, sanctumque est Deum laudare : imo quid melius eo? Actus namque specificantur et dignitatem sortiuntur a termino ad quem, seu ab objecto. Idcirco actus qui immediate tendunt in Deum, et circa ipsum directe versantur, optimi atque dignissimi sunt : quales sunt actus latriæ, scilicet adoratio, laudatio, oratio Dei. Imo laudatio Dei, orationem in dignitate excellit, quum sit actus omnino cœlestis atque angelicus, qui tunc in patria æternaliter permanebit, quando omnis cessabit oratio, prout Salvator locutus est : In illo die me non rogabitis quidquam. De perpetuitate vero laudationis dictum est supra : Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine : in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te.
paras.en: He says, then: [[146:1|Praise ye the Lord|Laudate Dominum]] with a devout and cheerful heart, with a strong and seemly voice, with virtuous works or a praiseworthy life, [[146:1|because psalm is good|quoniam bonus est psalmus]]: that is, the praise of God is good, and it is a holy thing to praise God; nay, what is better than this? For acts are specified, and take their dignity, from the term to which they tend, that is, from their object [a principle of the schools: an act is of the kind and of the worth of that to which it is directed]. Therefore the acts that tend immediately to God, and are directly concerned with him, are the best and most worthy: such are the acts of latria [that is, of the worship due to God alone], namely the adoration, the praise and the prayer of God. Nay, the praise of God surpasses prayer in dignity, since it is an act wholly heavenly and angelic, which will remain for ever in the fatherland when all prayer shall cease, as the Saviour said: [[John 16:23|in that day you shall not ask me any thing|In illo die me non rogabitis quidquam]]. And of the perpetuity of praise it was said above: [[Ps 83:5|Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord: they shall praise thee for ever and ever|Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine : in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te]].

paras.t: Deo nostro sit jucunda decoraque laudatio, id est ex spirituali lætitia nascens, et phantasmatibus ac distractionibus impermixta. Debet enim laudatio, qua Deum laudamus, esse jucunda, ita quod in laude Dei intime gloriemur, tanquam in optimo atque justissimo actu, prout Isaias profitetur : Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, et exsultabit anima mea in Deo meo. Quid enim tam justum et deliciosum, ut Creatorem a creatura laudari? Unde supra dictum est : Servite Domino in lætitia. Præterea laudatio Dei debet esse decora, id est pura et immaculata, tanquam ex fonte sereno seu corde mundo procedens : quod esse non valet, nisi vita laudantis fuerit virtuosa. Non enim est speciosa laus in ore peccatorum. Oportet etiam ut mens voci concordet, atque intenta sit sensui. De iis enim qui vago et dissoluto corde Dominum laudant, ipse per Isaiam testatur : Populus hic labiis me honorat ; cor autem eorum longe est a me. Non est ergo laudatio Deo exhibita, jucunda et decora, nisi anima fuerit spiritualiter læta, stabilis et virtuosa.
paras.en: [[146:1|to our God be joyful and comely praise|Deo nostro sit jucunda decoraque laudatio]]: that is, praise born of spiritual gladness and unmixed with idle images and distractions. For the praise with which we praise God ought to be joyful, so that we glory inwardly in the praise of God as in the best and most just of acts, as Isaias declares: [[Is 61:10|I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall be joyful in my God|Gaudens gaudebo in Domino, et exsultabit anima mea in Deo meo]]. For what is so just and so delightful as that the Creator be praised by the creature? Hence it was said above: [[Ps 99:2|serve ye the Lord with gladness|Servite Domino in lætitia]]. Moreover the praise of God ought to be comely, that is, pure and spotless, proceeding as from a clear spring, or from a clean heart; and this it cannot be unless the life of the one who praises be virtuous. For [[Ecclus 15:9|Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|Non enim est speciosa laus in ore peccatorum]]. It is needful also that the mind agree with the voice, and be intent on the sense. For of those who praise the Lord with a wandering and dissolute heart, he himself testifies through Isaias[[Is 29:13||]]: [[Matt 15:8|This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me|Populus hic labiis me honorat ; cor autem eorum longe est a me]] [Denis gives the words as Christ quotes them in Matt 15:8; the margin gives both places]. The praise offered to God, then, is not joyful and comely unless the soul be spiritually glad, steadfast and virtuous.

paras.t: Ædificans Jerusalem Dominus. Ad litteram Deus frequenter restauravit civitatem illam Jerusalem in Judæa. — Spiritualiter vero, est Dominus ædificans Jerusalem, id est Ecclesiam militantem, ex vivis lapidibus, scilicet hominibus fidelibus. Jerusalem vero supernam atque cœlestem Deus ædificat ex angelis et sanctis hominibus usque ad diem judicii. Similiter animam fidelem, quæ tropologice appellatur Jerusalem, id est Deum pacifice per fidem contemplans, ædificat Deus per virtutum et gratiæ infusionem.
paras.en: [[146:2|The Lord buildeth up Jerusalem|Ædificans Jerusalem Dominus]]. According to the letter, God often restored that city of Jerusalem in Judæa. — Spiritually, the Lord is building up Jerusalem, that is, the Church militant, out of living stones[[1 Pet 2:5||]], namely the faithful. And the Jerusalem above, the heavenly one, God builds up out of angels and holy men until the day of judgement. Likewise the faithful soul, which tropologically [that is, in the moral sense] is called Jerusalem, that is, one who peacefully contemplates God by faith [Jerusalem was commonly interpreted "vision of peace"], God builds up by the infusion of the virtues and of grace.

paras.t: Dispersiones Israelis, id est filios Israel per terram alienorum dispersos, congregabit, reducendo eos ad terram patrum suorum. Hoc Deus corporaliter fecit, quando per Zorobabel et Jesum filium Josedec sacerdotem magnum, per Esdram quoque et Nehemiam, filios Israel reduxit a captivitate Babylonica in Judæam. Unde per Moysen dixit : Si reversi fueritis ad me, ut custodiatis mandata mea, etiamsi abducti fueritis ad extrema cœli, inde congregabo vos, et inducam in terram quam dedi patribus vestris. Cur ergo modo non congregat, o Judæi, Deus dispersiones vestras a captivitate ista longissima, in qua nunc per annos mille trecentos et quinquaginta vel circiter fuistis? Utique, nisi aversi fuissetis ab eo aversione gravissima, nequaquam vos tamdiu relinqueret.
paras.en: [[146:2|the dispersed of Israel|Dispersiones Israelis]], that is, the children of Israel scattered through the land of strangers, [[146:2|he will gather together|congregabit]], bringing them back to the land of their fathers. This God did bodily when, through Zorobabel and Jesus the son of Josedec, the high priest, and through Esdras too and Nehemias, he brought the children of Israel back from the Babylonian captivity into Judæa[[1 Esd 2:1||]][[2 Esd 2:1||]]. Hence he said through Moses[[Deut 30:4||]]: [[2 Esd 1:9|if you return to me, and keep my commandments|Si reversi fueritis ad me, ut custodiatis mandata mea]], [[2 Esd 1:9|though you should be led away to the uttermost parts of the world, I will gather you from thence|etiamsi abducti fueritis ad extrema cœli, inde congregabo vos]], and I will bring you into the land which I gave to your fathers [the margin gives Deut. xxx, 1–5, and 2 Esdr. i, 9: Denis's words are closest to 2 Esd 1:9, where Nehemias recalls this word given through Moses; the last clause echoes Deut 30:5]. Why then, O Jews, does God not now gather your scattered ones from this most long captivity, in which you have now been for one thousand three hundred and fifty years or thereabouts? Surely, had you not turned away from him with a most grievous turning away, he would by no means have left you so long.

paras.t: Spiritualiter etiam, Christus per se ipsum et Apostolos congregavit dispersiones Israelis, id est populum Israeliticum per multas terras dispersum, colligendo eos per fidem et caritatem in unum ovile Ecclesiæ. Propter quod dicitur ab Evangelista : Jesus moriturus erat pro gente, et non tantum pro gente, sed ut filios Dei qui erant dispersi, congregaret in unum. — Mysticus vero sensus est : Dispersiones Israelis, id est populum christianum Deum fideliter contemplantem, per totum orbem diffusum, congregabit nunc in militanti Ecclesia per fidem et spem ac individuam caritatem, postmodum vero in patria per beatificam visionem et cohabitationem æternam prorsus dulcissimam.
paras.en: Spiritually too, Christ, by himself and by the Apostles, gathered together the dispersed of Israel, that is, the Israelite people scattered through many lands, collecting them by faith and charity into the one fold of the Church. For which reason the Evangelist says: [[John 11:51|that Jesus should die for the nation|Jesus moriturus erat pro gente]], [[John 11:52|And not only for the nation, but to gather together in one the children of God that were dispersed|et non tantum pro gente, sed ut filios Dei qui erant dispersi, congregaret in unum]]. — The mystical sense is this: [[146:2|the dispersed of Israel|Dispersiones Israelis]], that is, the Christian people that faithfully contemplates God, spread through the whole world, [[146:2|he will gather together|congregabit]]: now in the Church militant, by faith and hope and undivided charity, and afterwards in the fatherland by the beatific vision and an eternal dwelling together, sweet beyond all things.

paras.t: Qui sanat, spiritualem salutem præstando, contritos corde, id est mente afflictos ac tristes bona tristitia, scilicet ex recordatione peccati, ex dilectione patriæ, ex compassione fraterna; et alligat, spiritualem applicando medicinam, contritiones, id est afflictiones seu mala eorum : dando videlicet consolationem internam, sacramentorum reparativam medelam, virtutum integritatem. Sacramenta namque sunt vasa medicinalia, gratiam continentia, morbosque animæ potenter sanantia.
paras.en: [[146:3|Who healeth|Qui sanat]], bestowing spiritual health, [[146:3|the broken of heart|contritos corde]], that is, those afflicted in mind and sad with a good sadness: from the remembrance of sin, from love of the fatherland, from brotherly compassion; [[146:3|and bindeth up|et alligat]], applying spiritual medicine, [[146:3|their bruises|contritiones]], that is, their afflictions or ills: giving, namely, inward consolation, the restoring remedy of the sacraments, and wholeness of the virtues. For the sacraments are vessels of medicine, containing grace and mightily healing the diseases of the soul.

paras.t: Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum, quum sit creator earum, omnia determinate cognoscens : quæ utique stellæ ab hominibus præ multitudine nequeunt numerari ; et omnibus eis nomina vocat, id est, proprias appellationes tribuit et imponit. Nomen enim imponitur a proprietate rei. Sicut igitur omnium stellarum virtutes ac proprietates distinctissime atque plenissime Deus cognoscit, sic singulis aptissima nomina tribuit.
paras.en: [[146:4|Who telleth the number of the stars|Qui numerat multitudinem stellarum]], since he is their creator[[Gen 1:16||]], knowing all things distinctly; which stars indeed cannot be numbered by men for their multitude[[Gen 15:5||]]; [[146:4|and calleth them all by their names|et omnibus eis nomina vocat]], that is, he gives and assigns them their proper names. For a name is given from the property of the thing. As, then, God knows most distinctly and most fully the powers and properties of all the stars, so he gives to each the most fitting names.

paras.t: Spiritualiter vero, stellæ sunt homines virtuosi et edocti, qui verbo, vita et fama aliis lucent : qui (sicut a Daniele dicitur) fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates. Quibus dicit Apostolus : Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei, in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ : inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi, verbum vitæ continentes. Talibus Christus ait : Vos estis lux mundi. Harum igitur stellarum multitudinem numerat Deus, quoniam sibi soli cognitus est numerus electorum, in superna felicitate locandus. Ideo Christus : Ego, inquit, scio quos elegerim. Et omnibus eis nomina vocat, id est, singulos eorum per approbationem distincte cognoscit, sicut ad Moysen ait : Te ipsum novi ex nomine. Scripta quippe sunt nomina eorum in libro vitæ. Unde Apostolus ad Timotheum dicit : Firmum fundamentum Dei stat, habens signaculum hoc : Cognovit Dominus qui sunt ejus. Denique Christus tanquam pastor bonus, cognoscit oves suas, et proprias oves vocat nominatim.
paras.en: Spiritually, the stars are virtuous and learned men, who give light to others by word, life and good name; who (as Daniel says) shall shine [[Dan 12:3|as stars for all eternity|quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]]. To them the Apostle says: That you may [[Phil 2:15|be blameless and sincere children of God, without reproof, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation: among whom you shine as lights in the world|Sitis sine querela, simplices filii Dei, in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ : inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi]], [[Phil 2:16|Holding forth the word of life|verbum vitæ continentes]]. To such Christ says: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. The multitude of these stars, then, God numbers, since the number of the elect, who are to be placed in the happiness above, is known to him alone. Therefore Christ says: [[John 13:18|I know whom I have chosen|scio quos elegerim]]. [[146:4|and calleth them all by their names|Et omnibus eis nomina vocat]], that is, he knows each of them distinctly, with approval [the knowledge of approbation: God's knowing of the just as his own], as he said to Moses: [[Ex 33:17|thee I have known by name|Te ipsum novi ex nomine]]. For their names are written in the book of life[[Phil 4:3||]]. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:19|the sure foundation of God standeth firm, having this seal: the Lord knoweth who are his|Firmum fundamentum Dei stat, habens signaculum hoc : Cognovit Dominus qui sunt ejus]]. Lastly Christ, as the good shepherd, knoweth his sheep[[John 10:14||]], and [[John 10:3|he calleth his own sheep by name|proprias oves vocat nominatim]].

paras.t: Magnus, imo immensus est Dominus noster, universorum creator ac princeps, et magna virtus, id est potentia ejus : ipse enim est sua virtus. Ideo, sicut ipse immensus est, sic virtus ipsius est immensa. Propter quod non potest in tot et tanta, quin possit in infinities plura atque majora. Et sapientiæ ejus non est numerus, id est finis, quum sit infinita, ineffabilis et incomprehensibilis, sicut divina essentia, cum qua substantialiter idem est. Nec solum sapientia mentis divinæ, qua se cognoscit, immensa est ; sed sapientiæ ejus, qua alia noscit, non est numerus. Deus namque cognoscit actualiter infinita.
paras.en: [[146:5|Great|Magnus]], nay immeasurable, [[146:5|is our Lord|Dominus noster]], the creator and prince of all things, [[146:5|and great is his power|et magna virtus]], that is, his might: for he is his own power. Therefore, as he himself is immeasurable, so his power is immeasurable. And so he cannot do so many and so great things without being able to do infinitely more and greater. [[146:5|and of his wisdom there is no number|Et sapientiæ ejus non est numerus]], that is, no end, since it is infinite, ineffable and incomprehensible, like the divine essence, with which it is in substance the same. And not only is the wisdom of the divine mind, by which he knows himself, immeasurable; but of his wisdom, by which he knows other things, there is no number. For God knows actually infinite things [that is, an infinity of things actually, not only in possibility].

paras.t: Suscipiens, id est pie custodiens, clementer exaudiens, paternaliterque conservans et regens, mansuetos, id est homines mites qui iram exstinguunt, Dominus : tales enim (teste Scriptura) multum complacent Deo. Propter quod scriptum est : Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris. Sicut autem (teste Salomone) ira in sinu stulti, sic mansuetudo in sinu sapientis requiescit. Humilians autem, id est deprimens, peccatores in vitiis permanentes, usque ad terram, id est usque ad ima, puta infernum, qui in medio terræ creditur situatus. Quum enim peccatores contra Deum intumescant, ejusque præcepta implere non curent, juxta illud Job, Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini : justum est ut usque ad infima humilientur a Deo, qui dicturus est eis, Ite, maledicti, in ignem æternum.
paras.en: [[146:6|The Lord lifteth up|Suscipiens]], that is, lovingly guarding, mercifully hearing, and in fatherly wise preserving and ruling, [[146:6|the meek|mansuetos]], that is, gentle men who quench anger: for such men (as Scripture witnesses) are very pleasing to God. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 3:19|My son, do thy works in meekness, and thou shalt be beloved above the glory of men|Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris]]. And as (Solomon witnessing) [[Eccles 7:10|anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|ira in sinu stulti]], so meekness rests in the bosom of the wise. [[146:6|and bringeth|Humilians autem]], that is, pressing down, [[146:6|the wicked|peccatores]] who persist in their vices, [[146:6|down even to the ground|usque ad terram]], that is, to the lowest places, namely hell, which is believed to be situated in the middle of the earth. For since sinners swell up against God and care not to fulfil his commandments, according to that word of Job, [[Job 24:13|They have been rebellious to the light|Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini]], it is just that they be brought down to the very lowest by God, who will say to them: Go, [[Matt 25:41|you cursed, into everlasting fire|maledicti, in ignem æternum]] [Denis has *Ite*, "Go", for the Vulgate's *Discedite a me*, "Depart from me"].

paras.t: Præcinite Domino in confessione duplici, scilicet laudis divinæ et propriæ culpæ. Et quia peccator idoneus non est Deum laudare, idcirco præcinite (id est, primo canite) Domino in confessione propriæ culpæ : quoniam in confessione hac omnia lavantur, et justus in principio accusator est sui. Sicque purgati, præcinite Domino in confessione laudis divinæ, eum in omnibus per sacra verba laudando. Psallite Deo nostro, id est, Deum laudate, in cithara spirituali et figurata, videlicet in operatione bona atque morali. Non enim sine laude operis sufficit laus sermonis.
paras.en: [[146:7|Sing ye to the Lord with praise|Præcinite Domino in confessione]], a twofold one, namely of the divine praise and of one's own guilt [*in confessione*, "with praise", is literally "in confession", a word used both of praising God and of acknowledging sin]. And because a sinner is not fit to praise God[[Ecclus 15:9||]], therefore first sing (*præcinite*, that is, sing first) to the Lord in the confession of your own guilt: for in this confession all things are washed away, and [[Prov 18:17|The just is first accuser of himself|justus in principio accusator est sui]] [Denis reads *in principio*, "at the beginning", where the Clementine text has *prior*]. And so cleansed, sing first to the Lord in the confession of the divine praise, praising him in all things with holy words. [[146:7|sing to our God|Psallite Deo nostro]], that is, praise God, [[146:7|upon the harp|in cithara]], a spiritual and figurative one, namely in good and moral works. For the praise of speech is not enough without the praise of works.

paras.t: Qui operit cœlum nubibus, quantum ad nostrum adspectum. Deus enim elevat nubes de terra in aerem : sicque inter cœlum et nostrum adspectum positæ nubes, operiunt illud nobis, ne ipsum in sua diaphaneitate seu puritate videre possimus. Non tamen operiunt totum cœlum, quum sint incomparabiliter eo minores. Et parat terræ pluviam, emittendo aquam de nubibus ad terram irrigandam. Qui producit in montibus fœnum ad sustentationem jumentorum, et herbam multiplicem servituti hominum, id est ad hoc ut hominum utilitati deserviat. Maximam enim virtutem herbis impressit ad solatium atque subsidium hominum. Unde in Ecclesiastico habetur : Altissimus de terra creavit medicinam.
paras.en: [[146:8|Who covereth the heaven with clouds|Qui operit cœlum nubibus]], as far as our sight is concerned. For God raises the clouds from the earth into the air; and so the clouds, set between the heaven and our sight, cover it from us, so that we cannot see it in its transparency or purity. Yet they do not cover the whole heaven, since they are incomparably smaller than it. [[146:8|and prepareth rain for the earth|Et parat terræ pluviam]], sending down water from the clouds to water the earth. [[146:8|Who maketh grass to grow on the mountains|Qui producit in montibus fœnum]] for the sustenance of beasts, [[146:8|and herbs|et herbam]] of many kinds [[146:8|for the service of men|servituti hominum]] [Denis reads *herbam multiplicem*, "manifold herbs"], that is, so that they may serve the use of men. For he has set a very great power in herbs, for the comfort and help of men. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 38:4|The most High hath created medicines out of the earth|Altissimus de terra creavit medicinam]].

paras.t: Qui dat jumentis, id est animalibus homini ministrantibus in vita humana, sicut sunt equi, boves, muli, vaccæ, escam ipsorum : providet enim eis de necessariis vitæ, prout Salvator ait : Pater cœlestis pascit volatilia cœli ; et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum, non per aliquam cognitionem Dei, sed per naturalem appetitum quo appetunt cibum, quem nonnisi Deo concedente percipere valent. Propter quod in libro Job inducitur : Quis præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagantes, eo quod non habeant cibos ? Speciali autem modo providet Deus pullis corvorum. Nam (ut ait Isidorus) corvi pullos suos non alunt, donec plumis nigrescant : tunc enim recognoscunt eos esse suos. Antequam autem nigrescunt, nutriri dicuntur rore cœlesti, seu muscis quibusdam circa eorum ora volantibus, quas hiando facile glutiunt.
paras.en: [[146:9|Who giveth to beasts|Qui dat jumentis]], that is, to the animals that serve man in human life, such as horses, oxen, mules, cows, [[146:9|their food|escam ipsorum]]: for he provides them with the necessaries of life, as the Saviour says: The [[Matt 6:26|heavenly Father feedeth|Pater cœlestis pascit]] [[Matt 6:26|the birds of the air|volatilia cœli]]; [[146:9|and to the young ravens that call upon him|et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum]], not by any knowledge of God, but by the natural appetite with which they seek food, which they cannot obtain unless God grants it. For which reason it is said in the book of Job: [[Job 38:41|Who provideth food for the raven, when her young ones cry to God, wandering about, because they have no meat?|Quis præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagantes, eo quod non habeant cibos]] And God provides for the young of ravens in a special way. For (as Isidore says) ravens do not feed their young until these grow black with feathers, since then they recognize them as their own. Before they grow black, they are said to be fed with the dew of heaven, or with certain flies flying about their mouths, which they easily swallow by gaping.

paras.t: Spiritualiter vero Deus operit cœlum nubibus, id est sacram Scripturam verborum et figurarum obscuritatibus, ut veritas occultetur indignis, exercitatis vero detur occasio fructuosæ inquisitionis : et de his nubibus parat terræ, id est Ecclesiæ in terra peregrinanti, pluviam spiritualis doctrinæ, per hoc quod corda doctorum illuminat ad exponendum sacram Scripturam pro informatione Ecclesiæ. Qui producit in montibus, id est in altis et magnis hominibus, ad Christum humiliter conversis, fœnum, id est spiritualis vitæ ac documenti fructum ; producit in his montibus et herbam, id est spiritualia medicamenta, videlicet recta consilia, servituti hominum, id est, ut talia caritative ministrent proximis suis indigentibus. Qui dat jumentis, id est hominibus adhuc rudibus atque carnalibus, escam ipsorum, id est spiritualem doctrinam seu gratiam eis proportionatam, quemadmodum Apostolus dicit : Ego, fratres, non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus : tanquam parvulis in Christo, lac vobis potum dedi, non escam. Deus enim unicuique dat secundum propriam virtutem. Et pullis corvorum, id est filiis idololatrarum, videlicet gentibus conversis, invocantibus eum in fide et caritate pro spirituali profectu seu alimento.
paras.en: Spiritually, God [[146:8|covereth the heaven with clouds|operit cœlum nubibus]], that is, covers Holy Scripture with the obscurities of words and figures, so that the truth may be hidden from the unworthy, while to those who are practised an occasion is given of fruitful inquiry; and from these clouds he [[146:8|prepareth|parat]] for [[146:8|the earth|terræ]], that is, for the Church on pilgrimage on earth, [[146:8|rain|pluviam]] of spiritual doctrine, in that he enlightens the hearts of the doctors to expound Holy Scripture for the instruction of the Church. [[146:8|Who maketh|Qui producit]] [[146:8|on the mountains|in montibus]], that is, in lofty and great men humbly converted to Christ, [[146:8|grass|fœnum]] to grow, that is, the fruit of spiritual life and teaching; on these mountains he brings forth also [[146:8|and herbs|et herbam]], that is, spiritual medicines, namely right counsels, [[146:8|for the service of men|servituti hominum]], that is, so that they may minister such things in charity to their needy neighbours. [[146:9|Who giveth to beasts|Qui dat jumentis]], that is, to men still rude and carnal, [[146:9|their food|escam ipsorum]], that is, spiritual doctrine or grace proportioned to them, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:1|And I, brethren, could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal. As unto little ones in Christ|Ego, fratres, non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus : tanquam parvulis in Christo]], [[1 Cor 3:2|I gave you milk to drink, not meat|lac vobis potum dedi, non escam]]. For God gives [[Matt 25:15|to every one according to his proper ability|unicuique dat secundum propriam virtutem]]. [[146:9|and to the young ravens|Et pullis corvorum]], that is, to the children of idolaters, namely the converted Gentiles, [[146:9|that call upon him|invocantibus eum]] in faith and charity, for their spiritual progress or nourishment.

paras.t: Non in fortitudine equi voluntatem habebit : id est, Deo placitum non est in robore equi aut equitis : sicut prædictum est, Fallax equus ad salutem ; nec in tibiis viri beneplacitum erit ei : id est, non in bona dispositione naturalis formationis corporis humani, non in homine ad gradiendum bellandumque forti, seu curiose ornato, complacet Deo, quasi propter ista victoriam tribuat vel salutem. Unde ait : Non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua ; et iterum, Peribit fuga a veloce, et fortis non salvabit animam suam. Non autem sunt hæc sic intelligenda, quasi equus aut homo, seu alia creatura, quantum ad sua naturalia, Deo displiceat, quum dictum sit, Lætabitur Dominus in operibus suis ; et in libro Sapientiæ, Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti ; sed ideo dicitur Deus non habere beneplacitum aut voluntatem in istis, quia propter ea neminem spiritualiter salvat, nec quantum ad vitam æternam acceptat.
paras.en: [[146:10|He shall not delight in the strength of the horse|Non in fortitudine equi voluntatem habebit]] [literally "he shall not have his will in the strength of the horse"]: that is, God's good pleasure is not in the might of horse or horseman; as was said before, [[Ps 32:17|Vain is the horse for safety|Fallax equus ad salutem]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxvi, 17; the words are Ps 32:17]; [[146:10|nor take pleasure in the legs of a man|nec in tibiis viri beneplacitum erit ei]]: that is, God is not well pleased with a good disposition of the natural build of the human body, nor with a man strong for marching and fighting, or curiously adorned, as though for these things he would grant victory or salvation. Hence it is said: [[Jer 9:23|let not the strong man glory in his strength|Non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua]]; and again: [[Amos 2:14|flight shall perish from the swift|Peribit fuga a veloce]], [[Amos 2:14|neither shall the strong save his life|et fortis non salvabit animam suam]] [Denis joins two clauses of the verse, *fortis non obtinebit virtutem suam* and *robustus non salvabit animam suam*]. Yet these things are not to be understood as though the horse or man or any other creature, as to its natural being, displeased God, since it is said: [[Ps 103:31|the Lord shall rejoice in his works|Lætabitur Dominus in operibus suis]]; and in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:25|thou lovest all things that are, and hatest none of the things which thou hast made|Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti]]. But God is said to have no good pleasure or will in these things for this reason, that for their sake he saves no one spiritually, nor accepts anyone with regard to eternal life.

paras.t: Sed hoc modo Beneplacitum est Domino super timentes eum filiali et casto timore, et in eis qui sperant super misericordia ejus, non in propriis meritis, viribus, divitiis, aut simili aliquo : qui quum fecerint omnia quæ præcepta sunt eis, dicunt: Servi inutiles sumus ; quod debuimus facere, fecimus.
paras.en: But it is in this way: [[146:11|The Lord taketh pleasure in them that fear him|Beneplacitum est Domino super timentes eum]] with a filial and chaste fear [that is, the fear of a son who dreads to offend, not the servile fear of punishment], [[146:11|and in them that hope in his mercy|et in eis qui sperant super misericordia ejus]], not in their own merits, strength, riches or any such thing; who, when they have done all that was commanded them, say: [[Luke 17:10|We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do|Servi inutiles sumus ; quod debuimus facere, fecimus]].

paras.t: Psalmum hunc occulta virtute atque ingenti dulcedine plenum, decet nos mente pura et intenta proferre, ut sit nostra laudatio jucunda, itemque decora ; et ut a Deo jugiter suscipi mereamur, mansueti esse curemus, sicut et Christus nos admonet : Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde.
paras.en: This psalm, full of hidden power and of great sweetness, it befits us to utter with a pure and attentive mind, so that our praise may be joyful and also comely; and that we may deserve to be lifted up by God continually, let us take care to be meek, as Christ too admonishes us: [[Matt 11:29|learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart|Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde]].

paras.t: Precatio. Contritiones populi tui, Deus Pater omnipotens, sana, et omnes dispersiones cordis ejus in bonis operibus congrega : ut pro beneficiis in confessione tibi laudis precemur, et in cithara virtutum tibi Deo nostro psallamus.
paras.en: Prayer. Heal, O God the Father almighty, the bruises of thy people, and gather together all the scatterings of their heart in good works: that for thy benefits we may pray to thee in the confession of praise, and sing to thee our God upon the harp of the virtues [*precemur*, "we may pray", as printed; perhaps for *præcinamus*, "we may sing", as in v. 7].

147.title: EXPLANATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI QUADRAGESIMI SEPTIMI : LAUDA, JERUSALEM, DOMINUM.
147.title_en: Explanation of the hundred and forty-seventh psalm: Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem.

paras.t: Habet psalmus nunc declarandus pro titulo, Alleluia Aggæi et Zachariæ. In aliquibus tamen Bibliis non ponitur nisi, Alleluia. Quid autem Alleluia significet, sæpe prædictum est. Additur autem, Aggæi et Zachariæ, quoniam psalmus iste loquitur de cœlesti Jerusalem, cujus figura erat Jerusalem illa terrena, de cujus reædificatione prophetaverunt Zacharias et Aggæus.
paras.en: The psalm now to be explained has for its title: Alleluia, of Aggeus and Zacharias. In some Bibles, however, nothing is set down but Alleluia. What Alleluia means has often been said before. Of Aggeus and Zacharias is added because this psalm speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem, of which that earthly Jerusalem was a figure, of whose rebuilding Zacharias[[Zach 1:16||]] and Aggeus[[Agg 1:1||]] prophesied.

paras.t: Alloquens ergo Propheta Ecclesiam triumphantem, quæ appellatur Jerusalem, propter plenissimæ pacis abundantiam, et Sion, propter Dei clarissimam speculationem (Jerusalem enim visio pacis, Sion vero speculatio interpretatur), ait: Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum, quem facie ad faciem felicissime contemplaris; Lauda Deum tuum, quem perfectissime colis, et intime diligis, o Sion, id est, Ecclesia triumphans.
paras.en: Addressing, then, the Church triumphant, which is called Jerusalem because of the abundance of the fullest peace, and Sion because of its most clear beholding of God (for Jerusalem is interpreted "vision of peace", and Sion "watch-tower" [Latin *speculatio*, a looking out or beholding]), the Prophet says: [[147:1|Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem|Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum]], whom thou contemplatest most happily [[1 Cor 13:12|face to face|facie ad faciem]]; [[147:1|praise thy God|Lauda Deum tuum]], whom thou dost worship most perfectly and love inwardly, [[147:1|O Sion|o Sion]], that is, Church triumphant.

paras.t: Quoniam confortavit seras portarum tuarum. Portæ et seræ cœlestis Jerusalem, non sunt corporaliter intelligendæ: sed admissio, qua aliquis electus admittitur ad consortium Beatorum, ingrediendo regnum cœlorum, accipi potest et dici porta cœlestis Jerusalem; sera vero intelligi potest confirmatio Beatorum in Deo. Itaque confirmavit seras portarum tuarum, id est, confirmationes civium tuorum in se fecit immobiles et securas, ita quod nulla culpa, nulla miseria, nullus adversarius potest irrumpere. Immobiliter ergo conjuncti sunt Deo omnes Beati in patria. Metaphorice itaque dicuntur divinitus confirmatæ seræ portarum cœlestis Jerusalem: quoniam sicut civitas hujus mundi, dum fuerit fortibus seris clausa, secura est, nec valet hostis intrare, nec cives exire: sic cœlestis Jerusalem omnino securissima est: quam, sicut reprobi nequeunt ingredi, ita Beati nec volunt, nec valent hanc egredi, benedictionem amittendo. Benedixit, id est, omnium spiritualium deliciarum cœlestiumque bonorum munera contulit, filiis tuis, id est universis Beatis habitantibus in te. Quemadmodum autem viatores fideles, dicuntur filii Ecclesiæ militantis: sic comprehensores beati, dicuntur filii Ecclesiæ triumphantis.
paras.en: [[147:2|Because he hath strengthened the bolts of thy gates|Quoniam confortavit seras portarum tuarum]]. The gates and bolts of the heavenly Jerusalem are not to be understood bodily: rather, the admission by which one of the elect is admitted to the fellowship of the Blessed, entering the kingdom of heaven, may be taken for and called a gate of the heavenly Jerusalem; and the bolt may be understood as the confirmation of the Blessed in God [that is, their being made firm in good so that they can no longer fall away]. So he hath made firm the bolts of thy gates, that is, he hath made the confirmation of thy citizens in himself immovable and secure, so that no fault, no misery, no adversary can break in. All the Blessed in the fatherland, then, are joined to God immovably. Thus the bolts of the gates of the heavenly Jerusalem are said metaphorically to be made firm by God: for as a city of this world, while it is shut with strong bolts, is secure, and the enemy cannot get in nor the citizens get out, so the heavenly Jerusalem is altogether most secure: as the reprobate cannot enter it, so the Blessed neither will nor can go out of it and lose their blessing. [[147:2|he hath blessed|Benedixit]], that is, he hath bestowed the gifts of all spiritual delights and heavenly goods, [[147:2|thy children|filiis tuis]], that is, all the Blessed dwelling [[147:2|within thee|in te]]. For as the faithful wayfarers are called children of the Church militant, so the blessed comprehensors [that is, those who have reached the goal and see God, as against wayfarers still on the road] are called children of the Church triumphant.

paras.t: Qui posuit fines tuos pacem, id est pacificos, ita quod muros et terminos tuos nullus valet turbare aut circumvallare, sed posuit fines tuos pacem, in tantum ut pax sit finis tuus. Verumtamen quum in Evangelio dicatur Regni ejus non erit finis, mirum videtur quomodo cœlestis Jerusalem (de qua quotidie dicimus: Pater, adveniat regnum tuum) fines habere dicatur. Et respondendum, quod regni Christi seu cœlestis Jerusalem non est finis durationis: habet tamen suæ finem essentiæ atque virtutis. Per fines vero, hoc loco, non oportet corporeos intelligere terminos civitatis supernæ, sed interiores spiritualesque fines singulorum Sanctorum in patria, loquendo de finibus consummantibus seu perficientibus, non de finibus consumentibus. Finis autem consummans cujuslibet Beatorum, est visio Dei per speciem. Hunc vero finem posuit Deus in quolibet comprehensore, pacem, id est tam securum et interminabilem, ut aptius nuncupetur tranquillitas seu pax, quam pacificus et tranquillus. Vel, Posuit fines tuos pacem, ita quod pax est finis omnium filiorum tuorum, quoniam pacem finaliter appetunt: non quod pax sit essentialiter ultimus finis Sanctorum, sed proxima quædam dispositio ad ultimum finem. Huic quoque Jerusalem Dominus per Isaiam ait: Ponam visitationem tuam pacem, et præpositos tuos justitiam. Et adipe frumenti, id est beata fruitione Divinitatis, satiat te, repletus in bonis desiderium tuum. Ipsa namque superessentialis Divinitas, cibus est omnium Beatorum: cujus visio sive fruitio merito dicitur adeps frumenti, id est dulcis refectio panis æterni. Hæc refectio atque satietas est essentiale præmium Beatorum, quo tam plene ditantur, ut plus nequeant desiderare.
paras.en: [[147:3|Who hath placed peace in thy borders|Qui posuit fines tuos pacem]], that is, hath made them peaceful, so that no one can trouble or besiege thy walls and bounds; he hath set thy borders as peace, so far that peace is thy end [the Latin *fines* means both "borders" and "ends"; Denis plays on both senses]. Yet since it is said in the Gospel, [[Luke 1:33|of his kingdom there shall be no end|Regni ejus non erit finis]], it seems strange how the heavenly Jerusalem (of which we say daily: [[Luke 11:2|Father|Pater]], [[Luke 11:2|Thy kingdom come|adveniat regnum tuum]]) can be said to have ends. And the answer is that the kingdom of Christ, or the heavenly Jerusalem, has no end of duration, yet it has an end of its being and power. By *ends* here we need not understand the bodily bounds of the city above, but the inward and spiritual ends of each of the Saints in the fatherland, speaking of ends that complete or perfect, not of ends that consume. Now the completing end of each of the Blessed is the vision of God face to face [Latin *per speciem*, that is, by sight, not by faith]. This end God hath placed in every comprehensor as peace, that is, so secure and endless that it is more fittingly called tranquillity or peace than peaceful and tranquil. Or: he hath set thy ends as peace, so that peace is the end of all thy children, since they seek peace as their end: not that peace is in its essence the last end of the Saints, but a disposition next to the last end. To this Jerusalem too the Lord says by Isaias: [[Is 60:17|I will make thy visitation peace, and thy overseers justice|Ponam visitationem tuam pacem, et præpositos tuos justitiam]]. [[147:3|with the fat of corn|Et adipe frumenti]], that is, with the blessed enjoyment of the Godhead, [[147:3|filleth thee|satiat te]], filling thy desire with good things. For the superessential Godhead itself is the food of all the Blessed: the vision or enjoyment of which is rightly called the fat of corn, that is, the sweet refreshment of the eternal bread. This refreshment and fullness is the essential reward of the Blessed, by which they are so fully enriched that they can desire nothing more.

paras.t: Qui emittit eloquium suum terræ, id est legem divinam, sacram Scripturam, revelationes cœlestes annuntiat hominibus per angelos sanctos: qui omnes sunt administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi, secundum Apostolum; per quos revelationes divinæ deferuntur ad nos, secundum Dionysium. Unde Stephanus ait Judæis: Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum. Emisit quoque Deus eloquium suum terræ, mittendo Filium suum in mundum, annuntians pacem per Jesum, et per eum evangelicam legem hominibus donans ac prædicans. Velociter currit sermo ejus: id est, prædicatio verbi cœlestis, seu annuntiatio evangelicæ legis, cito atque celeriter per mundum diffusa est, et hominibus patefacta per Apostolos ac apostolicos viros. In omnem enim terram exivit sonus eorum. Emisit plane Christus eloquium suum terræ, dicendo Apostolis: Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. Velociter vero cucurrit sermo ejus, quando Apostoli exsequebantur et impleverunt quod Christus eis prædixit: Eritis mihi testes in Jerusalem et in omni Judæa et Samaria, et usque ad ultimum terræ.
paras.en: [[147:4|Who sendeth forth his speech to the earth|Qui emittit eloquium suum terræ]], that is, the divine law, holy Scripture, heavenly revelations, he announces to men through the holy angels, who are all [[Heb 1:14|ministering spirits, sent to minister|administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi]], according to the Apostle; through whom divine revelations are brought down to us, according to Dionysius. Hence Stephen says to the Jews: You [[Acts 7:53|have received the law by the disposition of angels|Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum]]. God also sent forth his speech to the earth by sending his Son into the world, [[Acts 10:36|preaching peace by Jesus|annuntians pacem per Jesum]], and through him giving and preaching the law of the Gospel to men. [[147:4|his word runneth swiftly|Velociter currit sermo ejus]]: that is, the preaching of the heavenly word, or the announcing of the law of the Gospel, was spread quickly and swiftly through the world, and made known to men by the Apostles and apostolic men. For [[Ps 18:5|Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth|In omnem enim terram exivit sonus eorum]]. Christ plainly sent forth his speech to the earth when he said to the Apostles: [[Mark 16:15|Go ye into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature|Euntes in mundum universum, prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]. And his word ran swiftly when the Apostles carried out and fulfilled what Christ had foretold them: [[Acts 1:8|you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth|Eritis mihi testes in Jerusalem et in omni Judæa et Samaria, et usque ad ultimum terræ]].

paras.t: Qui dat nivem sicut lanam, nebulam sicut cinerem spargit. Impressiones enim meteorologicæ principaliter fiunt a Deo, tanquam a prima causa: et sic ipse dat nivem sicut lanam, quoniam cadit per modum parvarum partium lanæ; nebulam sicut cinerem spargit, videlicet per partes minutas, et per modum cineris coloratas.
paras.en: [[147:5|Who giveth snow like wool|Qui dat nivem sicut lanam]], [[147:5|scattereth mists like ashes|nebulam sicut cinerem spargit]]. For the effects of the weather [Latin *impressiones meteorologicæ*, the scholastic term for what happens in the air: rain, snow, mist and the like] are brought about principally by God, as by the first cause; and so he giveth snow like wool, since it falls in the manner of little tufts of wool; he scattereth mist like ashes, that is, in tiny particles, and coloured like ash.

paras.t: Mittit crystallum suam, quæ est glacies fortissime indurata, sicut buccellas, id est per modum frustorum candidi panis. Ante faciem frigoris ejus quis sustinebit? id est, quis ferre poterit præsentiam frigoris a Deo causati, si vellet Deus illud intendere? quasi dicat, Nemo. Quædam enim loca inhabitabilia sunt propter frigiditatis excessum. Emittet Deus verbum suum, id est præceptum seu voluntatis suæ effectum, puta calorem seu simile aliquid, et liquefaciet ea, id est, crystallum seu glaciem mollificabit; flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ, quæ prius stabant congelatæ. Potest autem per spiritum intelligi ventus glaciem resolvens; vel ipsa Dei voluntas, seu Spiritus Sanctus, quo flante, id est virtutem suam exercente, fluunt aquæ quæ erant solidatæ per frigus. Hæc ad litteram plana sunt.
paras.en: [[147:6|He sendeth his crystal|Mittit crystallum suam]], which is ice frozen very hard, [[147:6|like morsels|sicut buccellas]], that is, in the manner of pieces of white bread. [[147:6|who shall stand before the face of his cold?|Ante faciem frigoris ejus quis sustinebit?]] That is, who could bear the presence of the cold caused by God, if God willed to make it severe? As if to say: No one. For some places are uninhabitable because of the excess of cold. [[147:7|He shall send out his word|Emittet Deus verbum suum]], that is, his command or the effect of his will, say heat or something like it, [[147:7|and shall melt them|et liquefaciet ea]], that is, will soften the crystal or ice; [[147:7|his wind shall blow, and the waters shall run|flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ]], which before stood frozen. By *spiritus* [which means both "wind" and "spirit"] may be understood the wind that thaws the ice; or the very will of God, or the Holy Ghost, by whose blowing, that is, by whose exercise of his power, the waters flow that had been made solid by the cold. These things are plain according to the letter.

paras.t: Porro spiritualem intelligentiam assequendo, dat Deus nivem sicut lanam, dum peccatorem vitiorum frigore induratum, ad pietatem pœnitentiamque convertit: ut sit mollis et capax gratiæ Dei, qui fuerat durus et frigidus. Nebulam, id est vitiosam consuetudinem, seu vitiorum accumulationem, sicut cinerem spargit, id est, per gratiam dissipat, dando compunctionem et confessionem, omnia mala expellentem. Mittit ad obedientiam et incorporationem Ecclesiæ, crystallum suam, id est peccatores quosdam obstinatos, quos interdum clementissime respicit, sicut buccellas: id est, sic mittit eos, ut incorporentur Ecclesiæ per fidem et caritatem, atque ut alios nutriant verbo doctrinæ cœlestis. Ante faciem frigoris ejus quis sustinebit? id est, quis pati valebit ultionem divinæ justitiæ, qua in præsenti et futuro peccata ulciscitur, non solum infligendo pœnam sensus, sed etiam pœnam damni, indurando videlicet seu infrigidando corda reproborum, saltem permissive per gratiæ subtractionem?
paras.en: Further, following the spiritual understanding: God [[147:5|giveth snow like wool|dat Deus nivem sicut lanam]] when he turns a sinner hardened by the cold of vices to piety and penance, so that he who had been hard and cold becomes soft and able to receive the grace of God. [[147:5|mists|Nebulam]], that is, a vicious habit, or a heaping up of vices, [[147:5|like ashes|sicut cinerem]] he [[147:5|scattereth|spargit]], that is, he dispels it by grace, giving compunction and confession, which drive out all evils. [[147:6|He sendeth|Mittit]] to obedience and incorporation into the Church [[147:6|his crystal|crystallum suam]], that is, certain obstinate sinners, on whom he sometimes looks most mercifully, [[147:6|like morsels|sicut buccellas]]: that is, he so sends them that they are incorporated into the Church through faith and charity, and nourish others with the word of heavenly doctrine. [[147:6|who shall stand before the face of his cold?|Ante faciem frigoris ejus quis sustinebit?]] That is, who will be able to endure the vengeance of divine justice, by which he punishes sins in the present and in the future, not only by inflicting the pain of sense but also the pain of loss [the two punishments of the damned in scholastic teaching: suffering inflicted, and the loss of God], namely by hardening or chilling the hearts of the reprobate, at least permissively, through the withdrawal of grace?

paras.t: Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob. Multa enim futura revelavit Deus per spiritum prophetiæ Jacob patriarchæ: ut patet in Genesi, ubi ait, Congregamini ut annuntiem vobis quæ ventura sunt in diebus novissimis; illicque de Christo copiose et evidenter prophetat. Annuntiat etiam justitias, id est decem præcepta moralia, et judicia sua, id est præcepta judicialia, Israel, id est populo Israelitico. Non fecit Deus taliter, id est tam gratiose et pie, omni nationi, id est ceteris gentibus; et judicia sua, id est veteris legis præcepta, non manifestavit eis, sicut populo Judæorum. Quoniam enim Deus incarnari elegit ex semine Jacob, idcirco tam ipsi quam filiis ejus, et maxime tribui Juda, specialem gratiam præstitit, convertendo eos ad unius veri Dei cultum, et Christi expectationem. Decuit namque populum illum, de quo nasciturus fuerat Christus, ab aliis populis dividi, et singulari sanctitate ornari. Propter quod Moyses: Te, inquit, elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram. Et Apostolus: Quid amplius est Judæo? Multum per omnem modum: primo quidem, quoniam credita sunt illis eloquia Dei.
paras.en: [[147:8|Who declareth his word to Jacob|Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob]]. For God revealed many things to come, through the spirit of prophecy, to Jacob the patriarch, as appears in Genesis, where he says: [[Gen 49:1|Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you the things that shall befall you in the last days|Congregamini ut annuntiem vobis quæ ventura sunt in diebus novissimis]]; and there he prophesies copiously and clearly of Christ. He declareth also [[147:8|his justices|justitias]], that is, the ten moral precepts, [[147:8|and his judgments|et judicia sua]], that is, the judicial precepts, [[147:8|to Israel|Israel]], that is, to the people of Israel. God [[147:9|hath not done|Non fecit]] [[147:9|in like manner|taliter]], that is, so graciously and kindly, [[147:9|to every nation|omni nationi]], that is, to the other peoples; [[147:9|and his judgments|et judicia sua]], that is, the precepts of the old law, [[147:9|he hath not made manifest to them|non manifestavit eis]], as he did to the Jewish people. For since God chose to become incarnate of the seed of Jacob, he therefore showed special grace both to him and to his sons, and above all to the tribe of Juda, turning them to the worship of the one true God and to the expectation of Christ. For it was fitting that the people of whom Christ was to be born should be set apart from the other peoples and adorned with a singular holiness. Wherefore Moses says: [[Deut 7:6|The Lord thy God hath chosen thee|Te, inquit, elegit Dominus]], [[Deut 7:6|to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis qui sunt super terram]][[Deut 14:2||]]. And the Apostle: [[Rom 3:1|What advantage then hath the Jew|Quid amplius est Judæo]]? [[Rom 3:2|Much every way. First indeed, because the words of God were committed to them|Multum per omnem modum: primo quidem, quoniam credita sunt illis eloquia Dei]].

paras.t: Nunc vero quoniam Christum quem exspectant, præsentem spreverunt, nec in eum hucusque credere voluerunt; propterea ista nunc non eis, sed populo christiano, conveniunt. Ut sit sensus: Qui annuntiat verbum suum, id est prædicationem Evangelii, seu Christum Filium suum, Jacob, id est populo christiano vitia supplantanti; justitias et judicia sua, id est præcepta atque consilia in nova lege contenta, Israel, id est eidem populo cœlestia contemplanti. Non fecit taliter omni nationi, videlicet Sarracenis, Tartaris, Judæis nunc excæcatis; et judicia sua, id est ea quæ ipse judicat esse justa, non manifestavit eis, illuminando corda eorum interius, quamvis forte exterius audierunt. Unde Paulus ait quibusdam: Tempora prioris ignorantiæ despiciens Deus, nunc annuntiat ut omnes ubique pœnitentiam agant.
paras.en: But now, since they spurned the Christ whom they await when he was present, and have not been willing to believe in him to this day, these things now befit not them but the Christian people. So that the sense is: [[147:8|Who declareth his word|Qui annuntiat verbum suum]], that is, the preaching of the Gospel, or Christ his Son, [[147:8|to Jacob|Jacob]], that is, to the Christian people supplanting vices [Jacob means "supplanter"]; [[147:8|his justices and his judgments|justitias et judicia sua]], that is, the precepts and counsels contained in the new law, [[147:8|to Israel|Israel]], that is, to the same people contemplating heavenly things [Israel being taken to mean "a man seeing God"]. [[147:9|He hath not done in like manner to every nation|Non fecit taliter omni nationi]], namely to the Saracens, the Tartars, the Jews now blinded; [[147:9|and his judgments|et judicia sua]], that is, the things that he himself judges to be just, [[147:9|he hath not made manifest to them|non manifestavit eis]], by enlightening their hearts within, although perhaps they have heard outwardly. Hence Paul says to certain men: [[Acts 17:30|God indeed having winked at the times of this ignorance, now declareth unto men that all should every where do penance|Tempora prioris ignorantiæ despiciens Deus, nunc annuntiat ut omnes ubique pœnitentiam agant]].

paras.t: Denique quidam exponunt hunc psalmum de Ecclesia militanti, quæ dicitur Jerusalem et Sion, propter causas ubertim præhabitas. Hanc ergo in primo versiculo excitat ut Dominum laudet: cujus rationem annectit: Quoniam confortavit seras portarum tuarum. Portæ Ecclesiæ sunt virtutes, præsertim fides, spes, caritas, quibus intratur ad Deum. Seræ autem portarum istarum, dici possunt sacramenta seu dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ per virtutes muniuntur. Has igitur seras confortavit Dominus, dando sacramentis efficaciam sanctificandi, virtute dominicæ passionis, usque ad finem mundi. Possumus quoque per portas Ecclesiæ intelligere sacramenta; per seras vero portarum, virtutes sacramentorum. Benedixit filiis tuis, id est fidelibus, in te, id est in ecclesiastica unitate perseverantibus, dando eis munera gratiarum. Qui posuit fines tuos pacem, id est, particulares Ecclesias fecit pacificas. Christus enim annuntiavit, annuntiarique jussit pacem hominibus. Unde in Michæa habetur: Pax erit in terra nostra quum venerit. Et Christo nato angeli cecinerunt: Gloria in altissimis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Et adipe frumenti, id est corpore Christi, quod in pane de frumento facto consecratur, satiat te spirituali satietate, quemadmodum Christus testatur: Caro mea vere est cibus. Qui manducat meam carnem, in me manet, et ego in eo. Itemque: Qui manducat hunc panem, vivet in æternum. Cetera exponuntur sicut nunc patuit.
paras.en: Lastly, some expound this psalm of the Church militant, which is called Jerusalem and Sion for the reasons given at length above. In the first verse, then, he stirs her up to praise the Lord, and adds the reason for it: [[147:2|Because he hath strengthened the bolts of thy gates|Quoniam confortavit seras portarum tuarum]]. The gates of the Church are the virtues, above all faith, hope and charity, by which one enters to God. The bolts of these gates may be called the sacraments or the gifts of the Holy Ghost, which are made secure by the virtues. These bolts, then, the Lord hath strengthened, giving the sacraments the power to sanctify, by virtue of the Lord's passion, until the end of the world. We may also understand by the gates of the Church the sacraments, and by the bolts of the gates the power of the sacraments. [[147:2|he hath blessed thy children|Benedixit filiis tuis]], that is, the faithful, [[147:2|within thee|in te]], that is, those who persevere in the unity of the Church, giving them the gifts of graces. [[147:3|Who hath placed peace in thy borders|Qui posuit fines tuos pacem]], that is, hath made the particular churches peaceful. For Christ announced peace to men, and commanded it to be announced. Hence it is found in Micheas: Peace shall be in our land when he cometh[[Mich 5:5||]] [the margin gives "Cf. Mich. v, 5, 6"; Denis quotes loosely: the Douay-Rheims has "this man shall be our peace, when the Assyrian shall come into our land"]. And when Christ was born the angels sang: [[Luke 2:14|Glory to God in the highest: and on earth peace to men of good will|Gloria in altissimis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis]]. [[147:3|with the fat of corn|Et adipe frumenti]], that is, with the body of Christ, which is consecrated in bread made of wheat, [[147:3|filleth thee|satiat te]] with a spiritual fullness, as Christ testifies: [[John 6:56|my flesh is meat indeed|Caro mea vere est cibus]]. [[John 6:57|He that eateth my flesh|Qui manducat meam carnem]], [[John 6:57|abideth in me: and I in him|in me manet, et ego in eo]]. And again: [[John 6:59|He that eateth this bread shall live for ever|Qui manducat hunc panem, vivet in æternum]]. The rest is expounded as has now been shown.

paras.t: Quidam vero exponunt psalmum istum de illa terrena urbe Jerusalem et Sion; sed expositio hæc non videtur fructuosa, neque conveniens: propter quod eam non prosequor. Verumtamen si in Hebræo, vel translatione Hieronymi juxta Hebræum, haberet hic psalmus titulum illum, quem habet in aliquibus Bibliis nostris, videlicet, Alleluia Aggæi et Zachariæ; tunc litteraliter psalmus præsens loqueretur de Jerusalem illa terrena, de cujus reædificatione vaticinabantur prædicti Prophetæ. Sed in Hebræo psalmus iste sine titulo est.
paras.en: Some, again, expound this psalm of that earthly city of Jerusalem and Sion; but this exposition does not seem fruitful or fitting, and so I do not pursue it. Yet if in the Hebrew, or in Jerome's translation from the Hebrew, this psalm had the title it has in some of our Bibles, namely, Alleluia, of Aggeus and Zacharias, then the present psalm would speak literally of that earthly Jerusalem, of whose rebuilding the aforesaid Prophets prophesied. But in the Hebrew this psalm is without a title.

paras.t: Ecce psalmum omnino jucundum ac elevatum audivimus: qui mentes nostras ad cœlestia dirigit; in quo Ecclesia militans seu quilibet fidelis, Ecclesiam triumphantem ad Creatoris ac beatificatoris sui laudem invitat: non quod illa nostra indigeat admonitione, sed ut nos ei congratulemur, ejus beatitudinem contemplemur, et adipisci conemur. Dum igitur psalmi hujus primum versum proferimus, cor nostrum ad supercœlestis palatii gaudia erigamus, cœlestem Jerusalem oculis fidei circumspiciamus, ad ejus beatitudinem suspiremus, ob cujus amorem universa sensibilia atque carnalia aspernari debemus. Cogitemus ut possumus quanta sit Beatorum felicitas, quorum civitas ita munita est ut nihil adversi in eam possit incurrere, nullum periculum propinquare: cujus cives æterna et incessanti benedictione replentur, cujus fines sunt pax, ita ut inæstimabili securitate de sua perpetua confirmatione lætentur omnes Beati, qui summi boni beatifica fruitione æternaliter satiantur, æternæ pacis suavissimo gustu pascuntur, atque in sui Creatoris amplexibus invariabiliter requiescunt.
paras.en: Behold, we have heard a psalm altogether joyful and lofty, which directs our minds to heavenly things; in which the Church militant, or any one of the faithful, invites the Church triumphant to the praise of her Creator and the Giver of her beatitude: not that she needs our admonition, but that we may rejoice with her, contemplate her beatitude, and strive to attain it. While, then, we utter the first verse of this psalm, let us lift up our hearts to the joys of the palace above the heavens, look round upon the heavenly Jerusalem with the eyes of faith, and sigh for its beatitude, for love of which we ought to despise all things of sense and of the flesh. Let us think, as far as we can, how great is the happiness of the Blessed, whose city is so fortified that nothing hostile can break into it and no danger come near; whose citizens are filled with an eternal and unceasing blessing, whose borders are peace, so that all the Blessed rejoice with inestimable security in their everlasting confirmation; who are filled eternally with the beatifying enjoyment of the supreme good, are fed with the sweetest taste of eternal peace, and rest unchangeably in the embraces of their Creator.

paras.t: PRECATIO. Terroribus, Domine, ac bellis spiritualis nequitiæ sedatis, pone placatus fines nostros in pace; conforta seras portarum domus tuæ, et benedic nobis filiis novæ gratiæ; et non sinas tenebrarum filios adversum nos ultra prævalere.
paras.en: Prayer. O Lord, calming the terrors and wars of spiritual wickedness, be appeased and set our borders in peace; strengthen the bolts of the gates of thy house, and bless us, the children of the new grace; and suffer not the children of darkness to prevail against us any more.

148.title: ELUCIDATIO PSALMI CENTESIMI QUADRAGESIMI OCTAVI : LAUDATE DOMINUM DE COELIS.
148.title_en: Elucidation of the hundred and forty-eighth psalm: Praise ye the Lord from the heavens.
148.note: Some words are lost in the transcription in the paragraph on v. 3 (p. 686), marked […].

paras.t: Titulus demum psalmi jam exponendi est: Alleluia. In aliquibus tamen Bibliis additur, Aggæi et Zachariæ, propter causam in præcedenti articulo introductam. Est autem hic psalmus cœlesti dulcedine atque deifica jucunditate repletus, in quo ardentissimus Dei amator, zelo divini honoris succensus, universa creata ad omnipotentis exhortatur præconium Creatoris, et ait:
paras.en: Lastly, the title of the psalm now to be explained is: Alleluia. In some Bibles, however, there is added: Of Aggeus and Zacharias, for the reason brought forward in the preceding article. Now this psalm is filled with heavenly sweetness and godlike delight; in it the most ardent lover of God, kindled with zeal for the divine honour, exhorts all created things to the praise of the almighty Creator, and says:

paras.t: Laudate Dominum de cœlis; laudate eum in excelsis. Iste versiculus dupliciter explanatur. Primo, ut sit invitatio omnium creaturarum ad laudem divinam; eritque sensus: Laudate Dominum de cœlis, id est Dominum cœlestem in cœlis habitantem, o cuncta creata; laudate eum in excelsis, id est in altis exsistentem, in sublimibus demorantem, videlicet in mentibus contemplativis ac puris, in thronis cœlestibus, summisque cœlis. Secundo exponitur, ut sit invitatio excellentium creaturarum ad laudandum Deum, ut sit sensus: Laudate Dominum de cœlis, id est, vos qui estis in cœlis, videlicet creaturæ superiores atque cœlestes; laudate eum in excelsis, id est, vos qui estis in magnis dignitatibus, in excelsis ordinibus constituti; vel, Laudate eum in excelsis, id est magnis perfectionibus, summisque laudibus, adscribendo ei prædicata non parva aut mediocriter magna, sed omnino excelsa. Dupliciter autem laudatur Deus sublimis et benedictus ab intellectu creato. Primo in se ipso, attribuendo videlicet ei sublimia attributa, ejus increatam perfectionem designantia, sicut dum dicimus: Deus æternus, immensus, omnipotens, felix, justus, misericors. Secundo, commemorando opera ejus, et in illis ipsum opificem collaudando, sicut dum dicimus: Tu creasti cœlum et terram, et omnem ornatum eorum.
paras.en: [[148:1|Praise ye the Lord from the heavens|Laudate Dominum de cœlis]]; [[148:1|praise ye him in the high places|laudate eum in excelsis]]. This little verse is explained in two ways. First, as an invitation to all creatures to the divine praise; and the sense will be: Praise ye the Lord from the heavens, that is, the heavenly Lord who dwells in the heavens, O all created things; praise ye him in the high places, that is, him who exists on high and abides in the lofty places, namely in contemplative and pure minds, on the heavenly thrones, and in the highest heavens. Secondly, it is explained as an invitation to the excellent creatures to praise God, so that the sense is: Praise ye the Lord from the heavens, that is, you who are in the heavens, namely the higher and heavenly creatures; praise ye him in the high places, that is, you who are set in great dignities, in lofty orders; or, Praise ye him in the high places, that is, with great perfections and the highest praises, ascribing to him predicates not small or moderately great, but altogether lofty. Now God, sublime and blessed, is praised by a created intellect in two ways. First, in himself, namely by attributing to him sublime attributes which signify his uncreated perfection, as when we say: God eternal, immense, almighty, blessed, just, merciful. Secondly, by recalling his works and praising the Maker himself in them, as when we say: Thou hast created heaven and earth, and all their adornment[[Gen 2:1||]][[2 Esd 9:6||]] [the margin gives Gen. ii, 1 and II Esdr. ix, 6; Denis's words are a free blend of the two].

paras.t: Laudate eum, omnes angeli ejus; laudate eum, omnes virtutes ejus. Nomen Angelorum, et nomen Virtutum, interdum ponuntur pro specialibus choris sive ordinibus spiritualium substantiarum, quas Dionysius communiter nominat supermundanos animos, deiformes intellectus, cœlestes essentias, quarum sunt tres hierarchiæ, et ordines novem. Sed hoc loco angeli et virtutes non accipiuntur pro specialibus ordinibus; imo utrumque ipsorum significat omnes prædictas spirituales substantias. Omnes enim appellatæ sunt angeli, quoniam omnes sunt aliquo modo administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi propter electos, eo modo quo Dionysius docet. Omnes quoque dicuntur virtutes, eo quod sint fortes et viriles atque idoneæ ad exsequendas omnes operationes divinas eis divinitus præstitutas. Hos ergo angelos et virtutes, custodes et dominos nostros alloquimur, invitantes eos ad Dei præconium, non quasi indigeant, aut torpentes seu lassi fieri queant in laude Altissimi; sed quasi congratulantes eis, ut dictum est plenius in præcedenti articulo. Sic enim loquimur operanti quod nobis placet, Age, age. Porro nequaquam debemus ista sine attentione diligenti proferre, sed triumphantis Ecclesiæ cives ac Regem corde sereno adspicere, cogitando quam hilariter, indesinenter, ac speciose Deum collaudent omnes sancti angeli, quemadmodum apud Isaiam inducitur: Clamabat alter ad alterum: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus Deus exercituum; plena est omnis terra gloria ejus. Unde Dominus ait ad sanctum Job: Ubi eras quum me laudarent astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei?
paras.en: [[148:2|Praise ye him, all his angels|Laudate eum, omnes angeli ejus]]; [[148:2|praise ye him, all his hosts|laudate eum, omnes virtutes ejus]] [Latin *virtutes*, literally "powers", also the name of one of the nine choirs of angels]. The name of Angels and the name of Virtues [or Powers] are sometimes used for particular choirs or orders of the spiritual substances, which Dionysius commonly calls supermundane spirits, deiform intellects, heavenly essences, of which there are three hierarchies and nine orders. But in this place angels and virtues are not taken for particular orders; rather, each of them signifies all the aforesaid spiritual substances. For all are called angels, since all are in some way [[Heb 1:14|ministering spirits, sent to minister|administratorii spiritus, in ministerium missi]] for the sake of the elect, in the way that Dionysius teaches. All are also called virtues, because they are strong and manly and fit to carry out all the divine operations divinely assigned to them. These angels and virtues, then, our guardians and lords, we address, inviting them to the praise of God, not as if they had need of it, or could become sluggish or weary in the praise of the Most High; but as rejoicing with them, as was said more fully in the preceding article. For so we say to one who is doing what pleases us: Go on, go on. Moreover, we must by no means utter these words without diligent attention, but behold with a serene heart the citizens and the King of the Church triumphant, thinking how joyfully, unceasingly and beautifully all the holy angels praise God, as is set forth in Isaias: [[Is 6:3|they cried one to another|Clamabat alter ad alterum]]: [[Is 6:3|Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory|Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus Deus exercituum; plena est omnis terra gloria ejus]]. Whence the Lord says to holy Job: [[Job 38:4|Where wast thou|Ubi eras]] [[Job 38:7|When the morning stars praised me|quum me laudarent astra matutina]], [[Job 38:7|and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|et jubilarent omnes filii Dei]]

paras.t: Laudate eum, sol et luna, laudate eum, omnes stellæ, videlicet astra fixa et planetæ, et lumen sensibile et insensibile, naturale et supernaturale. Si autem poneremus corpora cœlestia animata, sicut posuerunt summi philosophi, scilicet Aristoteles, Plato, Socrates, Avicenna, et sequaces eorum: quos etiam Judæorum præcipui theologi atque philosophi, scilicet Rabbi Moyses, et David auctor libri de Causis, multique alii sunt secuti: quibus christianorum quoque doctorum aliqui consenserunt, videlicet Origenes, sicut beatus Thomas in prima parte testatur; ipse quoque sanctus, sublimis et gloriosus Hieronymus idem sentire videtur, exponens illud Ecclesiastæ, Lustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus: si, inquam, taliter poneremus corpora cœlestia, […] videlicet orbes et astra, solem ac lunam, invitare ad laudem Dei, quemadmodum angelos. Quamvis Augustinus super Genesim et in Enchiridio, sub dubio relinquat, an corpora ista sint animata; non autem relinquit sub dubio quin, si animata essent, pertinerent utique ad societatem angelorum. Si vero amplius complacet opinio S. Basilii et Damasceni, dicentium quod corpora cœlestia sunt inanimata, quod etiam communius existimatur: tunc invitantur ad laudem Dei eo modo quo cetera inanimata et irrationalia. Generalis etenim modus quo omnis creatura Deum laudat, est, quod ejus bonitatem, sapientiam atque potentiam repræsentat, ejusque voluntati obedit, agendo et patiendo quod ipse præfixit. Laudant igitur sol et luna, stellæ et lumen Dominum, quoniam suo decore, dignitate atque potestate inducunt intellectuales creaturas ad laudem ac admirationem Creatoris. Et item quia a suo officio atque obsequio non recedunt, ipsorum motus et servitium laus Dei est.
paras.en: [[148:3|Praise ye him, O sun and moon|Laudate eum, sol et luna]]: [[148:3|praise him, all ye stars|laudate eum, omnes stellæ]], namely the fixed stars and the planets, [[148:3|and light|et lumen]], sensible and insensible, natural and supernatural. Now if we held the heavenly bodies to be animate, as the greatest philosophers held, namely Aristotle, Plato, Socrates, Avicenna and their followers (whom the chief theologians and philosophers of the Jews also followed, namely Rabbi Moses, and David the author of the book *On Causes*, and many others; with whom some of the Christian doctors also agreed, namely Origen, as blessed Thomas testifies in the First Part; and the holy, sublime and glorious Jerome himself seems to think the same, expounding that saying of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:6|the spirit goeth forward surveying all places round about|Lustrans universa in circuitu pergit spiritus]]); if, I say, we held the heavenly bodies to be such, […] namely the spheres and stars, sun and moon, to be invited to the praise of God as the angels are [some words seem to be missing here; the sense is that on this view they would be invited as rational creatures]. Augustine, indeed, on Genesis and in the *Enchiridion*, leaves it in doubt whether these bodies are animate; but he does not leave it in doubt that, if they were animate, they would certainly belong to the fellowship of the angels. But if the opinion of St. Basil and of Damascene pleases more, who say that the heavenly bodies are inanimate (which is also the more common view), then they are invited to the praise of God in the same way as the other inanimate and irrational things. For the general way in which every creature praises God is that it represents his goodness, wisdom and power, and obeys his will, by doing and undergoing what he has appointed. The sun and moon, the stars and light, therefore praise the Lord, since by their beauty, dignity and power they lead intellectual creatures to the praise and admiration of the Creator. And again, because they do not withdraw from their office and service, their motion and service is the praise of God.

paras.t: Laudate eum, cœli cœlorum, id est cœli majores et principaliores, videlicet cœli qui sunt supra septem cœlos planetarum. Vel, per cœlos cœlorum designat cœlum empyreum; ponitque plurale pro singulari, quia, secundum Chrysostomum, hoc nomen, Cœlum, in Hebræo caret numero singulari. Unde et alibi Scriptura singulariter exprimit, Cœlum cœlorum, juxta illud Nehemiæ: Tu, Domine, fecisti cœlum cœlorum, et omnem exercitum eorum. Et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt, laudent nomen Domini. Quid per aquas has intelligendum sit, diversimode assignant doctores. Antiqui enim doctores, præter Augustinum, dicunt supra firmamentum seu cœlum stellatum, esse veras aquas, quas Beda asserit glaciali soliditate supra firmamentum per modum crystalli esse suspensas: et ita essent ejusdem naturæ cum aqua elementari. Moderni vero doctores, Augustinum sequentes, communiter dicunt nequaquam esse aquas veras supra cœlos, sed per aquas has intelligendam esse nonam sphæram mobilem: quæ dicitur cœlum crystallinum seu aqueum, non quod sit de natura aquæ, sed quia cum aqua convenit in diaphaneitate: quemadmodum cœlum empyreum dicitur igneum, non quasi de natura ignis existens, sed tanquam cum igne in luciditate seu claritate conveniens. Verumtamen, secundum Thomam super secundum Sententiarum, cœlum empyreum non dicitur ideo lucidum, quod sensibiles radios fundat, quum non sit compactum (talis namque luciditatis causa, est congregatio seu compactio partium diaphani, ut dicunt Avicenna et Averroes, propter quod ignis in propria sphæra non lucet); sed dicitur lucidum, quoniam naturam lucis habet in se, quum sit maxime formale. Ad nonam sphæram seu cœlum aqueum reducunt astrologi motum cœli stellati ab occidente in orientem. Ponunt autem quidam eorum et decimam sphæram mobilem, quam dicunt esse causam diurni motus firmamenti seu cœli stellati ab oriente in occidentem.
paras.en: [[148:4|Praise him, ye heavens of heavens|Laudate eum, cœli cœlorum]], that is, the greater and more principal heavens, namely the heavens that are above the seven heavens of the planets. Or, by the heavens of heavens he means the empyrean heaven; and he puts the plural for the singular because, according to Chrysostom, this noun, Heaven, has no singular number in Hebrew. Hence elsewhere too Scripture says in the singular, The heaven of heavens, according to that saying in Nehemias: [[2 Esd 9:6|Thou thyself, O Lord|Tu, Domine]], [[2 Esd 9:6|hast made heaven, and the heaven of heavens, and all the host thereof|fecisti cœlum cœlorum, et omnem exercitum eorum]] [Denis's text has only "thou hast made the heaven of heavens, and all the host thereof"]. [[148:4|and let all the waters that are above the heavens|Et aquæ quæ super cœlos sunt]] [the margin adds *omnes*, "all", the Vulgate reading] [[148:5|Praise the name of the Lord|laudent nomen Domini]].
